(`lion_sources_collect()`). At a key the map is asked after every group standing there has copied
its container under its pin, and before any of them moves past it: `lion_count_container()`'s
order, for all of them at once. A key the copy has nothing at, and a group whose intersection there
is empty, ask the map nothing, and the pins let go of past them had nothing counted from them. A
group whose set holds no pin - located past the pin budget, or a private copy - trusts no map (its
own `novm`), as its count alone would; every group does while a row filter applies (§17, "A query
known only at run time"), whose rows all go to the heap. Under SERIALIZABLE a group counted from
the map takes its blocks' predicate locks through the ordinary path.

**When.** A single GROUP BY column walked by its index's entries, once its WHERE is collected, when
every count is that one set ANDed with the group's own: not beside a range walked with it (§32, a
range too large to collect that the plan walks), and not for `GROUP BY coalesce(g, c)`, which adds
two entries into one group. The group counted before the collection - the first, over groups that
span the heap - is counted as it always was. **Not taken**: an IN list that drives its own groups
(§15), whose sets are the clause's; two GROUP BY columns (§20), whose pairs each AND two groups'
sets; count(DISTINCT) (§26), whose tests stop at a row. They count against the collected copy one
count at a time, as before.

**Parallel.** As first written the walk was serial, as every LionCount path but the FK-side join
of §27 was: `parallel_safe` false, no workers. With `max_parallel_workers_per_gather` 4 the repro's
grouped count still planned as the serial node, and the plan without the pushdown - a Parallel
Bitmap Heap Scan of four workers under a partial HashAggregate - took 1,138 ms. The walk and the
collection split by ranges of container keys, and do now: "A GROUP BY in parallel", below. An
ungrouped count is still serial.

**Cost.** A grouped count whose WHERE the executor will collect (`lion_cost_where_collected()`, the
rule of `lion_where_describe()` from the planner's sources: two or more, or one of several sets -
a union, or a multi-key query of several keys, which the merge prices as one set) is priced as the
collection - the WHERE
sources' merge as an ungrouped count's (`lion_merge_cpu_cost()`), and a container of the copy
written at each key it keeps (`LION_FKJOIN_COPY_CONTAINER_COST`, the same copy the FK-side join
makes) - plus, per group, its containers at the keys the copy has, each `LION_CONTAINER_COST`,
`LION_MEMBER_COST` a member and a heap sift of log2(batch) `cpu_operator_cost`, plus, per batch,
the copy's containers made images, and `LION_ENTRY_COUNT_COST` a group; the WHERE's pages are read
once. It was priced as every group's merge with each WHERE set probed in memory
(`LION_MEMORY_PROBE_COST` a set a key) and each union's sets set up again (`LION_UNION_SET_COST`),
which the batched walk does neither of.

**Measured**, the node before (the library before this subsection and before §15's, `base`), with
only §15's change (`c1`), and now:

| grouped count | base | c1 | now | cost, before and now | units a ms, base and now |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `grp ... WHERE f1 AND NOT f2 AND lvl = 1 AND tags && '{4}'` | 394.4 ms | 281.0 | 68.4 | 217,468; 44,857 | 551, 656 |
| `c20 ... WHERE tags && '{1,2}' AND NOT f1` | 116.2 | 38.3 | 24.0 | 36,747; 10,068 | 316, 419 |
| `lvl ... WHERE tags2 && '{1,5,9}' AND c20 IN (1, 2)` | 92.7 | 30.4 | 26.1 | 20,359; 11,198 | 220, 428 |
| `grp ... WHERE f2 AND lvl = 1` | 355.8 | 260.2 | 52.5 | 121,973; 32,293 | 343, 615 |
| `grp ... WHERE c20 = 3 AND tags && '{2}'` | 124.0 | 85.6 | 43.5 | 99,621; 28,222 | 803, 648 |
| `grp ... WHERE tags && '{1}'` (one set, too large to copy) | 348.8 | 256.7 | 47.5 | 76,520; 27,694 | 219, 583 |
| `c20 ... WHERE tags && '{1000,1001,1002}' AND f1` (a WHERE of 1,500 rows) | 6.5 | 6.3 | 6.2 | 7,758; 5,097 | 1,201, 823 |

The first of them went from 5.5 times its ungrouped count (72 ms) to 3.8 times (18 ms, §15),
most of the difference a group's own set read from its pages: some 90 ns a group's container,
against half a microsecond before. Its profile now: the walk itself (inlined, 32%),
`lion_page_item_fetch()` and `lion_cursor_take_page()` (the groups' posting pages, 21%), the images
(`container_or_bitset()`, 13%, the collection's too), the collection's ANDs and copies (11%),
buffer lookups (5%). Priced as before, the batched counts ran at 860 to 2,900 units a
millisecond, overpriced up to six times; they are at 419 to 823 now.

One plan the regression suite pins moved with it: `pushdown.sql`'s `SELECT a, count(*) FROM
lion_pdpo WHERE a = 17 OR b = 3 GROUP BY a`, 200 groups over two partitions of 50,000 rows, is the
node now (a Finalize HashAggregate over it) where it was a HashAggregate over each partition's
BitmapOr: 0.63 ms against 1.15, the node before this change 1.17.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE prints `Group Batches` and `Groups Counted in Batches` when there were any.
`test/sql/groupwhere.sql` reports the batches of every shape it checks - one per relation that
collected, none where the groups are an IN list's or pairs - and adds a table of 600 groups and a
NULL one, counted in three batches and, at a work_mem of 64 kB, in twenty; groups whose containers
are RUNs; a WHERE that is a BITSET at every key, and one of a row or two a key, ANDed directly; a
HAVING, a LIMIT inside a batch, SERIALIZABLE, the order an ORDER BY relies on across two batches with
no Sort, and a dirty heap - each against a sequential scan with the pushdown off.

### A GROUP BY in parallel (2026-09-28)

The walk above divides by container key: a group's count is the sum over any cut of the heap's keys
of its rows at the keys of each piece, and the collected WHERE of a piece is the whole copy's
containers at its keys. So the grouped count is offered, besides the serial node, as a
parallel-aware one below a Gather and core's Finalize HashAggregate:

    Finalize HashAggregate
      Group Key: grp
      ->  Gather
            Workers Planned: 3
            ->  Parallel Custom Scan (LionCount)
                  Lion Indexes: rp_lion.grp (grp), rp_lion.f1 (f1 = true), ...
                  Group Key: grp

- **Ranges.** When the Gather sets up its shared memory the heap's container keys are cut into
  ranges, a few for each participant the plan was made for (`lion_key_ranges()`: four each, at most
  64, no fewer than 16 keys a range - `pg_lion.parallel_range_keys` at run time, a testing knob;
  the planner prices the default), as evenly as whole keys go, the last one open-ended for a heap
  that has grown since. The shared copy of §27's FK-side join is cut the same way, and no longer
  leaves its last chunks empty when the keys do not divide. Each participant claims the next range
  nobody has from a shared counter (`LionJoinShared.nextchunk`, the struct the FK-side join keeps
  in the Gather's DSM; its sums carry the workers' counters to EXPLAIN), collects the WHERE of that
  range alone (`lion_sources_collect_range()`: the sources sought to the range's first key, the
  merge stopped at its end, `LionCollect.ranged`), walks the entries from the first and counts
  every group against the range's copy a batch at a time, exactly as above - a partial row per
  group with rows in the range - and claims the next. A range whose copy is empty walks nothing.
- **Why it is exact (§9).** Each range is the walk above over a copy of its keys: every group's set
  located afresh by the participant's own walk under its own pins, the map asked once a key after
  every group there has copied its container, the copy pinless and made after the snapshot was
  taken (workers run under the leader's). The ranges cover every key once, so every row is counted
  in one range by one participant, and the Finalize Agg adds a group's partial counts up - and
  applies the HAVING, which the node's partial target (`lion_make_partial_target()`, as for a
  partitioned table, §16) leaves to it.
- **When.** One GROUP BY column walked whole over one table, whose WHERE the planner prices as
  collected (`lion_cost_where_collected()`), with a positive clause that is positive whatever its
  value - an equality, an IN list, `IS NULL`, a multi-key literal without a prefix lexeme; a
  multi-key parameter, a literal tsquery whose prefix the run finds too common to expand (§17,
  "Prefix lexemes") and a jsonpath, whose keys are all prefixes (§43.2), may narrow nothing at run
  time and turn into a negated source, and a WHERE of negated sources alone has nothing to collect
  by range - and no range taken as a source; a grouping core can hash and aggregates it can split,
  and the table, the target and the clause values parallel-safe. Not a partitioned table, two
  GROUP BY columns, count(DISTINCT), an IN list that drives the groups, and not during recovery,
  where the WHERE is never collected. `GROUP BY coalesce(col, c)` divides too
  (2026-10-19): its group of c is the NULL entry's rows and those of the entry the grouping
  equality finds equal to c, which the serial walk adds up as it meets them (`LionCoalState`);
  in a range each of the two goes up as a partial row of the value c itself
  (`lion_next_group_ranged()`), and the Finalize Agg, which groups by `coalesce(col, c)`, adds
  them to each other and to the group's rows of other ranges like any partial rows of one key -
  the classes of one index being disjoint, no other entry is c's. A group of c with no row
  visible in any range has no partial row, and so no row, as serially. A parallel-aware
  node run without the Gather's shared memory (a Gather that cannot use parallel mode sets none up)
  is the only participant and counts every group whole, the serial walk.
- **Workers.** What a parallel scan of the grouping column's posting pages would get
  (`compute_parallel_worker()` over them, `lion_index_column_posting_share()` of the index's pages),
  capped by `max_parallel_workers_per_gather`; the table's `parallel_workers` decides alone.
- **Cost**, one participant's: the serial node's price before its HAVING divided among the
  participants (`get_parallel_divisor()`'s rule), since the collection, the groups' containers and
  the pages they lie on all divide by key; plus, for its share of the ranges, what each range pays
  again - the entry walk, the column's share of the directory and not its sets, whose pages each
  range reads its own share of ("Dense sources"), and for each group and each WHERE source a
  descent to the range's first key: `LION_ENTRY_COUNT_COST` and `LION_PROBE_COST` a group,
  `LION_PROBE_COST` a source, a page each (`LION_RANGE_DESCENT_PAGES`); plus a `cpu_tuple_cost` a
  partial row, a group's per range it has rows in. The Gather prices its rows and
  `parallel_setup_cost`, core's Finalize Agg its own work.

Two things the ranges made worth doing in the walk itself, serial or not. A group's cursor now
begins at the copy's first key (`lion_cursor_init_at()`: a CHAIN set's first leaf comes from a
descent for that key, an INLINE set skips to it, a copy is sought) where it began at the group's
first container and was sought from there; and the walk's cursors copy their leaves into page
images the node allocates once (`gbimages`), where each batch allocated and freed a page per group:
one participant counting the repro's first GROUP BY below as 16 ranges took 18 ms more than the
serial walk (65 ms) while each batch allocated its pages, much of it page faults and `brk()`, and
takes 7 ms more now.

**Measured** on the repro above, the library of this change with `max_parallel_workers_per_gather`
at 0, 2 and 3 - medians of 24 runs each, the settings' order rotated round by round, on four cores
that other work shared (the one-minute load rose from 1 to 3 while it ran); plans and costs are the
planner's own, every parallel one the node below a Finalize HashAggregate:

| grouped count | serial | 2 workers | 3 workers | cost: serial, 2, 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `grp ... WHERE f1 AND NOT f2 AND lvl = 1 AND tags && '{4}'` | 69.3 ms | 44.1 | 36.0 | 44,857; 21,115; 16,998 |
| `c20 ... WHERE tags && '{1,2}' AND NOT f1` | 22.2 | 19.8 | 19.2 | 10,068; 5,397; 4,464 |
| `lvl ... WHERE tags2 && '{1,5,9}' AND c20 IN (1, 2)` | 25.6 | 23.9 | 21.8 | 11,198; 5,728; 4,679 |
| `grp ... WHERE f2 AND lvl = 1` | 55.6 | 39.8 | 33.4 | 32,293; 15,869; 12,933 |
| `grp ... WHERE c20 = 3 AND tags && '{2}'` | 43.8 | 32.0 | 27.4 | 28,222; 14,173; 11,620 |
| `grp ... WHERE tags && '{1}'` | 51.1 | 32.4 | 28.2 | 27,694; 13,948; 11,444 |
| `c20 ... WHERE tags && '{1000,1001,1002}' AND f1` | 6.9 | 11.1 | 12.6 | 5,097; 3,326; 2,861 |

Every parallel plan here starts its workers first, and on this machine that takes about 6 ms
whatever the plan: core's own Parallel Seq Scan of a table of 1,000 rows took 6 ms with one worker
or three, against 0.05 ms serially, with the library loaded or not. `parallel_setup_cost` prices it
at 1,000 - 2 ms at the 500 units a millisecond the model is fitted to - so the counts of 20 to 25 ms
gain a little, and the last one, 7 ms, loses: it goes parallel as core's plans of its price would,
and takes 11. At a `parallel_setup_cost` of 3,000, what the start is worth here, it stays serial
with two workers. The larger counts gain 1.6 to 1.9 times with three workers on the shared cores;
over a larger table the walk grows and the start does not. Serially the library is the one before
this change within the noise (12 rounds of the same seven, the two alternated: -3% to +1%).

The per-range price was fitted with the leader alone (`max_parallel_workers = 0`, so the Gather
launches nothing and its node counts all 16 ranges): the four-clause GROUP BY above took 73 ms
against the serial 65 (perf's task clock, 60 runs), 500 us a range for the repro's groups, priced at
245 units; the 1,500-row WHERE took 6.9 ms against 5.6, 83 us a range for 20 groups, priced at 35.

`test/sql/groupparallel.sql` checks the plans - the node below a Gather with two workers and one, the
serial node with none or with the table's `parallel_workers` at 0 - and, at ranges of one key (a
table of fourteen keys, cut into twelve ranges for three participants), the answers of filters, a
negated filter and the NULL entry as one, an IN list, an OR across columns, multi-key queries, a
filter in two ranges of the twelve and groups that lie in one range or two, the NULL group, counts of
columns, a printed filter column, a HAVING, an ORDER BY with LIMIT, `GROUP BY coalesce(col, c)`
with c a key of the column or none, the leader alone with no worker
started, SERIALIZABLE, a generic plan's parameters and a heap the map cannot vouch for - each against
the same query run serially and with the pushdown off - and the ranges, collections and batches the
participants counted; and the shapes that stay serial, a WHERE whose positive clauses are literal
prefixes too common to expand, a tsquery's or a jsonpath's, among them.

### A count in parallel (2026-10-19)

The GROUP BY above divides by container key because a count is a sum over any cut of the heap's
keys; so does the node of ONE row - the count of a WHERE, or a sum over a column's entries (§14),
with filtered counts, `count(col)`s, residual clauses, OR lists and ranges beside it. It is offered,
besides the serial node, as a parallel-aware one below a Gather and core's Finalize Aggregate,
which adds the participants' partial counts up and applies the HAVING:

    Finalize Aggregate
      ->  Gather
            Workers Planned: 2
            ->  Parallel Custom Scan (LionCount)
                  Lion Indexes: t_f.f1 (f1 = 1), t_f.f2 (f2 = 0), ...
                  Count Filter 1: t_s (s = 3)

- **Chunks** (`lion_count_ranged()`). The heap's container keys are cut into ranges when the
  Gather sets up its shared memory, exactly as for a GROUP BY (`lion_key_ranges()`: four for each
  participant, at most 64, no fewer than `pg_lion.parallel_range_keys` keys a range), and the
  work into one chunk for each range of each RUN - the WHERE's count and each filtered count's
  (`nrun`, "Filtered counts"). Each participant claims the next chunk nobody has from the shared
  counter, chunk c being range `c % nranges` of run `c / nranges`, and counts that run at the keys
  of that range alone (`lion_count_range()`). The counter only grows, so a participant meets the
  runs in order: it locates a run's WHERE once, at its first chunk of the run, and releases it
  before it locates the next, as the serial node does (`lion_count_runs()`). Its counts go into
  `runcount` - the row's filtered counts are read from there as they are serially - and the
  partial row is emitted once the counter has run out.
- **A window of keys.** Each count of a chunk is the serial count, its cursors confined to the
  range [lo, hi): the range is set on the visibility cache every count of the node is handed
  (`lion_vis_cache_set_window()`, cleared after the chunk and by a rescan), and the count context
  reads it from there (`LionCountCtx.windowed`), so no caller of the count changes. The merge seeks
  its positive cursors to lo - nothing passed over is counted - and stops at hi
  (`lion_count_one_set()`, `lion_run_merge()`, the copy's `lion_run_merge_copy()`, the multi-key
  evaluator's `lion_wide_fill()`); a range walked at every count (§32) collects the keys of the
  window alone (`lion_range_probe_begin()` over `lion_sources_collect_range()`); and the heap scan
  of a WHERE nothing narrows (§17, "A query known only at run time") reads the window's blocks
  (`heap_setscanlimits()`, no synchronized scan). A grouped or decoded walk refuses a window; it is
  never handed one. A run with an IN list too long to locate at once ("A list too long to locate
  at once") is cut by its batches instead: range `sub` counts the batches b with `b % nranges ==
  sub`, at every key - a window would locate every batch again for each range - and the list's
  count is the sum of its batches' for the reason that section gives.
- **Why it is exact (§9).** The ranges of a cut cover every container key once - the last has no
  end, for a heap that has grown since - and a row lies at exactly one key, its block's. Every
  count the node makes is a count of rows: the merge of its sources, the disjoint sum of a list
  (§15), a walk's sum over entries (§14), a complement OR's two counts (§35), a range walked at
  every count, a probed walk's final count (§28), the heap scan of a WHERE nothing narrows; each
  identity they rest on - the entries of a scalar column are disjoint, `|F ∧ (P ∨ ¬M)| = |F ∧ ¬M|
  + |F ∧ M ∧ P|` - holds of the rows at any set of keys as it holds of all of them, so the
  ranges' counts add up to the serial node's. Each is an ordinary count of the containers at its
  keys: the containers in between are put to the visibility map before the page they came from is
  let go, under the pins the serial count holds; what the map does not vouch for - and every row
  a residual clause tests - goes to the heap under the leader's snapshot, which every worker runs
  under, the row filter (§17, residual clauses) tested there as serially; and SERIALIZABLE's
  predicate locks are taken as the serial count takes them, in whichever participant. A
  participant's sets are its own, located under its own pins. Run without the Gather's shared memory, the node is the only
  participant and counts every run whole.
- **When** (`lion_count_path_add()`, and `lion_count_priv_check()`'s "malformed parallel count"):
  no GROUP BY, or one folded away (a sum over the column's entries, §14); one table, not a
  partitioned one, and not the FK-side join, which is parallel its own way (§27); not a
  count(DISTINCT), whose values may have rows in two ranges and which core cannot split anyway;
  not the aggregates over keys (`sum(k)`, `min(k)`, §37), which have no partial form here; not a GROUP BY a WHERE equality folds to a constant
  (`LION_FLAG_SINGLEGROUP`), whose row is missing when no row matches, which a plain Finalize
  Aggregate cannot leave out; not during recovery; and aggregates core can split, the table, the
  target and the clause values parallel-safe. Everything else the serial node takes is taken:
  filtered counts, residual clauses, complement ORs, ORs across columns, IN lists, multi-key
  queries literal or known at run time, ranges as sources or bounding the sum, `count(col)`, a
  HAVING and expressions over the counts.
- **Workers.** What a parallel scan of the pages the count reads would get
  (`compute_parallel_worker()` over `LionRangeCost.pages`: the WHERE's posting and recheck pages
  and the walk's, as the serial price has them), capped by `max_parallel_workers_per_gather`; the
  table's `parallel_workers` decides alone. A count that reads a page or two gets none. A range is
  counted by one participant, so a heap the executor would cut into one range - fewer than 32
  keys, about 2,000 pages, at the default `pg_lion.parallel_range_keys`, read here as it is set -
  gets no parallel count at all, and the divisor below is never more than the ranges.
- **Cost**, one participant's (`lion_add_parallel_count_path()`): its share (core's
  `get_parallel_divisor()` rule) of the serial node's price before its HAVING, but for what every participant pays whole (`LionRangeCost.whole`: the
  lookups that locate the WHERE, and the ranges taken as sources it collects); that whole; and
  what each of its share of the chunks pays again (`countrange`, every run's, summed by
  `lion_count_rel_range_price()`): every set of the WHERE sought to the range's first key, a
  descent of `LION_RANGE_DESCENT_PAGES` and a `LION_PROBE_COST` a set (a range source's copy at
  `LION_MEMORY_PROBE_COST`), and a walk's entries counted again, each sought there, with the
  walk's pages read again; plus a `cpu_tuple_cost` for its row. The Gather prices its rows and
  `parallel_setup_cost`, core's Finalize Aggregate its own work. Both terms are in the node's
  units (`lion_units_price()`).
- **EXPLAIN ANALYZE** prints `Key Ranges`, the chunks counted - the ranges times the runs - and
  every counter of the scan a worker moves is summed into the leader's (`LionScanWorkerSums` in
  `LionJoinShared`), so that none of them prints the leader's share alone, or nothing where the
  leader takes no part. A range source is collected by each participant that counts a range of
  its run, but `Range Sources Collected` counts the sources of the query, not the collections: each
  clause marks how it was taken (`LionClauseState.counted`), and a worker ORs its marks into an
  array after `LionJoinShared` that the leader reads at shutdown (`LION_JOIN_SHARED_COUNTED()`).
  It counted collections before the 2026-10-23 review: 2 over two partitions, 3 over three
  rescans, 2 or 3 in a parallel plan, for the one range.

**Measured** on the release build (PostgreSQL 18.6 at -O2 without assertions, the library at -O2),
on four cores other sessions' work shared (a one-minute load of 1.6 to 2.0 throughout),
`shared_buffers` 2 GB with everything resident, `pg_lion.parallel_range_keys` at its default: a
synthetic table of 4,000,000 rows on 58,788 pages (919 container keys) - nine filters of two to
four values in one multicolumn lion index, an `int[]` of three keys of 2,000, a tsvector of four
words of 120. Medians of 21 runs (15 for the dirty heap), the settings' order rotated round by
round, `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF)`'s execution time; plans and costs the planner's own, every
parallel one the node below a Finalize Aggregate:

| count, heap all-visible | serial | 2 workers | 3 workers | cost: serial, 2, 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 9-source AND, `f1 = 1 AND ... AND f9 = 1` (870 rows) | 2.2 ms | 10.9 | 7.7 | 4,471; 2,885; 2,466 |
| ... three of the nine IN lists (20,800 rows) | 4.4 | 7.5 | 10.9 | 8,181; 4,442; 3,674 |
| `tags && '{0, ..., 199}'`, 200 keys (1.08M rows) | 30.7 | 15.0 | 13.7 | 5,702; 3,779; 3,256 |
| the same array from a subquery (an InitPlan) | 5,898 (seq scan) | 19.9 | 15.6 (two planned) | 108,892; 46,431; 46,431 |
| tsquery, eight ORs of ANDs (§17) | 4.3 | serial | serial | 245 |

| count, 1% of rows updated, 69% of pages not all-visible | serial | 2 workers | 3 workers | cost: serial, 2, 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 9-source AND | 3.7 ms | 6.4 | 9.1 | 5,726; 3,408; 2,871 |
| ... three of the nine IN lists | 13.0 | 13.3 | 16.0 | 22,711; 10,496; 8,361 |
| `tags && '{0, ..., 199}'` | 89.2 | 54.5 | 56.7 | 56,281; 24,853; 19,572 |
| tsquery, eight ORs of ANDs | 15.8 | 14.2 | 16.3 | 21,976; 10,162; 8,095 |

The counts of tens of milliseconds gain - the wide overlap 2.0 to 2.2 times on the clean heap, 1.6
on the dirty one, where 800,000 TIDs go to the heap - and the third worker adds little on four shared
cores. The leader alone (`max_parallel_workers = 0`) counted the overlap's twelve ranges in 96 ms
against the serial node's 97: a range costs next to nothing over its share there. The InitPlan's
array is a value the serial price cannot estimate (§17), priced as the ordinary plan's work, so the
serial node lost to the sequential scan by a hair and the parallel one won by its divisor - an
accident of that price. The counts of a few milliseconds lost in these runs: the 9-source AND went
parallel and took 7.7 to 10.9 ms for 2.2, because the serial node was priced at 4,471 units for
2.2 ms - 2,000 units a millisecond against the 500 the model is fitted to ("The units") - and a
worker's start, about 2 ms here and more under load, is more than the whole count: with
`parallel_setup_cost` and `parallel_tuple_cost` at 0 it took 3.6 ms with two workers and 3.8 with
three, against 1.6 serially in the same runs. The tsquery's serial price, 245, kept it serial; made
parallel the same way it took 5.3 and 5.6 ms against 4.3. The parallel GROUP BY had the same
exposure ("A GROUP BY in parallel"): a serial price that overstates a short count by more than
`parallel_setup_cost` sends it parallel. The serial price of an AND of dense sources was what was
wrong, not this path's, and is fixed ("Dense sources" below): the 9-source AND is priced at 620
units for 1.2 ms and the three IN lists at 1,024 for 3.0 ms, both serial at every worker count, and
over 40M rows they and the GROUP BYs of 9 to 33 ms still go parallel and gain 1.4 to 2.6 times.

`test/sql/countparallel.sql` checks the plans - the node below a Gather with two workers and one,
the serial node with none or with the table's `parallel_workers` at 0, a HAVING the Finalize
Aggregate's - and, at ranges of one key (fourteen keys cut into twelve ranges), the answers of
ANDs, the NULL entry, negated sources, IN lists alone and ANDed, ORs across columns and with a
complement arm, multi-key queries, filtered counts, `count(col)`, a residual clause, a filter in one
range of the twelve, sums over every entry, over every non-NULL one and bounded by a range, ranges
as sources, a HAVING, the leader alone, SERIALIZABLE, a generic plan's parameters (a runtime
tsquery among them, and one no key narrows, read from the heap a range at a time), an InitPlan's
value, a list of 5,000
values located in batches, and a heap the map cannot vouch for - each against the same query run
serially and with the pushdown off - and the chunks, batches and skipped heap blocks the
participants counted. `test/isolation/count_parallel.spec` runs a REPEATABLE READ snapshot's
parallel count against updates, deletes, inserts and VACUUM, and two SERIALIZABLE parallel counts
whose inserts conflict.

**Not done: count(DISTINCT k) in parallel.** Investigated, and left serial. Its count is
not a sum over the heap's keys: a value with rows in two ranges is one value, so the ranges'
partial answers do not add up, and core will not split a DISTINCT aggregate either (no
`GROUPING_CAN_PARTIAL_AGG`). Two divisions were weighed. By key ranges, as here, each range would
emit the values with a visible row there and core would count the distinct ones over the Gather:
every entry is then tested once per range, up to `nranges` times the serial walk's tests, and as
many rows go through the Gather - worst exactly where the walk is long, with many values. By
ENTRIES, each participant would take a share of k's entry walk and test each of its entries over
every key, exactly the serial test (§26, so §9 unchanged), the shares' counts then adding up since
the entries of a scalar column are disjoint; but the entry walk has no parallel division yet (a
shared cursor over the directory's leaves, or key bounds cut from it when the Gather sets up), and
the plan would have to turn the query's `count(DISTINCT k)` into a partial count the Finalize
Aggregate adds up, which core does not do for a DISTINCT aggregate. That is the shape to build if
it is wanted: the existence tests, the IN-list driver and the grouped form (§26 shape 2, by the
outer column's entries) all divide by entries.

### The units (2026-09-27, release build)

Every lion constant used to be fitted on the assert-enabled development build (-O1, cassert),
whose assertions inflate lion's own code far more than core's - so each of them was off, against
core's units, by a factor nobody knew. This pass fitted them again on a RELEASE build: PostgreSQL
18.6 at -O2 without assertions, on a 4-core, 15 GB VM, `shared_buffers` 5 GB with every relation
of the test database resident (the production target is warm), `work_mem` 64 MB, and every core
cost GUC at its default (`random_page_cost` 4, `seq_page_cost` 1, the `cpu_*` and parallel costs as
shipped). Numbers in this section and in the cost sections that cite it are from that build and
machine; §31 has the data sets and the decision matrix. The first measurements are medians of five
`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF)` runs on a quiet machine; once other work shared it, the backend's
own CPU time (`/proc/<pid>/schedstat`) over a DO loop that plans a query once and runs it many
times, alternatives interleaved - serial plans only, which is what it can measure.

**Core's units on this machine.** Cost units per millisecond of core's own plans over 5M-row
tables (`s`: 66,667 narrow pages; `w`: 102,639 wide ones; §31):

| core plan | cost | ms | units/ms |
|---|---|---|---|
| seq scan, `count(*)`, narrow rows | 129,189 | 210 | 617 |
| ... one int qual / two ANDed / three ORed | 129,252 / 141,693 / 154,860 | 263 / 265 / 341 | 491 / 534 / 454 |
| ... `sum()` | 129,189 | 313 | 412 |
| seq scan, `count(*)`, wide rows / one text qual / four quals | 165,157 / 165,400 / 190,262 | 238 / 394 / 474 | 695 / 419 / 401 |
| btree index-only scan, 25k / 250k / 2.5M rows | 614 / 6,609 / 77,410 | 1.28 / 12.3 / 187 | 480 / 536 / 415 |
| btree bitmap heap scan, 500 / 25k / 250k rows scattered | 1,834 / 49,218 / 74,525 | 0.41 / 28.9 / 137 | 4,419 / 1,702 / 544 |
| hash aggregate over a seq scan, 200 / 20,000 groups | 141,692 / 141,888 | 680 / 905 | 208 / 157 |
| sort and group aggregate, 200 groups | 778,903 | 1,115 | 699 |
| hash join 2M x 1,000 / 5M x 200k (4.4k and 140k rows hashed) / 5M x 2M (1.4M) | 45,201 / 110,063 / 122,632 / 178,551 | 161 / 390 / 664 / 3,148 | 280 / 283 / 185 / 57 |
| nested loop into a btree, 4.4k outer rows | 14,154 | 13.4 | 1,057 |
| parallel (2 workers) seq scan `count(*)` / one qual / wide, four quals | 93,730 / 93,756 / 140,159 | 102 / 118 / 210 | 915 / 797 / 667 |
| parallel hash join / hash aggregate | 80,029 / 104,341 | 365 / 337 | 219 / 309 |

Core is not consistent with itself, and three things account for most of it. A page is charged
as I/O whether or not it is in memory: a warm sequential page costs 0.6 us against the 2 us a
`seq_page_cost` stands for at 500 units a millisecond, and a warm random one about 1 us against 8,
which is why plans that read scattered pages run at 1,700 to 6,300 units a millisecond. Operators
are charged by count, not by type: an int `=` costs 10.6 ns a row, a text one 31 ns, both one
`cpu_operator_cost` (5 ns at 500). And hashing is charged far below what it costs: 94 ns a row into
a hash aggregate against one or two `cpu_operator_cost`, which puts every plan with a hash
aggregate or a large hash join at 57 to 310 units a millisecond.

**The reference.** Lion's CPU constants are fitted at **500 units a millisecond** - the middle of
core's CPU-bound scans (sequential scans 400 to 700, index-only scans 415 to 535) - so a
microsecond is 0.5 units, a `cpu_tuple_cost` 20 ns and a `cpu_operator_cost` 5 ns. Lion's I/O
terms keep core's convention: a page read in order at `seq_page_cost`, a random one at
`random_page_cost`, interpolated by `lion_heap_page_cost()` where core would interpolate, so that
lion and core overcharge a warm page alike and `random_page_cost` moves both the same way. Against
core's hash aggregates and hash joins that rate makes lion honest and them cheap: where a grouped
count competes with a hash aggregate on close to equal terms, the aggregate wins in the model and
loses on the machine (§31 lists the cases). Pricing lion at the hash aggregate's rate instead would
make it beat sequential and index-only scans it is up to twice as slow as. *(Since 2026-10-01 a
lion custom path is priced at the rate of the plan it competes with - its price, as fitted here,
times that kind of plan's rate over this reference - and a site can ask it to beat that plan by a
margin (§39).)*

**The merge** (`lion_merge_cpu_cost()`; every count, every group and pair of a GROUP BY, the AND of
a lion index scan's sets in `lioncostestimate()` - since 2026-09-28 with the lookups, unions and
pages around it, one price for both, `lion_cost_set_and()`, §29.11). Fitted to the backend CPU time
of 35 counts over the 5M-row `s` - eleven single sets holding 1 to 4,500 rows a container (sparse
arrays, dense arrays, bitsets, RUN containers), eighteen pairs, five triples and a quadruple of them
ANDed - by non-negative least squares on the features the planner can compute (the driver's
containers and members, the probes after the early exit, the running intersection's members, the
probed pages):

| constant | value | fitted | what |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LION_CONTAINER_COST` | 8 `cpu_operator_cost` | 32 to 39 ns | a container the driver reads and counts |
| `LION_MEMBER_COST` | 0.15 `cpu_operator_cost`, up to `LION_MEMBER_CAP` (1,024) a container | 0.74 ns | a member of it: the visibility-map mask is built from them; a bitset costs what an array of a thousand does (800 ns) |
| `LION_PROBE_COST` | 40 `cpu_operator_cost` | 210 ns | a seek of another source's posting tree to a driver key, and the container found; the leaves the seeks cross fit at 0.7 us a page and are charged as I/O (`lion_probed_pages()`) |
| `LION_MEMORY_PROBE_COST` | 30 `cpu_operator_cost` | 100 to 200 ns | the same into a set copied into memory (a GROUP BY's WHERE sets after their first use, §9; a two-column GROUP BY's outer set); 20,000 groups of 219 containers and 1,000 of 38 |
| `LION_AND_MEMBER_COST` | 0.8 `cpu_operator_cost` | 4 to 5 ns | a member of the running intersection ANDed with what a probe found |
| `LION_UNION_KEY_COST` (2026-09-28) | 30 `cpu_operator_cost` | 150 ns | the union of a list's containers built at a key: a bitset image cleared and counted (§29.11, "Unions probed") |
| `LION_UNION_MEMBER_COST` (2026-09-28) | 0.25 `cpu_operator_cost` | 1.2 to 1.5 ns | a member set in that image, or of the intersection tested against it |
| `LION_BITMAP_WORD_COST` (2026-10-20) | 0.07 `cpu_operator_cost` | 0.27 to 0.36 ns | a word of a bitmap container passed over, ANDed, united, subtracted or counted ("Dense sources") |
| `LION_BITMAP_MEMBER_COST` (2026-10-20) | 0.2 `cpu_operator_cost` | 0.86 to 0.93 ns | a member of an ARRAY looked up in a bitmap container ("Dense sources") |

The k'th source is sought only at the keys the first k - 1 left a row at, `1 - exp(-lambda)` of
them (§25's early exit, which was never priced). Median residual 27%. Re-costing the 35 counts
with the model moved them from 87 to 46,239 units a millisecond (a ratio of 530 between the
cheapest and the dearest) to 283 to 3,724 (13); the high end is counts of a few containers, whose
time is a directory lookup priced as a random read, as btree's leaf is. The per-container charge
it replaces - two `cpu_operator_cost` whatever the container held, members and probes free - was
calibrated in §10's first version, before the posting tree, and never again.

**The counts around the merge.**

| constant | before | now | fitted on the release build |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LION_DESCENT_COST` (a directory level of a lookup: a count's, an IN list value's, an FK join's) | 50 `cpu_operator_cost` (25 in the FK join) | 120 | 0.6 us a directory page read, from the FK join's 23 shapes (§27), median residual 9% |
| an IN list value's search | nothing but its leaf's page | a descent (§21: a leaf's binary search, the levels above it too when the values are sparser than the leaves) | 1,000 values over 1M keys: 7.6 ms, chosen over a 1.8 ms btree index-only scan at 1,032 |
| `LION_ENTRY_COUNT_COST` (each count of a GROUP BY: one per entry of its column, per pair of two) | `cpu_tuple_cost` | 50 `cpu_tuple_cost` | 1.0 us a test of a walk of 20,000 entries; 1.3 us a group of 200 of six RUN containers |
| `LION_LIST_GROUP_COST` (the same, a group of an IN list that drives them) | `cpu_tuple_cost` | 18 `cpu_tuple_cost` | 0.35 us a group over 1,000 of them |
| `LION_UNION_SET_COST` (a set of a union source, rebuilt by every count of a GROUP BY; `LION_FKJOIN_SET_COST` is it) | 0 (80 `cpu_tuple_cost` in the FK join) | 100 `cpu_tuple_cost` | 2 us a set for 4 groups ANDed with a 1,000-value list; 2.7 and 6 us for 200 groups ANDed with a two-arm OR and a two-value list |
| `LION_RECHECK_TID_COST` / `LION_RECHECK_GROUP_TID_COST` (a candidate TID of the heap recheck) | `cpu_tuple_cost` | 1.5 / 6 `cpu_tuple_cost` | 24 to 29 ns a TID on pages holding 68 to 150 candidates, up to 70 ns at 34; 130 ns in a 200-group count of a wholly dirty table, 1.6M of 2M pages answered from the visibility cache |
| `LION_DISTINCT_TEST_COST` | 50 `cpu_tuple_cost` | unchanged | 1.0 us (§26) |

A GROUP BY is charged one merge per ENTRY of its column - the executor counts every entry and
skips the empty ones after - with the entry's own set a source. Before, each group was charged
the containers of its share of the WHERE's rows: `c20k, count(*) FROM s WHERE c20 = 3 GROUP BY
c20k` cost 6,550 for 1,091 ms (6 units a millisecond, against the hash aggregate's 142,000 for
905); it now costs 502,000. How many containers one key's rows lie in follows its column's
correlation (`lion_key_containers()`: one a row when scattered, their share of the heap when
stored in value order, interpolated by the correlation's square): a GROUP BY over 365 days of a
table loaded in date order cost 4,650 for 0.6 ms when every day was taken to be scattered, and
costs 317.

### Dense sources (2026-10-20)

The serial price of an AND of many dense sources was about four times its time. That sent short
counts parallel ("A count in parallel": the 9-source AND, priced 4,471 for 2.2 ms, took 7.7 to
10.9 ms there) and chose a partial index's sum over a whole index's merge that ran faster (§45.6).
On a table of that section's shape - 4,000,000 rows on 68,966 pages (58 a block), 1,078 container
keys, the release build, warm - `f1 = 1 AND ... AND f9 = 1` was priced at 4,266 units for 1.21 ms,
3,519 units a millisecond. About 4,000 of them were the merge's (`lion_merge_cpu_cost_sets()`): 397
for the driver's containers (`f8 = 1`, 928 rows a key), 836 for the other eight sought at every
key at a `LION_PROBE_COST` each, and 2,773 for `LION_AND_MEMBER_COST` a member of the running
intersection at each of those seeks - 928 members, then 232, 77, 26 and on down. Both terms are an
ARRAY's: two sorted lists of members merged, and a seek that descends to its key. Neither is what
these sets are.

- **What a container is.** A build, an insert that writes an item and a VACUUM write each
  container as the smallest that holds it (`lion_container_optimize()`, §38): an ARRAY of up to
  256 k members, and past them a NARROW of width k, 512 k bytes - k the words a heap block takes,
  one at 58 rows a block; an ARRAY added to in place grows past that only by its slack, a few dozen
  members. The merge ANDs two bitmaps in one pass of the narrower's words whatever they hold
  (`lion_container_and_raw()`), and looks an ARRAY's members up in a bitmap a bit each: the nine
  sets take 1.2 ms as NARROWs and 8.8 ms as ARRAYs of up to 2,048 members and BITSETs past them.
  The price follows the containers (`lion_set_bitmap_words()`): a set of more than 256 k members a
  container is taken as NARROWs, one of fewer as ARRAYs. Two new constants, from the containers of
  heaps of 58, 120 and 226 rows a block:

  | constant | value | measured | what |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `LION_BITMAP_WORD_COST` (`pg_lion.bitmap_word_cost`) | 0.07 `cpu_operator_cost` | 0.27 to 0.36 ns | a word of a bitmap passed over: two NARROWs ANDed in 23, 38 to 43 and 69 ns at one, two and four words a block; a bitmap counted into the visibility mask, 0.34 ns a word |
  | `LION_BITMAP_MEMBER_COST` (`pg_lion.bitmap_member_cost`) | 0.2 `cpu_operator_cost` | 0.86 to 0.93 ns | a member of an ARRAY looked up in a bitmap, to AND or subtract the two; two ARRAYs merged take 1.5 ns a member, `LION_AND_MEMBER_COST` |

  The driver's container is read and counted at `LION_CONTAINER_COST` and a pass over its words
  (`lion_container_members_cost()`); a source sought ANDs the running intersection with what it
  finds in a pass over the narrower bitmap's words, a bit tested a member of whichever of the two
  is an ARRAY where the other is a bitmap, or `LION_AND_MEMBER_COST` a member where both are
  ARRAYs - and the intersection stays a bitmap as long as both are.
- **A seek that stays on its leaf** (§22). A source's seeks move it forward through its posting
  leaves, never back, so no more of them than the leaves it has can find their key on another
  leaf. The rest step to the item that holds it on the leaf the cursor stands on,
  `LION_PROBE_STEP_COST` (10 `cpu_operator_cost`; 60 to 85 ns in this AND). Priced as descents,
  `LION_PROBE_COST`, each was charged 210 ns.
- **Pages by bytes.** A set's posting pages are its share of its column's container pages by the
  bytes it takes (`lion_set_bytes()`, `lion_column_set_pages()`), not by its rows: a bitmap
  container takes its bytes however many members it holds, and by rows the tenth of a two-value
  column was given a ninth of the pages its other value was where the two have as many. A
  column's own share of the index weighs a dense set as the NARROW it is
  (`lion_index_column_posting_share()`). The pages a walk of a column reads - a GROUP BY's, a
  sum's over its entries (§14), the inner column of two (§20) - are its share of the directory by
  entries and its share of the container pages by bytes (`lion_column_walk_pages()`). Split by
  entries alone, the five dense entries of a partial index's column beside a column of a thousand
  were given half a percent of the index's pages, where they fill a ninth of them (§45.6). A range
  of a parallel GROUP BY ("A GROUP BY in parallel") walks the entries again but reads only its
  own share of their sets, so the directory's share is what each range pays again. Charged the
  column's whole sets again each range, the 40M-row GROUP BYs below were priced higher in
  parallel than serially, though they ran in half the time.
- **A driving union** - an IN list or a multi-key `&&`, the source with the fewest rows - is built
  into a bitset image at each key its sets meet at (`lion_or_hot_raw()`), unless it is a few
  ARRAYs' members folded pairwise (`LION_OR_FOLD_MEMBERS`, 128, now in lion_count.h beside
  `LION_OR_BITSET_MIN`), and the AND takes the image as the bitmap it is. ANDed member by member
  instead, an IN list of three values ANDed with three dense sets was priced at 3,082 units a
  millisecond.
- **Negated sources** - `IS NOT NULL`, `<>`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, a multi-key NOT (§14, §35) -
  are located as any clause is and priced where the merges subtract them
  (`lion_count_rel_negated()`, `lion_count_rel_subtract()`). Each is sought at the keys the AND
  leaves, a step or a probe, and taken out of the intersection by what the two are: a pass over
  the intersection's words where both are bitmaps, a bit cleared for each of the source's members
  where only the intersection is, a bit tested for each of the intersection's members where only
  the source is. Unpriced, `count(*) WHERE c1 <> 3` cost what `count(*)` cost, and a partial index
  that subtracts per entry was chosen at 1.7 ms over the whole index's one merge at 0.38 (§45.6).
- **A filtered run over a sum of every row** ("Filtered counts", §35) that has a source of its own
  that selects rows - an equality, a list, `IS NULL`, an array column's reserved entries (§17), an
  OR with no range and no complement arm - is counted as that source's intersection with the rest
  (`lion_run_count()`), and is priced as one (`lion_count_run_plain()`), not as the sum.
- **Residual rows over a partial index** (§45). The rows a residual clause is tested on are those
  the restrictions select within the index's predicate: each predicate clause the restrictions do
  not imply restricts the rows fetched (`lion_residual_rows()`). Without it, an index `WHERE w > 5`
  read under `w > 7 AND b = 4` was priced as fetching every row with b = 4, as the whole index
  does, where it fetches 40% of them in half the time.

**Measured** on the release build, warm, on four cores other work shared; medians of 21 runs (11
for the 200-key overlap and the GROUP BYs over 4M rows) of `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF)`, the
plans and prices the planner's own with `max_parallel_workers_per_gather` at 0, 2 and 3, "before"
the library without this change. The 4,000,000 rows above:

| 4M rows | before: price; serial; 2 and 3 workers | now |
|---|---|---|
| 9-source AND, `f1 = 1 AND ... AND f9 = 1` | 4,266; 1.21 ms; parallel, 3.59 and 3.11 ms | 620; 1.20 ms; serial |
| ... three of the nine IN lists | 5,826; 2.97 ms; parallel, 3.89 and 3.91 ms | 1,024; 3.08 ms; serial |
| `tags && '{0, ..., 199}'` | 5,780; 13.3 ms; parallel, 11.6 and 11.0 ms | 5,552; 14.5 ms; parallel, 11.1 and 9.5 ms |
| tsquery, eight ORs of ANDs | 29; 2.5 ms; serial | the same |
| `f8, count(*) ... WHERE f1 = 1 AND ... AND f5 = 1 GROUP BY f8` | 7,997; 3.05 ms; parallel, 3.82 and 3.82 ms | 644; 3.02 ms; serial |
| `f9, count(*) ... WHERE f1 = 1 AND f6 = 1 GROUP BY f9` | 3,618; 1.54 ms; parallel, 3.21 and 3.29 ms | 356; 1.50 ms; serial |
| `f8, count(*) ... WHERE tags && '{1,2,3}' AND f1 = 1 GROUP BY f8` | 1,993; 0.96 ms; serial | 448; 0.94 ms; serial |

The same table at 40,000,000 rows, 689,656 pages (5.4 GB), 10,776 container keys, its nine
filters' index 156 MB:

| 40M rows | before: price; serial; 2 and 3 workers | now |
|---|---|---|
| 9-source AND | 44,184; 11.9 ms; parallel, 7.55 and 6.44 ms | 7,489; 11.8 ms; parallel, 7.38 and 6.65 ms |
| ... three of the nine IN lists | 61,533; 32.1 ms; parallel, 16.3 and 15.2 ms | 12,581; 33.3 ms; parallel, 17.0 and 14.0 ms |
| `tags && '{0, ..., 199}'` | 62,082; 133 ms; parallel, 53.7 and 41.4 ms | 59,672; 135 ms; parallel, 53.2 and 47.0 ms |
| tsquery, eight ORs of ANDs | 269; 25 ms; serial | the same |
| `f8 ... GROUP BY f8`, five filters | 81,687; 33.1 ms; parallel, 16.6 and 13.1 ms | 7,611; 33.2 ms; parallel, 16.3 and 13.0 ms |
| `f9 ... GROUP BY f9`, two filters | 36,815; 15.5 ms; parallel, 9.30 and 8.37 ms | 4,173; 15.6 ms; parallel, 8.54 and 7.40 ms |
| `f8 ... GROUP BY f8`, the overlap and a filter | 20,778; 9.87 ms; parallel, 7.15 and 6.00 ms | 5,245; 9.44 ms; parallel, 7.22 and 6.52 ms |

The counts of a millisecond or a few stay serial now, where they went parallel and took two to
three times as long; the counts and GROUP BYs of 10 ms and more over 40M rows still go parallel,
and gain 1.4 to 2.6 times. The AND is priced at 518 to 633 units a millisecond at both scales.
ARRAY sets ANDed with dense ones - the whole index of §45.6, 4M rows of 157 a block, its `g` and
`c2` sets ARRAYs and its three dense ones NARROWs of three words a block:

| `count(*) FROM pp WHERE ...` | before: price; ms; units a ms | now |
|---|---|---|
| `g = 5 AND f1` | 351; 0.216; 1,626 | 139; 0.208; 666 |
| `g = 5 AND f1 AND f2 = 'a' AND f3 = 'n'` | 910; 0.582; 1,564 | 306; 0.576; 531 |
| `c2 = 7 AND f1 AND f2 = 'a' AND f3 = 'n'` | 467; 0.295; 1,583 | 168; 0.299; 562 |
| `g IN (1, 2, 3) AND f1 AND f2 = 'a' AND f3 = 'n'` | 2,093; 0.679; 3,082 | 457; 0.684; 668 |
| `c2 < 20 AND f1 AND f2 = 'a' AND f3 = 'n'` (a summed range) | 3,443; 4.61; 746 | 3,229; 4.74; 682 |

**Not done.** A GROUP BY's own work is priced below its time: the GROUP BYs with dense filters
above at 210 to 280 units a millisecond. The WHERE collected for the groups ("The
WHERE sets, collected once") costs about twice its count, the first group is counted by the merge
that collects it, and each group after it takes 450 to 550 ns a key against the 70 it is priced
at: the batch's own work - a step, the copy's image narrowed to the group's width, the block mask
of the result - is not in the model.
A summed range's counts and a range taken as a source (§32), and the FK-side join's sets (§27),
still price a container's members at `LION_MEMBER_COST`, whatever the container; complement ORs
and summed ranges leave their negations unpriced; and a tsquery of many keys is priced far below
its time (269 units for 25 ms above, §17).

`test/sql/costdense.sql` checks it on 60,000 rows indexed twice, built and grown by inserts: the
NARROWs each has, and the same AND over both priced in the same units - a member ANDed priced ten
times as dear moves neither price, a word of a bitmap both, a step on the leaf both - an IN list
that drives the AND priced as the bitmap image it is built into, and a `<>` beside the AND
subtracted, priced, and dearer where a seek leaves its page; every count against a sequential scan
with the pushdown off.

### Shapes rewritten to the node's counts (2026-10-11)

Each of these is a query the node answers with the counts it already makes; nothing in the count
engine or its visibility rules (§9, §11) changes, so every one is exact wherever the plain count
is. `test/sql/countshapes.sql` checks each against a sequential scan, over NULLs and over dead
and updated rows the visibility map no longer covers.

**Expressions over the counts.** `SELECT count(*)::int`, `100.0 * count(*) / n`, `g, round(100.0 *
count(*) / n, 2) ... GROUP BY g` or `g || '!'` of a group column: the grouped target holds the
expression, and the checks used to refuse anything in it but a column or an aggregate. Now an
expression is taken apart into what it reads - its aggregates whole and its columns, an expression
column (§41) as one - and each must pass the rules of a target entry of its own
(`lion_count_path_having()`); a SubPlan or a window function in it declines. The plan keeps the
expression in the CustomScan's target list and puts only what it reads in `custom_scan_tlist`, so
setrefs.c makes it the node's projection, evaluated once per row the node emits - once a group, as
the Agg's projection would; a volatile function in it is called as often. Under a Finalize Agg (a
partitioned table, a parallel or decoded GROUP BY, the FK-side join and the semi join) the partial
target already held only the aggregates and columns, and the Finalize Agg computes the expression.
The grouping `coalesce(col, c)` is still the one expression the node emits itself, and only that
exact expression: `coalesce(count(*), 0)` is an expression over a count. 1M rows: `count(*)::int`
with two filters 23 ms to 0.3 ms; the grouped `round(...)` 97 ms to 3 ms.

**count(1).** `count(c)` of a constant that is not NULL counts every row, which is `count(*)`
(`lion_agg_is_count()`), as the FK-side join already took it: `count(1)`, `count('x')`, and a
constant expression `eval_const_expressions()` has folded. `count(NULL)` and a Param or stable
argument are not taken. The plan classifies it as `count(*)`, and the top k accepts it as one.
1M rows: 23 ms to 0.2 ms.

**count(col) of a nullable column.** Without a GROUP BY, where every aggregate is `count(col)` of
one column that nothing proves non-NULL (§14), the count is `count(*)` of the rows the WHERE
selects AND `col IS NOT NULL`, which the posting sets answer (§14, §35: the NULL entry subtracted,
or skipped when the column drives a count of every row). `lion_count_path_countcol()` adds the
clause as if the query had written it, and EXPLAIN lists it (`cs_n (n IS NOT NULL)`); a column
whose index cannot answer it declines as such a WHERE would. With a GROUP BY it is not taken: a
group whose rows all have `col` NULL is a row of 0 in the query and no row at all under the
clause. Beside `count(*)` or a count of another column it is not taken either, since the clause
would change those. 1M rows, `count(nullable) WHERE c20 = 3`: 23 ms to 0.3 ms.

**NOT IN (list).** `col NOT IN (a, b)`, which the parser makes `col <> ALL ('{a,b}')`, is the
conjunction `col <> a AND col <> b` (`lion_all_as_and()`), and each conjunct is a §35 `<>`
clause - a negated source, the entry of its value and the NULL entry subtracted. Both forms are
false or unknown where `col` is NULL, and agree element by element everywhere else, so the
rewrite is exact. A NULL element makes the ALL unknown for every row and an empty array makes it
true for every row; both are left to the ordinary plan, as is an array known only at run time (a
generic plan's `NOT IN ($1, $2)`), whose elements cannot be taken apart at plan time, and a list
longer than §15's 1000. The conjuncts share the restriction's position, so a partition whose
bounds imply the whole restriction leaves all of them out (§16). The FK-side join's and the semi
join's fact filters go through the same code. 1M rows, `count(*) WHERE c20 NOT IN (3, 4, 5)`:
91 ms to 1.1 ms.

**Window functions over the counts.** A window function is evaluated by a WindowAgg above the
grouping, over the grouped rel's rows. With windows in the query the grouped rel's target is
`make_window_input_target()`'s: the grouping columns and every aggregate and column a window's
arguments, PARTITION BY or ORDER BY read, flattened out of the window expressions. That target
goes through the same checks as any other, so a window that reads something the node cannot
produce - `sum(count(u)) OVER ()` of a count it cannot answer - declines through them, and the
query-level refusal of window functions is gone. The top k (§36) still declines a query with
windows, whose rows it would cut before the window saw them. 1M rows, `c20, round(100.0 *
count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2) ... GROUP BY c20`: 109 ms to 1.3 ms.

**GROUP BY or DISTINCT with no aggregate.** `SELECT c20, c200 FROM fact GROUP BY 1, 2` and `SELECT
DISTINCT c200 FROM fact` ask for the keys that have a row, each once - which is what a GROUP BY
walk emits already: a group is emitted only when its count of visible rows is not 0, under the
same visibility rules as any count (§9, §11), so a key whose rows are all dead, or not yet visible
to the snapshot, is not emitted, as a sequential scan would not see it. The checks used to require
an aggregate; a GROUP BY with none is taken now, its target holding only grouping columns and
expressions of them. A DISTINCT is planned at UPPERREL_DISTINCT, where the hook now acts too when
the stage's input is one base relation - no GROUP BY, aggregate, window, set-returning function or
DISTINCT ON below it (`lion_try_distinct_path()`). Its keys are the groups of a GROUP BY of the
same columns: for the build, `processed_groupClause` and `parse->groupClause` are the DISTINCT's
(core's `processed_distinctClause`, without the columns a WHERE equality pins, which makes the
query one group as a GROUP BY's do), and the target is the input rel's - core leaves the distinct
rel's own target empty and its paths carry their input's. The grouping extra is the one a
partially aggregatable GROUP BY gets, so the parallel, decoded and partitioned forms work as for
counts, with a Finalize HashAggregate of no aggregates above them. The claimed sort order is the
GROUP BY's (§21): `SELECT DISTINCT ... ORDER BY` gets a Sort above the node when it is not that
order. PostgreSQL 18's B-tree skip scan does not compete here: core's DISTINCT over a B-tree is a
Unique over a full index-only scan, priced as such, and the cost model decides. 1M rows: `SELECT
DISTINCT c200` 128 ms to 4.6 ms (51 ms with a B-tree on c200); `c20, c200 ... GROUP BY 1, 2`
127 ms to 15 ms (decoded walk).

### Grouping sets (2026-10-11)

`GROUP BY ROLLUP (...)`, `CUBE (...)` and `GROUPING SETS (...)` over one table
(`lion_plan_gsets.c`). Every grouping set is a subset of the union of the sets - the finest
grouping, which is `parse->groupClause` - so each group of a set is the union of some groups of
the finest grouping, and an aggregate of a set's group is an aggregate over theirs. The node
counts the finest grouping as the plain GROUP BY it is, one row a group with its count `n`, and
core's own grouping sets Agg forms every set's groups over those rows, with each aggregate
rewritten over them as the FK-side join's rows mode rewrites it (§27, "Every aggregate over the
node's rows"):

| the query's aggregate | over the finest grouping's rows |
|---|---|
| `count(*)` | `lion_join_count(n)` |
| `count(x)`, x of grouping columns | `lion_join_count(n) FILTER (WHERE x IS NOT NULL)` |
| `sum(x)`, x an int2 or int4 of grouping columns | `lion_join_sum(x * n)` |
| `min`, `max`, `bool_and`, `bool_or` of grouping columns | as it stands |
| any aggregate over `DISTINCT` grouping columns | as it stands |
| `GROUPING(...)` | as it stands |

A FILTER over grouping columns is kept, ANDed with the `IS NOT NULL` of a `count(x)`. The
aggregates left as they stand are the ones a group's repeated rows do not change: those with a
sort operator in `pg_aggregate` (the aggregate is the first of its input in that order) and those
over DISTINCT arguments, whose distinct inputs are the same over the finest grouping's rows as
over the table's. `lion_join_count` is 0 over no rows, so the empty grouping set of an empty
input is one row of count 0, as `count(*)` gives.

The plan is a LionJoinAgg over a GroupAggregate over the node, sorted for the first rollup:

```
Custom Scan (LionJoinAgg)
  ->  GroupAggregate                 core's, the aggregates rewritten
        Group Key: a, b
        Group Key: a
        Group Key: ()
        Sort Key: b                  a CUBE's second rollup, sorted by the Agg
          Group Key: b
        ->  Sort
              Sort Key: a, b
              ->  Custom Scan (LionCount)   GROUP BY a, b, each group with count(*)
```

The LionJoinAgg is §27's: the grouped rel's target is the query's own, which what core puts
above (a Sort for `ORDER BY count(*)`, a window, a projection) finds its aggregates in by
`equal()`, and the Agg below computes the rewritten ones.

**The finest grouping.** `lion_try_gsets_path()` builds a rel of its own for it, a copy of the
grouped rel with an empty path list and a target of the grouping columns - with their
sortgrouprefs, as they are below the grouping step: from PostgreSQL 18 on, a grouping column
above it is nulled by the grouping step's RT index, which `remove_nulling_relids()` takes off -
and a count(*). `lion_try_count_path()` then plans the plain GROUP BY into that rel, with the
query's `groupingSets` and `limitCount` cleared and `processed_tlist` below the grouping for the
call: the top k (§36) would cut the finest grouping to the query's LIMIT, which is the sets'.
Every form of the plain GROUP BY is open to it - the nested loop of §20, the decoded walk of §34,
a partitioned table's Finalize Agg, the parallel GROUP BY - and its paths are priced in the units
pinned for the grouped rel (§39, `lion_units_pin_move()`), whose competitor is core's grouping
sets plan.

**Rollups.** The sets are chained greedily from the largest down, each to the first chain whose
last set holds it; a chain is one sorted pass of the Agg, its grouping clause the columns of its
smallest set, then those its next set adds, so that every set of it is a prefix. The first chain
holds the largest set and reads the node's rows sorted by its clause; core sorts them again for
each other chain (`create_groupingsets_plan()`). Every rollup is sorted, never hashed: the
finest grouping's rows are few, which is what makes the node worth using. A set's group count is
`estimate_num_groups()` over the node's rows. The Agg claims no order, since its first rollup
need not be the one core's `group_pathkeys` were made for, and an ORDER BY gets a Sort above the
LionJoinAgg. The cost is core's `cost_sort()` and `cost_agg()` over the node's path, and
`add_path()` chooses between the plan and core's own. The Agg's aggregate costs are the query's,
computed for it (`get_agg_clause_costs()`, `AGGSPLIT_SIMPLE`, as core prices its own Agg over the
table), not read from the `GroupPathExtraData`: core sets that struct's `agg_final_costs` only
when it builds partially aggregated paths (`partial_costs_set`), which grouping sets and a
DISTINCT aggregate never allow, and leaves it otherwise as its stack held it. Read there, the
first version's Agg was priced at whatever a backend's stack held - its real cost in one session,
1e108 in a fresh backend on PostgreSQL 16, where core's plan then won - and countgsets.sql checks
the price in a fresh backend (`\c`).

**Privileges.** The Agg below asks EXECUTE on what it runs - the extension's aggregates and those
left as they stand - and the node on `count()`; the query's rewritten aggregates (`sum(int4)`,
`count("any")`) would be asked by no one, so the LionJoinAgg path carries them in its
`custom_private` and the node asks EXECUTE on each when it starts, as ExecInitAgg would
(§9, "Privileges"; `test/sql/node_contracts.sql` has the line). The plan asks one privilege more
than the ordinary plan where the query has no `count(*)`: `count()`, of the node's own count, and
the extension's `lion_join_count` and `lion_join_sum`, which are looked up at plan time.

**Declined**, to the ordinary plan: an aggregate that reads a column outside the grouping, or one
not in the table above (`avg`, `array_agg` without DISTINCT, `bit_xor`, a `sum` of a bigint); an
aggregate that reads a column whose equality is not its value's identity (a numeric, a float;
"DISTINCT aggregates over a finer grouping", below);
an aggregate with ORDER BY other than those left as they stand; a volatile function or a
subquery inside an aggregate, which would run once a group of the finest grouping and not once a
row; an ordered-set aggregate; a grouping expression that is not a plain column of the table; a
set that names a column twice; DISTINCT, set-returning functions, joins; and a finest grouping
the node does not count (a column without a lion index, a WHERE it cannot answer).

5M rows (two columns of 20 and 2 values, one of 200): `ROLLUP (c20, c2)` 885 ms to 46 ms, `CUBE
(c20, c2)` 1,237 ms to 46 ms, `GROUPING SETS ((c20), (c200), ()) WHERE c2 = 1` 577 ms to 52 ms.
`ROLLUP (c20k, c200)` and `ROLLUP (c1m)`, whose finest groupings run to millions of groups, stay
core's MixedAggregate, at 4.8 s and 2.4 s. `test/sql/countgsets.sql` compares every shape with
the sequential plan, over NULL grouping keys and dead and updated rows VACUUM has not seen, and
of a partitioned table, and checks that the declined shapes are declined.

### DISTINCT aggregates over a finer grouping (2026-10-11)

`SELECT a, b, count(DISTINCT c) FROM t GROUP BY a, b` is the number of groups of `GROUP BY a, b,
c` with `c` not NULL within each group of `(a, b)`, and in general a DISTINCT aggregate of a
group is the same aggregate over the distinct values its rows hold - which the groups of the GROUP
BY with the aggregate's columns added are, one row each. §26's distinct walk takes one grouping
column at most and one distinct column; `lion_try_distinct_agg_path()` (`lion_plan_gsets.c`)
takes the rest the way grouping sets are taken (above): the GROUP BY with every column of every
DISTINCT aggregate appended - under fresh sortgrouprefs, as resjunk entries of a copy of the
target list - is the finer grouping, counted by the node into a rel of its own, and core's sorted
Agg forms the query's groups over its rows below a LionJoinAgg, every aggregate rewritten over the
counts by the same rules (`lion_gsets_mutator()`): the DISTINCT aggregates stand as they are,
`count(*)`, `count(x)` and `sum(x)` of the finer grouping's columns become `lion_join_count` and
`lion_join_sum` of the counts, min, max, bool_and and bool_or stand as they are. An aggregate
over any other column declines, so `max(u)` beside `count(DISTINCT c)` leaves the query to core.

```
Custom Scan (LionJoinAgg)
  ->  GroupAggregate
        Group Key: a, b
        ->  Sort
              Sort Key: a, b, c
              ->  Finalize HashAggregate
                    Group Key: a, b, c
                    ->  Custom Scan (LionCount)   decoded walk of a, b, c (§34)
```

The Agg's input is sorted by `root->group_pathkeys`. When an aggregate's DISTINCT can use a
sorted input, core appends its keys to those pathkeys and marks the aggregate presorted
(`adjust_group_pathkeys_for_groupagg()`), and nodeAgg then only skips consecutive duplicates
instead of sorting each group's values; the Agg relies on that order over the node's rows as it
would over the table's, and the sort supplies it. With `enable_presorted_aggregate` off the
pathkeys are the GROUP BY's alone and the Agg sorts each group's values itself.

It is tried only where the node has not counted the GROUP BY as it stands: §26's walk of one
grouping column and one distinct column keeps its plan, and a second form of the same query would
only compete with it. Where §26 declines - two or more grouping columns, two distinct columns, a
DISTINCT aggregate other than `count`, a partitioned table (whose (g, k) groups the Finalize Agg
under the node merges, so the distinct counts above it are exact) - or loses to core on price,
the finer grouping is offered. The cost is core's sort and Agg over the node's path, its
aggregate costs computed as for grouping sets, above, and `add_path()` chooses.

A column the finer grouping adds is grouped by its type's default equality, so one value of each
equality class reaches the Agg; every column an aggregate reads must therefore have an equality
that is its value's identity (`lion_type_equalimage()`), or `count(DISTINCT n::text)` of a
numeric n, whose 1.0 and 1.00 are one group, would count one text where the table has two. The
same rule holds for grouping sets. Its grouping equality is one privilege more than the ordinary
plan asks: nodeAgg compares a single DISTINCT column through an unchecked function (§26), while
the Finalize Agg under the node checks the equality of every column it groups by.

5M rows (two grouping columns of 20 and 2 values, a distinct column of 200): 3,252 ms to 92 ms.
100k rows, `g200, count(DISTINCT k50) ... GROUP BY g200`, which §26's walk loses to core: 19 ms
to 2.2 ms. `test/sql/countgsets.sql` compares each shape with the sequential plan over the same
table, with and without `enable_presorted_aggregate`, and checks the declines.

### Filtered counts

`count(*) FILTER (WHERE c)`, `count(CASE WHEN c THEN 1 END)`, `sum(CASE WHEN c THEN 1 ELSE 0
END)` and `sum(CASE WHEN c THEN 1 END)` each count the rows the WHERE selects - or the group
holds - for which `c` is true. A row where `c` is NULL is one where it is not true, in a FILTER
and in a CASE alike, and a clause the posting sets answer selects exactly the rows where it is
true, so a condition the WHERE could take is one more set to intersect with the WHERE's.
`lion_agg_filtered()` (`lion_plan_target.c`) recognises the forms and the way each reports an
empty answer:

| form | `LION_FCOUNT_*` | no row has `c` true | no row at all |
|---|---|---|---|
| `count(*) FILTER (WHERE c)`, `count(k) FILTER (WHERE c)` of a non-NULL constant, `count(CASE WHEN c THEN k END)` | COUNT | 0 | 0 |
| `sum(CASE WHEN c THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` of int4 or int2 | SUM | 0 | NULL |
| `sum(CASE WHEN c THEN 1 END)`, `sum(1) FILTER (WHERE c)` | SUMNULL | NULL | NULL |

`count(col) FILTER (WHERE c)` is the COUNT form where every row it counts has `col` non-NULL:
proved by a clause of the WHERE or of `c` itself that implies it, or by a NOT NULL column (§14);
otherwise it declines. Anything else - another constant, a second arm, an ELSE but 0, a CASE
inside a FILTER, DISTINCT or ORDER BY - is not a filtered count, and with the generic checks of
this section it leaves the query to the ordinary plan.

**The planner.** Each distinct condition (by `equal()`) is a filter, numbered from 1 in the order
the target list and HAVING meet it; two forms of one condition share it. After the strategy is
settled, `lion_count_path_filters()` takes each condition through `canonicalize_qual()` and
analyses each conjunct as a WHERE restriction is (`lion_count_path_filter_clause()`): the same
rewrites, an OR as one source (§19), `NOT IN` as its `<>` clauses, `IS NOT TRUE`, a multi-key
clause (§17), a range. A conjunct no posting set answers, or a condition that is a constant,
declines the whole query: what the node would count without it is not the query's answer. The
clauses are appended to the clause lists after the WHERE's, a filter's together, each
`LionClauseInfo` with its filter's number; they constrain no column of the result, so what they say
of their columns (positive, pinned, non-NULL) is the filter's alone and is restored for the WHERE
after each filter. A duplicate is dropped only within one filter. A filter's clause is no
restriction of the relation, so a partition's bounds never imply it away (§16), and a range in a
filter bounds no walk: it is a range taken as a source (§32), which needs a pinned source in the
same run - the walk, or a positive clause of the WHERE or of the filter - as the WHERE alone does.

**Runs.** The node counts the WHERE alone (run 0) and then the WHERE with each filter (run f):
run f's clauses are the WHERE's followed by filter f's, and each run is an ordinary count with its
own sets, located, counted and released before the next run's are located
(`lion_select_run()`, `lion_count_runs()`). Every rule of §9 holds within a run; the runs share
the executor's snapshot, so each counts what that snapshot sees whatever happens to the table
between them. A run touches only its own clauses: `lion_clause_in_run()` keeps the others out of
the row filter, and a range source's other bounds are looked for in its own filter's clauses only
(`lion_clause_window()`). EXPLAIN prints run 0's clauses as `Lion Indexes` and each filter as
`Count Filter N: index (clauses)`.

- **Without a GROUP BY** (the count of the WHERE, its sum over every row of §35, a partitioned
  table's sum over its partitions) the runs' totals make the one row: a COUNT form prints run f's
  total, SUM prints NULL when run 0's is 0, SUMNULL when run f's is. Where the WHERE alone is
  summed over every row (§35), a filter's run with a pinned source of its own - an equality, a
  list, a null test, an array column's reserved entries (§17), or an OR with no range and no
  complement arm - is counted as a plain count instead. An OR with a complement arm selects nothing by itself (§35, "Complements in an OR"), and
  a run whose only source it is is summed over every row as the WHERE's run is.
- **With a GROUP BY** - one column, two (§20), the decoded walk (§34), on a table or a
  partitioned one - every run emits its groups as partial rows below core's Finalize HashAggregate:
  a row of run r holds run r's count in the columns of filter r, and in the others what adds
  nothing, 0 for a COUNT form or the base `count(*)`, NULL for SUMNULL, and for SUM 0 in run 0's
  rows and NULL in the rest, so the Finalize Agg's sum of a group is NULL only when run 0 had no
  such group. A group is emitted only when its count is not 0, as without filters. The query must
  allow partial aggregation (`GROUPING_CAN_PARTIAL_AGG`) with a hashable grouping, and the path
  claims no sort order. The decoded walk is taken only when every filter's run has a source
  positive whatever its value, in the WHERE or in the filter - an equality, a list, a null test, a
  literal multi-key clause other than a jsonpath and without a prefix lexeme, or an OR of those -
  and no range source.

**Declined with filters**: the FK-side join (§27), `count(DISTINCT)` (§26), the aggregates over
keys (§37), a `coalesce` group, expressions of the grouping columns that are not grouping columns,
the top k (§36) and the parallel GROUP BY ("A GROUP BY in parallel" above). They leave the query
to the ordinary plan.

**Price.** The runs' prices added up: each run is priced by the cost functions of its strategy
with the other filters' clauses left out (`lion_count_run_targets()`), and a grouped path's rows
are its groups once per run. Where the WHERE selects most of a small table one pass over the rows
can be cheaper than a count per filter, and the cost model then keeps the ordinary plan.

**custom_private.** `LION_PRIV_FILTERS` (member 20, shape 24): an IntList of the number of filters
and each clause's filter, and at the path stage the conditions themselves; the residual clauses
("Residual clauses" below, member 21) and the target-list kinds (member 22) follow it. `LION_TL_FCOUNT(f, form)` is a filtered count's target-list kind.
`lion_count_priv_check()` requires the clauses' filter numbers to rise by at most one and end at
the number of filters, no RANGE clause in a filter, an OR's leaves inside one filter, and no join,
DISTINCT, aggregate over keys, top k, parallel walk or coalesce group beside filters.

**Privileges.** A filter's operators are clauses of the node like the WHERE's, and the operators
of every aggregate argument and FILTER the node stands in for are recorded for the EXECUTE check
(§9, "Privileges"): revoking EXECUTE on a filter's operator refuses the query as it refuses one
on a WHERE operator. `test/sql/countfilter.sql` checks every form against a sequential scan, on a
table with NULLs and with deleted and updated rows not vacuumed, through a generic plan with a
multi-key condition only the run knows, and through a cursor whose rows are read one at a time
with rows deleted between them; `test/sql/node_contracts.sql` checks the privilege.

Measured on a synthetic table of 5M rows (columns of 100, 10, 5 and 13 values, a lion index on
each), with the ordinary plan against the node:

| query | ordinary plan | LionCount |
|---|---|---|
| `count(*) FILTER (WHERE b = 1), count(*) FILTER (WHERE c = 3), count(*) ... WHERE a = 2` | 94 ms | 7.6 ms |
| `sum(CASE WHEN b = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), sum(CASE WHEN c = 3 THEN 1 END), count(*)` | 373 ms | 28 ms |
| `count(*) FILTER (WHERE b = 1), count(*) ... WHERE a = 2 AND g = 7` | 15 ms | 0.7 ms |
| `g, sum(CASE WHEN b = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), count(*) ... GROUP BY g` | 692 ms | 68 ms |
| `a, b, count(*) FILTER (WHERE c = 3), count(*) ... GROUP BY a, b` (decoded) | 628 ms | 100 ms |
| `g, a, b, count(*) FILTER (WHERE c = 3) ... GROUP BY g, a, b` (decoded) | 636 ms | 158 ms |

### Residual clauses (2026-10-11)

A WHERE clause no posting set answers - `payload LIKE 'ab%'`, `id > 2500000` on a column with no
lion index, `length(t) = 3`, `n % 2 = 0` on one with - used to leave the whole count to the ordinary
plan, which then fetched every row the other clauses select from the heap anyway, through a bitmap
heap scan. Now such a clause is RESIDUAL: the node counts as before, and every row its counts are
handed is fetched and tested.

**Which clauses.** `lion_count_path_where()` tries each restriction as it always did; one the
posting sets do not answer - or that only an index the table does not have would answer
(`lion_where_indexed()`, asked here rather than when the indexes are matched, which declined the
whole query) - is residual when `lion_residual_ok()` takes it: a table's count, or a partitioned
table's (§16, "Residual clauses over a partitioned table"), not an FK-side join's; Vars of the
table's own user columns only (no system column, no whole row); nothing volatile, no subplan.
Whatever the analysis had appended for it (the first
arms of an OR, a range's bound) is undone from a snapshot of the build taken before it
(`lion_count_path_snapshot()`): its own copy of every list the analysis appends to, the per-column
lists of range bounds inside `rangecls` and `rangepos` included, which are appended to in place - a
bound left in its column's list would name the position the next clause takes, or one past the end
of the lists. A restriction every partition's bounds imply (§16) is taken back from the same
snapshot. The query is then taken only when the other
clauses SELECT rows - a positive clause, an OR of them or a range taken as a source (§32) - and the
shape counts rows rather than entries: not a sum over every row's entries or a range's on the
column it walks (§28, §35), §37's aggregates over keys, the decoded walk, the parallel GROUP BY, or
beside a multi-key query known only at run time (§17), whose candidates may be every row. And the
rows the other clauses select must be at most half the table (`LION_RESID_MAX_SHARE`): past that,
fetching them one by one loses to the sequential scan that reads them page by page whatever the
prices say (5M rows, `c2 IN (0, 1)` with a residual: 2.2 s against 1.1).

**How it is carried.** The clauses travel in custom_private's RESID member (21) at the path stage,
and `lion_plan_custom_path()` appends them to custom_exprs after the aggregates' arguments
(`LION_FLAG_RESID`, shape 25). `LION_TL_RESID` kinds lie above the filtered counts'
`LION_TL_FCOUNT` range, so neither encoding can be read as the other. Every column they read is a column of `custom_scan_tlist` - one the
target list prints already, or a resjunk `LION_TL_RESID` one no row prints (it is emitted NULL) -
so setrefs.c rewrites their Vars into references to it, records their functions as plan
dependencies, and SS_finalize_plan() sees their Params: a LATERAL value in a residual rescans the
node.

**How it is evaluated.** `lion_begin_residual()` initialises the clauses with ExecInitQual() over a
virtual slot of the node's scan tuple, as the ordinary plan's scan initialises its quals, which
checks EXECUTE on every function they call and calls the object access hook - at executor start,
plain EXPLAIN included, and as the role that runs the plan. The test of a row
(`lion_resid_test()`) copies the columns they read from the heap tuple into their places in that
slot and evaluates the qual: a NULL result rejects the row, as a qual's does. The columns are
read at the numbers the relation counted gives them, looked up when it is made so
(`lion_open_relation()`, `lion_heap_attno_in()`): the plan's are the parent's (§16). It is the row
filter's `rowtest` (`LionRowFilter`, §17), set on the visibility cache every count of the
execution is handed (`lion_build_filter()`), so every count the node makes - a plain count, each
group of a walk or a batch, each test of a count(DISTINCT), the top k's candidates, both counts of
an OR with a complement arm (§35) - sends every candidate to the heap whatever the visibility map
says, resolves its HOT chain under the snapshot there (`lion_recheck_heap_filtered()`), and counts
the visible row only when it passes. A row the snapshot does not see is never tested, so a
residual `100 / w > 20` raises nothing over a deleted row whose w is 0, as the ordinary plan
