    nothing again (`LionMatSet.posfiltered`, `LionCountCtx.posdone`) - a join's thousands of keys,
    a GROUP BY's groups.  A count that reads the filters' sets themselves - one that probes them,
    or the WHERE of a walk that collects none - decides its own candidates, and its cursors start
    again at their lexemes' first members.  Deciding positions at a moment of the scan's own
    choosing is safe for the reason below ("Why reading positions at any moment of a scan is
    safe"): a row the snapshot sees keeps its TID and its positions, and a TID that changes hands
    in between is a row the snapshot does not see, which a copy may keep or drop as a stale copy
    may (§27, "Why a stale copy is safe").
  - **The price** (`lion_cost_posfilter()`).  A cursor decodes its chunk's members up to the
    candidate's, so a count whose candidates lie close together - a copy's, a count of every
    row - decodes each member of its lexemes once, and one whose candidates lie further apart than
    a chunk holds decodes part of one at each: 1,606 to 1,703 members a seek, measured over trees
    of 400,000 to 7.5 million members of one position (`LION_POS_SEEK_MEMBERS`, 1,650).  Each
    member decoded is `pg_lion.position_member_cost` (2.4 `cpu_operator_cost`), and each
    candidate `pg_lion.position_check_cost` (4.3) a lexeme beyond that, `TS_execute()` and its
    callbacks: 11.4 to 12.8 ns, the leaves a cursor steps and descends to included, and 21.6 ns
    on the release build (§10, "The units"), at the reference's 5 ns a `cpu_operator_cost`.
    *(Fitted on 2 and 10 million rows, `foo` and `bar` in three rows of four and `new` and
    `york` in a fifth, where the probing counts run at 453 to 487 units a millisecond and a count
    of every row at 476 to 511.  A fit on 400,000 rows, whose trees are a few leaves, comes to
    1.8 and 1,000, which over the larger trees prices the probing counts at 211 to 263 units a
    millisecond and takes the FK-side join of `new <-> york` at 3 and 20 keys of 2 million rows -
    2.5 ms against the nested loop's 0.37, 15 against 3.5 - and at 20 keys of 10 million, 21
    against 2.7; at 2.4 and 1,650 each of those takes the nested loop.  At 200 keys of 10 million
    the join still collects the filter, 144 ms against the nested loop's 30: core prices that
    nested loop at its own rate, which §39 holds out.)*  The candidates are the SUPERSET's rows,
    not the clause's (`lion_tsquery_pos_shape()`): each operand is estimated as core estimates a
    query of it alone, the clause and its superset are combined from those as core combines a
    tsquery's operands, and the candidates are the rows the caller's filters select times the
    superset's share over the clause's - 1 for `foo <-> bar`, whose superset `foo & bar` core
    estimates as it estimates the phrase, and 8 for `foo <-> !bar` of `foo` in every row and
    `bar` in seven of eight - and never more than the superset holds: `!foo <-> bar` where every
    row has `foo` is estimated at next to no rows, and its candidates are the rows with `bar`.
    The operands' shares are combined over the rows whose column is not NULL
    (`lion_tsvector_nonnull()`), as core combines them: an operand's share alone carries the
    NULLs once, and a product of n of them n times - with three rows of four NULL, that would
    price `new <-> york` at three times its candidates and `foo <-> !bar` at under half.  The AND of the
    superset's lexemes is as the intersection probe measures it (§29.11, "Correlated sets"):
    `new <-> york` of two lexemes in the same tenth of the rows is a hundredth of them by core's
    product, and its candidates are the whole tenth.  The probe's measure is taken however near
    core's product (`lion_isect_measured_factor()`): the three times §29.11 asks of a measure
    before it moves the rows estimate - which the plans above it are sized from, and which
    ANALYZE's per-column estimates and the probe's sample both wobble - is no reason to price a
    filter over rows it does not decide.  `alpha <-> beta` of two lexemes in the same two rows
    of five, 2.5 times core's product, would be priced over that product, and the FK-side join
    taken at 3 keys of 20,000 rows at 0.41 ms over a 0.04 ms nested loop (release build).  A
    partition is probed in its own columns, as the planner hands it its restrictions
    (`lion_clause_in_child()`): a clause in the partitioned table's columns matches no key of the
    partition's index, and a count of a partitioned table would price its filters from core's
    product: `new <-> york`'s, over 10,000 rows in two partitions, at 11 against 31 on the same
    rows unpartitioned.  A cursor is a lexeme's, one for each the query names, those under a
    NOT too, and its members are the rows that have the lexeme.  Priced from the clause's own rows
    and the superset's one lexeme, `foo <-> !bar` would come to a sixteenth of what it takes:
    over 400,000 rows and 2,000 keys, the FK-side join would be taken at one to ten keys over a
    nested loop into a btree of the fact's key that runs 8 to 40 times as fast (1.2 ms against
    18 ms at two keys, on the release build); and the correlated phrase's probing counts would be
    priced at a fifth of their time.  The copy is priced once for its candidates, and every
    other count for its own, its lexemes decoded up to them - which an FK-side join's probing
    counts, their candidates a few of every part of the heap, pay at almost every one.
    The heap recheck (`lion_cost_recheck()`) charges such a clause nothing.  An AM scan, plain or
    bitmap, is priced the same way once a scan (`lion_cost_scan_posfilter()`, from
    `lioncostestimate()`): its cursors begin again at every scan, so a nested loop's inner scan
    pays the seeks to its key's candidates at every repetition: a nested loop over 20 keys of a
    dimension into the fact's lion index, 3,000 candidates 2,000 rows apart, takes 68 ms, against
    19 ms for the FK-side join that collects the filter once.
  - **Under an OR** no recheck sees a leaf alone: the row passes when any arm holds, and the
    other arms are answered from posting sets.  A leaf the sets only bound is taken there when it
    is a literal an index that stores positions can follow (`lion_query_posexact()`;
    `lion_match_index()` then takes only such an index), and its tree is wrapped in a
    `LION_KN_POSFILTER` node: one child, the superset, whose every container the node's cursor
    puts through a filter of its own as it gets there, skipping the containers it empties.  The
    child is built eagerly and the node is never pending, so a leapfrog, a union or a probe above
    it sees an ordinary built container; the child stands at the key while its positions are
    read, so its pins carry §9 as any node's do, and a wide union opens the node a window at a
    time like any child.  Its cost is the filter's, per candidate, as above.
  - **What a filter holds** grows with its query, and the node is charged that against the open
    budget (§15, "Bounded cursors"; `lion_posfilter_mem()`): a cursor per distinct lexeme, each a
    copy of its position tree's leaf and a pointer per item that leaf may have (24 kB) or an INLINE
    entry's chunk - which of them is not known before the entry is read, so every operand is
    charged a tree's - beside the filter's two member arrays (128 kB). So an OR of filters too big
    for work_mem is read as a windowed union, one filter open at a time. The charge used to be a
    flat 160 kB, and a phrase of a thousand lexemes allocated 24 MB under it (2026-10 review). The
    filter is in a memory context of its own, of sizes aset.c keeps no deleted context for
    (`LION_POSFILTER_CXT_SIZES`), so that what it holds is the same whatever context it is begun
    in and whatever the backend did before, and the charge is an upper bound of it: every buffer
    and array past 512 bytes is a block of its own, its size and the headers. A recycled small
    context keeps the chunk limit of the context it was first, and one first begun to grow to
    8 MB put each 8 kB leaf in a block of 16 kB, so that the same filter held a third more in
    one session than in another. What only finding the cursors' keys takes - the opclass's
    extracted keys, the entry lookups - goes with a context of its own when the filter begins,
    and what `TS_execute()` allocates for a candidate - a phrase's positions - goes after each
    candidate, not after each container's thousands of them.
  - Why reading positions at any moment of a scan is safe: a member's TID can change hands only
    after VACUUM has removed the old row's positions, and the new row is then inserted after the
    scan's snapshot was taken, so it is invisible to the scan and its page is not all-visible to
    it either.  A mix of two rows' positions can therefore only be applied to a TID the heap
    visit drops.

  - **`@@ ANY (array)`**: a bitmap scan emits each element through its own filter
    (`lion_emit_multikey()`), and a plain index scan under an MVCC snapshot wraps each element's
    superset in a `LION_KN_POSFILTER` node of its union (`lion_scan_col_tree()`), so neither
    rechecks unless an element has a prefix lexeme.  The count takes a multi-key operator over a
    literal array (`tsv @@ ANY`) as the OR of one clause per element
    (`lion_multikey_any_as_or()`, §19), so an element the sets only bound is decided from the
    positions there as under any OR.  An index stores them for every key column whose opclass has
    support function 5 (`tsvector_ops`) unless it is built `WITH (store_positions = off)`: the
    reloption is an enum, `auto` (the default), `on` or `off`, with `true` and `false` kept as `on`
    and `off` from when it was a boolean defaulting to off.  `auto` is GIN's choice - a tsvector
    index keeps its positions without being asked, at about twice the size, so that phrases,
    weights, NOTs and BM25 are answered from it - and an index with no such column builds without
    them, where `on` is an ERROR (`lion_settle_store_positions()`).  The build records what it did
    on the meta page (`LION_META_POSITIONS` in `order_flags`, set only on an index that has a
    column storing them; no format change), so `ALTER INDEX` changes nothing until a `REINDEX`
    (docs/REFERENCE.md, "Reloptions").

### Ranking: BM25 from the index (2026-10-07)

`lion_bm25(index, query, k, k1, b, col)` (lion_bm25.c) ranks the rows of an index by one key column
that stores positions, by Okapi BM25, in Lucene's form: `idf = ln(1 + (N - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5))`
and `tf * (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1 * (1 - b + b * |d| / avgdl))` per query lexeme, for any finite `k1` of
at least 0 and `b` between 0 and 1 (`lion_bm25_params_ok()`, which both functions and the LionBm25
planner ask). Each term is computed with its top and bottom divided by `k1 + 1`, as `idf * tf / (tf /
(k1 + 1) + k1 / (k1 + 1) * (1 - b + b * |d| / avgdl))`, which no finite `k1` overflows. Written as the
first, a `k1` near 1e308 makes both infinite and the term infinite or NaN, and an infinite `k1`
makes every term NaN; a NaN ranks below nothing, so once its heap is full a walk admits no other
row, and the LionBm25 scan would return fewer rows than the sort of the same scores.

- **tf** is the npos of the row's member under the lexeme, a stripped lexeme counting once, read
  from the position tree with a counts-only cursor that steps over the positions. **df** is the
  lexeme's entry's `ntids`.
- **|d|**, the row's length, is its lexeme occurrences. The extraction files every row that has a
  lexeme under the EMPTY TEXT key as well, with one "position" holding the length in all 16 bits of
  a WordEntryPos (capped at 65535). The empty key is free: `tsvector_in()` and `array_to_tsvector()`
  refuse an empty lexeme and no tsquery can name one, and the extraction drops one that arrives
  some other way. It is an ordinary VALUE entry, so insert, build, parallel build, VACUUM and
  verify carry it with no change, and it costs one member per row (about 2 MB at 500k rows).
- **N** is the empty key's `ntids`. **avgdl** is the mean of its members' lengths; reading it walks
  the whole key, so a backend keeps it per index column until the key's `ntids` moves by more than
  1/64 or the index is rebuilt.
- **The column.** Keys are per key column (§24), so every column that stores positions has an empty
  key and lexeme entries of its own: its N, df, |d| and avgdl count that column alone, and a column
  of a multi-column index ranks exactly as an index on that column alone would, bit for bit.
  `col` names it as the index's own pg_attribute does (the Column of `\d index`): a plain column by
  the table column's name at CREATE INDEX, an expression by the name CREATE INDEX chose
  (`to_tsvector`, `to_tsvector1` on PostgreSQL 19; the names differ between versions). NULL, the
  default, is the index's one column that stores positions, and an error whose hint names the
  candidates when there are several (`lion_bm25_column()`); a name the index lacks, or a column
  without positions, is an error too.
  The functions are declared CALLED ON NULL INPUT for col's NULL, and give no rows (a NULL score)
  for a NULL in any other argument, as STRICT would.

The query's lexemes are its operands not under a NOT, once each; a prefix among them is refused, and
one under a NOT scores nothing, as every operand there does (`'w1 & !w7:*'` ranks by `w1`).
Candidates stream out of a merge of the lexemes' cursors in TID order, each scored as it comes, with
the empty key's cursor moving forward beside them; a min-heap keeps the best `L = k + 16`. Those are
sorted and fetched best first under the caller's snapshot, the TID following a HOT chain to the
visible version, until `k` are visible; when dead rows leave fewer, the walk is made again for the
next `4L`: the rows ranked strictly below the last one already tried, by (score, TID). A row's score
depends only on its members and on the prepared query (N, df and avgdl are read once per call), so
that is exactly where the last walk stopped. An offset into a bigger walk is not: a row inserted
meanwhile, invisible to the snapshot but in the index, moves every row ranked below it down a place,
and one row would be returned twice and another never. Dead rows count in N, df and avgdl until
VACUUM removes them, as a search engine's deleted documents do until a merge.

The walks stop only at one that returns fewer than it asked for, never on a count: rows inserted
since the query was prepared are in the index too, and a walk that counted them towards the rows
the lexemes had at the start stopped one short of the last visible row. Each walk asks for at most
one row past that count, so in the usual case the walk that reaches the end comes up short and no
further walk is made.

Ranking must answer what an ordinary scan of the index would, so `lion_bm25()` refuses, as the
direct count functions do, a table with row-level security enabled (it cannot apply the policies),
and so does `lion_bm25_score()`: N, df and avgdl count the hidden rows, so under a policy any
score, even one of a made-up document, would tell whether hidden rows hold a lexeme and how many.
The index `lion_index_usable()` rejects for the snapshot (an `indcheckxmin` index built
over a broken HOT chain holds the newest version only, which no heap recheck can repair). Its
lookups - the empty key's, each lexeme's, found or not - take the predicate locks of §9,
"SERIALIZABLE", as the LionBm25 scan's do, so a SERIALIZABLE search that finds nothing still
conflicts with a later insert of what it looked for.

**MaxScore** (Turtle and Flood) prunes the merge. A lexeme adds less than `idf * (k1 + 1)` to any
row, since `tf / (tf + norm) < 1` (infinite for a `k1` near the largest double, which leaves every
lexeme essential); with the lexemes in ascending order of that maximum, the first
ones whose maxima sum to no more than the heap's worst score, once the heap is full, are
non-essential: a row with none of the others cannot get in. Only the essential lexemes' members are
candidates. The non-essential ones are sought for a candidate only, from the largest maximum down,
and only while what is left of them could still lift it past the heap's worst. The heap's worst
only rises, so the essential set only shrinks. Equal scores rank by TID and candidates come in TID
order, so a candidate needs a score strictly above the worst to get in; the maxima are nudged up by
one part in 10^9 so a sum of them rounded down cannot pass for a score.

This pays most when a common lexeme sits beside rarer ones: on a synthetic 500k-row benchmark, top
10 for one very common lexeme and two rarer ones went from 41 ms to 16 ms. When every lexeme is
common, each one's maximum is close to the scores at the top, nothing becomes non-essential, and
the walk still reads every member. Block-max bounds (a maximum per chunk, not per lexeme) would
skip whole chunks there, but need a maximum tf and a minimum length stored per chunk, which the
format does not have.

**The planner path.** `lion_bm25_score(doc, query, index, k1, b, col)` is the score of one row,
computed from its tsvector with the N, df and avgdl of the index column `col` names, read once per
call site. Its tf, length (every occurrence of every non-empty lexeme, capped at 65535) and order
of addition are the walk's: both add a row's terms in descending order of idf, ties in query order,
so a row gets the same float from either, bit for bit, as an incremental sort over the scan's order
needs.

`LionBm25` (lion_bm25_scan.c) is a CustomScan offered from `set_rel_pathlist_hook` for a base table
whose query's first pathkey is `lion_bm25_score(doc, Const, Const, Const, Const, Const) DESC`, the
index a lion index on that table whose key column the function ranks indexes `doc`, a plain
column. The planner resolves `col` with the function's own `lion_bm25_column()`, and the walk ranks
that key column, which the plan records. Anything else is left to the ordinary plan, which calls
the function for each row, so that the rows and scores are the function's in every plan: a `doc`
that is another column, an expression, or a key column other than the one named is a tsvector the
walk does not read, and a `col` that settles no column (NULL on an index with several, a name it
lacks) is an error the function raises. Nor is the column ever taken from `doc`: the function
cannot see where its tsvector came from, so the scan would rank where the function raises an
error. The order is claimed only when the walk's candidates hold every row the scan may return, so
a restriction `doc @@ q2` must be there that no document without the scored lexemes matches.
`lion_bm25_where_covered()` evaluates q2 with `TS_execute()` in ternary logic: each scored lexeme
is absent, and every other operand - another lexeme, a prefix - is unknown. q2 is covered when the
answer is no whatever the unknowns are, NOTs and phrases included. Every row that passes it
therefore has a scored lexeme and is a candidate. The usual query has the same q in both places,
or a narrower q2: `'w1 & w2'`, `'w1 & !w9'` or `'w9 <-> w1'` under a score of `'w1'`. Not
`'w1 | w2'`, `'w9 & !w1'` or a bare prefix, which a row without `w1` can match.

The scan asks the walk for the best `L` rows: the planner's `limit_tuples` plus 16, or 64 when the
LIMIT is not known. It fetches them best first under the scan's snapshot, following HOT chains, and
applies the restrictions as its qual. When the node above pulls past them, it repeats the walk for
the next `4L` rows ranked below the last one it had, as `lion_bm25()` does, until the walk returns
fewer than asked.

The scan also returns each row's score: the ORDER BY expression is the last column of its scan
tuple (`custom_scan_tlist`, after the table columns the plan uses), and setrefs.c replaces every
copy of the expression above the scan with it. Evaluated on its own, `lion_bm25_score()` would read
N, df and avgdl when the first row is fetched, the walk when the executor started; a cursor whose
table gained rows in between would show scores out of the order it ranked by. With no call left
above the scan for ExecInitFunc() to check, the scan checks EXECUTE on `lion_bm25_score()` for the
current user itself, every time it is initialised and under plain EXPLAIN too (§9, "EXECUTE on what
a count replaces"), so a cached plan answers a REVOKE or a SET ROLE as the ordinary plan does
(test/sql/security_exec.sql). A relation locked
`FOR UPDATE` or the like is left to the ordinary plan, since EvalPlanQual hands a scan the table's
row rather than that tuple, and so is one with LATERAL references (`rel->lateral_relids`: a
PlaceHolderVar it computes for a LATERAL subquery pulled up from under an outer join), every path of
which is parameterized by the relations they name - the scan's is not, and its plan would compute
that value from a column of a relation it does not scan. So are parameters the function refuses,
whose error it raises. Its startup cost is
two index tuples and two operators per member of the scored lexemes (their `ntids`, read at plan
time from the lexemes' entries alone, `lion_bm25_plan_ncodes()`: a plan reads no row's length for
avgdl, which the price does not use, and takes none of a search's predicate locks, which a plan
that is never run would leave behind in a SERIALIZABLE transaction). Each row then costs a random
page, a tuple and the restrictions. Against a bitmap scan that
fetches, scores and sorts every match, on the synthetic 500k-row benchmark (top 10): 120 ms to 20
ms for two mid-frequency words, 157 ms to 51 ms for two common ones, and 160 ms to 21 ms for one
very common word with two rarer ones. A rare AND keeps the bitmap scan, which is the cheaper plan.

### Prefix lexemes (2026-10-08)

The tsvector opclass's keys are text compared under the C collation, so the key directory is in
byte order and every key starting with `foo` is one contiguous run of it.
`lion_tsquery_expand_prefixes()` (lion_multikey.c) rewrites each `foo:*` in a tsquery into the OR
of the index keys in that run, keeping the item's weight mask on every key: a walk from `>= foo`
that stops at the first key not starting with `foo`.  The rewrite runs at scan time (bitmap
scan, index scan, count pushdown), never in the planner, so new lexemes are always seen.

- **Exactness.**  A row visible to the scan's snapshot was indexed under all its lexemes before
  it committed, so its `foo...` lexemes are all in the run and the OR selects exactly the rows
  `foo:*` does.  Keys that only dead or uncommitted rows have add candidates and no matches.
- **Anywhere in the query.**  An OR of lexemes stands where the prefix stood, so under a phrase
  (`foo:* <-> bar`), a NOT or a weight it means what the prefix meant, and the position filter
  decides it like any other query.
- **Nothing matches.**  An empty run becomes the bare lexeme `foo`, which is not in the index
  either (an indexed `foo` would be in the run), so it selects no row.
- **The cap.**  At most `LION_MAX_QUERY_KEYS` (1000) lexemes over the whole query.  Past it the
  original query is kept and the old path applies: the prefix is every row and the heap rechecks.
  So a literal query with a prefix may narrow nothing at run time, as a parameter's may: the count
  pushdown does not take it for a clause positive whatever its value (`plainpositive`), which a
  parallel GROUP BY or count by cells collects by range and a filtered count's decoded walk begins
  from (§10).  Nor, with no such clause beside it and no walk driving each count, does it take a
  negated clause on an expression column or an OR with a complement arm beside it, which the heap
  scan of a WHERE that narrows nothing does not test ("A query known only at run time" above,
  `prefixmulti`).
- **Planner.**  Costing and the count pushdown's mode choice see the query with its prefix flags
  cleared (`lion_tsquery_strip_prefixes()`), the closest stand-in for an expansion they cannot
  do.  A prefix under an OR of clauses in the count pushdown is refused: that path has no
  recheck to fall back on if the expansion goes past the cap.

### Long lexemes (2026-10-19)

A tsvector lexeme can be 2047 bytes long (`MAXSTRLEN`: text input stops at 2046, a dictionary or
binary input does not), and a key with its 4-byte header at most `LION_MAX_KEY_SIZE` = 2047 (§4).
So `tsvector_ops` puts every lexeme through `lion_lexeme_key()` (lion_multikey.c), in its
extractValue and extractQuery wrappers and in the ranking:

- A lexeme of up to `LION_LEXEME_KEY_MAX` = 2043 bytes is its own key.
- A longer one is filed under a key of exactly 2043 bytes: its first bytes, as many whole characters
  as fit in `LION_LEXEME_KEY_KEEP` = 1978, then `#` up to byte 1979, then the 64 hex digits of the
  SHA-256 of the whole lexeme. Facets show the lexeme itself (§7, "Facet counts").
- **Exactness.** A 2043-byte key is ambiguous: it is a 2043-byte lexeme or the key of a longer one,
  and a 2043-byte lexeme can be spelled like another's key. So the extractQuery wrapper turns a
  query that names one into `LION_SEARCH_MODE_LOSSY`: every candidate is rechecked in the heap (the
  bitmap scan's recheck, the index scan's `xs_recheck`, the count pushdown's row filter), and the
  position filter stays out, since `lion_tsquery_item_keys()` needs the default search mode. The
  planner asks the same wrapper (`lion_multikey_query_is_exact()`, `lion_query_posexact()`), so such
  a literal under an OR of clauses stays with the ordinary plan. Lexemes of up to 2042 bytes keep
  every exact path.
- **Prefixes.** A long lexeme's key begins with its first 1978 bytes, or up to
  `pg_database_encoding_max_length() - 1` fewer where a character straddles byte 1978, so its key
  is in the run of every prefix no longer than `lion_lexeme_prefix_max()`, and that key, being
  ambiguous, makes the expansion rechecked. A longer prefix is not expanded: the query keeps the
  path past the cap above, every candidate rechecked.
- **Ranking.** BM25 scores keys: `lion_bm25_lexemes()` returns the query's keys, deduplicated, and
  `lion_bm25_score()` finds a row's term frequency by key (`lion_bm25_doc_lexeme()`), so the two
  agree with the index. A lexeme that shares its key with no other scores as itself. Two lexemes of
  one row with one key count as one term with the positions of the first in the tsvector's order,
  which is the one the extraction keeps; the row's length counts both.
- **Other keys**: array_ops hashes long text, varchar and bytea elements the same way ("Long
  elements" below); a scalar key past `LION_MAX_KEY_SIZE` is stored compressed (§4, "Long keys").

`test/sql/tsvector_long.sql`: lexemes of 1990 to 2047 bytes (the 2047-byte ones through binary
COPY), long ones that share their first 2030 bytes, multibyte ones, and a 2043-byte lexeme spelled
like another's key; AND, OR, NOT, phrases, weights and prefixes at and past the longest a key
keeps; bitmap, index, count and literal paths with and without positions against a sequential
scan and GIN; BM25 against SQL and the LionBm25 scan against sorting; writes, VACUUM, REINDEX and
verify; a scalar and an array key past the limit.

### Long elements (2026-10-19)

GIN takes an array element of any length whose compressed index tuple fits in ~2712 bytes. array_ops
names `lion_array_extract_value()` and `lion_array_extract_query()`, which call `ginarrayextract()`
and `ginqueryarrayextract()` and treat an element as tsvector_ops treats a lexeme: one of more than
2043 bytes is filed under `lion_long_key()` of it - its first bytes, `#`, its SHA-256 in hex, 2043
bytes in all - and a query that names an element of 2043 bytes or more is
`LION_SEARCH_MODE_LOSSY`, every candidate rechecked, with the same planner behaviour as a long
lexeme. So a long element is never an error, where GIN's limit applies to the compressed one.

Only for an element type whose equality is equality of its bytes, so that a hash of the bytes is
the same for two equal elements: text and varchar under a deterministic collation (the column's,
as the extraction is called with it), and bytea, whose first bytes are cut anywhere rather than at
a character. A hashed key is the type's own value - the directory calls the type's comparison and
hash on it - and is equal only to a value spelled the same, which is 2043 bytes long and so
rechecked as well. An element of any other type (numeric, citext, jsonb, ...) is a key as it is or,
past the limit, compressed (§4, "Long keys"), and an ERROR when that does not fit, as GIN's is. The
decision depends on the element's raw length alone, never on how well it compresses, so an insert
and a query always agree on whether an element is hashed.

`lion_index_facets()` shows a hashed key's elements, each with its own rows (§7, "Facet counts").
`test/sql/long_keys.sql`: text, varchar and bytea elements of 2042 to 100000 bytes, multibyte and
incompressible ones and one spelled like another's key, under `@>`, `&&` and `<@`, bitmap and count
paths against a sequential scan and GIN, before and after writes, and the facets.

### Non-empty arrays (2026-10-20)

A filter that asks whether an array has an element - `array_length(tags, 1) IS NOT NULL`,
`cardinality(tags) > 0`, `tags <> '{}'` - was a heap filter beside the count: a function of the
column is no clause of any kind the pushdown knows, and `<>` is no operator of array_ops.  Every row
of an array_ops column is in exactly one of five classes, which its entries tell apart ("The
reserved EMPTY entry" above): the column is NULL (the NULL entry, §14); it has no element and no
dimension (EMPTY), no element and a first dimension of length 0 (EMPTYDIM), or no element and a
first dimension of length 1 or more (EMPTYINNER); or it has an element (NULLELEMS or the entries of
its elements).  A predicate whose truth is the same for every row of a class is then a union of
reserved entries or the complement of one, and is answered with no heap visit.

**The classes, as PostgreSQL's arrays make them.**  An array with no element has no dimension
nearly however it was made: `'{}'`, `'{{},{}}'`, `array_fill(1, ARRAY[0])`, an empty slice,
`trim_array()` and `array_remove()` down to nothing and `string_to_array('', ',')` all come out as
the one empty array of `construct_empty_array()`, and the binary input makes one of any array with
no element.  The exceptions are the empty `int2vector` and `oidvector`, `[0:-1]`, their casts to
`int2[]` and `oid[]`, and what keeps their dimensions: `array_cat()` of them, and `ARRAY[]` and
`array_agg()` of them, `[1:2][0:-1]`.  Any other array has one to six dimensions of at least one
element each, whatever its lower bounds and whether its elements are NULL.  So over (NULL, EMPTY,
EMPTYDIM, EMPTYINNER, has an element):

    array_length(a, 1)                 NULL, NULL, 0,      >= 1,   >= 1
    cardinality(a)                     NULL, 0,    0,      0,      >= 1
    array_ndims(a)                     NULL, NULL, 1 .. 6, 2 .. 6, 1 .. 6
    array_lower(a, 1), array_upper(a, 1)   NULL, NULL, any integer, any, any
    a = '{}'                           NULL, true, false,  false,  false
                                       (array_eq() compares the dimensions first)

**Which predicates** (`lion_nonempty_test()`, lion_plan_nonempty.c).  Each clause is evaluated over
the five classes, a class's answer being true, false, NULL for every row of it, or mixed; a clause
with no mixed class is taken, and what it selects is the classes where it is true.  The values are
those of the table: the integer functions above with the dimension the constant 1, and
`coalesce()` of one with an integer constant; compared with an integer constant of any width by an
operator of the integer btree family, either way round, or with `IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM`, or tested
`IS [NOT] NULL`; the column compared with `'{}'` - an empty array constant with no dimension - by
`=`, `<>` or `IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM`; and any of these under `NOT` and `IS [NOT] TRUE / FALSE /
UNKNOWN`.  A value over a class is a range (`>= 1`, 1 to 6, any integer), so `array_length(a, 1)
>= 0` is true of every class with dimensions and `array_length(a, 1) > 1` is mixed.  Declined, and
left to the heap: a mixed class (`array_length(a, 1) = 1`, `array_ndims(a) = 1`, `array_ndims(a) >
1`, `array_lower(a, 1) = 1`, `tags <> '{1}'`); an empty constant with dimensions
(`''::int2vector::int2[]`, which a row of EMPTYDIM equals or not by its lower bound); a dimension
other than the constant 1 (`array_length(a, 2)` is NULL for a one-dimensional array with
elements); a bound that is not a constant at plan time (the classes a parameter selects depend on
its value); and a predicate true of every row or of none (`coalesce(cardinality(a), 0) >= 0`),
which has nothing to read.

**The count** (`lion_nonempty_leaf()`, first in `lion_analyze_leaf()`).  The classes a clause
selects become one of two clause kinds, whose value is a mask of the column's reserved entries -
one or more of EMPTY, EMPTYDIM and EMPTYINNER, and the NULL entry or not (`LION_RESERVED_MASK_OK()`):

- `LION_CLAUSE_RESERVED`, the rows of the entries named - `a = '{}'` EMPTY's, `cardinality(a) = 0`
  the three empty entries', `array_length(a, 1) = 0` EMPTYDIM's, `array_length(a, 1) IS NULL`
  NULL's and EMPTY's - a positive source, located as the OR of those entries' sets
  (`lion_locate_leaf()`), and a plain one for the one-set counts as an equality's set is;
- `LION_CLAUSE_NOTRESERVED`, every row outside the entries named - `cardinality(a) > 0` outside the
  NULL and the three empty entries, `a <> '{}'` and `array_length(a, 1) IS NOT NULL` outside NULL
  and EMPTY, `array_length(a, 1) > 0` outside those and EMPTYDIM, `a IS DISTINCT FROM '{}'` outside
  EMPTY alone - a negated source subtracting their union, as `<>` subtracts its value's entry and
  the NULL one (§35).
- The NULL class alone, or every row but it, is `a IS NULL` or `a IS NOT NULL`
  (`cardinality(a) IS NULL`, `cardinality(a) >= 0`), the NULL and NOTNULL kinds of §14, now taken on
  a multi-key column too: from its NULL entry, when no index holds the column as a scalar one (a
  whole-array class, below) to answer them instead (`LION_CLAUSE_ANY_COLUMN()`,
  `lion_match_index()`, `lion_index_col_for_kind()` in the executor).

The rows with an element alone are never read as a union - NULLELEMS and every element's entry,
a row under each of its elements - only as what is left of the others.  Both kinds are multi-key
kinds, resolved on the column's multi-key index, and only on one whose class extracts an array's
elements (`lion_nonempty_index()`, `lion_extracts_array_elements()`), which is what files the five
classes in entries apart: a class of whole arrays, one key per row, has no key-less entry, and
tsvector's and jsonb's classes extract other values.  Both are taken wherever their models are,
under the same rules: beside positive clauses, under a GROUP BY and a count(DISTINCT), in a
filtered count, in parallel, on a partitioned table, as an arm of an OR (§19) and as a complement
arm (§35), and beside nothing that selects rows, where the count of every row drives (§35).  A
RESERVED clause read from a partial index holds the count to the predicate's rows, as an equality
does (§45, `lion_partial_anchor_kind()`): its entries hold the predicate's rows alone.
`count(col)` reads the column as NOT NULL beside a RESERVED clause without the NULL entry and a
NOTRESERVED one with it.  Beside a multi-key query known only at run time ("A query known only at
run time" above), which may narrow nothing and leave the rows to the row filter, the row filter
tests a NOTRESERVED mask on each row the snapshot sees - the array in none of the empty entries
named, which `lion_array_empty_flag()` reads off its dimensions, and with the NULL entry among them
not NULL; without it a NULL array passes, as it passes `IS DISTINCT FROM`
(`lion_filter_with_negated()`, `LionRowFilterClause.reserved` and `nullpass`).  Two copies of one
NOTRESERVED clause - `array_length(a, 1) IS NOT NULL AND array_length(a, 1) >= 0` - are counted
once.  EXPLAIN prints the classes in one spelling whatever the query's (`lion_explain_reserved()`):
`a = '{}'`, `a <> '{}'`, `a IS DISTINCT FROM '{}'`, `cardinality(a) = 0`,
`coalesce(cardinality(a), 0) = 0`, `cardinality(a) > 0`, `cardinality(a) IS DISTINCT FROM 0`,
`array_length(a, 1) IS NULL`, `array_length(a, 1) = 0`, `array_length(a, 1) > 0`,
`coalesce(array_length(a, 1), 0) = 0` and `array_length(a, 1) IS DISTINCT FROM 0` - the twelve sets
of classes one clause can select.

**The estimates** (`lion_nonempty_rel_clauses()`, §29.11 "The relation's rows").  Core estimates
each spelling as a function of the column, with no statistics of it: a null test at 0.995 or 0.005,
an inequality at a third, multiplied with the others.  `array_length(a, 1) IS NOT NULL AND
array_length(a, 1) >= 0` over a column with an element in 80% of its rows came out at a third of
the rows, 2.4 times short, and `array_length(a, 1) IS NULL` at 0.5% where 19% were.  Lion's estimates
take every such clause of one column of a lion array_ops index together, AND the classes each
selects, and put in their place the one clause core estimates from the column's own statistics for
the same rows (`lion_nonempty_clause()`): `a <> '{}'`, `a = '{}'`, `a IS DISTINCT FROM '{}'`,
`NOT (a <> '{}')` (the empty array's share and the NULLs'), `a IS NULL`, `a IS NOT NULL`, or false.
Those clauses tell three classes apart, NULL, `'{}'` and the rest, and core's statistics count an
empty array with dimensions among the rest, as the clause does. So the EMPTYDIM and EMPTYINNER rows
are taken from the column's most common values (`lion_ne_dims_clause()`): the frequencies of those
that are empty arrays with dimensions come off the clause's estimate where the test selects the
arrays with an element and not their class, and go on where it selects their class and not the
arrays with an element - the clause then a RestrictInfo whose cached selectivity says so, as a run
of `<>` is one (§29.11, "A run of `<>` is one exclusion"). A test of those rows alone
(`array_length(a, 1) = 0`) is its own clause at their share. A value too rare to be a common one
counts as none: such arrays come from a cast of an `int2vector` or `oidvector`, and a column with
few of them loses little. A test alone that already is the clause it comes to (`a = '{}'`) is left
as it is, and changes nothing. The relation's rows are corrected wherever this changes a clause, as
wherever the intersection probe measures a correlation.

**Planning cost.**  Every estimate of a relation lion indexes takes its clauses through
`lion_nonempty_rel_clauses()`, at least once per relation and again for each index path's quals,
and the count pushdown takes every clause of its WHERE through `lion_nonempty_leaf()`, a table with
no lion index included; nearly none is a test of whether an array is empty.  So both look at a
clause's shape first, with no catalog lookup (`lion_ne_shape()`: one of the five functions above,
`coalesce()` of one, array `=` or `<>`, or a null test), and only a clause of the shape is evaluated
over the classes, its operator looked up last; a list with no clause of the shape and fewer than
two null tests of a column is handed back as it is, without an allocation.  Measured with
callgrind on 18 (2026-10-21), the planning of a query with three or eight scalar clauses on a table
with lion indexes spends 0.3-0.5% of its instructions there, where it spent 3-4.5%: 600 of 199,000
where it was 6,400 of 207,000 for three clauses, and 2,100 of 468,000 where it was 22,400 of 493,000
for eight under a count.  A count on a table with no lion index spends 900 of 293,000 (0.3%) where
it spent 8,400 of 301,000 (2.8%), and a query with no count none, as before.

**The scans.**  There is no route.  Core hands an index only the clauses whose operator is in the
index's operator family, and null tests of its columns (`match_clause_to_indexcol()`): a function of
the column never reaches the access method, nor does `<>`, which is no operator of array_ops.
`a = '{}'` does, as array `=` (strategy 17), and is answered as every row with a recheck, as above;
`a IS NULL` and `a IS NOT NULL` are answered exactly (§14).

`test/sql/nonempty.sql` runs every spelling, the taken and the declined, against the pushdown off,
as multisets both ways, over NULL arrays, empty ones, `'{NULL}'`, `'{NULL,NULL}'`,
`'{{NULL},{NULL}}'`, two-dimensional ones and lower bounds of 0 and -3; beside GROUP BY, filtered
counts, ORs and complement arms, `@>` and `&&` on the same and another column, a query known only
at run time (with `'{}'`, the row filter's case), a text[] column under "C", a domain over int[],
a multicolumn index, a partitioned table (one partition without the index declines), a whole-array
class and a class of the user's over `ginarrayextract()`; after updates, deletes and inserts that
move rows between the classes, before and after VACUUM; the plans; the rows estimated against core's
and the truth; and what reaches the scans.  `test/sql/nonempty_dims.sql` does the same for the
empty arrays with dimensions - `''::int2vector::int2[]`, `array_cat()` of two, `ARRAY[]` of them in
two and three levels, `''::oidvector::oid[]` - beside `'{}'`, NULLs, `'{NULL}'` and arrays with
elements and lower bounds of 0: every spelling, the empty constants with dimensions and the
multi-key operators, alone and beside a key; the plans; GROUP BY, filtered counts, count(DISTINCT),
ORs, the row filter beside a query known only at run time with each mask, counts by cells, the
parallel node, a partial index the clause holds the count to, the facets, and inserts, updates,
deletes, VACUUM and REINDEX moving rows between all five entries, with lion_index_verify() after.

### Cardinality guard

Reloption `max_entries` (int, default 0 = unlimited, ShareUpdateExclusiveLock).  Exceeding it is a
WARNING, once per backend per index (a static HTAB keyed by relation Oid), and never rejects a row.

- Build: exact.  Pass 1 has just counted the distinct keys, so the test is `ndistinct > max_entries`.
- Insert: a running estimate, and only on the one path that can add a key - creating a new entry.
  **The heuristic is `entries on this directory leaf + 1, times the leaves`** (§21), the leaves
  being the meta page's count of directory pages less the directory's height, and one at least
  (`lion_insert_new_entry()`).  The index's other blocks - posting and position trees, free pages -
  hold no entries: a column of five keys with 100,000 rows each is 62 blocks and one leaf.  The
  leaf is already locked, and the meta page comes after it in a split's lock order.  It is
  deliberately crude: counting the whole index per new key would read every leaf.

### Not supported

`<@` from the posting sets (a row matches when it has no key OUTSIDE the query array, which the index
cannot tell); prefix, phrase and weighted tsqueries from the posting sets, except as a superset
rechecked in the heap (above); `col op ANY (...)` in the count pushdown (only
in the bitmap scan); a query known only at run time under an OR (above);
a multi-key index as the GROUP BY or sum-over-all driver;
`lion_index_count(idx, key)` on a multi-key index (it needs a strategy-1 operator and errors out);
a test of whether an array is empty in a plain or bitmap scan ("Non-empty arrays" above).

### Measured (2026-09-20, 1M rows, 521 MB heap, all-visible, warm cache)

`tags text[]` of 5 tags out of 1000; `tsv tsvector` of 30 lexemes out of 20000 (4.99M and 29.98M
(key, row) pairs).

    column   roaring build   roaring size   GIN build   GIN size
    tags          18.4 s         37 MB        2.9 s      23 MB
    tsv          107.6 s        390 MB       19.3 s     157 MB

The posting-set BYTES are competitive - 20.4 MB for tags and 177 MB for tsv against GIN's 23 and 157
- and the size difference is entirely the page-granularity floor of §12 item 3: every one of the
1000 / 20000 keys is too big to stay inline (5000 and 1500 members) and so owns whole container
pages, 4 and 2 of them, leaving 10.8 MB and 214 MB of free space inside them.  Sharing a container
page between keys is what would close that gap, and it is the same item that was already the top
open one before this section.  The build time is the second half of the same story: 30M (key, row)
pairs go through one tuplesort and then into 40000 pages that are each written once.

    count(*) WHERE ...                     rows   pushdown   roaring bitmap+Agg   GIN bitmap+Agg
    tags @> '{t17,t42}'                      16    0.14 ms        0.39 ms            0.72 ms
    tags && '{t17,t42}'                   10031    0.38 ms        7.6 ms             8.0 ms
    tsv  @@ to_tsquery('w17 & w42')            1    0.09 ms        0.11 ms            0.23 ms
    tsv  @@ to_tsquery('w17 | w42')         2915    0.21 ms        2.3 ms             2.3 ms

The bitmap paths are at parity with GIN, heap-bound as §12 measured for scalar keys.  What the
multi-key classes are for is the first column: the pushdown answers the 10031-row `&&` in 0.38 ms
against 7.6 ms, because it never visits the heap - `Heap Blocks Skipped via VM: 9358, Heap TIDs
Rechecked: 0, Containers Visited: 2071`.

## 18. VACUUM cost, entry deletion, and page reuse (format version 3)

Measured problems (bench/COMPARISON.md, bench/results/2026-09-21-stress): a VACUUM over the 1M-row,
eight-index portfolio takes 1,141 ms and 316 MiB of WAL against btree's 380 ms / 137 MiB; in the
changing-key churn test the fifth-cycle VACUUM takes 1,017 ms against btree's 41 ms, 600,000 historical
entries remain for 100,000 live rows, and the two-index portfolio grows from 7.6 to 34 MiB until REINDEX.

**Measured first** (bench/vacuum_micro.sh, assert build, relative numbers only; the raw runs are in
bench/results/vacuum-micro-before and bench/results/vacuum-micro-after).  ambulkdelete reports its own breakdown at DEBUG1 -
cleanup-lock waits, container filtering, GenericXLog apply, INLINE entry work, pages visited/changed,
records, items rewritten/deleted - and pg_walinspect splits the WAL by resource manager.  On the
1M-row eight-index portfolio with 1% of the rows deleted, the index side of the VACUUM was 696 ms of
the 1,050 ms total, and it went:

    INLINE entry handling                423 ms (61%)   ix_c1m alone 278 ms
    container filtering (the callback)    96 ms (14%)
    GenericXLog apply                     30 ms ( 4%)
    bucket/chain page walking            147 ms (21%)
    cleanup-lock waits                   1.0 ms

with 82 MiB of generic WAL (49 MiB of it full-page images) in **20,222 records** against btree's
58 MiB in 8,312.  Two things stood out and shaped everything below.

1. *The INLINE work was almost all wasted.*  A VACUUM that removes 1% of the rows leaves 99% of the
   entries unchanged, and the old code found that out only after copying the payload out, filtering
   it into a StringInfo and building a new entry tuple.  632,130 entries × ~400 ns of allocation is
   the 278 ms.  So the filter now runs a read-only PROBE first, straight out of the page (the
   cleanup lock makes it stable) into the shared work buffer, and only an entry that really loses a
   member pays for the second pass that builds its payload.
2. *One WAL record per changed ENTRY, each carrying the whole tail of its page.*  20,222 records for
   1,422 changed container pages: the rest were INLINE entries, one `lion_replace_entry()` record
   each, and because the entry shrank, PageIndexTupleOverwrite() moved every entry after it and the
   GenericXLog delta covered all of that - 33 MiB of deltas for a few hundred KiB of real change.
   Hence the two rules below: an entry keeps its bytes, and a bucket page's entries are written in
   ONE record.

**Shrink in place.** Removing members from an ARRAY/RUN/segment item must not move the rest of the
page: the item keeps the bytes the page has allotted it and the freed bytes become slack (§4 growth
slack), so PageIndexTupleOverwrite() moves nothing and the GenericXLog delta is the item alone.  An
item that has lost more than `LION_ITEM_SLACK_VACUUM` = 256 bytes gives the space back and pays the
page-tail delta once; `LION_ITEM_SLACK_BOUND` is the larger of that and the insert path's bound, and
is what verify() accepts and what lion_index_stats() reports as `slack_bytes`.  A page whose filter
removes nothing is never registered for WAL (already the rule).  The same applies to an INLINE
entry's payload on a bucket page: a filtered payload is written back into the entry's existing bytes
with the remainder ZEROED, up to `LION_ENTRY_SLACK_BOUND` = 256 bytes.  No length field was needed
for that - no item kind has type 0, so `lion_inline_fetch()` stops at the first zero item header and
the padding is self-describing; verify() bounds it and checks that every byte of it really is zero.

**One record per bucket page.** Pass 1 collects every INLINE entry of a bucket page that changed and
writes them all in a single GenericXLog record.  Entry offsets survive PageIndexTupleOverwrite(), so
the writes do not disturb each other.  A payload that outgrew its entry still spills onto container
pages in records of its own (rare: it needs a RUN container to become a BITSET while losing
members; "The spill" below says how many records).

**Entry deletion.** An entry with ntids = 0 and ncontainers = 0 is deleted by VACUUM:
- The deletion happens in a final step for that bucket page, after every chain of that page's
  entries has been walked, under a cleanup lock, with all of the page's dead entries in ONE record.
  Emptiness is re-decided *there*, not from what pass 1 or pass 2 saw: an insert may have put a TID
  back, and then the entry stays.  An INLINE entry that pass 1 emptied is still written back empty
  first - its dead TIDs have to leave the page under that cleanup lock - and deleted afterwards.
  Reserved NULL/EMPTY entries are deleted like any other; inserts recreate them on demand.
- **Entry offsets on a bucket page never change.**  This is the invariant readers rely on, and it is
  what `lion_delete_entries()` buys by going through `PageIndexTupleDeleteNoCompact()` instead of
  `PageIndexMultiDelete()`: the item's bytes are freed but the line pointer array is left alone, the
  deleted entry shows up as an unused line pointer that every walk already skips, and nothing else
  moves.  The freed line pointers are marked so that the next `lion_add_entry()` reuses them.
  *(Deviation from the first draft of this section, which had readers copy the whole bucket page
  under a SHARE lock and iterate the copy.  Offset stability is strictly cheaper - no BLCKSZ memcpy
  per page per reader - and it is the only thing the copy was for: `lion_entry_scan_next()` gives up
  its lock between two entries of one page and comes back to an offset.  An INLINE posting set still
  keeps its bucket page PINNED until its containers have been through the visibility-map check, as
  §9 requires; that was always separate from the copy.  It also needed no change to
  LionPostingSet/LionEntryScan, which live in a header this wave does not own.)*
- A group cannot come back twice by the other route either - the entry deleted and the key inserted
  again further along the page - because only an EMPTY posting set is deleted, and a posting set
  whose members are all dead to every snapshot has nothing the scan's snapshot could have counted
  before.  test/isolation/vacuum_entry_delete.spec parks a one-column and a two-column GROUP BY
  between two entries of a bucket page while a VACUUM deletes half of them.
- Inserts are unaffected: they hold the bucket page EXCLUSIVE for the whole insert and look entries
  up by key.

**Whole-chain free.** When a CHAIN entry is deleted its chain is freed: (1) delete the entry (one
record; from here the chain is unreachable for new readers and inserts), then (2) for each chain
page, under ConditionalLockBufferForCleanup (skip the page on failure; it is merely leaked, and the
walk stops because the rightlink cannot be read without the lock), check that the page still claims
this chain and is empty, mark it LION_PAGE_DELETED, store `safexid = ReadNextFullTransactionId()` in
the page body (as nbtree's BTDeletedPageData), WAL-log, and keep it for the free space map, which
gets it once it is reusable ("Reuse" below).  Step 2 runs with
the bucket page unlocked, because VACUUM never waits for a page while holding another LWLock (§11).
A crash between (1) and (2) leaks pages, which is harmless: they are unreferenced and the sweep
below finds them (test/recovery/run.sh phase 1b puts the crash exactly there).  The leaves of a
LIVE key's set that VACUUM empties are taken out of the set one at a time and recycled the same
way (§22, "Empty leaves").

**Reuse.** *(§22 adds one thing to the sweep below: a leaked posting set's ROOT is an INTERNAL page
with downlinks on it, not an empty one, so the sweep runs in ROUNDS - an unreferenced internal
posting page is freed once every one of its downlinks names a DELETED page, which the round before
made true of its leaves. A LIVE internal page can never pass that test: every leaf of a live posting
set was visited by pass 2 and is therefore never swept, and a page a concurrent insert created since
then is full of the items a split just put there. verify() reports such a page as the ordinary leak
it is, with a WARNING.)*

**The free space map holds only pages that may be handed out**, nbtree's rule since PostgreSQL
14: a page out of the index's trees - LION_PAGE_DELETED, or an UNLINKED posting leaf (§22, "Empty
leaves") - is recorded in it once GlobalVisCheckRemovableFullXid(heaprel, safexid) is true (no scan
that could still hold a link to it is running), and not before.  `lion_alloc_page()` then takes
what the map offers, as
`_bt_allocbuf()` does: GetFreeIndexPage() takes a block off the map, the page is locked with
ConditionalLockBuffer and taken if it is all-zero or passes the same test, and otherwise the next
block is asked for, until the map has none left and the relation is extended.  A block refused is
not put back.  It is one the map is wrong about - the map is not WAL-logged, so a crash or a
promotion can leave live pages listed, which must leave it - or a free page a reader holds locked,
which the next VACUUM records again.  Recording a page before it is reusable would fill the map
with blocks every allocation reads and refuses: the map offers them by block, so young pages in
front of old ones would have the inserts after a VACUUM extend the index while the old ones wait,
and under a long snapshot every allocation would read one.  heaprel comes from `heapRel` in aminsert and
`info->heaprel` in VACUUM; a NULL heaprel means "never recycle", which is what ambuildempty wants.
ambuild never reuses.  amvacuumcleanup calls IndexFreeSpaceMapVacuum().

So a page VACUUM frees is handed out by the first VACUUM that finds it reusable.  That may be the
same one: ambulkdelete keeps the pages it freed, and the ones its sweep found not reusable yet,
with their safexids (bounded by work_mem, as nbtree's `_bt_pendingfsm_add()`; one past the bound
waits for the next VACUUM), computes the horizon afresh at its end and records those that are
reusable by then (`lion_vac_pending_record()`, nbtree's `_bt_pendingfsm_finalize()`) - a page
freed early in a long VACUUM, beside short transactions, usually is.  A page freed with no
transaction started since is not, and the next VACUUM with rows to remove records it, as does one
without them once such pages are more than a twentieth of the index (below).  Leak recovery:
ambulkdelete keeps a bitmap of the blocks it accounted for - the meta page, every bucket page it
walked, every container page it reached from a live entry, and every page it freed - and sweeps the
rest at the end of ambulkdelete: an all-zero page goes into the FSM, a DELETED page or an UNLINKED
posting leaf goes there once it is reusable, and an
unreferenced EMPTY container page becomes a DELETED one first, and so does an unreferenced FULL
leaf whose root is not a live root of its key (the leftover of an interrupted spill, "The spill"
below).  A page already out of the trees is only read, under a SHARE lock, as
`lion_vacuum_recycle()` and nbtree's `btvacuumpage()` read one; only a page the sweep may free is
cleanup-locked, conditionally.  So a free page that the checkpointer or the background writer has
pinned to write it out is recorded all the same, where a cleanup lock would leave it to the next
VACUUM.  The pages out of the index's trees that are not reusable at the end of ambulkdelete - the
ones it did not record - are counted on the meta page (the special area's `maxckey`, nbtree's
`btm_last_cleanup_num_delpages`), and a VACUUM that calls no ambulkdelete reads every block of the
index for them when they are more than a twentieth of it, nbtree's `_bt_vacuum_needs_cleanup()`
rule, recording the ones that are reusable now (`lion_vacuum_recycle()`).  In a healthy index nothing but its free pages is unaccounted for, so the sweep reads
those and nothing else.  Every page ambulkdelete's walk and its sweep read goes through VACUUM's
ring of buffers (`info->strategy`, `lion_vac_read()`; `vacuum_buffer_usage_limit`), as nbtree's
do, and so does every other page VACUUM reads to its own ends: the descent to the leftmost leaf
that the walk, and the count of the keys in amvacuumcleanup, start from
(`lion_dir_leftmost_leaf_ext()`); the descents and walks right that find an entry or a summary
again after an insert moved it (`lion_vac_ref_relocate()`); the root of a set the sweep asks is
live (`lion_posting_root_live()`); and what taking pages out of the trees reads - a directory page
deletion's leaf, siblings and parents (§21, "Page deletion") and an empty posting leaf's neighbour
and parent (§22, "Empty leaves"), which a VACUUM that empties a run of leaves reads once per
leaf.  What is left reads without it, as the inserts it shares the code with do: the meta page,
which every scan reads; and the pages of the writes a VACUUM makes beside its filtering through
the inserts' code - a directory leaf split by an entry the filtering rewrote larger, with the
parent its downlink goes to and any split left unfinished that the write finishes on the way
(§21); a container that grew, put back by a split of its posting tree (`lion_vacuum_regrow()`),
with the head a push-down copies, the parent and any unfinished split (§22); a page a payload
spills to; and every candidate the free space map offers an allocation, up to the one it takes
(`lion_alloc_page()`).  So a VACUUM leaves no more of the index in shared buffers than the ring
holds, besides the meta page and the pages those writes read, split or allocate - as many as the
writes need, and none when its filtering rewrites nothing larger.  It checks for interrupts at
every block, with nothing locked, and each page it reads passes the cost-based delay first, as
every page the walk reads does, so a sweep of a great many free pages answers a cancel and paces
its reads and records.  A page of a LIVE set is
never mistaken for a leak, because pass 2 visits every page of every chain it found, and a chain
created after pass 1 read its bucket page has no empty page in it (a spill and a split both fill
every page they allocate inside the record that allocates it, under the lock they hold
throughout) and names a root that is live.
lion_index_stats() reports deleted_pages; VACUUM is told the counts below.

**Page counts.**  IndexBulkDeleteResult has three: `pages_newly_deleted`, the pages this VACUUM
freed; `pages_deleted`, the free pages the index holds; and `pages_free`, those the next allocation
could take already.  A page is counted once: a whole-set free counts the pages it marks DELETED
as freed and as free and marks them visited, so the sweep passes them by, and the directory pages
a deletion frees (§21) are counted as freed there and as free by the sweep, which meets them
unvisited.  `pages_newly_deleted` is ADDED UP over the calls of a VACUUM that calls ambulkdelete more than once
(dead TIDs past maintenance_work_mem), as nbtree does it, and the other two describe the index as
the call leaves it - the sweep counts them afresh every time, the earlier calls' pages among them -
with a page reusable when it is all-zero, or DELETED with its safexid behind every snapshot, which
is exactly lion_alloc_page()'s test.  A page freed a moment ago is free and not yet reusable: of an
index whose lion_index_stats() says 30 deleted pages, all freed by this VACUUM, `VACUUM VERBOSE`
says "30 newly deleted, 30 currently deleted, 0 reusable".  (A VACUUM that needs no ambulkdelete at all reports
them only when it reads the index for the pages an earlier one could not hand out yet, above;
otherwise counting them would mean reading every page of the index.)

**Statistics.**  `num_index_tuples` becomes the index's `pg_class.reltuples`
whenever it is not marked estimated, and the planner reads that as ROWS - a partial index's size
is estimate_rel_size()'s tuples-per-page density of it, clamped to the table's rows - and ANALYZE
writes rows there too.  So ambulkdelete reports rows, not Σ ntids over every entry, which counts
the NULL entry, every column of a multicolumn index, every element of a multi-key one and every
SUMMARY entry (§32) all over again: every VACUUM would put a multiple of the rows there and every
ANALYZE the rows back, and plans would flip between the two.  It reports
Σ ntids over the entries of the index's FIRST SCALAR key column, SUMMARY entries left
out, which is exact because a scalar column files every row the index holds under exactly one
entry, the NULL entry for a NULL (§14, §24); for a partial index that is the count ANALYZE only
estimates.  An index whose key columns are all multi-key files a row under any number of entries,
the key-less entries included (§17), and nothing short of their union counts its rows, so it reports
the heap's row count instead, exact when the heap's is - `ginvacuumcleanup()`'s answer, and wrong
for a partial index the same way. `tuples_removed` stays a count of postings, as GIN's is. ambuild
reports as `index_tuples` the rows it added, each participant's summed (`lion_spool_nrows()`) -
not, as GIN's does, the postings it wrote - so that a partial index is sized by its rows from the
start (§45.3).

**The spill.**  An INLINE posting set that outgrows its entry moves onto
container pages (§4, §5), and VACUUM's filtering can make it outgrow the entry by an order of
magnitude (§5, VACUUM step 2), so `lion_entry_spill()` writes as many leaves as the payload needs:

1. the ROOT first, with reuse = false and held EXCLUSIVE to the end - every page of a set is
   stamped with its root's block, and a root block is never handed out twice (above) - and
   LOGGED first, as an internal page of the set with no downlink yet, in a record of its own:
   an extension no record touches is one an OS crash can lose, and the next extension would
   then hand the same block out again as the root of another set, whose stamp the leaves the
   crashed spill had written could not be told from (every summary's hash and
   every NULL entry's is 0, §32).  Replaying the record extends the relation past the root
   whatever blocks the leaves took, so the block is never a root again;
2. then each LEAF, filled, linked to the next one and logged in a record of its own that
   registers that one buffer.  The next leaf is allocated just before the record of the one in
   front of it, because that record carries the rightlink and a record may not allocate (§25), so
   at most two leaves are pinned at any time;
3. then the root's downlinks - ONE internal level: a leaf takes at least one item, a spilled
   payload has no more items than the INLINE payload it came from, which is at most
   LION_MAX_INLINE_LIMIT bytes of items of at least a header each, 512 against the 678 downlinks
   an 8 KB root holds (a static assertion keeps it so) - and the rewritten entry, together, in the
   LAST record.  A set that fits one leaf is that leaf and its entry in one record, which is every
   spill an INSERT makes.

The entry changes in the last record and in no other, so it is INLINE until the whole set is on
disk and CHAIN from the moment it is, never half of each.  An ERROR or a crash before the last
record loses nothing - the entry still holds the payload it held, dead TIDs included, which the
next VACUUM removes - and leaves FULL leaves that nothing references, stamped with a root that
has no downlink.  The next VACUUM's sweep collects them: of an unreferenced leaf that is not
empty it asks the leaf's ROOT (`lion_posting_root_live()`), and a leaf is an orphan when
the page at its owner_head is not a live container page stamped with that same (owner_hash,
owner_head), with a downlink on it when it is an internal page.  Every page of a set that exists
passes - its root is live until the entry is gone and the set freed, is internal only with a
downlink (a push-down makes it one with one, in one record), and the whole-set free only frees
EMPTY sets, whose leaves the sweep frees for being empty - and a spill that is still writing
holds its root EXCLUSIVE, which the sweep's conditional lock reads as live.  A root seen
unwritten, without a downlink, DELETED or stamped for another set under its lock stays that way
for every leaf stamped with it, because the spill that stamped the leaf has ended and no block
is a root twice.  The root itself is freed by the same sweep: an internal page all of whose
children are DELETED - here, none - is dead (§22).  lion_index_verify() reports such a leaf as the
leak it is, with a WARNING, like an empty one (which extends what §4 says verify() tolerates), and
the root as an empty page.
`test/isolation/vacuum_spill_interrupted.spec` stops a VACUUM's spill between the leaves and the
root with an ERROR (injection point `lion-spill-leaves-written`), and `test/recovery/run.sh`
phase 1e with a crash.

**Hot standby.** Generic WAL cannot raise recovery conflicts - nbtree's XLOG_BTREE_REUSE_PAGE has no
equivalent - so on a standby a reader holding a stale chain link could land on a page that replay has
already reused.  Every container page therefore carries its owner in the special area, and readers
validate it:

    typedef struct LionPageOpaqueData {       /* version 3: 24 bytes */
        BlockNumber rightlink; uint32 minckey; uint32 maxckey;
        uint32      owner_hash;   /* owner stamp of the entry this chain belongs to (§21; 0 but for a value entry) */
        BlockNumber owner_head;   /* head block of that chain, fixed for the life of the chain */
        uint16 flags; uint16 page_id; }

Every reader that reaches a container page through an entry's head or a rightlink (scan, count
cursors, insert, VACUUM, verify) checks: CONTAINER flag set, DELETED clear, and the owner equal to
the entry's.  A mismatch means the chain was freed after the reader copied the entry, which can only
happen when the posting set held nothing visible to anyone: the reader treats it as the end of the
chain (a count contributes nothing further).  It is never an error outside verify(), except on the
paths that hold the entry's bucket page throughout - insert and VACUUM's own walk - where the chain
cannot go away and a mismatch is corruption.

**owner_head alone identifies a chain**, for the whole life of the index, and that is deliberate: a
chain's HEAD page is the one page `lion_alloc_page()` never takes from the free space map
(`lion_entry_spill()` passes reuse = false), so a head block always comes from extending the
relation, is a block number that has never been handed out before, and is therefore never reused as
a head. Since §22 the head is the posting tree's ROOT rather than its first leaf, and the rule is
unchanged because a root split is a PUSH-DOWN that keeps the root at its block: `head` never moves
for the life of the set, so owner_head is still an identity nothing else can collide with.  A reused page always belongs to some other chain, whose head block differs.  *(Deviation
from the first draft, which relied on the pair (owner_hash, owner_head) and accepted "a simultaneous
32-bit hash and head-block coincidence".  The reason for the change is not the coincidence but
reachability: the count cursor's LionPostingSet carries only the head block, not the entry's hash,
and LionPostingSet lives in a header this wave does not own - so making owner_head sufficient is
what lets the count path validate at all.  It is also strictly stronger than the pair check, since
the freed head block is exactly the block the FSM is most likely to hand back.  The cost is that a
freed head block can only ever come back as a non-head page.)*  owner_hash stays as the second half
of the check for the readers that do have the entry in hand, and is what lets verify() prove that a
chain belongs to its key.

LION_VERSION becomes 3; older indexes are refused with the existing REINDEX hint.  The bump is
unavoidable and not merely advisory this time: the special area grows from 16 to 24 bytes, which
moves every item on every page.

**Measured after** (same script, same cluster; bench/results/vacuum-micro-before and bench/results/vacuum-micro-after).  The
78 MiB of XLOG/FPI_FOR_HINT in the WAL column is the heap's own, identical on both sides, so the
column that matters is the index's:

    portfolio, 1M rows, 8 indexes, DELETE id % 100 = 1, one VACUUM
                          VACUUM ms   total WAL   index WAL (of which FPI)   index records
      before (lion)          1050      162 MiB     82 MiB (49 MiB)              20,222
      after  (lion)           728      138 MiB     58 MiB (49 MiB)              10,198
      btree (control)         585      138 MiB     58 MiB (58 MiB)               8,311

    ... of which ambulkdelete itself (sum of the DEBUG1 breakdowns)
                          total    inline   filter   apply   walk   cleanup-lock wait
      before                696 ms   423      96       30     147     1.0
      after                 418 ms   186      89       28     115     0.6

    churn, 100k rows, unique bigint key + two-valued key, UPDATE every key then VACUUM
                       cycle 1                          cycle 5
                   ms      WAL     size   entries    ms      WAL     size   entries
      before      1343    428 MiB  14 MiB  200,000   1456   379 MiB  34 MiB  600,000
      after        135    4.6 MiB  14 MiB  100,000    140   6.2 MiB  15 MiB  100,000
      btree         58    3.3 MiB 5.8 MiB     -        60   3.3 MiB  10 MiB     -

The index WAL of the portfolio VACUUM is now exactly at btree's, and all but 9 MiB of it is
full-page images that the first touch of a page after a checkpoint costs whatever the AM is; the
deltas went from 33 MiB to 9 MiB.  The churn index no longer grows: entries stay at one per live row
instead of accumulating a cycle of history each time, the VACUUM is ten times faster and writes
sixty times less WAL, and the pages the dead keys owned are handed straight back through the free
space map (deleted_pages is 0 at the end of every cycle because the next cycle's inserts have
already taken them).  What is left between lion and btree on the portfolio is ix_c1m, whose 628,508
single-TID entries cost 196 ms of the 418: probing 990,000 dead-TID lookups in hash order, one
bucket page at a time.

**The §9/§11 proof is unchanged**: TIDs are still only removed under a cleanup lock taken in chain
order on every page; a page is freed only after it has been cleaned and found empty under that
lock, so a reader's pin on a page it took containers from still blocks everything that could make
those TIDs' heap pages all-visible.

### Measured, 2026-09-23: parallel VACUUM, and the callback asked once per TID

The focused benchmark of 2026-09-23 (PostgreSQL 18.6, release build,
bench/results/2026-09-23-eb1579e-pg18-focused) had `VACUUM (ANALYZE)` of the 5M-row, seven-index
scalar table after its maintenance sequence at B-tree 3,399 ms, GIN 3,823 ms and lion 4,374 ms. **Most of that gap was not lion's code at all: lion
declared `VACUUM_OPTION_NO_PARALLEL`**, and the benchmark runs VACUUM with the default
`max_parallel_maintenance_workers = 2`, so B-tree's seven indexes were vacuumed by three processes and
lion's by one. Measured separately (below), lion's serial VACUUM was 14-20% slower than B-tree's
serial one, and its default (parallel for B-tree only) one 38-47% slower.

*Set-up* (release builds, -O2 and no assertions, PostgreSQL 19beta4; shared_buffers 512MB,
maintenance_work_mem 512MB, max_wal_size 8GB, checkpoint_timeout 1h, fsync and synchronous_commit on,
autovacuum off, max_parallel_maintenance_workers left at 2 - the benchmark's settings). Two clusters,
one without and one with `shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_lion'`, so every index is generic-WAL in
the first and rmgr-WAL in the second (§25). One run is: `CREATE TABLE fact AS SELECT * FROM fact0`
(fact0 is the benchmark generator's table, `bench/comprehensive/workloads.py` scalar_data(), built
once), `VACUUM (FREEZE, ANALYZE) fact`, the seven single-column indexes of ONE family (c2, c20,
c200, c20k, c1m, skew, nullable; `none` for the heap alone), the benchmark's maintenance sequence
(`INSERT` of 1% new rows, `UPDATE fact SET c200 = (c200 + 1) % 200 WHERE id <= rows/100`,
`DELETE FROM fact WHERE id % 100 = 1`), `CHECKPOINT`, and then the timed statement, `VACUUM fact` or
`VACUUM (PARALLEL 0) fact`, with `client_min_messages = debug1` to collect ambulkdelete's own
breakdown. The old and the new `pg_lion.so` were swapped (rename, restart) between every round, the
configurations alternate inside a round, and the machine was shared with other work, so each cell is
a median with its [min-max] and anything under 10% is noise. (The driver was a throwaway shell
script around exactly these statements and is not in the tree; bench/vacuum_micro.sh measures the
older eight-index portfolio above.)

*Where the time goes* (5M rows, rmgr, serial, old code; ms, sum over the seven indexes):
1,224 ms of ambulkdelete, of which chain-page filtering 400, INLINE entry work 618, WAL apply 94,
cleanup-lock waits 1, and the walk itself the rest. Filtering is almost all the dead-TID callback:
c2's 5M TIDs filter in 82 ms, 16 ns a TID, and every index has 5M TIDs, so the callback alone is
about half of ambulkdelete. nbtree asks the same callback about the same TIDs, and the API gives no
cheaper question to ask (it is opaque; a range test against the dead-TID store would need the
store, which is not the AM's), so that half is the floor. The INLINE work had one real waste: an
entry that changes was filtered TWICE, a probe pass to find out whether anything changes and then a
second pass - asking the callback again - to build the new payload, and on c20k (twenty thousand
entries of 250 TIDs) every entry changes. A cycle-counter split of pass 1 (temporary, on the new
code) shows what is left: on c1m (a million entries of five TIDs) 40% is filtering the unchanged
entries, 41% writing the changed leaves - one record per leaf, each with its full-page image after
the checkpoint, the same as nbtree pays per leaf - and 9% the 95k entries that change; on c20k 62%
is filtering the entries that change, now once, and 30% writing them.

What changed:

1. **`amparallelvacuumoptions = VACUUM_OPTION_PARALLEL_BULKDEL`** (§6, `lion_am.c`). §11 has the
   argument for why the interlock holds whatever process runs an index's ambulkdelete;
   `test/isolation/vacuum_parallel.spec` makes a worker run one (it reports `f` with the old
   setting) and checks the result. amvacuumcleanup stays with the leader: it only vacuums the FSM.
2. **One pass over an INLINE payload**: the callback is asked about every member once
   (`lion_vacuum_inline_filter()`). The items in front of the first one that loses a member are
   copied from the page when it turns up; `lion_container_optimize()` is a function of the member
   set, so the payload built is byte for byte the old one (`test/sql/vacuum.sql`, "INLINE entries
   whose FIRST items lose nothing", drives the prefix copy through ARRAY, RUN and sparse items).
3. An INLINE entry that is not about to be deleted is not kept past pass 1 and its key is not
   copied: one allocation less per entry. Not measurable on its own.

Neither protocol nor WAL changed: the WAL of every run is identical before and after (the column).

    VACUUM wall ms, median [min-max]       old lion              new lion              btree          WAL MiB (lion / btree)
    1M rows (5 rounds)
      rmgr,    default (parallel)       561 [492-619]         471 [451-501]         370-392 [354-454]   139 / 136
      generic, default (parallel)       658 [640-694]         505 [497-552]            -                147
      rmgr,    PARALLEL 0               596 [568-651]         537 [520-596]         483-504 [452-544]
      generic, PARALLEL 0               654 [590-718]         662 [611-2027]           -
      heap alone (no index)             301-329 [275-375]
    5M rows (3 rounds)
      rmgr,    default (parallel)     3,350 [3061-4012]     2,638 [2568-2794]     2,314-2,544 [2223-3628]  579 / 644
      generic, default (parallel)     3,347 [3283-4027]     2,648 [2551-3062]          -                580
      rmgr,    PARALLEL 0             3,391 [2991-3466]     3,775 [3422-4837]*    2,888-2,983 [2791-4800]
      heap alone (no index)           1,781 [1650-3370]     (1,509 min)

    ambulkdelete, sum over the seven indexes (serial runs), median ms

      1M rows          293        262          372           350             44 -> 32

(*) the new serial 5M cell and the second heap-alone cell were hit by other work on the machine -
their minima are in line with the old ones; the ambulkdelete sums, which only time the index, went
down. A B-tree cell gives two medians: its runs alternated with the old and with the new lion build,
and it is the same B-tree both times.

So the VACUUM of the benchmark's portfolio is now 16-23% faster in both WAL modes: 4-14% slower
than B-tree's at 5M rows (from 38%), 20-27% at 1M (from 47%). What is left is shape, not overhead:
with three participants the wall time is bounded below by the longest index, and c1m - 632k INLINE
entries at 1M rows - is that index there (133 ms of the parallel run's 471). Its cost is one callback per TID, one pass over each
entry and one full-page image per leaf, which is what nbtree pays for the same column. Not done:
the REGROW path (§18, `lion_vacuum_regrow()`) filters a container that outgrew its slot a second
time - on skew, 561 containers at 5M rows, about 30 ms of that index's 128 - and could instead reuse
the first result when the container's bytes on the page are unchanged; below the noise here, and
it touches the one path that re-places containers, so it waits for a workload where it matters.

## 19. OR across columns in the count pushdown (v1, implemented)

`count(*) WHERE c200 = 17 OR c20 = 3` used to be declined and ran as BitmapOr + Bitmap Heap Scan
(19 ms at 1M rows on the optimized build, the same as btree, because 5% selectivity touches nearly
every heap page). The count evaluator already evaluates AND/OR trees over posting-set cursors
(multi-key classes, IN lists), so the whole of this is a planner and a plumbing problem.

**Planner.** A top-level `BoolExpr OR` in baserestrictinfo is accepted when every arm is an accepted
positive clause (equality, IN, IS NULL, exact multi-key) or an `AND` of such clauses, each on a plain
column of the same relation; the collation, opfamily, cross-type, Param, IN-list-cap and
