every count - `lion_merge_ops()` of the whole union prorated to the probed keys, and
`LION_UNION_SET_COST`'s 100 `cpu_tuple_cost` a set - from when the counts built it; they probe it
now, a seek of each set at the key's containers and its cursor set up, 217 ns a set. The IN list's
probing plans were priced at 2,149 to 16,139 units a millisecond (median 3,684), five to thirty
times what they take. The probe of a filter set too large to be copied into memory for the counts
(`LION_MATERIALIZE_MAX_*`) re-reads its posting tree at every count: from the second row on it is a
NOPIN set whose cursor starts at the root, 2.9 to 3.7 posting pages a probe where a key's one to ten
containers lie far apart, 0.34 to 0.68 where it has 100 or all 169 of the heap's container keys and
the seeks step right. `LION_FKJOIN_PROBE_COST`'s 80 had those pages in it, measured at one fanout. A
set that is copied is probed in memory, at `LION_MEMORY_PROBE_COST`, and the partitioned fact's
leaves' filter sets all are. The walk in key order was charged a page visit a row, where its
counters show 0.02 to 0.3 directory pages a key while the keys are dense, besides a batch row priced
as a page on purpose: a partitioned fact's lookups, a batch sorted once and walked in every leaf,
were priced at two to three times their time ("A dimension that is a join", §32 "What collecting a
range costs"). And the two counts' set-ups, 25 `cpu_tuple_cost` each, are 271 and 659 ns: probing a
key whose filters are in memory is cheaper than looking it up in a copy.

**What moved.** The model's shape: a union filter probed is its sets' seeks - no more of them than
the sets have containers - and `LION_FKJOIN_SET_COST` a set, a count; a probe is
`lion_fkjoin_probe_one()`: `LION_FKJOIN_PROBE_COST` and the pages it reads,
`LION_FKJOIN_PROBE_PAGE_COST` each, the posting tree's height and two where the key's containers are
eight container keys apart or more and a share of that where they are closer, or
`LION_MEMORY_PROBE_COST` where the set can be copied; a union collected is its sets' containers read
and its image built at each of its keys (`LION_UNION_KEY_COST`, `LION_UNION_MEMBER_COST`), as the
leapfrog builds a driving union, not a k-way merge; and a walked row is `LION_FKJOIN_LOOKUP_COST`
and `LION_FKJOIN_BATCH_ROW_COST`, with no page but the leaves it steps over. The constants, at 5 ns
a `cpu_operator_cost` and 20 a `cpu_tuple_cost`:

| setting (`pg_lion.`) | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| `fkjoin_count_cost` | 25 `cpu_tuple_cost` | 14 |
| `fkjoin_set_cost` (new; was `LION_UNION_SET_COST` and the prorated merge) | 100 `cpu_tuple_cost` | 11 |
| `fkjoin_probe_cost` | 80 `cpu_operator_cost` | 10 |
| `fkjoin_probe_page_cost` (new; was in `fkjoin_probe_cost`) | - | 54 `cpu_operator_cost` |
| `fkjoin_copy_count_cost` | 25 `cpu_tuple_cost` | 33 |
| `fkjoin_copy_probe_cost` | 5 `cpu_operator_cost` | 2 |
| `fkjoin_copy_member_cost` | 3 `cpu_operator_cost` | 3 |
| `fkjoin_lookup_cost` (new; was a page visit, `descent_cost`'s 120) | - | 75 `cpu_operator_cost` |
| `fkjoin_batch_row_cost` | 120 `cpu_operator_cost` | 75 |
| `fkjoin_row_cost` | 10 `cpu_tuple_cost` | 20 |
| `fkjoin_collect_container_cost`, `fkjoin_copy_container_cost` | 2, 20 `cpu_operator_cost` | unchanged (below) |

The run's account of "Probed, then collected" is kept at the same prices: a count that probes adds
its set-up and its union's sets, its filter containers sought and its posting pages read, less the
count against a copy it would have made - its set-up and its fk containers looked up - and the
account does not go below nothing, so that keys cheap to probe early in a run do not put off the
switch once dear ones come.

**Units a millisecond, before and after** - each forced plan's total cost over its untimed run, the
same 352 runs with the build before the refit and after it (the executor the same but for the
account); median, and the least and the most:

| forced plans | serial, before | serial, now | two workers, before | two workers, now |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| collected, plain (51 each) | 677 (156 to 2,308) | 605 (276 to 942) | 554 (303 to 2,070) | 648 (266 to 1,074) |
| collected, partitioned (10) | 808 (465 to 1,906) | 634 (446 to 1,282) | 658 (552 to 1,651) | 450 (363 to 1,290) |
| probed, plain (51) | 739 (193 to 16,139) | 419 (215 to 974) | 788 (119 to 15,377) | 410 (164 to 933) |
| ... of them the IN list (17) | 3,684 (2,149 to 16,139) | 383 (215 to 765) | 2,310 (703 to 15,377) | 373 (164 to 708) |
| probed, partitioned (10) | 3,966 (1,023 to 22,785) | 752 (631 to 1,412) | 1,635 (808 to 18,327) | 435 (362 to 1,401) |
| core's plans, pushdown off (27) | 223 (81 to 14,469) | 257 (117 to 15,686) | 289 (101 to 4,477) | 303 (163 to 5,925) |

The probing plans, priced at up to 45 times the 500 units a millisecond the rest of the model runs
at, run at 164 to 1,412; what is left low is the IN list probed over keys of a hundred or a thousand
rows (215 to 250 serially, below) and the two workers' probing counts, which take two to three times
a serial one's time each (164 to 183 over the ten-row fact's largest sets). Core's own plans are its
prices, unchanged: its hash joins run at 120 to 300 units a millisecond, its nested loops over a
hundred keys at 1,700 to 15,000 (they are priced for pages read at random that the warm cache
holds).

**The choices.** With nothing disabled, the IN list over each fact and dimension set and the
partitioned fact's semi join, against the fastest of the node collected, the node probed and core's
plan: serially the chosen plan took 1.05 times the fastest at the median where it took 1.07, 1.81 at
the 90th percentile where 2.17, and 2,251 ms in all where 2,794; in two workers 1.06, 1.83 and 1,386
ms where 1.09, 1.62 and 1,776. The mispicks the refit ends are the node's collected plan refused for
a hash join (serially, 10,000 keys of one row, 115 ms against 40, which two workers still refuse;
the partitioned fact's 10,000 keys, 131 against 45) and the probed plan chosen over the collected
one (1,000 keys of a hundred rows, 15.6 against 6.6; of a thousand rows, 32.5 against 20.9). The
mispicks left are hash joins that core prices at 120 to 270 units a millisecond, which the node at
600 loses to while it is up to two and a half times faster (20,000 keys of a hundred rows, 160 ms
against the node's 103; 2,000 of a thousand, 128 against 43), and a hundred keys of one row, where
core's nested loop, priced at 797 and run in 0.3 to 0.5 ms, now loses to the node's 585 and 0.8 to
0.9 ms. Over the suite's own small tables `fkjoin_distinct.sql`'s `count(DISTINCT d.attr)` over a
semi join of 300 dimension rows is now pushed down, in 0.6 to 0.7 ms against the nested loop's 1.0
to 1.1 it was left to.

**Walks over small fk indexes.** The refit takes the walk wherever the batch's keys lie closer than
a descent reads, which it did not over the suite's small fk indexes. Over 400,000 rows of 4,000 and
of 400 keys, whose descents read three directory pages a key, the walk and the descent were timed
side by side (the walk forced by pricing its rows at nothing, the descent by pricing the walk's
lookups out): the whole of 4,000 keys took 9.0 ms walked against 9.2 descended, their lookups 2.2 ms
against 4.3; 400 keys 1.1 against 1.1; 400 keys of a thousand rows 1.7 against 1.6 and 20.2 against
21.8 grouped. The walk is not slower where the refit now takes it, and saves half the lookups' time.

**The skewed star of "Probed, then collected", again** (the same machine and runs as there, three of
each). With nothing disabled the node, collected, is now chosen for 10,147 and 30,000 hot keys, in
315 and 770 ms, where core's nested loop into the fk index was, in 5,540 and 18,656: the collected
price came down with a union collected priced as its image rather than a k-way merge, below the
nested loop's price at the average rows a key. For 1,047 keys the nested loop stays, in 605 ms
against 120 collected. The probing plans switch after 19 keys where they switched after 8 (57 over
three participants where 24), at the account's lower prices, and take 1.0 to 1.3 times the collected
plan's time serially (160 ms against 120 for 1,047 keys, 819 against 769 for 30,000, 1,604 against
1,554 for 200,000) and 1.04 to 1.8 in two workers, where each participant collects for itself: 125
to 152 ms of collection over the three against 50 to 65 for the planned shared copy. Over the cold
keys of one row the 1,202 keys no longer switch and probe to the end, in 104 ms against 99
collected; the 40,542 switch after 1,144 keys, in 181 against 155.

**Not refitted, and found.** The collection's own terms, once a run
(`fkjoin_collect_container_cost`, `fkjoin_copy_container_cost`), are left as they were: one filter
of 201,111 rows in 169 containers took 0.45 to 0.6 ms to collect, where it is priced at some 20 us
(the three of the IN list, a union, took 1.1 to 1.5 ms, priced at 0.8 through the union's members),
and the skewed star's union of 592,134 rows took 27 to 36 ms. The data holds two sizes of collection
only, which cannot tell a fixed cost from one a row; the price is low for small dimension sets,
where it makes the planner collect for a few hundred microseconds more than probing would take, and
it makes the run's switch come early, which costs at most the collection. A count's containers that
hold visible rows cost some 0.8 us each more, fitted on `Visibility Map Checks`, in both ways; the
model has no such term. The AND of a key's container of a few members with a copy's container that
is an array walks the copy's members: the grouped count over a thousand rows a key, whose copy of
one filter holds 1,190 members a container, counts three to four times slower than the IN list's,
whose copy is of bitsets. A union filter probed over keys of a hundred or a thousand rows is priced
at half its time (215 to 250 units a millisecond): each of its containers at a key is probed as a
union of three sets, some 1.4 us, where the model has three seeks. And in two workers a count takes
two to three times what it does alone.

The suite's plans change in three ways, each checked: over its small fk indexes the lookups now walk
the keys in index order where they descended (`Join Key Lookups: in index order`); some small
dimension sets over filters held in memory probe them rather than collect them; and
`fkjoin_distinct.sql`'s `count(DISTINCT d.attr)` over a semi join of 300 dimension rows is pushed
down, in 0.6 to 0.7 ms against the nested loop's 1.0 to 1.1 it was left to. `costgucs.sql` lists the
three new settings. Where a test counts the copy's own counters (`fkjoin_perkey.sql`,
`fkjoin_semi.sql`, `fkjoin_walk.sql`) it now forces the collection with `pg_lion.fkjoin_count_cost`,
and `fkjoin_adaptive.sql`'s switches come a few keys later (13 where 10), its rescan case running
two dimension sets of twenty heavy keys so that each run still reaches the price.

### The semi and anti join as a join path (2026-09-29)

The node answered the FK-side semi and anti joins only as an aggregate over the whole query's join,
at the upper rel. Where the rows of `d ⋉ f` - the dimension rows that have a fact row under the fact
filters - were the INPUT of something else, core computed that semi join itself: a nested loop that
probes a btree on `f.fk` for each dimension row and tests the fact filters on the heap, or a hash
join over all of the fact's filtered rows. A benchmark had such a semi join over a large share of a
dimension's rows, a partitioned fact (list partitions, one sub-partitioned by range on a timestamp)
and fact filters that are a stable range on the timestamp beside an OR with an arm per value of the
partition key: 10 to 30 s through core's nested loop or hash semi join, where the same semi join
counted by the node (the reverse semi join) took some 150 ms. Its rows fed the node itself, as its
joined dimension ("A dimension that is a join", whose child is core's cheapest path of the join rel
`{d, f1}`), and other joins and aggregates.

So the semi and anti join is offered as a JOIN path of its own (`set_join_pathlist_hook`,
`lion_set_join_pathlist()`, chained to any hook installed before it): a CustomPath of the join rel
that emits the outer side's rows. Its child is a path of the outer side; for each of the child's
rows the node looks the key up in the fact's fk index and tests it under the fact filters - the
upper node's machinery unchanged: the filters collected once or probed, the lookups in key order a
batch at a time, a partitioned fact's leaves each looked up with the batch and matched by any (or
by none), the §9 interlock per leaf - and emits the row when the semi join has a match, or when the
anti join has none. EXPLAIN names it `Custom Scan (LionSemiJoin)` or `Custom Scan (LionAntiJoin)`,
prints `Join Rows: the outer rows with a match` (`without a match`; `, in their order` when it
claims the child's order, below) and every line and counter the upper node prints, and runs with
the upper node's executor: the same LionCount scan state under another plan name
(`lion_semijoin_scan_methods`), the rows mode of `count(DISTINCT)` (`LION_JOINFLAG_ROWS`) with
`LION_JOINFLAG_OUTER` (shape 16).

**Which calls it takes** (`lion_fkjoin_recognize_join()`). Core calls the hook once for each pair of
rels it joins into the join rel and each kind of join it tries for them. A semi join (`EXISTS`,
`IN`) comes as JOIN_SEMI, the special join's left side outer; as JOIN_RIGHT_SEMI the other way round
(PostgreSQL 18 and later); and as the right side made unique and inner-joined - JOIN_UNIQUE_INNER and
JOIN_UNIQUE_OUTER up to 18, from 19 JOIN_INNER with a rel of unique-ified paths. An anti join (`NOT
EXISTS`) comes as JOIN_ANTI, and as JOIN_RIGHT_ANTI the other way round (16 and later). Only the
plain JOIN_SEMI and JOIN_ANTI are taken, with the fact as innerrel: their rows are the outer side's,
each at most once, which is what the node emits; the right-hand forms have the fact outer, whose rows
the node never emits, and the unique-ified ones only repeat what JOIN_SEMI answers. Then:

- the special join is the call's own (`extra->sjinfo`), of the same kind, a semi join or the anti
  join of a NOT EXISTS - the anti join core makes of `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE f.fk IS NULL` is left
  alone, as the upper node leaves it;
- its minimal and its syntactic inner side are the fact alone, and innerrel is the fact: a plain or
  partitioned table with no LATERAL reference and no TABLESAMPLE (`lion_fkjoin_rel_ok()`), whose
  own restrictions are the fact filters - every one answered by posting sets, with a lion index on
  the fk and on each filter in every leaf that keeps it, exactly as the upper node asks
  (`lion_try_count_path()`, `lion_fkjoin_setup()`), RLS on the fact declining as there;
- the join's clauses (`extra->restrictlist`, everything the join evaluates) are exactly ONE: a strict
  operator between a plain column of the fact and a plain column of a table of the outer side,
  which the index must answer as a §10 equality (`lion_match_index()`). A second correlation (`f.y =
  d.attr`), an outer-side qual inside `NOT EXISTS` (which stays a join clause; inside `EXISTS` it is
  pushed to the outer side and is a filter of the child), or anything but a Var on either side
  declines;
- the outer side needs nothing from outside it (no `lateral_relids`, on it or on the join rel: a
  LATERAL subquery on the outer side is taken at the join rel that also holds what it references),
  its rows carry the key, and no pseudoconstant qual is anywhere in the query; the paths offered are
  unparameterized, over every unparameterized path of the outer side;
- the statement is a SELECT with no row marks: a row it locks or modifies would have its EvalPlanQual
  recheck run through a join the node stands in for, which it does not do.

The outer side may be anything else: a base relation of any kind, an inner or outer join, a join rel
holding other semi and anti joins - another LionSemiJoin among them - whatever core plans for it.

**What the rows carry.** The join rel's target, which for a semi or anti join names the outer side's
columns - of any kind, system columns and whole-row Vars included; the node reads them from its
child's row as it reads a dimension column - and nothing of the inner side but what an equivalence
class needs above the join. Two `EXISTS` correlated to one key make one class of the three columns
(`f1.fk = d.pk`, `f2.fk = d.pk`), core forces every member to be available up to the class's
relids, and the join rel `{d, f1}` then carries `f1.fk` for a join with f2 that may compare `f2.fk
= f1.fk`. Core's semi join hands up its first matching fact row's value; the node emits the outer
row's key in its place, which is every matching fact row's value when the fk and the key are of one
type, the join operator is that type's own equality, and it implies one representation under the
join's collation (`lion_fkjoin_fk_is_key()`, §10's value rule - "Grouped by the join key"). A key of
another type (`int4` fk against an `int8` key, joined by a cross-type class) or of a type whose equal
values are spelled differently declines, and so does any other fact column, an anti join's fact
column (it has no row to come from), and a PlaceHolderVar. No uniqueness is asked of the key: each
outer row is tested and emitted on its own, two outer rows with one key being two rows.

**Why the rows are the join's.** A semi join's rows are the outer rows for which some fact row
satisfies the join clause and the fact filters, under the query's snapshot; per outer row that is
§26's existence test of the key's fk set ANDed with the filters, which the upper node already makes
for a reverse semi join, and the anti join's rows are those for which it finds nothing. A NULL key
joins nothing under a strict operator: a semi join never emits its row and an anti join always does
(NOT EXISTS). `NOT IN` is no anti join: `x NOT IN (SELECT f.fk ...)` is not true for a NULL `x` nor
when the subquery yields a NULL, and core makes no anti join of it on 16 to 18. From 19 it does,
when it proves neither the outer expression nor the subquery's output can be NULL - where the two
are the same, and the node's anti join is right for it. Over a partitioned fact a row matches when
any leaf has a visible match (the leaves' rows are disjoint), and the anti join's when none has;
a leaf whose filters select nothing has no turn. Every count is the upper node's, so §9, "Why a stale
copy is safe", "One copy per query" and "A partitioned fact table" hold as they are: the node is the
upper node with the rows of a join instead of partial counts.

**Order.** A plan that looks the keys up a row at a time emits the child's rows in the child's
order. One that walks the fk index in key order, and every plan over a partitioned fact, reads the
child a batch at a time and sorts the batch into the index's key order. The join path tests such a
batch WHOLE before any of its rows goes up (`lion_join_count_batch()` for a plain fact,
`lion_join_count_parts()` for a partitioned one, each key's answer in its entry) and then hands up the
surviving rows in their own order: each row's place in the child's order is its `seq`, 0 to n - 1,
so `lion_join_batch_unsort()` swaps each row into its place - n swaps at most and no comparison. So
the path claims the child's pathkeys, as a nested loop claims its outer side's
(`build_join_pathkeys()`), and a Sort or a merge join above can use them; `LION_JOINFLAG_ORDERED`
says so, set when the join rel has a use for them. Testing a batch whole also keeps the walk's place
from one key to the next with no row going up in between, where the rows mode of the upper node
lets the walk's leaf go at each row it hands up. What putting the rows back costs was measured on
the data below (d's 200,000 kept rows semi-joined to the partitioned f1, serially, a build that
timed the put-back and one that skipped it): 0.9 ms of some 750, under 5 ns a row. The query ran in
736 to 759 ms over an ordered child (`LionOrdered` on d, or a btree index scan) with no Sort, and in
748 ms with a Sort above the path over an unordered child - the differences noise, as were those
with the put-back skipped (782 to 862 ms). The model charges nothing for it.

**Projection.** The path supports projection (`CUSTOMPATH_SUPPORT_PROJECTION`): over the topmost
join the query's target list is computed by the node from its row, with no Result above it. Its
tuple (`custom_scan_tlist`) is then every column of the join rel's rows, since core may hand it
another target list, or none - when it puts one on the plan afterwards (`create_projection_plan()`).

**Parallel.** A partial path over each partial path of the outer side, under the upper node's rules
("Parallel", "One copy per query"): the join rel, the fact rel and the outer side consider
parallelism and the clause values are parallel-safe; each participant tests the rows its share of
the child returns; the fact filters' copy is collected once, by the participants together, in the
Gather's shared memory; and the workers are what a parallel scan of the fk index pages the lookups
read would get, or the child's, whichever is more - unless the key's table has a `parallel_workers`
setting, which decides alone. Core puts the Gather (or a Gather Merge, over the claimed order) above
it, as over any partial path of a join rel; its rows are the join rel's divided as core divides a
partial path's. The serial path is parallel-safe when its child is, and a worker may run it whole
- under a parallel join's inner side, say - with a copy of its own. A parallel upper node over a
partial semi join path is two parallel-aware nodes, each with its shared state keyed by its own
plan node; each collects its copy before it reads a row of its child, so no participant waits at one
node's barrier while another waits at the other's.

**Rescans and parameters.** A rescan is the upper node's: everything a run built let go of, the
copy made again for new values of the fact filters, and the child rescanned, core's changed
parameters handed on to it. So the path is right as the inner side of a nested loop that rescans it
for every outer row, and inside a correlated subplan whose parameters are in the child's quals and in
the fact filters, a NULL one among them; a generic plan's parameters are evaluated once a run, in
every participant. A generic plan's `kind = $1` proves nothing of a partition's bounds (§16), and
needs a lion index on kind in every partition.

**Cost** (`lion_add_semijoin_path()`): the child's total cost, plus `lion_cost_fkjoin_path()` for
the child's rows - a lookup and an existence test per outer row, every row taken to find an fk entry
as the upper node prices a reverse semi join's (`found` = the rows, "Cost, revisited"), each leaf
of a partitioned fact for the keys it looks up - plus `cpu_tuple_cost` and the target's cost per row
emitted, as core charges a join's rows. The rows are the join rel's, core's estimate of the semi or
anti join, and a partial path's a participant's share of them. Nothing is taken off: not for the
outer rows core's estimate says have no match, and not for the fact rows the cost model has priced
at their average number a key where the kept keys hold more. What the fact side costs does not
depend on which of the outer side's paths the child is, and is computed once for all of them.

**Startup** (2026-09-29, the same day). No row goes up before the first batch is tested whole: one
batch of 200,000 rows at a `work_mem` of 64 MB, below, gave its first row at 978 ms of 992. The path
first started when its child did, which told a LIMIT above that its first rows came at once. Its
startup cost is now the child's startup, the child's run for the first batch's rows (their share of
its rows), and what the fact side does for them - `lion_cost_fkjoin_path()` for that many rows
under the choices the whole run made (`force`): the fact filters located, the copy collected, the
batch's lookups and existence tests. The total is as it was. The batch is what
`lion_join_fill_batch()` puts in one: rows until its memory context has `work_mem` allocated - its
first block, the array of entries, 1,024 at first and doubled when full, and each row's copy
(`lion_join_batch_rows()`) - never more than the child's rows; a plan that looks the keys up a row
at a time has a batch of one row, and its startup is the fact filters' collection and one lookup.
So over one batch the path's startup is nearly its total, and a Sort above it gives the rows of an
`ORDER BY ... LIMIT` as early and for less than the child's order does (the ordered path is shown
with sorts off in the test); at a `work_mem` of 64 kB, ten batches of a 4,000-row outer side, the
startup is some 14% of the path's cost and the ordered path under a LIMIT is taken with no Sort.

The upper node prices a row it hands up at `LION_FKJOIN_ROW_COST` (10 `cpu_tuple_cost`, "The cost
of a key, after the per-key path"), and the join path at one `cpu_tuple_cost`, core's price of a
join's row. For the rows of a reverse semi or anti join - the rows of a `count(DISTINCT)` of a
dimension column, a `GROUP BY` of one - the two plans do the same lookups and hand up the same rows,
and the model now prefers core's Agg over the join path to the upper node's rows by the difference.
Measured, neither price is the time. Through an anti join whose fact filter selects nothing -
2,000,000 outer rows, every one handed up and none looked up - the path took some 65 ns a row over
its child's own, about 3 `cpu_tuple_cost` at §10's units, and a `count(DISTINCT)` of a column of
those rows ran as fast through the upper node's rows as through core's Agg over the path (310 and
320 ms). The two plans run alike, and the prices are left as they are. A count alone keeps the
upper node, which hands up one row a participant.

**Composition.** The upper node over a dimension that is a join takes the join rel's cheapest path
as its child ("A dimension that is a join"); where that is the semi join path, the node counts one
fact against the rows the path emits for another:

    Finalize Aggregate
      ->  Custom Scan (LionCount)
            Lion Indexes: f2_df.fk (fk = d.pk), f2_df.doc (doc @@ '...'::tsquery)
            Fact Filters: collected once
            ->  Custom Scan (LionSemiJoin)
                  Partitions: f1_a_old, f1_a_new, f1_b, f1_cd
                  Lion Indexes: (fk = d.pk), (((kind = 'a') AND ...) OR ...), (ts >= (now() - ...))
                  Implied by Partition Bounds: ...
                  Refuted by Partition Bounds: ...
                  Join Key Lookups: in index order
                  Join Rows: the outer rows with a match
                  Fact Filters: collected once
                  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on dim d
                        ...

**Setting.** `pg_lion.enable_semijoin` (on) offers the paths; `pg_lion.enable_count_pushdown` off
turns them off with the rest of the pushdown. No `enable_*join` setting disables them: they are
join methods of their own. The FK-side join tests that pin the upper node's plans with core's join
methods disabled (`fkjoin*.sql` but this one, and `countmultikey.sql`) turn the path off: with it,
their reverse semi and anti joins went to core's Agg over the join path, by the row prices above,
with the same answers - the whole suite was run so once, and every answer agreed.

**Measured** (2026-09-29; PostgreSQL 18, release build, `shared_buffers` 256 MB, `work_mem` 64 MB;
medians of five warm runs; the machine shared with other work at a load of 4 to 9, so that a
difference under some 20% is noise). Synthetic data: a dimension `d` of 500,000 rows, a unique key,
a lion index over its filter columns and a filter that keeps 40% of it; `f1`, 20,000,000 rows
LIST-partitioned by `kind` into four lists, one sub-partitioned by range on `ts`, with a
partitioned lion index over its filter columns and the fk and a btree leading with the fk; `f2`,
10,000,000 rows with a lion-indexed filter column, a lion index over the fk, and a btree on the fk; 95%
of either fact's rows on the kept keys. f1's filters, a range on `ts` relative to `now()` beside an
OR with an arm per kind, keep 821,814 rows on 195,969 of the 200,000 kept keys; f2's keep 400,000
rows (two words ORed) or, marked narrow, 10,000 (two ANDed). The queries: (1) the count of d's
kept rows with a row in f1 and a row in f2; (2) the count of f2's rows whose fk is a kept d row
with a row in f1; (3) the rows of d ⋉ f1 feeding a Sort on another column, and, joined to a
100-row table, a GROUP BY of that table's label - the semi join below the join to it or, kept
apart in a subquery by `OFFSET 0`, above it (a hash join, where core's joins are enabled); (4) the
anti join feeding a Sort; (5) the rows of d ⋉ f1, and their count. Each cell is the plan, its cost and its median time; "the path"
has core's three join methods disabled, "without it" the same and `pg_lion.enable_semijoin` off,
and "core's nested loop" the pushdown off and the hash and merge joins disabled.

What they say:

- The path is the fastest way to the semi join's rows over f1's wide filters: 1.3 to 2.5 times
  core's hash semi join serially ((3), (4), (5)), 1.1 to 2.2 times with two workers, and 2 to 33
  times the plans core makes with its hash joins disabled - a nested loop into f1's btree, or over
  f1's rows made unique. For the counts (1) and (2) it is about as fast as core's hash semi joins
  serially, and as the upper node over core's parallel hash semi join - the node's child where the
  path is not taken - with two workers; with a narrow filter on f2 a plan that starts from f2's
  10,000 rows is faster (177 to 367 ms against 732 to 1,958), and the path is priced above it by
  as much.
- With nothing disabled it was chosen once, rightly: (3)'s GROUP BY with two workers, 399 ms
  against the 868 ms of the plan core takes with the path off. `enable_nestloop = off` changes no
  choice of it; it moves (1) with two workers off core's nested loop into f2's btree (9.2 s) to the
  upper node over core's parallel hash semi join (1.2 s), whose partial path is cheaper than the
  path's (233,299 against 350,092) and as fast.
- The path's price is its time: 370 to 680 units a millisecond serially and 310 to 520 with two
  workers, around §10's calibration. Core's hash semi joins over the partitioned fact run at 100 to
  240 (some 90,000 heap pages of fact rows read past `shared_buffers`, two million rows filtered),
  and its nested loop into f2's btree at 23. So the path loses on price where it wins on time:
  serially it costs 1.2 to 2.7 times core's hash semi join and runs faster. Nothing was taken off
  its price for that; a hash join priced at its time would lose to it.
- Core's estimate of d ⋉ f1 was 90,469 rows for 195,969 (ANALYZE's `n_distinct` of `f1.fk`,
  226,000 for 500,000): the join path's rows are the join rel's, and everything above them is
  priced for half the rows it gets, whichever path the join rel takes.

### Grouped by a fact column (2026-09-29)

`SELECT f.kind, count(*) FROM fact f JOIN dim d ON f.fk = d.pk WHERE ... GROUP BY f.kind` used to
be declined whatever indexes there were: the node's row for a dimension row is one count, the rows
of `fk = d.pk` ANDed with the fact filters, and nothing in that number says how the rows it counts
divide among `f.kind`'s values. A lion index on `kind` did not help, because the join never asked
for one. So the query was core's - over a partitioned fact table with an OR of a filter per kind, a
nested loop into every partition, at every dimension row. Written as a UNION of one ungrouped count
per kind, each branch was the node's, which is the whole of what this adds: the node counts each
dimension row once per GROUP of the fact column instead.

**What is counted.** For a dimension row `d` and a value `v` of the fact column `g`, the rows the
Finalize Agg's group `v` wants from `d` are `F(d) ∩ {g = v}`: the key's set, the fact filters, and
the posting set of `g = v` - one more source of the same count. The node counts that for each
group, and hands up a partial row `(d's columns, v, count)` for each count that is not 0; the
Finalize Agg adds up the rows of each `(v, d's grouped columns)` as it adds up a dimension column's.
A dimension row's rows in different groups are disjoint (a fact row has one value of `g`), so the
counts are exact per group and add up to the row's count. Grouping by `g` beside dimension columns,
or beside the fact's join key ("Grouped by the join key"), is the same rows with more columns.

**The groups are a relation's own.** In the plain table, and in a partition whose bounds leave `g`
several values, they are the entries of a lion index on `g` there: an entry is one group exactly
when the index's strategy 1 is the grouping equality under the grouping collation, and its stored
key is what the row prints, so the index has to pass §10's value gate - the same rules as a GROUP
BY's own driving index (`lion_collect_targets()`, given `g` as a driving column), which is why a
numeric `g` declines. A partition whose bounds give `g` one value needs no index at all: every row
of it is of that group, and a key's count there is the group's count, made as any partition's is
(`lion_leaf_bound_value()`). The proof is §16's for an implied clause - the constraint strongly
implies `g = c` under the grouping's own equality and collation - taken for the few constants the
constraint compares `g` with; and since `c` is what the rows print, the grouping equality has to be
the type's and imply an identical representation under that collation (`lion_type_equalimage()`),
which is §10's rule for a stored key. A partition of the NULLs alone gives the NULL group. So a
fact table LIST-partitioned by `kind`, one partition per kind, needs no index on `kind` for this; a
partition of several kinds, or a default one, needs one.

**Executing it** (`lion_next_join_group()`). The keys are read a batch at a time - the batches of
"Lookups in key order", taken for a plain table too - and each batch is taken to each relation in
turn, the plain table or every leaf partition. In a partition whose bounds give `g` its value, the
turn is the partition's ordinary turn (`lion_join_lookup_ent()`, with its copy of the filters and
its account of what probing them costs), each count put by with that value. Otherwise the entries of
`g`'s index - open, with the relation's others, for the life of the node (§16, "Why every leaf is
open for the whole run") - are walked a chunk of 64 at a time: the chunk's sets located - and
pinned, as an IN list's are - each key of the batch looked up once and counted against each of them
(`lion_join_count_groups()`: the key's set, the filters or their copy, and the group's set, ANDed by
the one count function every count goes through), and the chunk let go of before the next. The cost
model takes this for columns of few values; a column of more is correct, only slower, and a chunk
after the first walks the fk index from its start again. The rows a turn counted go up once the turn
is over: after the partition's turn has ended, as a partitioned fact's rows always go (§16), or,
over the plain table, once its sets have let go of their pins (`lion_pause_run()`). They wait in
memory until then - at most one per key and group with rows in the relation, no more than the
batch's join rows there. A turn whose filters select nothing has none. `Fact Group Key` names the
column in EXPLAIN, `Fact Groups From Partition Bounds` how many partitions' bounds give it, and
EXPLAIN ANALYZE's `Fact Group Counts` how many counts were made per group - none in a partition
whose bounds give the value.

**What is taken.** An inner join, and the forward semi join over its distinct keys, whose rows
stand for the fact's; a semi or anti join's rows are the dimension's, and the query above them names
no fact column. One fact column other than the join key, itself a column of the GROUP BY (an
expression of it is the Agg's, above the node), hashable, with counts alone beside it: the rows
carry no count per group for "Every aggregate over the node's rows" to rewrite, and a
`count(DISTINCT)` or a sum beside a fact column declines. Each row is a dimension row's in one
group - in one partition, over a partitioned fact - so "Grouped by the join key"'s rows-as-groups
Agg is never taken beside it. Parallel plans divide the dimension rows as for any FK-side join, and
each participant counts its share in every group.

**Cost.** A relation counts each key once per group, so `lion_cost_fkjoin_path()` multiplies its
per-key counts - against the filters or their copy - by its groups: one where the bounds give the
value, and otherwise the column's distinct values in the relation (`estimate_num_groups()` over its
rows, since every entry is counted whether or not the filters leave it rows). The key's lookup is
made once. The node's rows are its keys' times the groups, as many as the join's rows at most.

`test/sql/fkjoin_factgroup.sql`: every query against the pushdown off and serially, over a fact
table LIST-partitioned by kind (a sub-partitioned list, a list of one kind, one of two and a
default, NULL kind included) and a plain copy of it - grouped by the partition key, alone, beside
dimension columns and the join key, under an OR of a filter per kind with a range beside it and an
IN list of a dimension's keys, and by other columns, one of a hundred values and NULL, more groups
than one chunk; the forward semi join; HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT; filters that select nothing in some
partitions and in all; batches at a small work_mem; rescans and a dirty heap; the counters; and the
declines (an expression, two fact columns, a `count(DISTINCT)` beside, a numeric column, and a
partition of several kinds without an index on kind - which declines only where a partition needs
it).

### Grouped by a fact column, the keys united (2026-10-11)

`SELECT f.c20, count(*) FROM fact f WHERE f.c200 IN (SELECT id FROM dim200 WHERE region =
'region3') GROUP BY f.c20` over 5M rows counted each of the 29 keys in each of the 20 groups: 580
counts, every one of them reading its key's set again and seeking the group's set at each of its
containers, 871,740 key containers in all, 393 to 600 ms. The same keys given as an array, `=
ANY ((SELECT array_agg(id) ...))`, are an IN list - collected once, every group counted against it
- in 12 ms. Nothing in the rows needed the keys apart: no dimension column is in them, and the
Finalize Agg adds up a group's rows whatever key they came from.

**What is counted.** When the target and the HAVING read no column of a dimension row - none of
its own, nor the fact's join column standing for its key ("Grouped by the join key") - and the
aggregates are counts alone, a batch's keys are united: their sets located once, each letting go of
its pin as soon as it is located, made one union source of a collection with the fact filters - or
their copy - ANDed in (`lion_sources_collect()`), and each group of the fact column counted once
against that copy (`lion_join_unite_keys()`, `lion_join_count_united()`). A group's row then
carries the count of all the batch's keys together, and the Finalize Agg adds up the rows of each
group as before - one per batch and relation now, where it was one per key. EXPLAIN says `Fact
Groups Counted Against: united join keys`, and `Fact Group Counts` is the groups (times the
batches) rather than the keys times the groups.

**Why it is exact.** The union's count in a group is the sum of the keys' counts there because the
keys' fk sets are disjoint: a fact row has one fk value, and the keys are distinct under the
join's equality - an inner join's by the dimension's unique key, the forward semi join's because
they are its distinct keys - which is the fk index's, so no two keys locate one entry. And the copy
is safe on exactly the terms the fact filters' copy is ("Why a stale copy is safe"): it is read
after the query's snapshot was taken, so it misses no row the snapshot sees, and it is only ever
counted beside a group's set, located from the index and pinned as an IN list's is, which carries
the §9 interlock for any dead TID the copy still lists; the dimension rows are read by the child
under the same snapshot as before. A key the same bytes as the one before it in the batch - which
that proof says does not come - is left out of the union and counted key by key, so the rows would
still add up to the join's.

**Bounds and fall-backs.** The keys located at once are what work_mem holds of them
(`lion_array_batch_size()` sets at most, and no more than half of work_mem's worth of
`LionPostingSet`s, so the array of sets leaves room for the sets' copies); past that they are
united a share at a time, each share a copy of its own counted beside every group, which adds up
the same. A share takes one key at least whatever work_mem is left - `lion_array_batch_size()`
alone never falls below 1000 sets, whose array outgrows a work_mem of 96 kB before a key is
located - and the turn checks for interrupts before each. The copies take a hash table's
memory (`get_hash_memory_limit()`) and spill past it as the filters' copy does. A turn that cannot
be united - a hot standby, which makes no copy; a range the counts walk (§32), which is not a set
to collect; a copy that fails - is counted key by key, every key. A partition whose bounds give
the column its value has one group, and its turn counts each key as before. With dimension columns
in the rows, nothing changes: each key is counted in each group.

**Cost.** `lion_cost_fkjoin_path()` prices both ways and takes the cheaper (`*unite`). Per key,
each key is counted once per group, and every count after the first reads the key's set again;
every count also seeks the group's set at the key's containers (`lion_cost_fkjoin_group_counts()`).
Both of those used to be left out - only the count's set-up and its filter probes were multiplied
by the groups - which priced the 580 counts above at 77, against core's 125,094 for 345 ms; they
were chosen, rightly against core, at a twentieth of the time they took. United, the found keys'
sets are read once into the collection (a set's cursor, its containers, the union's image at each
container key, the filters sought at the keys of the sparser side, the survivors copied), and each
group is a count against the copy (`lion_cost_fkjoin_united_counts()`), once a batch. A plan that
unites makes no copy of the fact filters of its own: the union is ANDed with the filters as it is
made.

Measured (2026-10-11, 5M rows, `max_parallel_workers_per_gather` 2, `work_mem` 64MB, best of 3):

| query | before | after | core |
|---|---|---|---|
| `c20`, `c200 IN (29 keys of a region)` | 438 ms, 580 counts | 14 ms, 20 counts | 345 ms |
| the same as an inner join | - | 22 ms | 311 ms |
| ... and `f.c2 = 1` | - | 20 ms | 264 ms |
| `c20`, every key (200) | - | 43 ms | 592 ms |
| `c2`, `d.flag` (half the keys) | - | 15 ms | 503 ms |
| `c20k`, 29 keys (20,000 groups) | - | 209 ms | 412 ms |
| `c20, d.name`, 29 keys (per key, unchanged) | - | 391 ms | 351 ms |

The last row is a per-key plan, chosen and slower than core's: priced at 44,649 against core's
126,053 even with the key sets read again counted, the per-key counts remain underpriced against
core's aggregate on this table, a calibration question this change leaves alone.

`test/sql/fkjoin_unite.sql`: every answer against the pushdown off with sequential scans only - an
inner join grouped by a fact column under a dimension filter, a fact filter, both, HAVING, ORDER BY
and LIMIT; NULL dimension keys alone and among others; keys without fact rows; an empty dimension
result and a fact filter that selects nothing, each a value the planner does not see; a dimension
that selects every key, joined and as an IN; the forward semi join over a non-unique key - duplicated
and NULL keys, one key three times, an EXISTS; a dimension column and the fact's join key in the
rows, counted key by key; the counters (`Fact Group Counts` the groups, against the keys times the
groups per key); batches at a work_mem of 64 kB; a correlated subquery that rescans the node; and a
dirty heap before and after VACUUM. `test/sql/fkjoin_factgroup.sql`'s queries with no dimension
column in the rows - partitioned, parallel, an OR of filters per kind with a range - now unite, with
their answers unchanged.

### The dimension LEFT JOIN the fact (2026-10-11)

`SELECT d.name, count(f.id) FROM dim d LEFT JOIN fact f ON f.fk = d.pk GROUP BY d.name` - the count
of each dimension row's fact rows, a dimension row with none counted 0 - was declined: an outer
join was refused whatever its direction, and the plan was a hash join over the whole fact table
(1,144 ms on the 5M-row synthetic table below, against 18 ms for the inner join through the node).

**What is computed.** The join's rows are an inner join's pairs, and each dimension row with no
pair once more, null-extended. A dimension row `d` with `n = |F(d)|` fact rows under the fact
filters is therefore `max(n, 1)` of the join's rows: `n` holding a fact row, or one holding NULL in
every fact column. The node looks the keys up exactly as for an inner join and hands up every
dimension row with its `n` - a NULL key, a key with no entry, a count of 0 and a fact filter that
selects nothing included, each a row with `n = 0` (`LION_JOINFLAG_LEFT`, which goes with the
counted rows of "Every aggregate over the node's rows" and nothing else). The Agg above aggregates
them as it does counted rows, over `m = GREATEST(n, 1)` where an aggregate counts the join's rows:

| the query's | over the dimension rows | why it is the join's |
|---|---|---|
| `count(*)`, `count(1)` | `lion_join_count(m)` | a dimension row is m of the join's rows |
| `count(f.x)`, x the fact's key or a column declared NOT NULL | `lion_join_count(n)` | x is NULL in the null-extended row, and not NULL in a joined one |
| `count(x)`, x an expression of dimension columns (the dimension's key among them) | `lion_join_count(m) FILTER (WHERE x IS NOT NULL)` | each of the row's m join rows holds its x |
| `sum(x)`, x such an int2 or int4 expression | `lion_join_sum(x * m)` | as for an inner join, over m |
| `count(DISTINCT x)`, `min`, `max` and the others of "Every aggregate over the node's rows", of dimension columns | as they stand | each dimension row is in the join at least once |

A group whose dimension rows have no fact row gets `count(f.x)` 0 from `lion_join_count`'s 0 over
rows of `n = 0`, as the ordinary plan's count of NULLs is; an empty dimension gives no group, or 0
and NULL without a GROUP BY. A NOT NULL fact column is the planner's `notnullattnums`, which leaves
out a constraint that is not valid. An inner join counts such a column as `count(*)` now too
(`lion_fkjoin_agg_is_count()`), which `WHERE f.x = 3` over a LEFT JOIN - strict, so core makes it
an inner join - needs.

**What is taken.** Recognising it (`lion_fkjoin_recognize()`) takes one LEFT JOIN as the only
special join of the query, its outer side one dimension table and its nullable side the fact, both
minimal and syntactic, its own relid the join rel's third member; the RIGHT JOIN spelling is the
same join. The dimension's key is proved unique as for an inner join, the same scope guard. The join
clause is the one clause between the two, and it has to be every join clause either table has:

- a condition of the ON clause on the fact alone is pushed down to the fact's scan by core, where
  it is a fact filter like any other - it decides which fact rows match, which is what the count
  is of;
- a condition of the ON clause on the dimension alone decides which dimension rows are
  null-extended, and stays a join clause, which declines;
- a WHERE condition on the fact that is strict makes the join an inner join before the hook runs;
  one that is not (`f.y IS NULL`, `coalesce(f.x, 0) = 0`) is evaluated above the join over the
  null-extended rows too, and is a join clause of the fact that needs the outer join's relid -
  which a pair's clauses do not include, so the join clauses are checked whole, and it declines.

The aggregates over a fact column are the counts above; `count` of a nullable fact column, `sum` or
`min` of one, a DISTINCT of the fact's key, a GROUP BY of a fact column and a key pinned to a
constant (core then joins the two on no clause at all) decline. The partitioned fact, parallel
plans, batches and the walk in key order are the inner join's.

**Cost.** The inner join's counted rows (`lion_add_fkjoin_paths()`), every child row a row: the
same lookups, and `LION_FKJOIN_ROW_COST` per dimension row rather than per one that joins.

Measured (2026-10-11, 5M rows, a 220-row dimension of which 20 keys have no fact row, `work_mem`
64MB, best of 5): `d.name, count(f.id) ... GROUP BY d.name` 1,144 ms to 16 ms; `d.region,
count(*)` 888 ms to 18 ms; with `AND f.c20 = 3` in the ON clause 168 ms to 106 ms.

`test/sql/fkjoin_left.sql`: every answer against the pushdown off with sequential scans only -
counts of the join's rows, of the fact's key and its NOT NULL id, of dimension columns, sums, min,
max, `bool_or` and a DISTINCT over a 400-row dimension with NULL keys and 100 keys past the fact's
range; grouped by a dimension column, by the key (the NULL keys one group), and not at all, folded
to constants, empty; fact filters in the ON clause, one that selects nothing at run time, a
subquery's; a dimension filter; HAVING `count(f.id) = 0`, ORDER BY and LIMIT; the RIGHT JOIN
spelling; the declines; the counters; batches at 64 kB; a rescan; a parallel plan; a partitioned
fact; and a dirty heap on both sides before and after VACUUM.

### A second dimension that only filters (2026-10-11)

`SELECT d.region, count(*) FROM fact f JOIN dim d ON f.fk = d.pk JOIN e ON f.e_id = e.id WHERE
e.flag GROUP BY d.region` - a fact counted per dimension row, a second table joined to it only to
filter its rows - was declined: three tables with no special join are an inner join inside the
dimension ("A dimension that is a join"), and the plan was core's hash joins over the whole fact
table.

**What is computed.** A table `X` inner-joined to the fact `F` by `F.x = X.k` alone, `X.k` unique
under the join operator, and nothing of `X` wanted above the join. Each fact row has one `x`, and
each value of it at most one row of `X`, so the join with `X` keeps the fact rows whose `x` is the
key of one of `X`'s rows that pass `X`'s own filters, each once, and adds nothing the rest of the
query reads. It is a fact filter:

    F.x = ANY (K),    K = { X.k of the rows of X under its filters, X.k NOT NULL }

the operator strict, so a NULL key joins no fact row and a NULL `F.x` none of the keys. The query
left is the join of `F` with the rest of its tables, with one more fact filter, which the node
answers as it answers any: the keys of the remaining dimension looked up under the fact filters,
the IN list among them.

**Recognition** (`lion_fkjoin_filter_of()`, for each table of the join tried as the fact):

- `X` is a plain table or a materialized view (not a partitioned or inheritance parent), in no
  special join - no semi or anti join's side and no outer join's - so that it is inner-joined;
- no column of `X` is in the join rel's target, which holds every column the query reads above
  the join (target list, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY): `X`'s columns are read by its own filters and
  the join clause alone;
- exactly one clause joins `X` to the rest of the join - the equivalence classes' clauses between
  `X` and every other table, and `X`'s joininfo clauses within the join - and it is the clause the
  pair `(F, X)` gives (same class, or the same joininfo clause). A table also joined to the
  dimension, by a second clause, or by a condition over it and the fact together (`e.flag OR f.x =
  1`), is not only a filter;
- that clause is a strict operator between a plain column of each, and `X.k` is unique under it
  (`lion_column_is_unique()`, as a dimension's key is proved);
- `X`'s cheapest path is unparameterized and carries the key, the key's type has an array type,
  and the rows the path is expected to return are no more than a count locates of one IN list at
  once (`lion_array_batch_size()`: a work_mem of 256-byte located sets, never fewer than a
  thousand), since the node holds the list's sets whole where the ordinary plan would hash `X`'s
  keys within its memory.

`lion_fkjoin_recognize()` folds every table that qualifies; the tables left are the dimension, taken
apart as ever (`lion_fkjoin_try_fact()`). When every table but the fact qualifies, each is tried as
the dimension with the others folded, and the cost model chooses - an ungrouped count with a filter
on each of two dimensions is either one's count against the other folded. Folded tables go only
with an inner join of the fact and the dimension (a LEFT JOIN, a semi or an anti join with the
dimension declines), at most `LION_MAX_JOIN_FILTERS` (8) of them.

**Execution.** Each folded table is a child of the node's, `custom_plans[1 + i]`, core's cheapest
path of `X`. Its clause is an ARRAY clause of the fact filters like any IN list - the lion index on
`F.x` matched for it by the join operator, a cross-type one (`int4` against `int8`) included - whose
value the node makes at the start of each run (`lion_eval_clause_values()`,
`lion_join_filter_values()`): the child is run whole, in the query's memory as every node is (its
scan descriptor outlives the values' context), the key read from its column of each row, NULLs left
out, the keys accumulated into an array in the values' context (past the cap, a tuplestore: "Past
the cap" below). From there it is an IN list among
the fact filters: located, collected into the copy or probed, counted. A rescan rescans the children
and collects the keys again, so a filter of `X`'s on an outer query's column is applied per outer
row. The clause's expression in `custom_exprs` is a NULL constant of the key's type that nothing
evaluates: a Param there would need an initplan to set it (`SS_finalize_plan()`). EXPLAIN prints it
among the `Lion Indexes` as `x = X.k`, deparsed from the child's column, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE counts
the keys collected (`Join Filter Keys`). The join operator's function is checked at executor startup
as the key's is (`lion_replaced_functions()`).

`custom_private`'s join member grows (shape 23) a `(clause, column)` pair a folded table, the
column its attnum at the PATH stage and its position in the child's target list at the PLAN stage
(`lion_plan_fkjoin_path()`, `lion_child_resno()`); the decoder checks the clause is in range, not
the key's own, and an ARRAY clause, and the plan check that there is a child each and that the join
is an inner one with none of the distinct-key, outer, LEFT or parallel flags.

**Cost.** The children run whole before the first key: their total cost is added to the node's
startup and total. The IN list is priced through a cost clause (`lion_fkjoin_filter_costclause()`):
`F.x = ANY (<n NULLs>)`, `n` the child's estimated rows, which `estimate_array_length()` counts, in a
RestrictInfo of the fact alone whose cached selectivity - `clause_selectivity()` returns it without
reading the array - is `n / max(nd(F.x), X's rows)`: each key one value of `F.x` with as many fact
rows as any other, and where `F.x` has values no key has, the keys' share of those. The same share
multiplies the fact filters' selectivity in the fact-side model (`lion_fkjoin_filters_sel()`), which
the fact rel's own estimate does not include. The uniform fk is an assumption: keys chosen by `X`'s
filters that hold most of the fact's rows make the plan cheaper than priced, never wrong.

**Not taken**, as yet: parallel plans (a participant would run each folded table whole; with one
the node is offered serial only).

**Past the cap.** The cap is the planner's estimate, which can be wrong by any factor. A folded
table that returns more keys than `lion_array_batch_size()` puts them in a tuplestore instead of the
array (`LionClauseState.valstore`), which keeps work_mem of them and spills the rest to a temporary
file, and the IN list is collected from it a batch of keys at a time into one set, as a parameter's
long list is (§15, "A list too long to locate at once"; `lion_locate_list()`): in each leaf of a
partitioned fact, and again at each rescan, the store ended before the values' context is reset
(`lion_clause_values_free()`). A table of a million flagged keys whose statistics said none were,
at work_mem 4MB on the assert build: 17 MB of the backend's own memory at the peak, in 2.3 s, where
the whole list in one array held some 287 MB in about the same time.

Measured (2026-10-11, 5M fact rows, a 220-row dimension of 10 groups, a 1,000-row filter table of
which a third is flagged, best of 5, PostgreSQL's own plan with its parallel workers): the flagged
rows' `GROUP BY` 776 ms to 54 ms; a filter leaving 19 keys 343 ms to 51 ms; one leaving 899 keys
1,294 ms to 131 ms.

`test/sql/fkjoin_star.sql`: every answer against the pushdown off with sequential scans only, over a
fact with NULL fks and a 400-row dimension with NULL keys and keys past the fact's range, and a
folded table with NULL keys and fact values it has no row for - grouped
by dimension columns and by its key, the folded table's own filters applied and none; two folded,
one compared across types (`int4` against an `int8` primary key); the fact's own filters beside
them; no GROUP BY, with every other table only filtering; the IN spelling; a folded table no row
of which passes its filter; HAVING, ORDER BY and LIMIT; the declines (a column of it grouped by or
counted, a non-unique key, a clause to the dimension or a second one to the fact, a condition over
it and the fact, an outer join of it and beside it, more keys than one list locates at 64 kB); the
`Join Filter Keys` counter; batches at 64 kB; a correlated subquery that rescans the node with a
new filter of the folded table's; parallel settings; a partitioned fact; and a dirty heap without
VACUUM - deletes and updates in the fact, the dimension and the folded table, whose rows move in
and out of its filter, and new rows with NULL and new keys. `node_contracts.sql` and
`exec_hook.sql` check the folded join's operator, `int48eq`, refused as the ordinary plan refuses it.

### The anti join over a small inner side (2026-10-20)

    SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE <clauses the count answers on t>
      AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM s WHERE s.a = t.k AND <filters on s>)

counts t's rows WITHOUT a qualifying inner row: a complement of the forward semi join's union,
which no count per key gives, and core's plan is an anti join over the whole of t. Where the inner
side is a few rows, the complement is cheap the other way round: count t's WHERE as the count
pushdown counts any, and take away the rows of it that some inner row matches, which a B-tree on
`t.k` finds a key at a time.

**What is computed.**

    count = C - |M|
    C = { rows of t visible under the snapshot that pass W }          (the count of W, §9)
    M = { r in C : some row of the inner side passes every join clause with r }

`W` is t's own restrictions (and, for `count(col)`, the `col IS NOT NULL` the count adds to them).
The node runs the inner side as its child, once. Each child row's scan keys - the values of the
inner expressions of the join clauses a B-tree on t looks up by - are evaluated; a row with a NULL
key matches nothing (every key is a strict operator) and is skipped; the rest go into a sort by
their keys in the B-tree's order ("One lookup a key" below; "The anti join within work_mem"), with -
where a join clause other than the keys' needs them - the inner columns the clauses read. Each key
is then looked up once in the B-tree under the query's snapshot, and every row found is tested on
`W`, and if it passes, on the join clauses with each inner row of its key in turn - the scan keys'
own hold of every row their lookup finds, and the others are tested; a row that passes is in M. A
key's inner rows alike in every column (by their bytes, `datum_image_eq()`) that the sort puts one
after another are kept once. With two clauses on the same column (`s.a = t.k AND s.b = t.k`) both
are scan keys of it: the B-tree's preprocessing makes an inner row whose `a` and `b` differ an empty
scan, and the clauses are tested on what is found anyway. Clauses that are not keys - `s.b <> t.g`,
a clause of t alone inside the NOT EXISTS, which belongs to the join - are tested the same way.

**The order the clauses are tested in.** Core's plan tests t's restrictions in its scan of t, and
the join clauses only on the rows the scan gives the join, the hash or index clauses first and the
others after them; each list cheapest first (`order_qual_clauses()`: by security level, then by the
cost of one test, in their written order where those agree). So does the node
(`lion_anti_order_quals()`, `lion_anti_join_clauses()`): W, in that order, on each row found, and
only on a row that passes it the join clauses, the scan keys' own first - true of every row their
lookup finds - and the others in that order. A clause core runs only on rows a cheaper one has kept
is not run here on a row that one rejects: `count(*) FROM t WHERE y <> 0 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
FROM s WHERE s.a = t.k AND s.b / t.y > 1)` divides by no zero `y`, nor does a WHERE of `10 / y > 1
AND x = 3` on a row whose `x` is not 3, where core's plan answers. Beside a count by cells the
predicates' truths are evaluated first (below): tests of a column against constants, which a lion
index answers and which fail on no row.

**Forms.** `count(*)`, `count(1)`, `count(col)` where the count answers it (a column declared NOT
NULL, or the `IS NOT NULL` clause it adds, which the subtraction tests too: a row with a NULL `col`
is in neither C nor M), a `count(DISTINCT col)` of a column proved unique (§26, "A unique column",
which is that `count(col)`), and a GROUP BY of one or two of t's columns that LionCount groups by
(§10, §20), with a HAVING, or folded by the planner to one group; and a count by cells (§10,
"Counts by cells"), a GROUP BY of expressions over predicates or a WHERE over them, whose cells
lose the rows found ("Counts by cells beside the anti join" below). Not: the decoded walk of a
GROUP BY's columns (§34), a `count(DISTINCT)` walked, filtered counts, the aggregates over keys
(§37), the top k (§36), a coalesce group, expression columns (§41), a partitioned or inheritance
parent - each counts in a way the subtraction would have to follow, and none is needed by the query
this is for.

**Recognition** (`lion_fkjoin_recognize_small_anti()`, from the join rel `create_upper_paths_hook`
is given at `UPPERREL_GROUP_AGG`, where §27's joins are recognised):

- a sublink anti join - NOT EXISTS pulled up by core, its RTE_JOIN not in the FROM list - whose
  outer side is exactly one table t and whose two sides make the whole join rel; any other special
  join lies inside the inner side; no PlaceHolderVars, pseudoconstant quals or LATERAL references;
- t a plain table or a materialized view as the fact of §27 is asked to be
  (`lion_fkjoin_rel_ok()`), not a parent; the inner tables base relations with no TABLESAMPLE
  (`lion_fkjoin_member_ok()`); the inner rel - one table, or the join rel of several - has a
  cheapest path that is not parameterized;
- the join clauses: the equivalence-class clauses between the two sides and t's joininfo clauses
  within the join rel, each non-volatile, with no SubPlan, aggregate, window function or set-returning
  function, over plain columns - t's, and the inner side's that its rel's target carries;
- at least one of them a strict binary operator between a plain column of t and an expression of
  the inner side alone: the keys.

`LEFT JOIN s ON s.a = t.k WHERE s.a IS NULL`, which core makes an anti join of, keeps its `IS NULL`
quals above the join, and is not a sublink anti join: it is left alone, as not free and asked for by
nothing. `t.k NOT IN (SELECT s.a ...)` is a hashed SubPlan on 16 to 18, which the node never sees.
19 makes an anti join of it where it proves that neither `t.k` nor `s.a` can be NULL (a NOT NULL
column, or a strict qual on it) and its operator is a B-tree's or a hash index's, which gives no
NULL for values that are not: then NOT IN and NOT EXISTS are the same join, a sublink anti join with
its own join entry, and the node takes it as it takes the NOT EXISTS - its answer is core's. A NOT
IN over a side that may be NULL stays a SubPlan there too.

**The B-tree** (`lion_anti_choose()`, lion_plan_anti.c): a B-tree of t's own that has
`amgettuple`, not hypothetical, whole or partial with a predicate t's restrictions imply (`predOK`:
a row outside it fails `W`, and is in neither C nor M), with an equality scan key on its first
column at least. A key is a scan key of index column c when the column is the key's t column, the
operator - commuted when t's column is its right operand - is the equality of c's operator family
with c's opclass type on the left, and its collation is the index's (or the index has none). The
scan keys cover a prefix of the columns, each with every key that is one of its; the B-tree that
covers the most columns is taken, and of those the smallest. None, and the query is core's. A key is
the scan key of the first column it is one of, and of no other: of a B-tree that names t's column
twice, the second's would be the same equality on the same value and narrow nothing. So each scan
key is a join clause of its own, and the join clauses the node tests lead with each once
(`lion_anti_join_clauses()`); the prefix searched by ends before the second, unless another key is
one of its, and a key of a column after it is a join clause tested on the rows found.

**One lookup a key.** The keys are sorted by the `<` of their B-tree column's operator family for
two values of the key's type (strategy 1 of the family for the operator's right type on both sides;
a family without one leaves the query to core), under the key's collation: they come in the
index's order, and keys equal under the family - numeric's `1.0` and `1.00`, strings a
nondeterministic collation makes equal - one after another, looked up once. Keys the sort keeps
apart are unequal under the family, whose operators are transitive across its types, as a B-tree
family's must be: a row found by the lookups of two of them would make them equal. So the lookups
find disjoint rows, and no row of M is found twice.

**Why the subtraction is exact.** The count and the lookups are made under one snapshot S,
`es_snapshot`:

- C is the count of W under S (§9: the interlock makes every count exact under the snapshot the
  query runs with, the visibility of each candidate row decided by S).
- An MVCC index scan returns, for one scan key, each row version visible under S whose key equals it
  once: a heap-only tuple through its chain's root entry, a version an index entry points at
  directly through that entry, and nothing for the entries of versions S does not see. Every
  version has an entry under its own key (or, heap-only, its root has one under the same key), so a
  row visible under S with `t.k = v` is found by the lookup of `v`.
- Every row found is tested on W on the version S sees: a row in M passes W and is visible under
  S, so `M ⊆ C`, and no row is subtracted that the count did not count. Every row of C with a
  matching inner row has a key equal under the join's operator to that row's, which is not NULL
  (the operators are strict), and the lookup of that value finds it: M is complete.
- Distinct lookups find disjoint rows: the keys the sort keeps apart are unequal under the B-tree's
  family ("One lookup a key"), so each row of M is found, and subtracted, once.
- The inner side is core's plan under S, as the ordinary anti join's is: the same inner rows.

So the count is `|{ r ∈ C : no inner row matches r }|`, which is what core's plan counts. §11's
rule - lion's VACUUM leaves a posting set's TIDs alone while a scan may need them - is about lion's
own sets, which C reads under it; the B-tree is core's, and core's VACUUM removes an entry only once
its version is dead to every snapshot, S among them. Each structure is exact under S on its own, so
nothing ties the two together. Rows the query's own transaction changed are seen as S's command id
says, by both.

**Execution** (lion_exec_anti.c). The run is made once, at the start of the first row's call, after
the clause values are evaluated and before the count locates anything, so that no lion pin is held
while the child runs. Reading the child, looking the keys up (the B-tree opened then, under
`AccessShareLock`, and checked to be a B-tree of t whose key columns the scan keys name), testing
each row found in a slot of the node's scan tuple - t's columns read from the heap tuple, W tested
over them, and on a row that passes each inner row's beside them in turn, the join clauses tested
over the two - and adding it to the subtraction: one total for an ungrouped count, or, for a GROUP
BY, each row's group (its grouping columns read from the heap tuple, hashed and compared with the
grouping's own equality and hash function, under its collation), or, beside a count by cells, the
row's cell (below); none of it held in memory past `work_mem` or `hash_mem` ("The anti join within
work_mem"). `lion_emit_keys()` takes each row's subtraction off its count: a group left with none is
no row, as a group with no rows to start with is not, and so is the one group of a GROUP BY the
planner folded; a plain count's one row stays a row, of 0. A subtraction larger than the count is an
error in a serial plan, which the argument above rules out. A rescan makes the run again: the child
is rescanned with the changed parameters core does not hand to `custom_ps`, and a parameter of t's
WHERE or of the inner side's filters is the new one's.

**Parallel.** The ungrouped count, offered as §10's parallel count: the participants divide the
count, and the participant that comes to the run first (an atomic flag in the node's shared memory,
`antiowner`) makes it - runs the child, looks the keys up, and takes the whole subtraction off its
partial count; the others take nothing off theirs, and the Finalize Aggregate adds them up. A partial
count may go below zero. The child is the inner side's cheapest path a worker may run, unparameterized
and not partial (the serial node's cheapest may be a Gather). Without a shared memory (none could be
made) the participant subtracts. A rescan of the Gather clears the flag. EXPLAIN ANALYZE's counters
are every participant's, summed. A parallel count by cells subtracts in every participant (below).
A GROUP BY of columns stays serial.

**Cost.**

    the count's price (converted, §39)
      + lion_units_price(the lookups)          (converted, as the node's own work)
      + the child's total cost                 (core's plan, in core's units, as a dimension's)

all of it before the first row. The lookups are priced as core prices an index scan repeated once
per outer row of a nested loop (`cost_index()`, `btcostestimate()`): `lookups` = the inner key
expressions' distinct values (`estimate_num_groups()`) over the child's rows, no more than the rows;
each finds t's rows over the distinct values of its key columns in the whole table
(`lion_anti_key_values()`) - a lookup finds every row of its key, and the restrictions are tested
after, where `estimate_num_groups()` would scale the values down to the rows the WHERE leaves: an
n-distinct extended statistics object's count of as many of the key columns together as one has
(the most, and of those the object of the fewest columns, as `estimate_num_groups()` picks one),
times each other column's `n_distinct` as `lion_fkjoin_fk_ndistinct()` takes it. The product of
the columns' own takes them as independent: over 3M rows whose two key columns make 1,000 pairs,
it makes a lookup of a pair a share of a row where it finds 3,000, and takes the node over core's
hash anti join at a third of its speed (334 ms against 122); with `CREATE STATISTICS (ndistinct)` on
the pair, core's plan is taken. A descent costs `ceil(log2(index tuples)) * cpu_operator_cost` and
`(height + 1) * 50 * cpu_operator_cost`; each index tuple read `cpu_index_tuple_cost` and a
`cpu_operator_cost` per scan key; the index pages over every lookup by `index_pages_fetched()` at
the random page cost; the heap a read for each row found (no order) or for each page of a lookup's
share of the table's pages (the index's order), as far between the two as the correlation squared
puts them, each read at the price of a page of the pages the reads come to, as many as
`index_pages_fetched()` makes them (`lion_anti_heap_page_cost()`: from `random_page_cost` towards
`seq_page_cost` as the table's share of `effective_cache_size` holds them, not by density, since
the lookups read the pages in the key's order). A read is a buffer looked up, pinned and locked
whether or not another lookup read the page before, and that, on a table the cache holds, is the
lookups' time; core's index scan, whose model this was, charges the distinct pages at the random
page cost and none of the reads again, which over the table below priced 10,000 lookups at 4.2
times their time and 100,000 at about once, `index_pages_fetched()` by then at every page of the
table. Each row found a `cpu_tuple_cost` and the clauses it is tested on; a `cpu_operator_cost` a
row for each grouping column; and each child row's keys evaluated, and the child's rows sorted by
them as `cost_sort()` prices a sort (`lion_anti_sort_price()`, after costsize.c's
`cost_tuplesort()`): of the keys' width, and the child row's where a join clause other than the
keys' reads it, with the pages written and read back past `work_mem`. A large inner side is many
descents and many rows, which the ordinary plan's one pass over t undercuts: the cost model, nothing
else, leaves it to core. On PostgreSQL 18 the path carries the child's disabled nodes.

**The plan.** `custom_private` grows (shape 29) an `ANTI` member, 24, after the cells' (§10): the
B-tree, its scan keys' columns, operators, collations and the `<` they are sorted by, the number of
keys, join clauses and restrictions, and the grouping columns' equalities, collations and a `<` of
each equality's family; at the PATH stage also the expressions - the keys' inner values, the join
clauses and the restrictions - which `lion_plan_custom_path()` appends to `custom_exprs` after the
residual clauses, where setrefs.c points their columns at `custom_scan_tlist`: t's as a residual
clause's are (`LION_TL_RESID`), the inner side's as `LION_TL_ANTI` entries naming their place in the
child's target list. The plan check requires its one child and refuses it beside the FK-side join,
partitions, the decoded walk of a GROUP BY's columns, a parallel GROUP BY other than a count by
cells' (below) and the other forms above. EXPLAIN prints, under the node's indexes:

    Join Type: Anti
    Join Rows: the rows counted, less those with a match
    Join Lookup Index: t_k_idx
    Join Cond: (s.a = k)

the join clauses deparsed as core prints a join's (t's columns bare, as in a `Residual Filter`), and
under ANALYZE `Join Child Rows`, `Join Keys Looked Up` (distinct keys, NULL ones not), `Join Rows
Fetched` and `Join Rows Subtracted`, with `Join Child Time` and `Join Lookup Time` under TIMING, and
`Join Spilled` where some of the run went past its memory ("The anti join within work_mem"). The
child is printed under the node. `pg_lion.enable_count_anti` turns it off.

**Beside the FK-side anti join.** A reverse anti join - `SELECT count(*) FROM dim d WHERE NOT EXISTS
(SELECT 1 FROM fact f WHERE f.fk = d.pk ...)` - is both §27's anti join, the dimension's rows
tested against the fact's posting sets, and this one, with the fact's rows as the inner side and the
dimension's primary key as the B-tree; the cost model chooses. The suites of the FK-side join that
pin its plans turn this one off.

Measured (2026-10-20, PostgreSQL 18, a synthetic table of 3M rows of some 240 bytes - 710 MB - whose
key has 1M values of three rows each scattered over the heap, a B-tree on the key and a lion index
on the WHERE's column; warm, best of 7 runs - of 5 for the larger inner sides - on a machine other
work kept busy; core's plan a parallel hash anti join with up to two workers):

| WHERE | inner keys | LionCount | core's plan | the model's choice |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a half | 2 | 15 ms | 181 ms | LionCount, parallel |
| a half | 2,000 | 26 ms | 172 ms | LionCount, parallel |
| a twentieth | 2 | 2.4 ms | 137 ms | LionCount |
| a twentieth | 2,000 | 12 ms | 139 ms | LionCount |
| a half | 20,000 | 149 ms | 240 ms | core |
| a twentieth | 20,000 | 128 ms | 152 ms | core |
| a half | 200,000 | 1,463 ms | 391 ms | core |
| a twentieth | 200,000 | 1,215 ms | 184 ms | core |

LionCount's times in the last four rows are with core's joins turned off. The model left the inner
side to core somewhere between 2,000 and 20,000 keys, where the node was still faster on a warm
cache, its heap fetches priced at the random page cost as core prices its own index scans' pages:
at a third of the keys where the two plans' times cross. Priced by the read (2026-10-23, a release
build, PostgreSQL 20devel, the same shape at 3M rows in 40,000 pages, `shared_buffers` 512 MB,
serial plans, medians of five warm runs):

| WHERE | inner keys | LionCount | core's plan | the model's choice, before | now |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a tenth | 2,000 | 10 ms | 115 ms | LionCount | LionCount |
| a tenth | 5,000 | 30 ms | 117 ms | LionCount | LionCount |
| a tenth | 10,000 | 54-56 ms | 111-139 ms | core | LionCount |
| a tenth | 20,000 | 101-108 ms | 128-150 ms | core | LionCount |
| a tenth | 50,000 | 259 ms | 145-166 ms | core | core |
| a tenth | 100,000 | 495 ms | 171-191 ms | core | core |
| a half | 10,000 | 49-72 ms | 399-414 ms | LionCount | LionCount |
| a half | 20,000 | 107-122 ms | 413-453 ms | LionCount | LionCount |
| a half | 50,000 | 277-291 ms | 495-718 ms | core | core |

The node's price is now 1.4 to 1.8 times its warm time at every size, against core's hash anti
join, whose price grows with the table where the lookups' does not: the conservative side of the
crossing, which a table of 50M rows moves further out. The last row is a hash join of a half of
the table priced at the hash join's rate (§39), below its time.

### Counts by cells beside the anti join (2026-10-21)

    SELECT CASE WHEN <score over predicates on t> >= 5 THEN 'high' ... END AS tier, count(*)
      FROM t WHERE <clauses> AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM s WHERE s.a = t.k ...)
     GROUP BY tier

is a count by cells (§10, "Counts by cells") of t's WHERE less the rows of it some row of s
matches - and so is the WHERE form, `count(*)` of the rows whose tier is one. The rows of a group
are the rows of the cells the group's expression maps to, so the anti join takes each row it finds
from its CELL, and core's Finalize Aggregate adds up what is left.

**What is computed.** With C and M as above, and `cell(r)` the cell of row r - the outcome of each
dimension its value or keys are in:

    count(c) = |{ r ∈ C : cell(r) = c }| - |{ r ∈ M : cell(r) = c }|

The count by cells makes the first term, as ever; the lookups find M, as for any count, and each
row of M is counted under its cell.

**A row's cell** (`lion_cells_code_of()`, lion_exec_cells.c). Each predicate - the expression of its
`LION_TL_CELLPRED` column of custom_scan_tlist - is evaluated on the heap tuple of a row of M
(`lion_anti_cells_truths()`), NULL a truth of its own: the truths that, in the count, the labels
