### Held out

The rates were fitted on the matrix's own 39 queries, whose choices barely depend on them (above).
`bench/calib/heldout.sql` and `heldout.py` are 41 queries the model was never fitted to, on a
different schema: 3M rows with 10% dirtied, a column of geometric skew, 24 runs of uneven length
in heap order, a 30% NULL column, 300 text tags, and dimensions of 64, 300,000 and 1.5M keys. A
release build of PostgreSQL 18, five repetitions, the margin at 1; a mispick is a chosen plan 15%
and 0.05 ms slower than the fastest of the matrix's arms.

```sh
python3 bench/calib/matrix.py --setup-only --rows 3000000 --dirty 10 --setup-file bench/calib/heldout.sql
python3 bench/calib/matrix.py --queries bench/calib/heldout.py --sweep pg_lion.pushdown_margin=1 \
    --repeats 5 --label default --out ho_default.json
```

| rates | calibration set (39): mispicks, time lost | held out (41): mispicks, time lost | held-out plans changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| hash aggregate 0.42, hash join 0.5, nested loop 2 | 3, 81 ms of 514 | 10, 509 ms of 4,549 | |
| all three at 1 | 3, 76 ms of 539 | 13, 1,182 ms of 5,254 | 9 |
| only `hashagg_rate` at 1 | | 13, 1,188 ms | 8 GROUP BYs |
| only `hashjoin_rate` at 1 | | 10, 562 ms | 1, `h.fk.semi.d10` |
| only the nested loop's at 1 | | 10, 557 ms | none |

Differences of about 50 ms in time lost with no plan changed are the fastest arm's noise.

- `hashagg_rate` carries most of the layer: at 1, six GROUP BYs over the whole table go to a hash
  aggregate 1.0 to 2.4 times slower (`h.group.c5` 261 ms to 461, `h.group.c50.c5` 197 to 476).
  The calibration set cannot show it: none of its GROUP BYs sits near the boundary.
- `hashjoin_rate` decides two near ties, `fk.status.kind` in the calibration set and
  `h.fk.semi.d10`. Timed seven times each on their own, the node is the faster in both (47 ms
  against 58; 52 against 73), though one matrix run had the hash join ahead in the second. It stays.
- The nested loop's rate moved nothing, and is gone.

What the held-out set found that no constant rate can fix: two GROUP BYs under a selective WHERE
(`h.group.tag.w.c50`, `h.group.c1k.w.geo`) where the node, chosen at any of these rates, takes 148
and 256 ms against a hash aggregate's 46 and 85.

### A hashed aggregate's own rate

Those two lost to one rate for every plan with a hash aggregate. Over `WHERE c50 = 9` (60,000 rows
by an index scan) core's HashAggregate costs 60,997 and runs in 49 ms warm, 1,245 units a
millisecond: its cost is the scan's, which runs near or above the reference, and its hashing is 314
of it. At 0.42 the node's own 76,157 came to 31,986 and won; it takes 150 ms.

So `pg_lion.hashagg_rate` is now the rate of the hashing alone - each hashed aggregate's cost less
its input's - and the rest of the plan is taken at the reference
(`lion_hashagg_plan_rate()`):

    rate = total / ((total - hashing) + hashing / hashagg_rate)

Fitted on the calibration matrix alone, its four whole-table GROUP BYs over a sequential scan
(their time less the scan's cost at 500 units a millisecond, over the aggregate's own cost):
0.106, 0.087, 0.116 and 0.110 for `c20`, `c200`, `c20, c2` and `c200, c20`; 0.1. A whole-table
GROUP BY comes to 0.35 to 0.43 as before, the two above to 0.96 and 0.88.

| | calibration set (39): mispicks, time lost | held out (41): mispicks, time lost |
|---|---|---|
| 0.42 for the whole plan | 3, 81 ms of 514 | 10, 509 ms of 4,549 |
| 0.1 for the hashing | 4, 93 ms of 560 | 9, 311 ms of 4,432 |

The plans that changed are the two above, now the hash aggregate (148 ms to 55, 256 to 127), and
`fk.status.kind` and `h.fk.semi.d10`, the hash join's near ties, which moved with the run's noise
and not with this rate: neither has a hashed aggregate over a scan. No GROUP BY of either set moved
to a slower plan.

What it gives back, in the regression suite: three small GROUP BYs. A whole-table one over a dirty
heap of wide rows (`pushdown.sql`) is a tie on the release build, 14.8 ms against 15.6, and goes to
the hash aggregate. A prepared top-k with its LIMIT a parameter (`topk.sql`) goes the other way, to
the node. And a GROUP BY under `d @@ ANY (...)` over 4,000 rows (`positions.sql`) goes to the hash
aggregate at 4.5 ms against the node's 2.4 (assert build): its input is a sequential scan whose `@@`
core charges one `cpu_operator_cost` a row, far below its time, and only the hashing is now priced
below its time. That error is the filter's cost, not the aggregate's.

### A nested loop's cold reads (2026-10-09)

A nested loop into a parameterized index scan is priced by core at `random_page_cost` for each page
`index_pages_fetched()` says its probes fetch. On a private workload that price was right warm and
far off cold: a semi join probing a table several times `effective_cache_size` was a little faster
than the FK-side join warm and orders of magnitude slower cold, and the two were priced alike. A cold
page costs a probe a synchronous read - nothing reads ahead of a parameterized scan - which is
tens of times what `random_page_cost` stands for, set low as it is for an SSD.

So against a nested loop whose inner side is one parameterized index scan, under a Material, a
projection or a Memoize (`lion_nestloop_cold()`, lion_plan_units.c):

- **its cold reads** are the pages core counts it fetching, a leaf a probe and the heap pages of the
  rows a probe fetches (`index_pages_fetched()` over the loops, as core counts them; over a
  Memoize's misses where one sits over the inner scan), in the share the cache cannot hold: one
  less the residency `lion_index_page_cost()` argues from, `effective_cache_size` over the query's
  tables and the index. Each is charged `pg_lion.cold_page_cost`, 50 `seq_page_cost` (100 us at
  the reference: a local SSD's synchronous read with the kernel's share), less the
  `random_page_cost` core charged it. In an upper rel's plan the loop is the one below a semi or
  anti join over it ("The join that reads the dimension", below);
- **the FK-side join's own cold reads** are counted the same way (`lion_cost_fkjoin_path()`'s
  `reads`): the directory leaves and fk sets of its lookups, the fact filters it locates, the heap
  of a recheck;
- **the path is priced with both added** (`lion_units_cold()`): (own x rate + its cold reads) over
  (the loop's cost + the loop's cold reads), of the loop's cost - a factor of the rate, each path
  of the relation with its own reads. The loop's cost is less its outer side where the path reads
  that side as its child at core's price (LionProbeJoin's fact: "The join that reads the
  dimension"). It is at most 1, so a path that reads more than the loop keeps its price, and at
  least 1 / `pg_lion.cold_max_discount`, 2 by default ("The cap" below).

The floor is what this costs warm. With the inner table's working set in the cache the loop runs at
core's price, and a lion path chosen over it can take up to `pg_lion.cold_max_discount` times its
time (2 by default). Nothing changes where the tables and the index fit in `effective_cache_size`,
which every table of the regression suite does but those of the tests that set it lower
(`fkjoin_cold.sql`, `competitor_cold.sql` and others), nor against any other kind of plan. Not
counted: the probes a semi join stops early, which the loop's reads overstate; the count paths
other than the FK-side join's, which compare with the loop at its price.

### A bitmap heap scan's cold reads (2026-10-23)

Core prices a bitmap heap scan's heap pages at `random_page_cost` falling to `seq_page_cost` with
the square root of the share of the table one scan reads (`cost_bitmap_heap_scan()`), as if each
page were cached or a device's cheap random read. On a private workload, over a fact heap almost
four times `effective_cache_size`, a covering walk of a B-tree on the fact's key, index-only over
the lion set (LionOrdered, §40), was priced at about 1.1M units against a parallel bitmap heap
scan's 605k, 1.82 times, and lost; cold it ran in 11.0 s against the scan's 24 s, 2.2 times
faster. The walk's price was right, 10 us a unit; the scan's 605k heap pages, which core charged
some 1.08 units each, took 40 us each, four times the walk's rate. They are not a loop's reads: a
bitmap heap scan asks for its pages ahead of itself (`effective_io_concurrency`), so that the
reads overlap one another and the scan's own work. On the same device a parallel bitmap heap scan
read 1.9M uncached pages at 33 us a page and this one 605k at 40 us, where a nested loop's
synchronous probe paid 270 to 300 us: 0.11 to 0.15 of it.

So against a competitor that reads through bitmap heap scans (`lion_bitmap_cold()`,
lion_plan_units.c), and the same way §39's loop is priced:

- **the competitor** is the cheapest core path of the relation the lion path is added to,
  `lion_competitor_path()`'s, pinned for the hook's paths as before - for a count and the FK-side
  join, `lion_units_for()`'s, where the loop's cold reads are not taken already (both are never
  added); for a base relation's covering walks, which have no rate, `lion_units_scan_cold()`'s, the
  cheaper of that path and the relation's cheapest unparameterized partial path under the Gather
  core puts over it (`parallel_setup_cost` and a `parallel_tuple_cost` a row, as `cost_gather()`
  prices it), taken before the walks are added, since `add_path()` frees what they dominate. A
  plain or parallel bitmap heap scan; an aggregate over one; a hash or merge join with one on
  either side; a nested loop's parameterized inner one, over the loop's outer rows; a Material
  scans its input once, a Memoize once a cache miss, at the hit ratio `cost_memoize_rescan()`
  prices it at (`lion_memoize_misses()`), a subquery's scan is followed into its plan under the
  subquery's own root, and a custom path reads nothing of core's;
- **its cold reads** are each scan's heap pages as `compute_bitmap_pages()` counts them, over the
  loops (`loop_count`, which pro-rates them, times the loops), and each bitmap leaf's index pages,
  its selectivity's share of the index and a page at least, over the loops as
  `index_pages_fetched()` counts them; in the share the cache cannot hold, one less the residency
  `lion_index_page_cost()` argues from - `effective_cache_size` over the query's tables and the
  bitmaps' indexes - each charged `pg_lion.cold_stream_page_cost` less the price core charged it:
  the heap page the scan's `random_page_cost - (random_page_cost - seq_page_cost) x sqrt(pages /
  T)`, the index page `random_page_cost`;
- **the lion path's own reads** are counted at the same per-page charge (`cold_stream_page_cost`
  less the largest scan's `random_page_cost`), since they too are read in an order the device or
  the kernel reads ahead of - posting chains, a B-tree's leaves in order, a recheck's heap through
  a read stream: an index-only covering walk's B-tree pages as its `amcostestimate()` counts them,
  its set's build (each lion leaf's share, as the scan's bitmap) and its heap fetches as priced
  (`lo_cost()`'s `reads`); a count's directory leaves, posting and summed pages and heap rechecks
  as its price counts them (`LionRangeCost.reads`), and the heap pages its residual clauses read,
  each count's candidates in block order as `compute_bitmap_pages()` counts the scan's
  (`lion_residual_pages()`); the FK-side join's as §39 counts them;
- **the path is priced with both added** as against the loop: (own x rate + its cold reads) over
  (the competitor's cost + its cold reads), of the competitor's cost, at most 1 and at least
  1 / `pg_lion.cold_max_discount` - a factor of the rate for a count and the FK-side join
  (`lion_units_bitmap_cold()`), of the walk's own startup and total for a covering walk
  (`lo_cold_price()`). A parallel walk's partial cost is one participant's share where the scan's
  is a whole plan's, so it is priced under the Gather core puts over it - `parallel_setup_cost`
  and a `parallel_tuple_cost` a row, as `lion_units_scan_cold()` adds to the scan's partial path -
  and the Gather's share taken out again (`lo_cold_price_partial()`). The margin divides the
  result as it divides any price.

`pg_lion.cold_stream_page_cost` is 6.25 `seq_page_cost`, an eighth of `cold_page_cost`'s 50: the
middle of the measured 0.11 to 0.15. The device measured is some three times slower than the
reference's local SSD under both kinds of read (270 to 300 us against `cold_page_cost`'s 100); the
ratio is what carries over, and 6.25 is 12.5 us at the reference. 0 turns the charge off.

Which paths: the index-only covering walks, LionOrdered's and LionBtreeScan's, serial and parallel;
the count of one relation, of its WHERE or its groups' sets, with its heap rechecks and residual
clauses; and the FK-side join, where its competitor is a hash join over a bitmap heap scan rather
than a loop. Not a walk in heap mode, which fetches each member's tuple as it meets it, a
synchronous read the stream's price would under-charge, nor §40.10's probes, nor LionProbeJoin
(§46), which reads the fact through core's own path as the competitor's scans of it do and the
dimension a descent at a time; it is priced against a loop's cold reads alone.

**The cap** is `pg_lion.cold_max_discount` (2 by default, 1 to 10), the loop's and the bitmap's
alike. It is the warm floor: where the cache holds what both plans read after all -
`effective_cache_size` set below the real cache, a hot working set - a lion path chosen for those
reads can take up to the cap times its competitor's time. The measured case:

| | the walk | the bitmap heap scan |
|---|---|---|
| priced | 1.1M | 605k |
| ran, cold | 11.0 s | 24 s |
| its pages, uncached | an estimated 95k of the B-tree's | 605k of the heap |
| their cold reads, x 0.74 uncached | 95k x 0.74 x (6.25 - 1.1) = 0.36M | 605k x 0.74 x (6.25 - 1.08) = 2.3M |

The factor, uncapped, is (1.1M + 0.36M) x 605k / ((605k + 2.3M) x 1.1M) = 0.28: the walk at 0.30M
against the scan's 605k. The walk's pages are an estimate, and move it little: none would make it
0.21, three times as many 0.41. The case needs a cap above 1.82 (1.1M / 605k). At 1.5 the walk is
priced at 733k and loses; at 1.82 it ties within `add_path()`'s fuzz; at 2 it is priced at 550k
and wins by 9%; at 2.5, at 440k. The model's own ratio, 2.9M against 1.46M, is 2.0 against the
measured 2.2.

**The default is 2**, Chinmay's choice after the measured cold and warm comparison (1.5 was
proposed, 2 recommended). It is the smallest round cap that takes the measured case with room past
the fuzz, and what it costs is bounded: only where `effective_cache_size` says the tables do not
fit, and there a third more than 1.5's worst case where they do after all - twice the competitor's
time where 1.5 allowed one and a half. A cap past 2 changes nothing in that case, and lets a path
priced 2.5 times core's through on the model's say alone.

Nothing changes where the tables and the indexes fit in `effective_cache_size`, and nothing
against a sequential scan, an index scan or an index-only scan. Not done:

- **A sequential scan's cold reads**: its pages are read ahead in long runs, near `seq_page_cost`
  even cold, and none are charged; a lion path against one keeps its price.
- **Core's plain index scans** read their heap pages synchronously outside a loop too; only the
  loop's are priced (§39 above).
- **A loop with a bitmap heap scan beside it**: a competitor with both kinds of cold reads takes the
  loop's alone.
- **The counts whose prices leave their reads out** - the decoded walk (§34), the top k (§36), the
  aggregates over entries (§37), a partitioned table's, beside an anti join, the cells' - and
  LionSemiJoin and LionAntiJoin, KNN and lion-column walks, keep their price against a cold scan.
- **One residency for every table**: a hot dimension and a cold fact are taken alike, as for the
  loop. A parallel scan's pages are counted whole, as core counts its I/O; several workers
  prefetching overlap more than one does (33 us a page against 40 above), which the one price does
  not see.

Tests: `bitmap_cold.sql`, with a cache of a megabyte as `fkjoin_cold.sql` has: a covering walk
taken over a bitmap heap scan cold and not where the tables fit, with the charge at 0 or the cap at
1; the walk's price over its price against the cold scan exactly the cap where it binds (1.5, 2) and
past 2 uncapped, and a parallel walk's the same under its Gather; the margin dividing the cold price and still a threshold on it; a GROUP BY's count
the same way, over an all-visible heap and with rows added since the VACUUM, which it rechecks; a
count whose residual clause reads more heap pages than the scan, not taken; the
FK-side join against a hash join over the fact's bitmap heap scan; the answers the same under
each plan; and a GROUP BY over a subquery whose plan holds a Memoize, estimated under the
subquery's root. `costrates.sql` lists both settings and their ranges, and `costgucs.sql` lists
`cold_stream_page_cost` among the cost settings.

### A Memoize under a LIMIT (2026-10-23)

Core prices a Memoize over a nested loop's inner scan at one hit ratio for all its calls
(`cost_memoize_rescan()`): of `calls` rescans over `ndistinct` keys, of which the cache holds
`est_entries`, `hr = (calls - ndistinct) / calls x est_entries / ndistinct` hit, each priced at the
lookup alone, and the rest at the inner scan's total cost. Under a LIMIT the planner takes the
loop's startup and the LIMIT's share of its run, and that share counts the hits of the whole walk.
But the loop stops after the share's first calls, which repeat only the keys among themselves. On
§47.9's bench a medium page's walk makes 625,513 calls over 188,097 keys, and core priced 70% of
them as hits; the LIMIT's 3,030 calls hit 0.8% of the time. The loop's price of its first 20 rows
was 2,847, where the same model with those hits is 3,982.

So against a nested loop over a Memoize (under a Material or a projection) in a query with a LIMIT
(`limit_tuples`, which the planner leaves -1 under a grouping, an aggregate or a window), whose
order gives the query at least its first sort key and of whose rows the LIMIT takes a share
`s < 1` (`lion_memoize_limit_extra()`, `lion_memoize_limit_scale()`, lion_plan_units.c):

- `n = s x calls` calls are made; of `ndistinct` keys drawn about uniformly they hold
  `d(n) = ndistinct x (1 - (1 - 1 / ndistinct)^n)` distinct ones;
- they hit `hits(n) = (n - d(n)) x min(1, est_entries / d(n))` times: every repeat where the cache
  holds every key met, and `est_entries / d(n)` of them where it holds fewer, as core takes
  `est_entries / ndistinct` of the whole walk's;
- the loop's price lacks `extra = n x (hr - hits(n) / n) x` the inner scan's total cost, where that
  is positive.

The figures are core's own: `calls` (`est_calls` from PostgreSQL 19), `est_entries`, `ndistinct` as
`cost_memoize_rescan()` estimates it (`estimate_num_groups()` of the cache keys, or the calls where
that falls back on a default; `est_unique_keys` from 19) and the hit ratio from them
(`est_hit_ratio` from 19). As with a cold loop's reads, the lion path's price is put into the loop's
units: it is multiplied by `memoscale`, the loop's price of the share (its startup and `s` of its
run) over that price plus the extra (`lion_units_price()`). That scale is not bounded by
`pg_lion.cold_max_discount`, since it is the competitor's own price, corrected; the cap bounds only
the cold reads on top, which take the loop at `nlcost / memoscale` (`lion_units_cold()`). Where the
loop's probes also meet a skewed key and the path is priced at its rows ("A skewed key's probes",
below), the two corrections add: the price is multiplied by `skewscale * memoscale`, and the cold
reads take the loop at `nlcost + nlextra + nlcost / memoscale - nlcost`. Every lion path priced
against such a loop through `lion_units_for()` sees it, and LionOrderedJoin weighs its own
competitor the same way (§47.3). A LionOrdered walk is priced against a scan of its relation, never
a loop, and its price does not change. `pg_lion.enable_memoize_limit` (on) turns it off.

Not counted: keys drawn other than uniformly. A skewed key column repeats more early, and a key
correlated with the loop's order (each run of the walk meeting the same few keys) hits more than
this model and core's both. A cache that evicts is taken at core's share of entries, not at the
hits its eviction order leaves. Tests: ordjoin.sql's page that is core's loop over a Memoize with
the setting off and LionOrderedJoin with it on.

### The join that reads the dimension (2026-10-24)

A NOT EXISTS over a small table puts its anti join at the top of core's plan, above the join of the
fact to the dimension: a `Hash Anti Join` hashing the small table over the `Nested Loop` into the
dimension's B-tree, or a `Nested Loop Anti Join` into the small table's B-tree over it. The plan's
time and pages are the loop's, and the anti join is the first join down from the top. So in an
upper rel's plan (`lion_competitor_through()`: the paths of the count, the FK-side join and
LionProbeJoin, which take every join below the aggregate):

- **past a semi or anti join over a join** (`lion_join_filters()`, `lion_competitor_below()`,
  lion_plan_units.c): a semi or anti join - `JOIN_SEMI` and `JOIN_ANTI`, and `JOIN_RIGHT_SEMI`
  (PostgreSQL 18) and `JOIN_RIGHT_ANTI`, which emit their inner side - whose emitted side reaches
  a join, down through the nodes that pass rows up, and costs at least what the semi or anti join
  adds over it, is passed through to that side. The competitor's kind is the join's below it
  (`lion_competitor_kind()`), and the nested loop whose cold reads, skewed probes and outer side
  are weighed is the first one below it (`lion_nestloop_cold()`, `lion_competitor_skew()`). A
  semi or anti join over a scan, or one that is most of the plan's cost itself, is its own kind. A
  join rel's lion paths - LionSemiJoin and LionAntiJoin as join paths - compete with that one join,
  their outer side core's child at core's price, and take the semi or anti join as it is.
- **through a Memoize** (`lion_nestloop_cold()`): a Memoize over the loop's inner index scan (one,
  under a Material or a projection) probes it once a miss, at the hit ratio
  `cost_memoize_rescan()` priced it at (`lion_memoize_misses()`, as the bitmap heap scans' reads
  count it): a leaf and the heap pages of a probe's rows for each miss.
- **in a subquery's plan** (`lion_nestloop_cold()`, `lion_competitor_skew()`): a loop below a
  subquery scan is the subquery's, and its pages, the residency over its tables and a Memoize's
  keys are looked up in the subquery's planner info, whose range table its Vars refer to.
- **the loop less its outer side** (`lion_units_cold()`, `LionUnits.nlshared`): where the lion path
  reads the loop's outer side as its child, at core's price beside its own price - LionProbeJoin's
  fact, the same rels as the loop's outer side (`pj_units()`, lion_probejoin.c) - its own price is
  weighed against the loop's cost less that side. The factor scales the path's own price alone,
  and the same scan inside both warm prices draws it towards 1 by its cost, which neither side's
  cold reads change. With the loop's own part L, the outer side S and the path's own price P, the
  path at P x f + S against L + S is (P + its reads) against (L + the loop's reads): the two plans'
  cold prices, short of the cap.
- **each LionProbeJoin path its own reads** (`pj_units()`): a participant of the parallel form
  probes its share of the fact's rows and makes every build, so the partial path's factor is of
  its loops' reads over its price with the builds whole. The serial node's factor would weigh the
  cold reads of every participant's probes against the builds of one. Its probes are priced at its
  own loops too (`lion_ordered_probe_price()`), as core prices a parallel loop's inner scan: fewer
  probes revisit fewer pages, each a little dearer.

Against a hash anti join over the loop, the loop's rate with its cold reads prices a lion path at
no less than the hash join's rate would: that rate, 0.5, is the cold factor's floor at the default
`pg_lion.cold_max_discount`. So where the cache holds the tables the path is the dearer for it, and
the dimension's cold reads count wherever an anti join of either method sits over the loop.

**Measured** (2026-10-24; PostgreSQL 18, the dev cluster - a VM of four cores shared with other
work; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF); warm, `shared_buffers` 2 GB, the median of seven runs; cold,
the server restarted and the relations' files dropped from the OS cache before each run, the median
of three). A 1,000,000-row dimension (a 503 MB heap, a 21 MB primary key, lion indexes on twelve
columns) and the 42,858 fact rows of one `grp` of 3,000,000, under §46's shape with a CASE of nine
predicates - ranges among them, which the node takes as cells with #178 - and a NOT EXISTS over
60,000 rows, at an `effective_cache_size` of about a quarter of the query's tables and a
`random_page_cost` of 1.1, in parallel: core's plan is a `Hash Anti Join` over the `Nested Loop`
into the dimension, cost 57,893. Against the loop, whose cold reads are 796,568 over its own 35,613
(57,893 less the fact's parallel bitmap heap scan, 22,280) - the serial node's 1,156,102 over its
86,138 (factor 0.62), the parallel form's 410,937 over 49,590 (0.40 before the cap, 0.5 applied) -
the node is 53,934, the plan, as it is at the hash join's rate. With the loop's whole cost the
parallel form's factor would be 0.63, and with the serial node's factor 0.62: core's plan either
way. The node runs it in 895 ms cold against core's 1,666 (404 against 1,274 with the dimension's
heap alone dropped), and in 295 warm against 184. The thirteen other settings and forms the query
was measured at keep their plans, and their prices but one: serially, with the cache holding the
tables at `random_page_cost` 1.1, core's plan is a hash anti join over the loop with a Memoize,
86,032, and the node 77,053 at the loop's rate (51,805 at the hash join's), still the plan.

`test/sql/competitor_cold.sql`, at the same settings and timed the same way (an 80,000-row
dimension of 1,231 pages, not all-visible until the last case; `effective_cache_size` '4GB' or
'1MB'; ms, the node; core's plan):

| query | settings | was | is | warm | cold |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 300 fact rows, the anti join of 300 | 4GB | the node | hash anti join over the loop | 2.72; 1.91 | |
| ... | 1MB | the node | the node | | 17.9; 37.1 |
| ..., hash and merge joins off | 1MB | nested loop anti join over the loop | the node | 2.05; 2.68 | 23.5; 35.2 |
| 4,500 rows over 3,000 keys, a Memoize | 1MB, the same | the loop over a Memoize | the node | 9.26; 9.65 | 40.8; 111.0 |
| 300 rows of a 200,000-row scan | 1MB, the same | nested loop anti join over the loop | the node | 11.5; 11.1 | 40.7; 44.2 |
| 10,000 of them, the anti join of 30,000, 2 workers | 1MB, the same, all-visible | core's plan, in parallel | the node, in parallel | 46.8; 36.3 | 64.8; 93.9 |

The cold column is a cache emptied once, each page read from the device at most once: the test's
1 MB stands for a cache a tenth of the dimension, which re-reads pages a cold run of a small table
does not, and the node's advantage there is the larger. Without the loop less its outer side the
fifth query is core's plan, and the sixth too; the sixth keeps the node with the serial node's
factor, which the 1,000,000-row fixture's does not. On the same tables with int keys, the warm
change of units moves the first query's plan from the node to core's loop at 1,000 and 3,000 fact
rows and `random_page_cost` 1.1, where the two tie (6.10 ms against 6.12; 11.6 against 11.4), and
at 300 rows at either `random_page_cost`, where core's is the faster (2.1 and 2.2 against 3.3).

The regression suite's other plans are unchanged: `make installcheck` passes on PostgreSQL 18 and
19.

### Tests

`test/sql/costrates.sql`: the settings and their ranges; the margin as a threshold - a GROUP BY the
node wins by far is chosen at a margin just above the ratio of its price to core's best and is not
just below it - that divides the node's and a LionOrdered's cost by exactly the margin, that core's
`enable_*` settings still force at the dearest margin (0.01) and lion's switches still leave out
with none; no margin and no rate where they hedge nothing - a count, a GROUP BY, a semi join and a
LionOrdered forced with core's settings cost the same at every margin and every rate, and a count
whose cheapest competitor is an aggregate over the AM's own index scan the same at every margin
while its rate still converts it; each kind of competitor made the cheapest by core's settings (a
plain aggregate over a sequential scan, a hash aggregate, the join methods) moving the cost of the
count, the GROUP BY, the FK-side join and the semi and anti join paths linearly with its own rate
and not at all with any other, and deciding the GROUP BY at the lowest and the highest rate; the
AM's scans unmoved by any rate or margin and LionOrdered by any rate; and every plan's rows against
the pushdown off and sequential scans only. `costgucs.sql` lists 38 cost settings with
`resident_page_cost`.

**The expected outputs regenerated.** No answer changed. Eight plans did, each timed against the
plan it replaced (assert build, the median of five, two or three times over):

| test | query | was | is | ms, is against was |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pushdown` | `g, count(*)`, 1,000 groups, never vacuumed | hash aggregate | LionCount | 13.8 to 14.3 against 15.0 to 15.8 |
| `pushdown` | `a, b, count(*) WHERE c = 'c1'`, decoded walk off | hash aggregate | LionCount | 2.4 to 2.9 against 3.2 to 3.5 |
| `pushdown` | ... `WHERE c = 'c1' OR n = 2` | hash aggregate | LionCount | 2.2 to 2.5 against 3.9 to 5.1 |
| `multicolumn` | `a, b, count(*) WHERE c = 'c1'`, one two-column index | hash aggregate | LionCount | 2.2 against 4.2 to 5.5 |
| `multicolumn` | ... over single-column indexes | hash aggregate | LionCount | 1.7 to 1.8 against 4.2 to 5.2 |
| `fkjoin_mixed` | `d.grp, count(*)`, `f.x = 3 AND d.attr = 2` | hash aggregate, hash join | partial counts | 1.0 to 1.25 against 1.35 to 1.66 |
| `fkjoin_mixed` | ... `, max(d.name)` | hash aggregate, hash join | counted rows | 1.28 against 1.62 to 1.74 |
| `fkjoin_distinct` | `d.region, count(DISTINCT f.fk)`, `f.x = 3 AND f.t = 't4'` | sorted aggregate, hash join | LionCount | 0.63 to 0.65 against 0.42 to 0.51 |

The first seven are the hash aggregate's and the hash join's rates finding the node where it is the
faster plan and dc7cd29 refused it; the tests' comments say so. The eighth is a loss, accepted: the
hash join's rate prices this small join's node at 0.82 of the hash join, and it runs 1.35 times
slower, where the matrix's `fk.status.kind` is priced at 0.91 and runs 1.25 times faster. To give
each to its faster plan the rate would have to be at least 0.57 and below 0.555 at once (EXPLAIN at
each); 0.5 keeps the larger, 12 ms against 0.17. At 0.8 the margin had moved four more -
`fkjoin_semipath.sql`'s GROUP BY to a sorted aggregate (a tie) and its two picks to a nested loop
(1.56 ms against 1.36) and from a LionCount (1.20 against 1.36), `orderedsemi.sql`'s LionOrdered
under a LIMIT to an index scan three times slower (0.13 to 0.15 ms against 0.04 to 0.05) - which at
1 are dc7cd29's plans again.

`make installcheck` passes in both WAL modes, 104 tests and 35 isolation tests in each, and so does
`make unit`.

### Not done

- **Three of lion's mispicks** in the matrix are formulas, not units: the IN lists' unions
  (`eq.c20k.in100`, `eq.c1m.in1000`, priced at 0.78 and 0.60 of an index-only scan's aggregate
  and 1.3 to 2.2 times slower) and the 20,000-entry GROUP BY (`group.c20k`, priced 1.09 times a
  sorted aggregate over an index-only scan and 1.4 times faster). Neither the rates nor the margin
  is the tool for them, and this section refits none of the 37 constants they are made of.
- **The rates on a release build.** This run's build was assert-enabled, and its own run's medians
  disagree with the defaults in both directions depending on what they are taken over (above). A
  release build's matrix, the rates fitted to its near ties, is the measurement that could move
  them.
- **LionOrdered** is not converted: its competitors are the reference or have no one rate. The
  matrix measured the one it meets most - a btree's index scan in order under a LIMIT - at 40 to
  115 units a millisecond, a fourth to a twelfth of the reference; a rate of its own would favour
  LionOrdered, but four queries are too few to set one.
- **Bitmap heap scans** have one rate for plans that run at 70 and at 4,400 units a millisecond;
  splitting the kind by what the scan's price is made of (pages or TIDs) would let §22's BitmapAnd
  have its own rate. Every bitmap scan the matrix timed was the AM's own, priced by lion's model,
  and measures nothing of the rate.
- **The parallel GROUP BY's participants** are priced with the serial node's competitor; core's
  partial paths are not searched for one of their own.
- **One residency for both sides' common reads.** A B-tree leaf a probe is counted for the loop and
  for LionProbeJoin alike, at the share of `effective_cache_size` the key's size gets among the
  query's tables (`index_pages_fetched()`): the 1,000,000-row fixture's 21 MB key, probed 13,467
  times by a participant, is some 10,000 reads of its 2,745 pages, which any cache keeps while the
  probes revisit them. Both sides' alike, they draw the factor towards 1: without them the serial
  node's 0.62 and the parallel form's 0.40 would both be far below the cap. A residency a relation,
  an index the probes revisit as hot as its size allows, would weigh the heap pages the node avoids
  alone.
- **The FK-side join's factor** weighs its own price against the loop's whole cost, the dimension
  scan it reads as its child at core's price inside it: `nlshared` is LionProbeJoin's alone, and
  the same pull towards 1 is not measured there.
- **The other readers of the loop.** A skewed key's probes (`lion_competitor_skew()`) are looked
  for past a semi or anti join but not through a Memoize; a Memoize under a LIMIT
  (`lion_memoize_limit_scale()`) only on the plan's top join.
- **A semi or anti join that is most of its plan's cost** is its own kind and rate: a hash anti join
  of a large table at the hash join's 0.5, a nested loop anti join at the reference. And a join
  rel's semi and anti join paths compete with their one join as it is, its kind the semi or anti
  join's.

### A skewed key's probes (2026-10-23)

§33's "The rows of a probed key" has the rows a probe of a key the plan does not know meets, on a
column whose keys are skewed: from Σn², and many times the per-key rows core prices it at. Lion
prices its own probes of such a key there. Its competitor was priced at core's rows, so the
comparison was between a lion path at the rows it meets and a core path at a sliver of them, and
the lion path lost to plans that run many times slower. A competitor at core's rows is under-priced
by however many rows it is short.

**Measured** (the same private workload as §33's). A nested loop from a dimension's small set of
keys into the fact table, its inner side the fact's B-tree on the key. Lion's probe of a key was
priced at 57 a call, 54 of that about 13 container seeks of about 4 random pages each. Core's
B-tree scan was priced at 18.46 a call: the per-key rows, 13 heap pages at a `random_page_cost` of
1.1. The loop won. Run cold, each of its calls read about 4,700 heap tuples and took 1.7 s.

**R1: the rows are the same on both sides, or core's on both.** A lion path is priced at the
skewed rows only where its competitor meets them too. The competitor is priced at those rows as
well, and the lion path's price is put back into core's units by the competitor's price at core's
rows over its price at the skewed rows:

    price = lion's price at the skewed rows x competitor at core's rows / competitor at the skewed rows

So the two compare as they would at the rows both meet, and everything else the plan weighs them
against stays in core's units. Where no competitor meets the rows (none, or a sequential scan whose
price no key's rows change), the lion path keeps core's rows too. AM scans are core's scans of a
lion index and keep core's rows: they compete with core's paths of the relation by core's own
rules. An unparameterized one whose index clauses equate the key to a value the plan does not know
- a correlated subquery's scan, a generic plan's - is lion's plan of the relation, and is priced in
the units of its other plans (§40.12). Path rows never change.

**What the competitor costs at the skewed rows** (`lion_skew_scan_extra()`, lion_plan_skew.c) is
the difference between core's own price terms worked out at core's rows and at `factor` times
them:

- an index scan: `cost_index()`'s heap pages, Mackert and Lohman's over the loop's scans and
  interpolated by the index's correlation, which it takes from the AM's `amcostestimate`;
- the leaf pages `genericcostestimate()` prorates;
- a bitmap heap scan: `cost_bitmap_heap_scan()`'s pages and the price of a page;
- a CPU charge for each row, index tuple and restriction qual.

The descent, the start-up and everything above the scan are left as they were. The factor is the
largest of the figures (`lion_skew_param_factor()`) for the scan's index clauses that equate a
column to a value the plan does not know: a Param, or another relation's Var
(`lion_skew_clauses_factor()`).

**Against a nested loop** (`lion_competitor_skew()`, lion_plan_units.c). The inner side must be
one index scan or bitmap heap scan parameterized by the outer rows, under a Material or a
projection at most. The extra is what core's own model of the loop (`final_cost_nestloop()`)
charges more at the skewed rows. An inner join's every probe reads its key's rows: the extra is
the loops (the outer rows) times one scan's extra. A probe into an inner side core proved unique
stops at its key's first match, and that loop is left at core's price. Core prices a semi or anti
join's loop by its outer rows with a match and without one. A matched row's probe reads
`2 / (match_count + 1)` of a scan, and the match count grows with the key's rows, so the first
match comes no later at a heavy key. An unmatched row's probe costs a fraction of a scan where the
scan's index answers every join clause (`lion_competitor_key_only()`, core's static
`has_indexed_join_quals()` restated): the join has no clause left to evaluate itself, the inner
side is a parameterized index or index-only scan or a bitmap heap scan over one index scan, and
each clause its parameterization takes from the join's outer side is one of its index clauses or
of the same equivalence class as one, with at least one such clause. That loop is left at core's
price too. Otherwise core charges an unmatched row a full scan, which grows with the key's rows,
and the extra is the unmatched rows times one scan's extra: the outer rows less the join's rows
for a semi join, which emits the matched ones, and the join's rows for an anti join, which emits
the unmatched ones. The inner side's restriction clauses are left out of the test, as core leaves
them out: its match count already scales with the key's rows, so the first match past such a
clause comes no later at a heavy key, and an outer row with no match, which reads every row of its
key, is under-charged by core at any key - core's model, not the skew's. In
`test/sql/skew.sql`'s section 10 no figure is worked out for the probe of a semi or anti join on
the key alone, and the lion path weighed against it keeps its price; a probe with a clause beyond
the key is priced at the figure. A loop below a subquery scan is the subquery's, and its Vars are
looked up in the subquery's planner info (`rel->subroot`), not the outer root's. The paths that
price their lookups at the figure take it with `lion_units_take_skew()`, which sets the scale:

    skewscale = (nlcost - nlouter) / (nlcost - nlouter + nlextra)

That is the loop's price without its outer side, at core's rows over at the skewed ones. The outer
side is left out because the lion path takes it as its child at core's price, and it would dilute
the correction. The FK-side join and its semi join path do this, their lookups priced at the same
rows (`lion_fkjoin_fk_keys()`: the keys the skewed rows per key would make, n_distinct over the
factor).

**Against the relation's own paths** (`lion_skew_rel_scale()`): a walk of a B-tree keyed on the
column (`lo_cost()`), a LionCount whose WHERE equates it to a Param
(`lion_count_skew_units()`), and an unparameterized AM scan of a lion index that does
(`lion_skew_am_paths()`, §40.12). The competitor is the cheapest of core's paths of the relation
with the same parameterization, neither one of lion's custom paths nor disabled. The scale is its
price over its price plus its extra, for one scan or for the walk's loops. By the time the count
or the walk is costed, `add_path()` may have pruned that path in favour of a lion path. So the
scale is worked out once a planner run for each relation, outer rels and loops, and kept
(`lion_skew_scale_keep()`). The unparameterized one is worked out at the top of lion's
`set_rel_pathlist_hook` (`lion_skew_rel_note()`), from core's paths alone: the relation's paths
that read no lion index, and core's index paths and sequential scan built again over its other
indexes, which `add_path()` may have dropped for an AM scan of a lion index. Where the query level
stops at a count of rows - a LIMIT, an `EXISTS`'s first row - both sides are priced for the rows
they read until the count is found (§40.12, "A count of rows").

**The cold reads, on top.** `lion_nestloop_cold()` counts the loop's heap pages at the skewed
rows: one changed term, `indexselectivity x skew`. `lion_units_cold()` weighs the lion path
against the loop at its corrected price, nlcost + nlextra. The skew correction is the skewscale
`lion_units_price()` multiplies by, outside `pg_lion.cold_max_discount`, because it is the
competitor's own price corrected and not a guess about the cache. The cold reads' factor applies
on top of it, within that cap. In `test/sql/skew.sql` the LionCount against the loop is priced far
below the loop, past the cap at its default of 2 (`past_cold_bound`).

**Plans.** At the figure the measured loop's index scan meets about 2,396 rows a call, not about
15, and is charged for its heap pages and CPU at those rows. That is nearer the 4,700 tuples a call
it read than core's 13 pages were. This build has not been run on that workload. The regression
test's fixtures reproduce the plan's shape at a small scale: a skewed key column, its B-tree, a
lion index, a correlated subquery, a nested loop and a generic plan. `pg_lion.enable_skew_estimate`
off gives back the plans this section changes. `test/sql/correlated.sql`'s plans move with it, and
that test runs with the setting off (§33's subsection).

## 40. Lion-filtered walks of a covering B-tree, index-only (`LionOrdered`'s index-only mode and `LionBtreeScan`, lion_ordered.c; 2026-10-06)

The shape is

    SELECT <columns a B-tree holds> FROM t
    WHERE <clauses lion indexes answer> [AND <the B-tree's own quals>]
    [ORDER BY <the B-tree's columns> [LIMIT n]]

over a B-tree the user created to cover it - `(k) INCLUDE (...)`, as for an Index Only Scan - and
lion indexes on the filter columns. §30's node already filters a B-tree's walk through lion's set
before it touches the heap; what it fetched from the heap was the row's VALUES. When the B-tree
returns every column the node must produce, the values come from the index tuple and the heap is
read for visibility alone, on pages the visibility map does not call all-visible, exactly as core's
Index Only Scan reads it (`nodeIndexonlyscan.c`): a `LIMIT 10` of a selective filter then costs the
lion lookups, the entries walked and ten visibility-map tests. And since the walk pays without an
ORDER BY once the heap is out of it, the same node is offered for any B-tree path of the relation
whose index covers the query - a full walk of `(grp) INCLUDE (x, tags)` under `WHERE tags @> '{t}'
GROUP BY grp` included - under the name `LionBtreeScan` when it claims no order. Lion's part is the
membership test, which answers what a B-tree cannot hold: multi-key columns, a column behind a
high-cardinality leader, ANDs and ORs across independent indexes. This is what replaces the window
store (format version 9, reverted 2026-10-06): a value store partitioned by heap window cannot beat
a B-tree's clustering on a pinned key, and the B-tree is the user's to create.

### 40.1 What qualifies

- **The relation, the WHERE and the lion side**: §30.1 and §30.2, unchanged (`lo_rel_ok()`,
  `lo_lion_accesses()`). The target of an UPDATE, DELETE or MERGE, a relation with security quals,
  another table AM: declined as there. So is a relation the planner has proven empty
  (`IS_DUMMY_REL()`: a constant-false or NULL restriction, constraint exclusion) - core builds no
  index path for one and `make_one_rel()` leaves its pages out of `root->total_table_pages`, which
  `cost_index()` asserts they are in; before `LionBtreeScan` the hook never reached
  `create_index_paths()` for such a relation, because its path list held only the empty Append and
  there was no ordered path to match, but `lo_btree_paths()` runs it whenever a B-tree covers the
  target, and ordered.sql's `EXECUTE lo_p(NULL, 0)` tripped the assertion (2026-10-06).
- **Coverage.** The B-tree covers the node when every column it must produce is a plain column of
  the index - a key column (`indexkeys[i] != 0`) or an INCLUDE column - that the AM can return
  (`canreturn[i]`, true of every B-tree column). The columns the node must produce are decided per
  (ordered path, lion access) pair (`lo_needed_attrs()`, `lo_index_only()`): every Var of the
  relation in `rel->reltarget->exprs`, in the residual filter (`lo_residual()`: the clauses the
  node still tests itself, a partial lion index's predicate when the query spells it included), in
  the ordered B-tree's own clauses (its recheck under `xs_recheck`) and - only when a lion index
  clause is lossy at plan time (`IndexClause.lossy`), so that every member would need the recheck
  and heap mode is the honest plan - in the lion qual. The lion filter's columns are otherwise NOT
  required, where core's `check_index_only()` would ask for every restriction clause's: whether a
  set needs rechecking is a run-time property (an inexact source), and a member of such a set
  the B-tree cannot recheck is rechecked on its heap
  tuple, fetched for that alone (§40.4) - heap mode, the alternative, fetches every member's. So
  `(created_at) INCLUDE (id, title)` under `WHERE tags @> '{t}'` is covered. Lion's planner marks
  no clause lossy today (a tsquery prefix, NOT or weight widens the set to a superset the executor
  rechecks, §17), so the lossy branch is dormant until one does. The pre-filter that decides which
  B-trees get unordered paths at all (§40.2) tests the target's Vars alone, a necessary condition;
  the pair decides. An expression
  column matches no Var: it may still give the order, as in §30, but no value. A system column
  makes the index non-covering, as in core: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` adds the row mark's `ctid` to
  the target, so a locked relation is always heap mode, and EvalPlanQual never meets an index-only
  plan. So does a partial B-tree's predicate column when the query spells the predicate: the clause
  stays in the node's filter (§30.2 step 4 - core's index scan drops it, but the fetch-and-sort
  switch rechecks rows that did not come through the index, which the predicate does not hold for),
  so `(k) INCLUDE (x) WHERE flag` under `WHERE flag AND ...` is covered only with `flag` among the
  INCLUDE columns. The mapping of index columns to relation attnos goes into `custom_private`
  (`LO_PRIV_IOCOLS`), so that the executor looks nothing up per row.
- **`enable_indexonlyscan`**: off, there is no index-only mode - the ordered node keeps its heap
  mode, and no unordered path is offered.

### 40.2 Planner integration (`lion_ordered_set_rel_pathlist()`)

- **Ordered paths** (§30.2): as before, from `rel->pathlist`; each (ordered path, lion access)
  pair decides coverage (§40.1) and is priced in index-only mode when covered, in heap mode as
  before otherwise.
- **Unordered paths.** For each B-tree of the relation that holds the query's target columns (a
  necessary condition; the pair decides the rest, §40.1), `create_index_paths()` is run on a scratch copy of the RelOptInfo that sees that index ALONE
  (`lo_scratch_rel()`, the helper `lo_lion_accesses()` now builds its copy with; `lo_btree_paths()`)
  - alone, so that its paths compete with nothing: in the relation itself the full walk of a
  covering index without a qual, which core builds as an index-only scan whenever
  `check_index_only()` passes, loses to the sequential scan and never reaches `rel->pathlist`, and
  a path with quals may lose to another index's. Core builds, for that index, the paths with its
  matching quals - with pathkeys where the query finds them useful, without otherwise - a backward
  one where that order is useful, and the no-qual one; an IndexPath that `add_path()` dropped for a
  bitmap scan of the same index is taken from that scan's one-leaf `bitmapqual`. Core builds the
  no-qual path only where its order is useful or the index alone answers the query
  (`check_index_only()`, every restriction clause's columns among its own), which a B-tree lacking
  the lion filter's columns - a primary key under a lion filter on other columns - never does; when
  core built no unparameterized path of the index, `lo_btree_paths()` builds that walk of the whole index
  itself (`create_index_path()` with no clauses; a partial B-tree only where the query implies its
  predicate), and the pair decides coverage as for any other. Each resulting
  IndexPath - a B-tree, not hypothetical, `param_info == NULL` (the parameterized ones are §40.10's
  nested loop probes), no ORDER BY operators,
  `lo_indexpath_ok()` - whose twin is not among the ordered paths (the same index, direction and
  pathkeys: offered above already) is paired with each lion access from `lo_lion_accesses()`, as
  the ordered loop pairs them, less the pairs in which the lion access adds nothing: every clause
  of its every leaf, an OR arm's too, is one of the B-tree path's own index clauses
  (`lo_lion_adds()`), so every entry walked would be a member - the same RestrictInfo, or an
  `equal()` clause: 18 and later match an OR of equalities to each index as a `ScalarArrayOpExpr`
  RestrictInfo of that index's own (`match_orclause_to_indexcol()`), so the B-tree's `k = ANY` and
  the lion index's are two objects spelling one clause (`lo_same_clause()`, which `lo_cost()`'s
  shared-clause correction uses too, or the OR's selectivity would be squared and the node
  underprice itself against the plain Index Only Scan). A leaf with no index clauses at all - a
  partial lion index walked whole for its predicate, which `lo_lion_tree_ok()` allows - adds that
  predicate's selectivity and counts as adding; `lo_cost()`'s `lo_pred_implied()` correction
  prices it. The pair must cover (§40.1) and is priced in index-only mode. The CustomPath carries the IndexPath's pathkeys when
  it has them - a free order - under the name `LionOrdered`, and none otherwise under the name
  `LionBtreeScan`: a second `CustomPathMethods`/`CustomScanMethods` pair over the same plan
  function, state struct and executor functions. `pg_lion.enable_ordered_scan` keeps gating the
  ordered paths and the lion columns' walks of §30.11, and with it off the unordered paths claim no
  order whatever core found useful - a `LionOrdered` must not appear with its switch off - and are
  all `LionBtreeScan`s; `pg_lion.enable_btree_scan` (bool, default on) gates the unordered paths.
  Core's `enable_indexscan` disables both, as it disables the B-tree's own index scans (§39,
  "Core's switches"): the path is kept and marked disabled after it is priced, since its price
  comes from `indextotalcost`, which carries no `disable_cost`; a partial path is disabled as a
  parallel index scan is.
- **A clause core's AND leaves out** (`lo_lion_cover()`). The lion accesses are core's bitmap
  paths, and `choose_bitmap_and()` leaves out of a BitmapAnd an index whose bitmap costs more than
  the heap fetches it saves - `c3 IN (0, 1)`, two thirds of the rows, beside `c20 IN (1, 2)` -
  since the bitmap heap scan's Filter tests such a clause on the tuple it fetches anyway. Paired
  with such an access, a walk of a B-tree that lacks the clause's column has the clause in its
  residual, needs the column, and is not covered: from core's accesses alone no index-only walk
  is offered, and the plan reads the heap (a bitmap heap scan of every member of
  `c20 IN (1, 2)`). So when every one of
  core's accesses leaves one of the clauses a lion access answers - those whose columns a lion
  index's key has (`lo_knn_own()`) and some access of the pool answers - the AND that answers all
  of them is added to the accesses: built from core's and those of each lion index alone, greedily
  (`lo_cover_pool()`, `lo_cover_and()`), as §44.6's post-filter builds a lionvec order's. It is
  paired only where it makes the walk index-only - every unordered path, and an ordered one whose
  B-tree then covers; a walk in heap mode reads every member's tuple for its values anyway, and
  keeps core's accesses, whose sets are the cheaper to build. The price decides between the
  pairs: a clause that keeps most rows makes a set costly to build (on a 60,000-row table the
  `c3` set is 40,000 members), and under `ORDER BY k LIMIT 50` the walk over core's smaller set,
  fetching the few members' tuples, is the cheaper; for the aggregate the index-only walk is
  chosen over the heap. A clause no lion access answers (`c3 + 0 = 1`) is the Filter's whatever
  the set. On a synthetic 3,000,000-row table of 340-byte rows (a 1.1 GB heap, a 64 MB primary
  key), `SELECT sum(id) ... WHERE a IN (<10 of 20 values>) AND b IN (<2 of 3>)` over core's
  accesses alone is a bitmap heap scan of `a`'s half of the rows with `b` in its Filter, 1,049 ms
  (median of five, warm; 687 ms parallel); over the added AND it is an index-only walk of the
  primary key, 307 ms serially and 202 ms with two workers.
- **Partial paths** (§40.9): each pair is offered a second time as a partial path when the walk
  may be divided among a parallel plan's participants (`lo_parallel_ok()`), and every serial
  walk is `parallel_safe` when the relation is (`rel->consider_parallel`): whole, it may run in a
  worker - the inner side of a join a worker runs, or below a non-unique semi join's
  unique-ification (§27, "Forward semi joins over a non-unique key"), which takes a whole path
  under a Gather.
- **Partitions**: as §30.11, each leaf is scanned like a table under core's Append or MergeAppend.

### 40.3 Cost (`lo_cost()`, index-only)

§30.3's start-up (the lion lookups and the set), walk (`indextotalcost` plus a membership test per
entry) and shared-clause correction stand. The heap term changes: the `F` members' pages are
priced as `cost_index()` prices an index-only scan's - `index_pages_fetched()` for an uncorrelated
order and the members' share of the heap for a correlated one, EACH scaled by `(1 -
rel->allvisfrac)`, the fraction of pages the visibility map does not call all-visible, and
interpolated by the squared correlation as before - plus a visibility-map test per member at
`cpu_operator_cost`; `cpu_tuple_cost` per member (now the index tuple's deform) and the filter's
cost were charged already. `lo_margin` applies as §39 applies it. For an unordered path core has no
LIMIT to scale by, so the planner prices the whole walk, and a path whose walk is the whole index
competes on `indextotalcost + T × cpu_operator_cost` against the bitmap heap scan's heap pages,
which is right: on `btreescan.sql`'s 100,000 rows, whose heap is six times the covering B-tree,
the covering walk is chosen over the bitmap scan for a filter of a tenth of the rows, the bitmap
scan over it where only the wide `(k) INCLUDE (...)` B-tree covers the columns, and the lion
index's own scan for a filter of three in a thousand (§40.7, "the plan choice"). The recheck
from the heap (§40.4) is not priced: an inexact source is not knowable at plan
time, and the fetches it costs are bounded by the members - the bound heap mode pays for every
member. *(Since 2026-10-19 a qual the set leaves to the recheck at PLAN time is priced: the lion
access's IndexPaths are asked what a plain scan's source of them leaves (`lo_rechecked_quals()`,
`lion_path_rechecked_quals()`; a BitmapOr's arms are not followed), the set's members become the
CANDIDATES, the rows of the quals it does answer, and every candidate the walk meets is charged
its recheck and - in heap mode, and index-only when the btree does not return a column the lion
qual reads (`LO_FLAG_HEAPRECHECK`) - its heap fetch, all-visible or not, since the recheck reads
the tuple before the visibility map is asked. `IS NOT NULL` used to be such a qual (§14): priced
by its members, such a set chose an index-only walk that fetched 1.41M heap rows to throw half of
them away. A set made lossy by a lossy qual at run time stays unpriced.)* The planner also hands
the executor the entries the walk is expected to visit,
`indexselectivity × rel->tuples`, for the switch's density gate (§40.4; `LO_PRIV_EXPECTED`, a
float8 Const in `custom_private`, 0 when the ordered path is a lion column's walk).

**The probe's price** (2026-10-06). The walk is CPU-bound. On bench/quick.py's 5M-row `fact` table
(its covering B-tree `(c20k) INCLUDE (c1m)`, 107 MB, under `WHERE c20 = 3 GROUP BY c20k`, a 5%
filter) the covering walk took 830 to 925 ms for 5M entries, 170 ns an entry - the btree step, the
probe (a binary search over the container keys and a membership test) and the met-before mark -
against 85 ns a row for the sequential scan with its filter, which the planner charges
`cpu_tuple_cost + cpu_operator_cost` (0.0125). Priced at `indextotalcost`'s `cpu_index_tuple_cost`
plus one `cpu_operator_cost` for the probe, a fifth of that for twice the work, the walk came out at
97,072 against 102,912 for the lion index's own scan and HashAggregate, which run in 200 to 250 ms,
and was chosen at `random_page_cost` 1.1 as well (57,055 against 101,486). Each walked entry's probe
is now `LO_PROBE_TUPLES` (2) × `cpu_tuple_cost` + `cpu_operator_cost`, 0.0225, 1.8 times the
sequential scan's row, which puts that walk at 197,072 (157,055 at `random_page_cost` 1.1, against
the lion index scan's 101,486) and sends the query to the lion index's scan at either setting,
while the LIMIT walks keep the node (§40.7, "On the benchmark's tables"). The lion column walk of
§30.11 keeps its own pricing (`lo_cost_walk()`). Where the covering B-tree holds the filter's
column as well, core's own Index Only Scan with the filter walks the same entries for one
`cpu_operator_cost` each, and is now priced below the node; on btreescan.sql's 100,000 rows the two
run in the same time for `c200 = 17 ORDER BY k LIMIT 10` (0.5 ms either way), and core's filtered
scan of `tags @> '{t3}'` over 94,000 entries takes 18 to 28 ms against the node's 13 to 17, the
containment operator costing core more than the one `cpu_operator_cost` it is charged at.

**Warm and cold.** A full covering walk reads the B-tree (107 MB here) in place of the heap (751
MB) but spends those 170 ns an entry, so warm it loses to the lion index's own scan of a 5% filter
by four times and to the sequential scan by two; it pays when the heap would be read cold, or the
filter is far wider than the B-tree's share of the heap. The planner's I/O constants decide,
`pg_lion.enable_btree_scan` turns the unordered walks off and `pg_lion.enable_ordered_scan` the
ordered ones. Since 2026-10-23 an index-only walk against a bitmap heap scan whose
heap the cache cannot hold is priced with both plans' cold reads (§39, "A bitmap heap scan's cold
reads").

### 40.4 Execution

- **The slot.** The mode is fixed per plan, so the scan slot's type is: `TTSOpsBufferHeapTuple` of
  the relation's descriptor in heap mode, as before; `TTSOpsVirtual` of the relation's descriptor
  in index-only mode - the relation's, not the index's as core's node uses, so that the plan's Vars
  (`scanrelid`, no `custom_scan_tlist`) and the rechecks read it unchanged. `lo_create_state()`
  picks it from the plan's flags, not `BeginCustomScan`: `ExecInitCustomScan()` initialises the
  projection and the quals on the scan slot's type before `BeginCustomScan` runs, and the expression
  machinery specialises on it, so one plan never returns slots of two types.
- **A row.** `xs_want_itup` is set on the B-tree scan before `index_rescan()`. For a member TID
  (`lo_fetch_indexonly()`): `VM_ALL_VISIBLE(heapRelation, blkno, &vmbuffer)`, the map's buffer kept
  across calls and released at rescan and end, as `ioss_VMBuffer` is. All-visible, the row is
  visible to every snapshot, this one included, and the heap is not read. Not all-visible, the
  heap tuple is fetched into a slot of the table AM's kept for this alone (`index_fetch_heap()` on
  16 to 19, `table_fetch_tid()` and `table_tuple_fetch_row_version()` on 20 - `lo_fetch_btree()`,
  as heap mode fetches), counted as a heap fetch and kept in that slot until the row's rechecks
  are done (below); a TID with no visible version is skipped. Either way the values are the INDEX TUPLE's: `xs_itup` deformed with `xs_itupdesc` (or
  `xs_hitup`, had the AM returned a heap-format tuple) and laid into the virtual slot through the
  mapping, every other attribute NULL - the visible version reached from the root TID has the
  index's values for indexed and INCLUDE columns, since those are HOT-blocking (§30.5). A `name`
  column a B-tree stores as a cstring (`name_ops`'s storage type) is copied back into a Name of the
  node's, reused per row, as core copies it. The "met before" bitmap of §30.4 stands: a TID met
  twice is skipped before any of this.
- **The rechecks.** `ordrecheck` under `xs_recheck` and EvalPlanQual's `lo_recheck` evaluate on
  the scan slot as before; coverage guarantees the columns are there. So does `lionrecheck`, for
  an inexact set, when the B-tree holds the lion qual's columns. When it does not
  (`LO_FLAG_HEAPRECHECK`, decided at plan time from the lion qual's Vars against the mapping;
  `st->lionheaprecheck`), the member is rechecked on its heap tuple (`lo_lion_recheck()`): fetched
  now into the table AM's slot if the visibility test did not fetch it already - counted as a heap
  fetch, a TID with no visible version skipped - `slot_getallattrs()`, and `ExecQual(lionrecheck)`
  with that slot as `ecxt_scantuple`, which is sound although the qual was initialised for the
  virtual scan slot (§40.5). A row the heap was read for holds its tuple predicate lock
  (`fromheap`). The heap tuple is let go at the end of the row's iteration. The switch's rows, in
  index-only mode, are heap tuples copied whole into the scan slot, so their recheck reads the slot
  as before.
- **The fetch-and-sort switch** (§30.4) fetches members from the heap in TID order: in index-only
  mode each lands in the table AM's slot and is copied into the virtual scan slot
  (`ExecCopySlot()`, a deform) before the rechecks and the sort, so the slot type stays fixed, and
  each copy carries its row's TID. Its ratio is `LO_SWITCH_RATIO` (32) in both modes, the setting
  `pg_lion.ordered_switch_ratio` (§30.4). In index-only mode the walk would not have read the
  members' heap pages at all, so a switch pays for pages the walk never touches: a uniform full
  walk under no LIMIT - the aggregate shape - must never switch (it would fetch every remaining
  member from the heap; under the heap-mode rule alone a filter of a tenth of the rows switched
  three quarters of the way through the index and fetched the 2,300 members left), while the
  hazard the switch exists for (§30.3: a LIMIT walk whose members sit at the far end of the order)
  must switch, and a ratio large enough to spare the former - some 530 at the planner's page and
  entry costs - spares the latter too for any set over a fifth of a percent of the index. The two
  are told apart by density instead: at both decision sites (the lazy set's conversion trigger and
  the switch itself, `lo_switch_due()`) the switch is considered, in index-only mode, only when
  the walk has met markedly fewer members than a uniform spread predicts - `distinct <
  LO_SWITCH_DENSITY (0.5) × members × scanwalked / expected`, `expected` the entries the walk was
  expected to visit (§40.3; 0 when unknown, and a gate with no expectation passes); the lazy site
  uses `lazymembers`. A uniform walk meets `members × scanwalked / expected` members and never
  passes; the correlated hazard keeps `distinct` near 0 while `scanwalked` grows and switches at
  the measured 32 (§40.8 has the gate's blind spot). In heap mode the gate does not apply: the
  members the switch fetches would have been fetched by the walk anyway. Under ANALYZE a switch's
  heap visits count in `Heap Fetches` in index-only mode as the walk's do (§40.6). An unordered
  path has no sort keys and never switches, as a path whose pathkeys were not plain columns never
  did; the planner priced the full walk.
- **Unchanged**: the lazy set, the early stop, the spill, rescans with changed Params, the
  predicate locks of the lion lookups.

### 40.5 Correctness

§30.5's argument stands for which TIDs come out of the walk and are members. What changes is how a
member's visibility is decided and where its values come from, and both are core's Index Only
Scan's.

- **The visibility map.** A page's all-visible bit says every tuple on it is visible to every
  snapshot. It is cleared, under the page's lock, before a row is inserted on the page, and the
  B-tree entry for that row is inserted after; the walk reads a TID under the B-tree page's shared
  lock, serialised with the insert's exclusive lock, and the lock released between the clearing and
  the index insert is a full barrier - so a TID the walk meets whose row was inserted after the bit
  was set is met with the bit cleared (`nodeIndexonlyscan.c`'s "memory ordering effects" note,
  which `visibilitymap_get_status()` reading without a lock rests on). A delete clears the bit too
  and does not touch the index, but the deleted row stays visible to the snapshot until its
  deleter commits, and a snapshot that sees the commit was taken under ProcArrayLock after the bit
  was cleared. Lion adds no TID the B-tree did not return, so nothing new arises on its side.
- **A recycled TID, and a hot standby.** `xs_want_itup` makes nbtree keep its pin on the leaf page
  while the executor tests the map (its `dropPin` rule, nbtree's README): VACUUM cannot remove the
  page's TIDs from the index, and so cannot free the heap slots they name, until the walk has moved
  on - the interlock core's Index Only Scan relies on, and now the node's. The set's own hazard
  (§30.5, "A recycled TID") is unchanged: a member whose slot was reused names a tuple the snapshot
  cannot see, and on a page still marked all-visible no such tuple exists. On a hot standby the
  same pin rule protects the walk as it protects core's scan, and the lion side still reads no
  visibility map and holds no pin (§30.5).
- **SERIALIZABLE.** A row returned without a heap visit has no tuple to predicate-lock - a tuple
  lock needs the tuple's xmin, which was not read - so the node takes `PredicateLockPage()` on its
  heap page as core's Index Only Scan does, after the rechecks pass, for each row it returns; a row
  the heap was visited for holds its tuple lock from the fetch. The B-tree page locks and the lion
  relation locks are §30.5's. test/isolation/btreescan_serializable.spec is the write skew of two
  HOT updates of rows the other transaction read index-only: it must fail, and without the page
  lock neither update would conflict with anything the other read (a HOT update writes no index)
  and both would commit.
- **The recheck from the heap** (§40.4) evaluates `lionrecheck`, initialised for the virtual scan
  slot, on the table AM's slot. That is sound because the scan slot's type is fixed
  (`ExecInitScanTupleSlot()` sets `scanopsfixed`), so `ExecInitQual()` emitted no
  `EEOP_SCAN_FETCHSOME` step for it - `ExecComputeSlotInfo()` drops the step for a fixed virtual
  slot, and with it the slot-type check that step makes (`CheckOpSlotCompatibility`) - and the
  qual's Var steps read `tts_values[]` and `tts_isnull[]` directly, which `slot_getallattrs()`
  fills for the heap tuple. The tuple it tests is the version the snapshot sees of the TID the
  walk returned (the HOT chain followed from its root, as the visibility fetch follows it), so the
  recheck tests the values the row has for this snapshot, the same version whose indexed and
  INCLUDE columns the index tuple returned (§40.4).
- **EvalPlanQual** never meets an index-only plan: a row mark's `ctid` is in the target (§40.1).
  `lo_recheck()` asserts the test tuple's slot type is the scan slot's; the recheck from the heap
  is index-only mode's alone and never reaches it.

### 40.6 EXPLAIN

    Custom Scan (LionBtreeScan) on bs
      Index: bs_grp (index only)
      Lion Cond: (tags @> '{t3}'::text[])
      Lion Indexes: bs_tags

    Limit
      ->  Custom Scan (LionOrdered) on bs
            Ordered By: bs_k (backward, index only)
            Lion Cond: ((c200 = 17) AND (c20 = 3))
            Lion Indexes: bs_c200, bs_c20

`LionOrdered`'s lines are §30.7's; `index only` joins the `Ordered By` line's parenthesis in
index-only mode (heap mode prints as before, so no existing output changes), and a `LionBtreeScan`
names the index it walks under `Index`, with the same qual and counter lines. Under ANALYZE, `Heap
Fetches` counts in index-only mode the heap visits: the members whose page the visibility map did
not call all-visible, the members an inexact set had rechecked on their heap tuple
(§40.4) and the fetch-and-sort switch's, visible or not, as core's Index Only Scan counts its
visits (in heap mode, as before, the members with a visible version); `Heap Fetches: 0` on a
vacuumed table under an exact set, or an inexact one the B-tree can recheck.

### 40.7 Tests

test/sql/btreescan.sql, on a 100,000-row table - its heap six times its covering B-trees - with
covering B-trees `(k) INCLUDE (id, grp, x, c200, c20, nm)` and `(grp) INCLUDE (x, tags)`, two
partial ones and an expression one, and lion indexes on `c200`, `c20` and `tags`: every query run
through the node (every core scan off) and through the ordinary plan (both of the node's settings
off) and compared - in order under an ORDER BY, as multisets otherwise - with the node and its mode
named. A covered `=`, ranges and `IN` lists on the B-tree side with lion filters, lion `IN` lists, a
`name` INCLUDE column filtered and returned, DESC with a LIMIT, OFFSET, an empty answer, a LIMIT
beyond the match count; the aggregate shape under a GROUP BY and a plain aggregate, with a scalar
filter and a multi-key one (exact as well, §29.6); the counters (`Heap Fetches: 0` after VACUUM, `Rows Removed
by Lion Recheck` evaluated on the index tuple's values, the switch in index-only mode with its heap
fetches counted); rows inserted in the same transaction and a dirty heap (HOT and non-HOT updates,
deletes) before VACUUM, their heap fetches counted, and after VACUUM with none; `FOR UPDATE` (heap
mode); cursors fetched in pieces in both modes; a generic plan and LATERAL and correlated
subqueries rescanned with the outer value in the lion filter and in the B-tree's quals; the partial

each setting off; and the plan choice with nothing disabled. Then a B-tree lacking the lion
filter's columns (§40.1): an exact set (`Heap Fetches: 0`), an inexact one (each member fetched
for its recheck), rows not all-visible on an inexact set (fetched once), a set that spills past
`hash_mem` through a kept plan (as ordered.sql's section 10 does, on a 400,000-row table of its
own: `Lion Set: exact`, no heap fetch and nothing removed) and tsquery
prefix and NOT filters (supersets, rechecked from the heap); the switch in index-only mode
(§40.4): the far-end shape switches and matches the ordinary plan, a large
`pg_lion.ordered_switch_ratio` keeps it walking, the uniform GROUP BY walk and a uniform backward
walk to the end never switch and read nothing from the heap, and the same backward walk in heap
mode (a `ctid` in the target) switches as before; NULLs in key and INCLUDE columns, a NULL `name`
among them, over `(grp DESC NULLS FIRST, id) INCLUDE (x, nm)` walked both ways, `IS NULL` filters,
on a table with a dropped column (the mapping with a gap); `ctid`, `tableoid` and a whole-row Var
(heap mode), both settings off (no node), a SCROLL cursor fetched backward; and the pairs that add
nothing (§40.2) - `k = 1 OR k = 7` with a lion index on `k` and a B-tree leading with it, with
core's scans on and off: no node, its presence alone printed since the plan's text differs between
majors - against a partial lion index walked whole, which is offered; and a clause core's AND leaves
out (§40.2), on a 60,000-row table of its own: the AND's index-only walk chosen for the aggregate
with nothing disabled, `Heap Fetches: 0`, the answers of the aggregate, ordered walks both ways, a
B-tree filter beside the AND, the OR spelling of the IN list and a `<>` keeping nearly every row;
a LIMIT 50 in order that takes core's smaller set in heap mode; a column the B-tree lacks in the
target (heap mode, core's access) and a clause no lion access answers (the Filter's).
test/sql/btreescan_parallel.sql is §40.9's.
test/isolation/btreescan_serializable.spec is §40.5's write skew, and passes only with the page
lock; a step shows the read ran index-only with `Heap Fetches: 0`, so the conflict is the page
lock's.

**On the benchmark's tables** (2026-10-06): bench/quick.py's `fact` (5M rows) and `docs` (1M), warm,
through the node, with both of its settings off, and in heap mode (`enable_indexonlyscan = off`),
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF) three times each. `SELECT c20k, sum(c1m) FROM fact WHERE c20 = 3
GROUP BY c20k`: the lion index's scan and HashAggregate at `random_page_cost` 4 and 1.1 (the node
forced: the 5M-entry walk, §40.3). `... WHERE c200 = 17 GROUP BY c20k`: the same plan. `SELECT id,
payload FROM fact WHERE c200 = 17 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 2000` over `(id) INCLUDE (payload)`: the
node, index only, 400,000 entries walked and no heap read, against core's backward index scan with

payload FROM docs WHERE tags @> ARRAY['t1','t17'] ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 10` over `(id) INCLUDE
(payload)`: the node, index only, the set exact (§29.6) and `Heap Fetches: 0`. Timed on the dev
cluster after the probe was priced: the `c20 = 3` GROUP BY 217 to 247 ms through the lion index's
scan (the node forced: 973 to 1,002 ms), the `c200 = 17` one 40 to 48 ms (the node forced: 722 to
746); the LIMIT 2000 walk 28.8 to 29.6 ms through the node against 44 to 49 for core's backward scan
with a filter; the two-filter LIMIT 10 2.5 to 2.9 ms against 5.2 to 7.5; the `tags` LIMIT 10 over
`docs` 1.5 to 1.7 ms against 4.0 to 4.5.

### 40.8 Not done

- **The density gate's blind spot** (§40.4): members dense early in the order and the rest at its
  far end, under a LIMIT the early ones do not satisfy (a residual filter removes them, say), keep
  `distinct` at the uniform rate while the walk crosses the empty middle, so the gate never opens
  and the walk goes to the end where heap mode's rule would have switched.
- **The recheck from the heap is unpriced** (§40.3) for a source made inexact at run time (a
  lossy qual, a non-MVCC snapshot); its fetches are bounded by the members, every one of which
  heap mode fetches. A qual the set leaves to the recheck at plan time is priced since 2026-10-19.
- **Pending CI on 20.** `index_beginscan()`'s third argument and the `IndexScanDesc` fields the
  index-only walk reads (`xs_want_itup`, `xs_itup`, `xs_itupdesc`, `xs_hitup`) are taken as 16 to
  19 have them; an index-only walk whose `xs_want_itup` went unhonoured errors with "no index
  tuple returned", which the master job's btreescan run will tell.
- **A partial B-tree's predicate clause** stays in the filter (§40.1); dropping it as core's index
  scan does would need the switch's recheck to take the predicate on.
- **A faster probe.** Each entry's probe is a binary search over the set's container keys and then
  a membership test, about half of the 170 ns an entry (§40.3); a directory indexed by container key
  would find the container in O(1), and a bitset container's test is O(1) already where an array
  container's is a second binary search. The price above would then come down with it.
- **Expression columns** returning a value for a matching expression of the target.
- **The lazy set, the switch and the early stop in a parallel walk** (§40.9): the first two are
  off, the third is each participant's own and rarely fires.
- **Other heap reads a B-tree could spare.** The count pushdown's residual clauses (§10, "Residual
  clauses") are tested on each candidate's heap row even where a B-tree holds the clause's column;
  the plan competes on price with an aggregate over the walk, which wins where the heap reads cost
  more (on the synthetic table of §40.2, `count(*) ... WHERE b = 1 AND id % 7 = 3` ran in 252 ms
  over the walk against 800 ms for the pushdown's rechecks, medians of five). A partial B-tree's
  predicate column must be among its columns (§40.1) because the switch rechecks the predicate; an
  unordered or parallel walk never switches and could drop the clause. Reads by TID - the plain
  and bitmap scans of lion indexes, `lion_index_facets()`'s read of a few rows' keys, a BM25 scan -
  have no B-tree to turn to, since a B-tree is not searched by TID.


### 40.9 Parallel walks (2026-10-20)

A walk of a B-tree probed against lion's set is offered as a partial path too: the participants
of a Gather or a Gather Merge share core's parallel scan of the B-tree, which hands each of them
whole leaf pages in the walk's direction, as a Parallel Index Only Scan's participants get
theirs, and the set, built once.

    Finalize Aggregate
      ->  Gather
            Workers Planned: 2
            ->  Partial Aggregate
                  ->  Parallel Custom Scan (LionBtreeScan) on t
                        Index: t_pkey (index only)
                        Lion Cond: ((a = ANY ('{0,1}'::integer[])) AND (b = ANY ('{0,1}'::integer[])))
                        Lion Indexes: t_a, t_b

    Gather Merge
      ->  Parallel Custom Scan (LionOrdered) on t
            Ordered By: t_k (index only)
            Lion Cond: (c = 3)
            Lion Indexes: t_c

- **What qualifies** (`lo_parallel_ok()`): the relation may be read in a worker
  (`rel->consider_parallel`: its restriction clauses, which the node evaluates, and its target are
  parallel-safe, and it is not a temporary table), and the B-tree's access method has a parallel
  scan (`amcanparallel`). The lion column walks of §30.11 and a lionvec order (§44, which has a
  parallel scan of its own) are not divided. Every pair of §40.2, heap mode and index-only, ordered
  and not, is offered once more through `add_partial_path()`, its rows a participant's; core then
  builds the Gather and the Gather Merge above it, the partial aggregates, the parallel hash joins
