  with the walk on either side, and the parallel anti joins - §40.2's unordered paths are what these
  needed. A whole walk is `parallel_safe` with the relation, so that a worker may run it too.
- **Cost** (`lo_cost()` with `workers`), as `cost_index()` prices a parallel index scan: the
  workers are `compute_parallel_worker()`'s for the B-tree's pages and - in heap mode, or where the
  set's members are rechecked on the heap tuple - the heap pages the fetches read, an index-only
  walk's left out as core leaves an Index Only Scan's; the per-row CPU - the probe of each entry
  walked, the visibility map's test, the quals and the target - is divided by core's parallel
  divisor; the lion lookups and the set (the start-up), the B-tree's own cost and the heap's pages
  are each participant's whole. The partial path's rows are divided likewise.
- **The set, built once** (`lo_shared_set()`). A `LoShared` in the Gather's dynamic shared memory,
  the B-tree's parallel scan descriptor after it, holds the set's state. The participants that
  need the set build it together, a part of its container keys each ("Built in parts", below), as
  the serial node builds the whole, and copy each part into the query's DSA as one image while it
  fits the room a Parallel Hash's table would have - `get_hash_memory_limit()` for each participant
  planned, the leader among them (`lo_image_write()`: the container keys, each container's offset,
  the containers, and whether the part is exact); one with no part left sleeps on a condition
  variable while the others finish theirs (the wait event `LionOrderedSetBuild` on 17 and later,
  the generic `Extension` on 16), and then each reads the containers where they are
  (`lo_set_attach()`), with a directory, the container keys and the walk's visited bits of its own.
  A set larger than the room is built by each participant for itself, spilling as the serial
  node's does (§30.4), and so is every set under `pg_lion.enable_shared_set = off`. A builder's
  error ends the query: the leader rethrows it at its next interrupt check, which its wait makes,
  and its abort ends every worker.
- **What a participant does with an entry** is the serial node's, on the entries it is handed: the
  probe, the visibility map's test in index-only mode with a heap fetch for a page it does not call
  all-visible, the rechecks - the B-tree's under `xs_recheck`, and an inexact set's on the index
  tuple or, under `LO_FLAG_HEAPRECHECK`, on the heap tuple fetched for it (§40.4) - and the page's
  or the tuple's predicate lock.
- **Not in a parallel walk**: the lazy set (§30.4) - one set serves every participant, and each
  would reach other ranges first - and the fetch-and-sort switch, whose fetch of the members left
  would need every participant's; a parallel walk keeps the B-tree's order to its end, which a
  Gather Merge needs of each participant anyway. The early stop (§30.4, "Stopping early") is each
  participant's: it counts the members it met against the set's, which a participant meets all of
  only when the others met none, so it rarely fires; a count shared among them would need the
  met-before bits shared too.
- **Rescans.** Before a Gather's workers are launched again (`ReInitializeDSM`), the B-tree's
  parallel scan starts over (`index_parallelrescan()`) and the set's shared parts are freed, the
  leader's view of them let go first, to be built again by the next run, whose parameters may be
  others; the run is counted (`gen`), and a set a participant needs again in the same run - a
  lion Param changed under it, which no plan of this section's has - is its own. A Gather Merge that a LIMIT shut down and that is rescanned initialises its memory afresh.
- **EXPLAIN** names the node `Parallel Custom Scan (LionBtreeScan)` or `(LionOrdered)`. Under
  ANALYZE the counters are the leader's own and the workers' sums, which each worker adds as it
  shuts down and the leader takes as it does (a LIMIT that stops the Gather early leaves the
  workers' out, as §27's parallel node does); `Lion Set` shows the set as the leader had it, or its
  builders' when the leader took no part, `shared` when the participants read one copy, and `in N
  parts` when it was built in more than one. A walk
  that is not parallel-aware but ran in a worker only - under `debug_parallel_query`, or the inner
  side of a join a worker ran - prints no counters: they stayed in the worker, since a
  CustomScan's DSM hooks are called for a parallel-aware node alone, and the leader's zeros would
  mislead.

**Visibility.** §40.5's argument is per TID and holds in every participant. The snapshot is the
leader's, which every worker restores. The visibility map's bit is tested for each member after
the entry was read under the leaf page's lock, as in the serial walk, by whichever participant was
handed that page; the participant keeps its pin on the leaf while it tests the map
(`xs_want_itup`, nbtree's `dropPin` rule, which a parallel scan follows as a serial one does), so
VACUUM cannot free the heap slots the page's TIDs name until it has moved on. The set is built
after the query's snapshot was taken, as the serial node builds it, by whichever participant
builds it: §30.5's argument for a recycled TID rests on that order, not on the builder. Every
participant that reads the set reads the same members and exactness, and rechecks as the serial
node would. Under SERIALIZABLE the predicate locks a worker takes are the leader's transaction's
(core's parallel SSI): what the set's build reads of the lion indexes is locked as it is read (§9),
by whichever participant builds it, and each participant takes the heap page lock of each row it
returns without a heap visit.
test/isolation/btreescan_parallel_serializable.spec is §40.5's write skew read by parallel walks,
and must end in a serialization failure.

**Tests.** test/sql/btreescan_parallel.sql, on a synthetic 40,000-row table whose heap is several
times its B-trees, with every parallel cost at 0: each query run as CREATE TABLE AS - a plpgsql
cursor never runs in parallel - through the partial walk below its Gather or Gather Merge and
through the ordinary plan (the walks off, sequential scans only, serially), the answers compared in
order under an ORDER BY and as multisets otherwise, the node, its mode and the Gather named; and
the counters of each parallel walk, summed, against the serial walk's (the lazy set and the switch
off, a serial run first so that both meet the same index entries killed by an earlier heap fetch):
the members met, the heap fetches, the rows the recheck removed. ANDs, ORs, IN lists and
multi-key filters, a B-tree qual beside them, aggregates and a GROUP BY, both orders, a LIMIT, an
empty answer and heap mode; a vacuumed table (no heap fetch, the set built once and shared); rows
inserted in the transaction, HOT, INCLUDE-column, lion-column and key updates and deletes before
VACUUM, fetched by every participant; sets made inexact by a tsquery NOT, rechecked on the heap
tuple in every participant; the set each participant's own (`pg_lion.enable_shared_set = off`),
and shared at `hash_mem`'s least; rescans of a Gather on a nested loop's inner side and of a
Gather Merge a LIMIT shut down, a generic plan's and an initplan's parameter in the lion filter;
the leader taking no part;
the walk on either side of a parallel hash join and below an anti join; and §27's FK-side count
over the walk of its dimension, serially and as a parallel LionCount, for the inner, semi and anti
joins and a GROUP BY of a column the B-tree includes, chosen over the dimension's bitmap heap scan
at `random_page_cost` 4 and 1 and with the dimension's pages not all-visible.

**Measured** (2026-10-20, PostgreSQL 18.6 release build, a VM of four cores shared with other work,
`shared_buffers` 1 GB, warm; medians of five unless said). A synthetic table of 3,000,000 rows of
340 bytes - a 1.1 GB heap, 142,858 pages, and a 64 MB primary key of 8,228 pages - with lion
indexes on `a` (20 values), `b` (3) and `h` (2); `SELECT sum(id) ... WHERE <filter>`, the walk of
the primary key forced (every core scan off) and the plan without the walks:

| filter | walk, serial | 2 workers | 3 workers | without the walks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `h = 1` (50%) | 239 ms | 177 | 136 | 749 (bitmap heap scan); 244 (parallel sequential scan, 2 workers) |
| `a = 3` (5%) | 184 | 150 | 119 | 124 (the lion index's scan) |

The walk is CPU-bound - 60 to 80 ns an entry, the probe and the row - and divides less well than
its entries: 1.2 to 1.4 times faster on two workers and 1.5 to 1.8 on three, the set built before
the walk and the four cores busy. Planned with nothing disabled, the 50% filter takes the walk, parallel at two
workers; the 5% one takes it serially as well, warm the slower by 35 ms, the heap's pages priced
as reads (§40.3, "Warm and cold").

The set shared against one per participant, under `pg_lion.enable_shared_set`, for §40.2's `a IN
(<10 of 20 values>) AND b IN (<2 of 3>)`, a set of 2,233 containers that takes 26 to 32 ms to
build: 192 ms shared against 214 each its own on two workers, 152 against 197 on three (medians of
seven). Built in every participant at once, the set costs the same time on idle cores but as many
times the CPU and memory, which on four busy ones shows; shared, it is built once and held once.
So it is shared, and each builds its own only when it would not fit.

**Built in parts** (2026-10-26). The first participant to need the set built it whole while the
others waited, idle for the whole build - 1 to 2 s on the 85 GB dimension of §40.10, every worker
of the Gather waiting on one. An AND or an OR of sets is decided one container key at a time, so
the set's part at a range of container keys is the AND or the OR of its leaves' parts there, and
the whole set is its parts in key order: the participants can build it a range each, with nothing
to merge.

- **The parts** (`lo_parts_plan()`). The first participant to need the set cuts the relation's
  container keys - its blocks now, 64 to a key at 8 kB - into `LO_PARTS_EACH` (2) for each
  participant planned, at most `LO_SHARED_PARTS` (64), each of at least
  `pg_lion.shared_set_part_blocks` (16,384 blocks, 128 MB at 8 kB); the last part is open-ended,
  for the rows added since. A relation of fewer than twice that has its set in one part, built
  whole by one participant as before. Two for each participant, because the leader starts building
  before the workers have started and a participant that finishes early can take another; not
  more, because a part has a cost of its own: each walks a range's entries again ("Measured",
  below).
- **A part's build** (`lo_build_part()`). Each leaf's source is bounded to the part's keys
  (`lion_source_bound()`): a SETS stream is sought to the first key and left at the last; a LIST's
  batches and a WALK's entries are each sought as they open and left at the last key; a UNION's
  windows start at the first key and stop at the last; a WINDOW's other columns are sought
  likewise. A sparse segment can start below the key sought, and its keys below are skipped. The
  leaves are combined as for the whole. A part is exact when every leaf's source was; the set is
  exact when every part is. An index's scan is counted once, by the first part's build.
- **Taken, built, put in the DSA** (`lo_share_part()`). A participant takes the next part nobody
  has (`nextpart`, under the struct's spin lock), builds it in its own memory, copies it into the
  DSA when the room still has it, and lets its own copy go; the last part done ends the build
  (`LO_SHSET_SHARED`) and wakes the waiters. A part that does not fit the room ends the building:
  the parts nobody has taken are counted done, the last part done frees the ones put in the DSA,
  and each participant builds its own set (`LO_SHSET_OWN`). With no room at all
  (`pg_lion.enable_shared_set` off) nothing is built in parts. A participant's view
  (`lo_set_attach()`) reads each part's containers where they are, with the parts' container keys
  copied in order into a directory of its own - a set of one part reads its keys in place too.
- **What a waiter can wait on.** A participant takes a part only from inside the build, and
  finishes it without waiting on anything: the build reads lion indexes and its own memory, and no
  tuple queue. So every part taken ends, and the waiters with it, or the query ends with its
  builder's error.
- **The probe's set** (§40.10, "Parallel query") is built the same way: below a Gather a nested
  loop's probe is parallel-aware for its set alone.
- **The price** is not changed. A walk's (above) charges each participant the whole build, which
  a set built in parts takes about the participants' share of; a probe's spreads the build over
  the loop's scans, which at a participant's share of the scans is the build divided by core's
  parallel divisor - what the parts take of each, as long as the set has parts enough for every
  participant. A set of one part (a relation under 256 MB) is built by one participant while the
  others wait, and that probe's price is low by the divisor, on the cheapest builds.

**Measured** (2026-10-26, PostgreSQL 18.6 release build; the four-core VM shared with another
benchmark, load 2 to 3; a timer around `lo_shared_set()` in each participant, the longest
participant's time until the set is in hand, medians of five). A 4,000,000-row dimension of 665
MB - 85,107 blocks, 1,330 container keys - probed by a parallel nested loop of 10,000 outer rows,
two workers planned, at 1,024-block parts so that the parts are `LO_PARTS_EACH` for each
participant:

| set | whole, one builder | 1 part each (3) | 2 each (6) | 4 each (12) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| tags overlap of four, a bool, two IN lists (a SETS source each) | 10.1 ms (7.6 to 26.8) | 10.7 | 7.9 | 7.6 |
| a range over 3,000 of a column's 10,000 values, beside a bool | 119 (90 to 142) | 94 | 106 | 105 |

The workers start a few milliseconds after the leader, so on a build of ten the leader builds
most of the parts; a range's every part walks its 3,000 entries again, 25 to 30 ms a part on this
table, so that more parts cost more than they divide. At the default part size the table's set
is 5 parts, 88 to 104 ms for the range against 130 to 171 whole. A build of seconds - the 85 GB
dimension's - leaves the workers' start a smaller share of it; this machine holds no such table to
measure. The parts take the memory one set took, where each participant building its own took it
as many times over.

**Tests.** test/sql/btreescan_parallel.sql, section 11: at 64-block parts - six for the three
participants planned - the answers and the counters of parallel walks against the serial walk's
over a SETS source, a WALK of a range, a LIST longer than a batch, a UNION of a query that needs
every row, an OR, an empty answer and a WINDOW of a long range beside another column's set in one
index; the leader taking no part; no room; a Gather run again, its parts built again each run.
test/sql/btreescan_param.sql, section 8, the same for a parallel nested loop's probe, and its
answers with Memoize enabled (chosen over the probe or not by a near tie of the prices, which 18
and 19 break differently).


### 40.10 A nested loop's probe: the walk parameterized (2026-10-23)

The shape is

    SELECT d.id, count(*) AS n FROM dim d JOIN fact f ON f.dim_id = d.id
     WHERE <clauses lion indexes on d answer> AND <a selective filter on f>
     GROUP BY d.id ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 100

where the fact side's filter leaves few rows against the dimension's, so that core's plan is a
nested loop over them into the dimension's primary key: an Index Scan that fetches each outer row's
dimension row from the heap to test the filter on it, and throws most of them away. On a production
table of this shape - an 85 GB dimension heap, filters of array overlap, a bool and two enum
equalities - that was 603,000 heap fetches, 77% of them rejected by the Filter, read cold. Nothing
of §40 so far could be the loop's inner side: every path the node built was unparameterized (§30.8
declined parameterized paths, "an inner side needs no order"), and the walk of the whole primary key
under a hash join reads every entry of the key where the loop wants six hundred thousand. What the
inner side needs is not an order but §40's index-only half: the outer row's key looked up in the
B-tree, the entry tested against lion's set of the dimension's filter, the visibility map asked, the
values taken from the index tuple, and the heap read only for pages not all-visible.

    Nested Loop
      ->  Index Scan using fact_tsv on fact f
            Index Cond: (tsv @@ '''w7'' & ''x3'''::tsquery)
      ->  Custom Scan (LionBtreeScan) on dim d
            Index: dim_pkey (index only)
            Index Cond: (d.id = f.dim_id)
            Lion Cond: ((d.tags && '{t1,t3,t5,t7,t9}'::text[]) AND d.verified AND (d.hue = 'green'::hue) AND (d.grade = 'alpha'::grade))
            Lion Indexes: dim_tags, dim_verified, dim_hue, dim_grade

The probe is a `LionBtreeScan` parameterized by the outer relations, as core's parameterized Index
Scan is: its B-tree quals include the join clauses (`id = outer.fk`), and each rescan is a descent
to the outer row's key. Its set is built from the inner relation's restriction clauses that lion
answers - never from a join clause or an outer row's Param - once per execution of the plan, and
kept for every scan the loop makes. A scan then costs a descent, a membership test per entry, a
visibility-map test per member and the values from the index tuple.

- **Which paths** (`lo_btree_paths()`, the probe loop of `lo_set_rel_pathlist()`). Core's
  own: the scratch copy of the relation that sees one B-tree (§40.2) now keeps the relation's join
  clauses (`lo_scratch_rel()`'s `joins`), so `create_index_paths()` makes for that B-tree the
  parameterized IndexPaths it makes for an inner side - the join clauses as index clauses, beside the
  restriction clauses the B-tree matches: `(grp, k)` under `grp = f.g AND k = 3` probes both
  columns. (Its equivalence-class joins it made all along: `match_eclass_clauses_to_index()` asks
  `index->rel`, the relation itself, not the copy. Those paths were then dropped - and, being paths,
  stopped §40.2's whole walk of a B-tree core made no unparameterized path of, which kept a primary
  key's whole walk out of every join on it; the fallback now looks for an unparameterized path, and
  that bug is gone.) The parameterized paths kept are forward ones (a backward twin walks the same
  entries), one per parameterization and set of index clauses (`lo_same_indexclauses()`: an
  IndexClause has no `equal()` support), that pass `lo_indexpath_ok()`. Each is paired with every
  lion access of §40.2, which are unparameterized - built from the restriction clauses alone - and
  priced, less the pairs that add nothing (`lo_lion_adds()`); the residual (`lo_residual()`) is taken
  over the restriction clauses and the parameterization's join clauses (`ppi_clauses`), a join
  clause the B-tree's index clause answers left out - the same RestrictInfo, or one of the same
  equivalence class (`lo_ord_answers()`), as `create_indexscan_plan()` drops it as redundant - and
  the B-tree must cover what is left (§40.1), the outer side's Vars being Params. The path carries
  `get_baserel_parampathinfo()`'s ParamPathInfo and its rows, claims no order (an inner side's order
  is no use to a nested loop, and a merge join takes unparameterized inputs) and is never partial. Core
  then builds the nested loops, and the Memoizes above them, as for its own parameterized scans.
  §30.1's precondition that the relation have no LATERAL references stands: a LATERAL relation's
  paths are parameterized by what it references, not by join clauses, and the node's others are not.
- **The set** is the relation's, as for an unparameterized walk: the lion access's lookups, built
  after the snapshot is taken, held in the query's memory, and rebuilt on a rescan only when a Param
  of the lion quals changed (§30.4) - which an outer row's never is, since no join clause reaches the
  lion side. A correlated subquery's or a generic plan's Param in the lion filter still rebuilds it
  for each value, counted in `Lion Set`'s builds. It is built lazily (§30.4, "The set, lazily") when
  the loop's scans together are expected to meet fewer than `LO_SWITCH_MIN_WALK` (10,000) entries -
  a few outer rows probing a few keys, the memo of the keys probed kept across the scans - and at once
  otherwise (`LO_FLAG_BUILD`).
- **Cost** (`lo_cost()` with `loops` and `scans`; `lo_probe_scans()`). A scan's price is §40.3's
  with the walk the parameterized IndexPath's: core's `indextotalcost` for one scan (the descent,
  and the B-tree's pages amortized over the loop count by core's `amcostestimate`), each entry's
  probe at `LO_PROBE_TUPLES` × `cpu_tuple_cost` + `cpu_operator_cost`, a member's visibility-map
  test at `cpu_operator_cost`, the residual and the target per row; and the heap pages as
  `cost_index()` prices a parameterized index-only scan's - the fetches of all the loops' scans
  through the Mackert and Lohman formula, scaled by `1 - allvisfrac`, every fetch random, divided
  by the loops - which on a vacuumed table is nothing, where core's Index Scan pays a random page
  per outer row. The loops are what core's `get_loop_count()` makes of the parameterization: the
  fewest rows of the outer relations, a semi join's inner side as its distinct values. The set's
  build (the lookups, the copy, the spill) is the start-up, divided by the scans `S` it is spread
  over: core's nested loop charges an inner path's start-up again on every rescan (`cost_rescan()`
  of a CustomPath), so `S` scans of `build / S` charge it once. `S` is the loops when
  `enable_memoize` is off, and otherwise the distinct values the outer side hands the probe,
  `Min(D, loops)` with `D` from `estimate_num_groups()` over the outer side of each join clause (a
  clause Memoize cannot key on gives the loops): a Memoize rescans its inner side for a value it
  has not cached alone, and `cost_memoize_rescan()` charges a scan's price per expected miss, so a
  build spread over the loops would be charged only `misses / loops` of it in the plan core likes
  best. Spread over the distinct values, the Memoize's plan pays the build once and the plan without
  it `loops / D` times, though it builds once too: an overcharge that tips the choice only where the
  values repeat, and there the Memoize's `D` scans against the loops' are the faster plan anyway.
  `lo_margin` (§39) applies as to every `LionBtreeScan`: the price divided by
  `pg_lion.pushdown_margin`, 1 by default. Where the outer side is small the build is not spread
  far enough: three or twenty outer rows take core's Index Scan, which fetches their rows, eighty
  the probe, and a dimension of a few hundred rows takes a hash join of a sequential scan
  (test/sql/btreescan_param.sql, section 10).
- **The build's price** (`lo_build_excess()`). §30.3 prices the lookups as the lion access's bitmap
  paths (`cost_bitmap_tree_node()`, `lioncostestimate()`), a `cpu_index_tuple_cost` a TID - what a
  lion index's scan hands a bitmap. The set's build hands nothing over a TID at a time: each leaf's
  posting sets are read and combined a container at a time (`lo_build_leaf()`,
  `lo_set_combine()`), a dense container's members costing nothing apiece. For the walks of §40 the
  walk is most of the price and this did not decide; for the probe the build is the whole fixed
  cost, and it decided wrongly: four dense filters on a 6M-row dimension of 4,688 containers were
  priced 88,000 and built in 57 ms, on a 50M-row one of 12,808 containers 715,000 and 80 ms - 1.5
  and 0.8 us a container of a posting set, against the 10 ns a TID stands for at the reference's 500
  units a millisecond, and the error grows with the rows a container holds. So the probe charges a
  leaf at most `LO_BUILD_PIECE_TIDS` (80) TIDs a container of each entry it reads - 0.8 us a piece,
  the lower of the two measurements, where a tie should fall - and takes its TIDs past that back
  out; a sparse leaf keeps its price, and the other walks keep §30.3's.
- **Cold reads, declined.** §39's "A nested loop's cold reads" prices a loop's pages the cache
  cannot hold at `pg_lion.cold_page_cost`, and a probe saves core's scan one heap page an outer row.
  Taking the probe against core's scan that way (its leaf, its members' pages not all-visible and
  the lion indexes' pages once for the set, against core's leaf and heap page) was built and
  measured: with the build priced as above it moved none of the plans measured below - the probe's
  own price is the lower wherever its cold reads are the fewer - and on the regression tables, where
  the lion indexes' pages over a few dozen scans outweigh core's heap pages, it never applied. It
  was taken out rather than kept untested.
- **Execution** (`LO_FLAG_PROBE`, `st->probe`). Each rescan restarts the walk with its keys
  evaluated again (core's run-time keys, `ExecIndexBuildScanKeys()`), so a NULL outer key makes a
  strict operator's key unsatisfiable and the descent finds nothing, as in core's Index Scan. A
  probe marks nothing: the met-before marks of §30.4 are counted for the early stop and the
  fetch-and-sort switch, neither of which a probe has, and the visited bits' directory, remade for
  every scan, is as long as the set's places - O(the set) a rescan for a scan of a few entries. A TID
  met twice in one scan is then fetched twice; the second time it names a tuple written after the
  snapshot (§30.4, "A recycled TID"), on a page whose all-visible bit the write cleared, which the
  heap's visibility check skips. The lazy set's memo is not walked at each scan's reset for the same
  reason. The visibility map's buffer is kept across rescans, as core's Index Only Scan keeps
  `ioss_VMBuffer`: the next outer key is often on the same map page. `lo_begin()` refuses a plan
  that marks a probe parallel-aware, a lion column's walk, a lionvec order, setless or sorted.
- **Memoize, and rescans with no Param changed.** A nested loop puts its parameters in the inner
  side's `chgParam` for every outer row. Under a Memoize the probe's `chgParam` accumulates while the
  cache answers, and the probe is rescanned by its next `ExecProcNode()` with all of them; a rescan
  of the Memoize with none changed - its parent rescanned with the same values, a cursor moved back
  - rescans the probe directly (`ExecReScanMemoize()`) with `chgParam` empty. Either way the set is
  kept unless a lion Param is in `chgParam` (`lo_rescan()`): the probe restarts its walk with the
  same keys and the same set. Memoize's own purge on a non-key Param is untouched by any of this.
- **EvalPlanQual and row marks.** A row mark of the dimension - `FOR UPDATE OF d`, `FOR SHARE`, or
  the `ROW_MARK_REFERENCE` every other relation of a locking query or an UPDATE gets - puts its
  `ctid` in the target, which no index returns (§40.1): no probe is offered, and EvalPlanQual never
  meets one. `lo_recheck()` would evaluate the original clauses, the join clause with the outer row's
  Param among them, and the lion qual, as for any walk.
- **Parallel query.** The probe is `parallel_safe` when the relation is (`rel->consider_parallel`),
  so a partial nested loop below a Gather runs it whole in each participant, the outer side divided
  - a scan is a descent for one key, with nothing to divide. Core calls a CustomScan's DSM hooks
  for a parallel-aware node alone, so the probe is parallel-aware for its set: the join hook
  (`lion_ordered_join_probes()`, 2026-10-26) gives each partial nested loop core made over a probe
  - or over a Memoize over one - a copy of the probe marked `parallel_aware`, its own path left as
  it was for the serial loops. Its participants then build the set together and read it from the
  Gather's shared memory (§40.9, "Built in parts"), where each had built its own; the struct has no
  parallel scan of the B-tree, each participant descending it for its own outer rows. EXPLAIN
  names it `Parallel Custom Scan (LionBtreeScan)`, and its ANALYZE counters are the participants'
  sums, as a parallel walk's. A lazy set (above) stays each participant's own - the containers its
  own outer rows reach - and is built whole for itself when its probes have cost a build.
- **Partitions.** A partitioned dimension's Append takes each partition's probe when its
  parameterization is the Append's (`reparameterize_path()` gives a CustomPath none). A
  partitionwise join's nested loop joins a fact partition to the dimension partition of the same
  keys, whose probe is parameterized by the fact's parent and is moved to the partition by core
  (`reparameterize_path_by_child()`: at path time on 16, at plan creation on 17 and later) through
  `ReparameterizeCustomPathByChild` (`lo_reparameterize()`): the B-tree's IndexPath is
  reparameterized by core's own code; the lion access is the partition's and unparameterized, and
  the column mapping the B-tree's.
- **EXPLAIN** is §40.6's `LionBtreeScan` with core's `Index Cond`: the index quals with the key on
  the left, which core's Index Scan prints (its `indexqualorig` is that list) - `(d.id = f.dim_id)`
  however the query wrote the join. Every walk prints them now (`LO_EXPR_ORDQUALS` in place of the
  original clauses, `LO_EXPR_ORDORIG`, which stay the recheck): `100 > k` as `(k < 100)`, a prefix
  `LIKE` as the range it is searched by, with the `LIKE` in the Filter, as core's. No expected output
  of the suite changed; the old display printed such a `LIKE` in both. Under ANALYZE
  `Index Entries Walked`, `Lion Set Hits` and `Heap Fetches` are the sums over every scan, and
  `Lion Set` shows the set built once - `48 containers, exact`, with no builds count - or `N builds`
  where a lion Param made it rebuild; a Memoize above it prints its own hits and misses.
- **Correctness.** Per scan, §30.5's and §40.5's arguments hold unchanged: the B-tree's entries and
  the set's members are both HOT chains' root TIDs, the visible version reached from a root has the
  index's values, the visibility map's bit is tested under the leaf's pin, and a row returned
  without a heap visit takes the predicate lock of its heap page. Across scans the snapshot is the
  execution's, so a set built after it serves every scan of it, a cursor's pieces included.
  test/isolation/btreescan_param_serializable.spec is §40.5's write skew read through the loop's
  probes (two HOT updates of rows the other transaction read index-only): it must fail.
- **Settings.** No new one. `pg_lion.enable_btree_scan` gates the probe with the other unordered
  walks; core's `enable_indexscan` disables it as it disables the B-tree's own scans (§40.2), and
  `enable_indexonlyscan = off` takes it away, since the probe is index-only or nothing.
  `pg_lion.enable_plain_scan` and `pg_lion.enable_ordered_scan` do not touch it: it is neither a
  scan of a lion index nor an ordered walk. `enable_memoize` decides `S` above. With
  `enable_nestloop = off` the probe is still offered, and on 18 it then costs a parallel plan its
  partial hash join: 18's `add_partial_path_precheck()` compares a new partial path with the join
  relation's existing ones by cost alone, so the disabled partial nested loop over the probe, cheaper
  than the partial hash join, keeps that join out, and the plan is a hash join of two Gathers; 19 and
  later compare the disabled nodes first and take the hash join (test/sql/btreescan_parallel.sql's
  section 9 switches the probe off with the loop). Not offering the probe while nested loops are
  disabled would avoid it, and was not done: a disabled path is still the plan where nothing else
  joins, and the quirk is 18's alone.
- **A count over the join** (§27, §39). A `LionCount` meets core's plan above the join in the
  competitor's units, and the competitor (`lion_competitor_path()`) is core's cheapest path with no
  lion path inside: where the probe's nested loop is the join's cheapest path, every aggregate core
  builds over it holds lion, the competitor is none, and the count is priced at rate 1 where a hash
  join's 0.5 had been. test/sql/rangesource.sql's join of a ten-row dimension then planned the
  probe's loop over its count, 2.1 ms against 1.8; that section now runs with the walks off.

**Declined, and why.**

- *A heap-mode probe* (a B-tree that does not cover): a scan would fetch every member's heap tuple,
  which is core's Index Scan with lion's test in place of its Filter - the heap fetches of the members
  saved only where the set rejects most of them, and a plan that loses to core's wherever the set
  does not; the index-only probe is the one that removes the heap from the loop.
- *A parameterized ordered walk* (`LionOrdered`), a lion column's walk and a lionvec order: an inner
  side's order is no use to a nested loop, a merge join takes its inputs unparameterized, and a lion
  column has no descent to a key.
- *A set from the join clause* - the outer row's key in the lion side: a set per outer row, which is
  §30.4's rebuild per Param at a loop's scale; the B-tree's descent does that part.

**Not done.**

- The price of the build does not shrink with a LIMIT above the loop: a fraction of the loop's
  scans still pays its share of a build that happened whole on the first.
- Duplicate outer keys with `enable_memoize` on but no Memoize chosen are charged the build
  `loops / D` times; it is built once.
- A parallel nested loop's participants build the set together (§40.9, "Built in parts"), and
  are charged a participant's share of it; a set of one part, a relation under 256 MB, is built by
  one while the others wait.
- The container price of the build is the probe's alone. The walks of §40 keep §30.3's TID price,
  so a hash join over the dimension's whole covering walk carries a build priced several times the
  probe's for the same set: at 600,000 outer rows into 6M dimension rows the two plans tie on price
  and the probe's loop, chosen, runs twice as long (below). Refitting §30.3's price moves every
  walk's plans, each to be timed against the plan it replaces.
- A build is not repaid by warm heap fetches: 14,000 outer rows into the 6M-row dimension take the
  probe (a 57 ms build) and run 1.7 times as long as core's loop with its heap fetches in the cache.
  The probe is for a dimension the cache does not hold, and the planner's page costs are the
  user's statement of that.

**Tests.** test/sql/btreescan_param.sql, on a 100,000-row dimension - its heap several times its
primary key - with lion indexes on an array, a bool and two enum columns and a `(grp, k) INCLUDE
(id)` B-tree, and a 200,000-row fact table with a lion tsvector index and every fiftieth key NULL:
every query run through the probe (hash and merge joins off, lion's paths priced at a thousandth)
and through the ordinary plan (the walks off), the answers compared as multisets, the plan's shape
and Index Cond named. The production shape, chosen with nothing disabled (`Index Entries Walked:
714`, `Lion Set Hits: 135`, `Heap Fetches: 0`, the set built once), and core's plan with the switch
off; a few outer rows, NULL outer keys, a LEFT JOIN and an empty set; repeated outer keys with a
Memoize (`Hits: 26572  Misses: 2000`, two thousand walks) and without (28,572 walks), the set built
once either way; the two-column B-tree with a parameterized leader and a constant second column; a
generic plan's Param in the lion filter, a subquery rescanned with its Param in the fact's filter
(built once) and in the lion filter (built for each value); a cursor fetched in pieces; pages not
all-visible - inserts, deletes, HOT updates and lion-column updates in the transaction, then after
it and after VACUUM (`Heap Fetches: 0`); a parallel nested loop (CREATE TABLE AS, Gather over a
nested loop over a Parallel Seq Scan and the probe, parallel-aware: its set built in parts and its
counters the participants' sums, against the serial probe's; a Gather run again; no room to share;
few outer rows, each participant's lazy set; Memoize enabled); a partitionwise join of hash-partitioned
tables, the probe reparameterized per partition; the price with nothing disabled (above): 3, 20
and 80 outer rows and a 300-row dimension; and the settings - `enable_indexscan` and
`enable_indexonlyscan` off, `pg_lion.enable_plain_scan` and `pg_lion.enable_ordered_scan` off
(the probe stays), a column no B-tree with the key covers, `FOR UPDATE OF f` and `FOR SHARE OF d`
(no probe). Section 2 also has a semi and an anti join, the Index Cond printed key first however
the clause was written. test/isolation/btreescan_param_serializable.spec is the write skew above.

**Measured** (2026-10-23; PostgreSQL 16.15, the dev cluster: `shared_buffers` 2 GB, a VM of four
cores and 15 GB shared with other work; warm, the tables in the OS cache; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING
OFF), medians of five or seven). Two synthetic dimensions with the production shape's filters - an
array overlap of five tags of ten, a bool true in two thirds of the rows, enum equalities of 70% and
80%: 18.7% of the rows pass - each joined from a fact table whose tsvector search picks the outer
rows, `GROUP BY d.id ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 100`: 6M rows of 410 bytes (a 2.3 GB heap, a 129 MB
primary key) under 4M fact rows, and 50M rows of 134 bytes (6.4 GB, 1 GB) under 2M.

| dimension | outer rows | planned | its time | core's plan, the walks off | core's nested loop |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6M | 14,286 | the probe | 142 ms | its nested loop, 84 ms | (the same) |
| 6M | 100,000 | the probe | 536 | hash join over a bitmap heap scan, 3,206 | 655 |
| 6M | 300,000 | the probe | 1,573 | hash join, 3,420 | 2,199 |
| 6M | 600,000 | the probe under a Memoize | 3,322 | hash join, 3,662 | 5,302 |
| 50M | 7,143 | core's nested loop | 54 | (the same) | (the same) |
| 50M | 50,000 | the probe | 352 | its nested loop, 318 | (the same) |
| 50M | 150,000 | the probe | 1,016 | its nested loop, 1,045 | (the same) |
| 50M | 300,000 | the probe | 1,874 | hash join over a bitmap heap scan, 12,510 | - |

The 600,000-row line's other plan with the walks on, a hash join over the dimension's whole
covering walk, ran in 1,627 ms ("Not done"). The set took 57 ms to build on 6M rows and 80 ms on
50M, warm (84 and 170 ms the first time); a scan of the loop, the descent, the probe and the
visibility map's test, 4 to 5 us, within a microsecond of core's Index Only Scan rescanned for the
same keys without a filter (2.56 s for 600,000). Warm, then, the probe ties core's nested loop at
0.1 to 0.3% of the 50M rows and is 1.1 to 6.7 times faster where core's plan reads the dimension's
heap whole. What it is for is the cold case, which a table in the OS cache cannot show: at 150,000
outer rows of the 50M table core's Index Scan read 139,693 pages from outside `shared_buffers` and
the probe 61,753, the primary key's leaves and the lion indexes; on a dimension of 85 GB each of
core's is a synchronous read from the device, and the probe reads none of them. A
500M-row dimension was not built: its set's build grows with the heap's containers, 0.8 to 1.5 us
each of each posting set, some 1 to 2 s for 85 GB under four filters.

### 40.11 A correlated subquery's calls (2026-10-23)

The shape is

    SELECT d.id,
           (SELECT count(*) FROM fact f
             WHERE f.dim_id = d.id AND f.doc @@ '<a tsquery>'::tsquery) AS n
      FROM dim d WHERE <a filter on d>

or the same subquery as an `EXISTS`, or a scalar sub-select of another aggregate (`max(f.id)`):
a subquery that refers to the query around it, which the executor runs again for every outer row,
the outer row's value arriving as an exec Param. Core plans such a subquery as a query of its own,
with no loop count, prices each of its scans for one call, and `cost_subplan()` charges the plan's
price again per call. For core's scans that is the convention a heap page is charged in. For
lion's it charged every call the pages of the first: the posting trees a sought set reads, the
directory leaves its keys are looked up in, a set that §40.10's probe builds once and keeps across
rescans - the parts of a nested loop's inner side that core's parameterized paths spread over their
loops (`index_pages_fetched()` with the loop count, `cost_index()`), and that a correlated
subquery repeats exactly as a loop does. On a fact table with a lion index on the key and a
tsvector and a covering B-tree on the key, a correlated count over a thousand outer rows was
priced at a call as the same count in a prepared statement's generic plan, and the subquery's
lion paths lost to core's B-tree scans they beat inside a join of the same rows.

So a lion path whose quals hold an outer query's exec Param is priced as the inner side of a nested
loop over an assumed number of calls.

- **The calls** (`lion_outer_param_loops()`, lion_selfuncs.c). The subquery's exec Params are
  found in its quals (RestrictInfos and IndexClauses looked into) and each is looked up in the
  `plan_params` of the query levels above, where `replace_outer_var()` lists the outer Var it
  stands for while the subquery is planned, with that level's range table index. The calls are
  the rows of the Var's relation, and of several relations the fewest, as `get_loop_count()`
  takes the fewest rows of a parameterized path's outer relations. The outer level is still being
  planned and its relations not yet sized, so the rows are the relation's own -
  `pg_class.reltuples` scaled to its pages now (`estimate_rel_size()`), before the outer query's
  restrictions, read once per planner run (the run cache of §33). A filter on the outer relation
  makes the calls fewer than that, and the price a call's share of more calls than there are:
  index pages are spread further than they will be, which, as for a parameterized scan, matters
  only where the index is larger than `effective_cache_size` says the cache holds. Restricting the
  outer relation would need its clauses' selectivity before its level has its paths; it was not
  done.
- **What is not a loop.** A Param that is not an outer relation's Var - an InitPlan's output, an
  outer aggregate or PlaceHolderVar, a prepared statement's own (`PARAM_EXTERN`, its generic
  plan's `$1`) - is evaluated once, or once per execution, and its scan keeps the price of one
  call. A relation of no known size (a subquery's, a function's, a table neither vacuumed nor
  analyzed that `estimate_rel_size()` makes nothing of) gives no calls either.
- **The lion index's own scans** (`lioncostestimate()`). `genericcostestimate()` takes the loop
  count times the calls, so the directory leaves and the pages it prorates are spread over both;
  the price of a set AND (§29.11, "One price for the AND of sets") spreads its leaves and posting
  pages the same way (`setand.leafpages + setand.setpages`), its CPU a call's. The heap is core's,
  which prices a subquery's heap pages for one call, and `lion_plain_heap_correlation()` keeps
  core's loop count.
- **The walk of a covering B-tree** (`lo_cost()`, lion_ordered.c). The subquery's walk is a
  probe, as §40.10's: its B-tree's descents and pages priced by the B-tree's `amcostestimate`
  at the calls times the loops, the build priced by containers (`lo_build_excess()`), and the
  build's start-up divided by the calls as well as by §40.10's `scans`: a set no Param reaches is
  built once and kept for every call (`lo_rescan()` rebuilds it only when a lion Param changed). A
  set whose Lion Cond holds the outer Param - the subquery's key is in a lion column too - is built
  again at every call, as `Lion Set`'s `N builds` shows; its lookups' pages alone are spread over
  the calls (`lo_lion_amortized()`: each leaf of the lion access priced again at the calls, the
  difference taken off), the build's CPU a call's. Beside it the walk is offered the set without
  the Param, built once (§40.12, "A set without the key"). An InitPlan's Param in the Lion Cond is
  set once per execution, before the calls, and rebuilds nothing: only a Param the levels above
  hand down (`lion_has_outer_param()`, their `plan_params`) counts. The heap's pages are a call's,
  as core's.
- **The count** (`lion_cost_count_rel_one()`, `lion_count_rel_calls_share()`, lion_plan_cost.c). A
  `LionCount` whose WHERE holds the Param is located again at every call (its rescan re-locates
  everything), so nothing is built once; the pages it reads - the directory leaves at random, an IN
  list's buckets, the walked and the sought posting pages - are spread over the calls as fetches at
  random from the indexes its WHERE reads (`index_pages_fetched()` of the pages times the calls over
  those indexes' pages, divided back), the CPU of the lookups, the merges and the counts a call's,
  and the heap a recheck reads a call's.
- **Unchanged.** `cost_subplan()`: a SubPlan's price is still its plan's per call, and the whole of
  the change is what a call costs. A join's paths, which the planner sees inside their loop, carry
  Vars and no exec Params and are priced as they were; a parameterized path's own loop count is
  core's as before, the calls multiplying it only inside a correlated subquery. No setting: the
  price follows the shape, and the switches that remove the paths (`pg_lion.enable_count_pushdown`,
  `pg_lion.enable_btree_scan`, `pg_lion.enable_plain_scan`) remove them here too.

**Measured** (2026-10-23; the test's tables: 100,208 dimension rows, 300,000 fact rows - eight keys
of 5,000 rows, two hundred of 300 and the rest one to three - a lion index on the key and a
three-word tsvector, a B-tree on the key including `id`; the subquery called for the 1,003 keys of
one group; warm, `effective_cache_size` the default 4 GB). A call's price, before and after, the
generic plan's being what a call cost before:

| subquery's scan | a call, generic plan | a call, correlated | chosen there instead |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LionCount` | 11.6 | 2.3 to 3.0 | - |
| the lion index's Index Scan (the count off) | (core's bitmap scan of the B-tree, 16.3) | 6.3 | core's bitmap scan |
| `LionBtreeScan` (the count and the lion index's scans off) | (core's Index Scan, 16.5) | 2.8 | core's Index Scan |

The table being warm and small, the plans' times are close: 16 to 20 ms for the count, 19 ms for
the walk against core's Index Scan's 22, and 37 ms for the lion index's Index Scan against 17 for a
bitmap scan of it and 22 for core's Index Scan - a lion index scan's rescan costs a few dozen
microseconds of CPU that §29.11 prices, and that the cache hides from nothing here. What the change
prices is the index pages a cold loop reads once rather than at every call.

**Not done.** The outer relation's restrictions (above). A subquery's heap pages stay a call's
each: core's convention for its own scans, which lion's are compared with. A SubPlan core hashes
(`hashed SubPlan`, its Params none) is run once and is not a loop; a correlated subquery under a
Memoize does not exist in core's plans.

**Tests.** test/sql/correlated.sql: the correlated count, its price at a call under half the
generic plan's and an InitPlan's Param priced as the generic plan's; the lion index's Index Scan
and the walk chosen in the subquery where the generic plan takes core's bitmap and index scans; a
scalar `max()` sub-select and an `EXISTS` through the walk; the walk with an InitPlan's tsquery in
its Lion Cond, its set built once and kept through every call; every answer compared with core's plan, the lion
paths off; and the join of the same rows, its plans unchanged.

### 40.12 A correlated subquery's skewed key, in lion's units (2026-10-24)

The shape is §40.11's, on a skewed key column, and capped:

    SELECT d.pk,
           (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT 1 FROM fact f
                                   WHERE f.fk = d.pk AND f.tsv @@ '<a tsquery>'::tsquery
                                   LIMIT 21) s) AS n
      FROM dim d WHERE <a filter on d> ...

a count a row shows as "20 or more", or the plain count, in a page of a query with an `EXISTS`, an
outer join and an `ORDER BY ... LIMIT`. The subquery's scan equates the key to the outer row's
value, a probe of a key the plan does not know: on a skewed column it meets the rows §33's figure
has, not core's rows per key, and lion prices its probes there and puts the price back into core's
units by its competitor's two prices (§39, R1). A correlated subquery's level has no loop to weigh
it against; the competitor is the relation's own cheapest path (`lion_skew_rel_note()`), and the
comparison is fair only where both sides of it are priced at the same rows and the same cap.

**The competitor is core's own scan.** The scale of an unparameterized scan of a relation whose
restrictions equate a skewed key to a value the plan does not know is worked out once a planner
run, at the top of lion's `set_rel_pathlist_hook`, against the cheapest of:

- the relation's paths that read no lion index, are no custom path of lion's and are not disabled;
- core's index paths and sequential scan built again on a copy of the relation that sees its other
  indexes alone (`lion_skew_scratch()`): by then `add_path()` has dropped the core paths that an
  AM scan of the lion index beat at core's rows.

The relation is one core builds index paths for, as the copy builds them again, and with the scan
core plans for it (as `lo_rel_ok()` has it): a plain table or a materialized view, not an
inheritance parent, whose rows are its children's Append, nor a parent whose children the query
does not reach (`lion_rel_is_unexpanded_parent()`, §23), nor a sampled relation, which core reads
by its sample alone, nor one already proven empty, whose pages the planner leaves out of
`root->total_table_pages`, which `cost_index()` asserts they are in. Such a relation keeps core's
rows.

An AM scan of a lion index is lion's plan, not its competitor. Were it the competitor, it would
keep core's rows, its scale would be 1, and every lion path of the relation would keep core's rows
with it: in `test/sql/correlated_skew.sql`, where the AM's plain scan is the cheapest at core's
rows, the count would be priced at 2.36 a call, against the 0.12 it is priced at against core's
scan, with the AM's plain scans on or off.

**The AM's scans in the same units** (`lion_skew_am_paths()`, `lioncostestimate()`). Where the scale
is below 1, the relation's unparameterized paths whose index scans are all of lion indexes and whose
index clauses equate the key are taken out, serial and partial. The lion indexes' paths are built
again on a copy of the relation that sees them alone, with `lion_skew_am_rel` set, under which
`lioncostestimate()` prices a scan whose index clauses equate the key at their factor
(`lion_skew_am_factor()`):

- the index tuples and the pages `genericcostestimate()` prorates, at the selectivity times the
  factor (`lion_cost_prorate()`, the tail of `lion_cost_canonical_sel()`);
- each set of the AND at its clause's factor (`lion_cost_set_and()`'s `skewed`), the key's set at
  the rows a probed key meets, the others at their own;
- the heap, which core prices from the selectivity the AM returns.

Each such path's run is then cut to the share a count of rows takes (below), and the whole
multiplied by the scale (`lion_skew_reprice()`; before PostgreSQL 18 a disabled path's
`disable_cost` is left whole). A partial path takes the scale alone. A plain scan's remainder
(§29.11) is priced alike (`lion_plain_scale_remainder()`) and paid there
(`lion_plain_pay_remainders()`): lion's pass that pays remainders runs on the relation's paths
first in the hook chain, before this note, and these are built after it. The pass offers the bitmap
heap scan of the same index path beside each, priced from it at the same rows and put into core's
units alike. Core's paths of the copy above are then offered again at core's prices, against these
at their whole price. Path rows stay core's. A parameterized AM scan, a join's inner side, keeps
core's rows as §39 has it; a scan of a lion index on other columns meets no more rows at a heavy
key and keeps its price; a BitmapAnd of a lion index and another index is core's mixture and keeps
it too.

**A count of rows** (`lion_skew_limit_rows()`, `lion_skew_limit_read()`,
`lion_skew_limit_share()`). Where the query level is the relation alone and ends at a count k of
its rows - a LIMIT (core's `limit_tuples`, the LIMIT and OFFSET together), or the absolute count a
caller asks for (`tuple_fraction` at 1 or more: an `EXISTS` sub-select's first row) - and nothing
between the scan and the count reads more of it (no grouping, aggregate, DISTINCT, window,
set-returning function, ORDER BY or set operation), a scan stops once it has k rows. Core's scan
of the key's B-tree filters the key's rows by the rest of the WHERE, which passes p of them (the
relation's restriction selectivity over the index clauses'), and reads the key's rows until k
pass:

    read = N_key                      no count, or N_key x p <= k
         = core's rows                core's rows x p >= k
         = max(min(k / p, N_key), core's rows)  otherwise

with N_key the rows at the factor. The extra (`lion_skew_scan_extra()`) is priced at the rows it
reads. A bitmap heap scan builds its whole bitmap first: its index tuples are the key's every row,
its heap pages and rows those it reads. Lion's path at the factor returns `out = sel x N x factor`
rows, and is charged the share of its run that k of them take, over the share core's Limit node
takes of it at core's rows (k / rows where its rows pass k; core prices the Limit from the path's
own rows, and it would be counted twice):

    share = min((k / out) / (k / rows if rows > k, else 1), 1)      1 where out <= k

A start-up - a set built whole first - is charged whole. The AM's scans take the share
(`lion_skew_am_paths()`) and so does the walk (`lo_cost()`, an unparameterized and serial one). The
two sides of the comparison shrink alike under a cap: the AM's scan of the test's capped count is
priced the same, in core's units, under a LIMIT of 21 and one of 100,000.

**The walk's set at the rows** (`lion_skew_set_extra()`). A walk whose lion access equates the key
to the Param builds the set of the key's rows with the rest of its Lion Cond, and that set meets
the rows a probed key meets too: each such leaf's index side is priced again under
`lion_skew_am_rel` and the difference added to the set's price, its members at the largest factor
(`lo_cost()`). An unparameterized walk only; a remainder the AM notes while pricing it again is no
plain path's to pay (`lion_plain_remainders_drop()`).

**A set without the key** (`lo_set_rel_pathlist()`). In a correlated subquery the walk is offered,
beside the lion accesses of the relation's restrictions, those of its restrictions without the
clauses that hold the outer query's Param (`lion_has_outer_param()`). The walk keyed on the Param
answers the key; the set of the rest holds no Param and is built once and kept for every call
(`lo_rescan()`, §40.11), its build divided by the calls (`lion_outer_param_loops()`), where the set
with the key is built again at each. `Lion Set` shows no builds count for it; the test's ten calls
show `85 containers, exact`, against `50 containers, exact, 10 builds` for the set with the key.

**§33's n_distinct hook keeps n_distinct.** The figure is the rows one probe of a key the plan does
not know meets: a cost of the probe, and not the number of the column's distinct values. The hook
feeds every estimate of the column - GROUP BY's groups, a join's rows, `var_eq_non_const()` - and a
skew-weighted n_distinct would shrink them all by the factor. The figure stays lion's own, priced
into its paths and their competitors and nowhere else.

**Measured** (2026-10-24, release build, PostgreSQL 18). A dimension of 100,000 keys and a fact of
2.85 million rows on them: keys 1 to 16 have 100,000 to 220,000 rows each, keys 17 to 316 300
each, the rest one to three; `tsv` holds three words of 600; a lion index on (fk, tsv) and B-trees
on (fk) and (fk, id); the subquery called for the 316 keys of one group, keys 1 to 316. A
statistics target of 10 on fk gives the figure 86,314 rows against core's 28, and every row below
is at that target. At the default target every heavy key is in the MCV list and the figure is
what the sample's error leaves (below); the rows with `pg_lion.enable_skew_estimate` off stand for
that, the figure at core's rows. Warm, best of three; cold, the cluster restarted and the OS cache
dropped. `Q8` is an OR of eight phrases, `(w7 <-> w8) | ... | (w21 <-> w22)`.

| settings | tsquery, form | before: plan, warm, cold | after: plan, warm, cold |
|---|---|---|---|
| walk off, `random_page_cost` 1.1, `effective_cache_size` 1MB | `w7`, capped | B-tree Index Scan, 85 ms, 600 ms | lion Index Scan, 35 ms, 102 ms |
| ... and the count pushdown off | `w7`, count | B-tree Index Scan, 1,563 ms, 2,559 ms | lion Index Scan, 51 ms, 864 ms |
| walk off, as above | two phrases, capped | B-tree Index Scan, 1,658 ms, 2,719 ms | lion Index Scan, 128 ms, 143 ms |
| ... and the count pushdown off | two phrases, count | B-tree Index Scan, 1,684 ms, 2,625 ms | lion Index Scan, 141 ms, 152 ms |
| skew estimate off | Q8, capped | Bitmap Heap Scan of the (fk, id) B-tree, 2,684 ms, 3,848 ms | walk, set built once, 84 ms, 128 ms |
| skew estimate off | Q8, count | Bitmap Heap Scan, 2,657 ms, 3,755 ms | walk, set built once, 81 ms, 113 ms |
| skew estimate off | `w1:* \| w2:* \| w3:*`, capped | walk, set built at each call, 12,772 ms | walk, set built once, 190 ms |
| skew estimate off | `w1:* \| w2:* \| w3:*`, count | LionCount, 12,711 ms | walk, set built once, 544 ms |
| skew estimate off | `w7`, count | LionCount, 34 ms | walk, set built once, 125 ms |
| default | `w7`, capped | walk, 39 ms, 65 ms | lion Index Scan, 26 ms, 104 ms |
| default | Q8, capped | walk, 527 ms | lion Index Scan, 564 ms |
| default | `w1:* \| w2:* \| w3:*`, capped | walk, 12,757 ms | walk, set built once, 194 ms |

Where the plan is the same before and after (the count at the default settings, LionCount; `w7 &
w8` with the walk off, the lion Index Scan) the times are too. In the page around the subquery
(the `EXISTS`, an anti join, `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 100`), with the skew estimate off, the capped
count over Q8 took 2,572 ms before and 100 ms after, and the count 2,660 and 91 ms; `w7`'s count
43 ms after against LionCount's 18. At the default settings Q8's capped count took 130 ms before
and 99 ms after.

**What is worse.** A walk reads its key's every entry, and where the plan prices the key at core's
rows - the skew estimate off, or a figure blind to the key - the set built once makes it cheaper
than the count for a key it reads many times more of: `w7`'s count with the skew estimate off,
34 ms to 125 ms. Cold, the capped `w7` at the default settings moved from the walk (65 ms) to the
lion Index Scan (104 ms), which warm is the faster (39 ms to 26). An 8-phrase OR's capped count at
the default settings went from the walk to the lion Index Scan, 527 ms to 564.

**Not done.**

- A probe of a most common key. The figure is the rows a key outside the MCV list meets (§33, "The
  rows of a probed key", measured against the workload's probed sets), and a probe of a key in the
  list is priced at it too, below the rows it meets. The table above is that case: its heavy keys,
  1 to 16 of 100,000 rows and more, are probed by 16 of the 316 calls. At the default statistics
  target all of them are in the MCV list, and what the remainder keeps of them is the error of
  ANALYZE's sampled frequencies against the exact Σn²: six ANALYZEs gave 63, 351, 28, 28, 11,536
  and 28 against core's 28. At a target of 10 the list holds keys 7 to 16, keys 1 to 6 are left in
  the remainder, and the figure is 86,314. So the table's figure moves with the statistics target.
- A prefix union inside a count. With the skew estimate on, `w1:* | w2:* | w3:*`'s count goes to
  LionCount before and after, and takes 13 s, where core's own plan takes 1.8 s and the walk with
  the set built once 0.5 s: LionCount's price of the AND of a heavy key with a large OR of prefixes
  (§29.11) is well under what it costs, which is not this section's to price.
- The walk's calls are the outer relation's rows before its filter (§40.11's "Not done"), so the
  set built once is divided among more calls than there are.
- A parameterized AM scan of a lion index, a join's inner side, keeps core's rows (§39).

**Tests.** test/sql/correlated_skew.sql: the figure; the count priced the same with the AM's plain
scans on and off; the AM's scan of the lion index chosen at the figure for the capped count and the
count where core's B-tree scan is chosen at core's rows, and priced below a third of core's plan;
the AM's scan priced alike under a LIMIT of 21 and of 100,000; the walk's set without the key, with
the skew estimate off and on, built once for ten calls; the plans with every path on; every answer
compared with core's plan; and the relations left out - an inheritance parent planned as its Append,
a parent read alone (`FROM ONLY`) at core's rows, a sampled relation as its Sample Scan, and one
proven empty by its CHECK constraint, an index path of which fails `cost_index()`'s assertion on
an assert-enabled build. test/sql/correlated.sql and
test/sql/skew.sql, whose correlated plans weigh the count against core's scan, turn the walk off
there.

## 41. Expression columns in the count pushdown (2026-10-09)

A lion index on an expression - `(doc->>'status')`, `((doc->>'qty')::int)`, `(lower(email))` - is
a scalar column whose values the table does not store. Its entries are those values, one per row,
exactly as a column's are, so everything the count pushdown does with a column's entries holds for
it: a clause on the expression is a posting set, a GROUP BY on it is the walk of its entries, a
`count(DISTINCT)` of it is the number of entries with a visible row. The pushdown treats each
expression such an index holds as a column of its own, an **expression column**, numbered past every heap column (`LION_VCOL_ATTNO(i)`,
`MaxHeapAttributeNumber + 1 + i`, lion_customscan.h).

### Matching (`lion_vcol_collect()`, `lion_vcol_subst()`, lion_plan_match.c)

- **Which expressions**: those of the table's valid, non-partial lion indexes - and, in an attempt
  for a partial index (§45), that index's - under a scalar
  opclass, deduplicated, at most `LION_MAX_VCOLS` (64), collected when the pushdown is tried on one
  table that is not partitioned. A multi-key opclass over an expression (`to_tsvector(...)`) is not
  one: its entries are keys, not row values. Nor is a binary-coercible cast of a column, `(v::text)`
  of a varchar: stripped of its relabel it is the bare column, which the plan cannot carry as an
  expression column, and which an index on the cast does not answer as a column either (a clause on
  it declines, as before).
- **The query's expressions**: the GROUP BY items, the WHERE clauses, the HAVING and the target
  list are rewritten with every subexpression equal to an expression column - as core's
  `match_index_to_operand()` compares them, relabels stripped - replaced by a Var of that column's
  number. Everything downstream then sees `Var op Const`, a grouping Var or an aggregate's Var
  argument and takes the paths a column takes; an expression that is not one of them (`upper(doc->>'s')
  = 'A'` against an index on `doc->>'s'`) stays as it was and declines as before.
- **The index**: `lion_find_roaring_index()` answers an expression column with the first key column,
  in index order, whose expression is equal to it, as a column is answered by the first key column
  on it. The expression must be written as the index writes it, under its collation.

The rewrite lives only while the path is built: the scope is entered in `lion_try_count_path()` after
the relation is known and left in a `PG_FINALLY`, and anything that asks the planner's statistics -
`estimate_num_groups()`, `examine_variable()`, `clause_selectivity()` - gets the expression back
first (`lion_vcol_unvar()`), so that core finds the index expression's own statistics as it would
for the ordinary plan. The expression-statistics hook (§33) declines for a partitioned table or an
inheritance parent, as the column hook does: one index of the parent counts no partition's rows, and
a partitioned index has no pages to read a count from.

### The plan

- **VCOLS** (custom_private member 19, shape 22): the expression columns' expressions, renumbered
  to varno 1 when the plan is made (`lion_plan_custom_path()`); setrefs.c does not look into
  custom_private. The codec checks each is an expression of the table's columns, and
  `lion_count_priv_check()` that every expression column a member names is one of them, and that
  there are none with partitions or a join, and that a `coalesce` group is not one. A `coalesce` of
  a column beside a clause on an expression column (`GROUP BY coalesce(c, 0) ... WHERE doc->>'a' =
  '1'`) is planned: the clause is a posting set like any column's.
- **custom_scan_tlist** holds the expressions themselves, not the virtual Vars: setrefs.c matches
  the plan's target list and HAVING against it by `equal()`, and finds `doc->>'s'` there as it
  would a column. A HAVING that names an expression column is wanted as that expression, not as
  the columns inside it (`lion_vcol_refs()`), and so is the partial target of the decoded walk, a
  parallel GROUP BY or a partitioned one (`lion_make_partial_target()`): core's
  `make_partial_grouping_target()` would pull the columns out of a HAVING like `count(*) > 100 OR
  doc->>'a' = '2'`, or out of a printed expression that a WHERE equality took out of
  `processed_groupClause`, and the node cannot emit `doc`.
- **The executor** finds each key column the same way (`lion_index_col_for()` with VCOLS,
  `lion_index_col_is_vcol()`), comparing with the index's own expressions, which are of varno 1.
- **EXPLAIN** prints the expression, deparsed against the table, where it prints a column name.

### Privileges

The ordinary plan computes a grouped or counted expression in its scan's projection, so it checks
EXECUTE on the expression's functions; a WHERE clause's functions are in baserestrictinfo already.
The plan adds the functions of each expression column it uses to `exec_funcs`
(`lion_expr_functions()`), and `test/sql/node_contracts.sql` checks both a filtered and a grouped
expression column against the ordinary plan.

### Not done

- **Partitioned tables**: each partition's index would have to be matched to the parent's
  expression through the partition's own attribute numbers.
- **FK-side joins** (§27), **aggregates over keys** (§37) and **`coalesce()`** (§10) of an
  expression column.

### Tests

`test/sql/exprindex.sql`: jsonb fields and a cast, filtered (`=`, `IN`, `<>`, ranges, `IS NULL`,
OR), grouped by one, two and three columns (with a HAVING on a grouped expression, and with one
pinned by the WHERE), `count(DISTINCT)`, HAVING, a `coalesce` group beside an expression clause, an
index on a binary-coercible cast of a column next to the expression indexes, a generic plan's parameter,
through LionCount and through the ordinary plan before and after updates and deletes, only
differences printed; what declines; and EXECUTE on a function an expression calls.

## 42. jsonb containment and existence: `jsonb_contains_ops` (lion_jsonb.c, 2026-10-09)

A multi-key opclass (§17) for jsonb that answers `@>`, `?`, `?|` and `?&` with the rows a
sequential scan and GIN return, from the posting sets alone wherever the keys make that exact.
It is the DEFAULT for jsonb, as GIN's `jsonb_ops` is GIN's: `USING lion (doc)` is this class.
Lion's own `jsonb_ops` - whole documents under `=` and the ranges, btree's meaning of the name -
is kept beside it, not the default, for an index that answers `=`, the ranges and
`count(DISTINCT doc)`, which a multi-key column cannot (§17).
Strategies 11 .. 14 are its operators; it names its own extractValue and extractQuery
(`lion_jsonb_extract_value()`, `lion_jsonb_extract_query()`), which take lion's strategy numbers
(`lion_gin_strategy()` passes them through). STORAGE is bytea with `byteacmp` as the ordering, so
keys compare bytewise and the directory is ordered (§21).

### 42.1 Keys

Each key is a bytea whose first byte says what it is:

- `R` + `o` | `a`: the document is an object, an array. A raw scalar has none.
- `L` names value marks: a scalar at a path. `names` is each object key on the path from the root
  as `0x01`, its length (unsigned LEB128) and its bytes, then `0x00`; `value` is `z` (null), `t`,
  `f`, `n` + length + `numeric_normalize()`'s text, or `s` + length + the string's bytes; `marks`
  is, for each gap before, between and after the names, the number of array levels in it. Array
  indexes are not on the path, because `@>` matches an array element wherever it is.
- `C` names type marks: a container (`o`, `a`) at a path below the root.
- `E` name: a top-level object key, a string element of a top-level array, a raw scalar string,
  which is what `?` tests (`jsonb_exists()`).
- `H` + SHA-256: any of the above whose varlena would pass `LION_MAX_KEY_SIZE`.

A raw scalar document is a one-element array to the iterator, and gets the `L` key a scalar
element of a top-level array gets: `'["foo"]' @> '"foo"'` and `'"foo"' @> '"foo"'` are both true,
`'"foo"' @> '["foo"]'` is false (no `R a`). Numbers go through `numeric_normalize()`, as GIN's
jsonb_ops does, so `1`, `1.0`, `1e0` and `-0`/`0` agree; strings are bytes, as jsonb equality
compares them. The names come before the value and the array levels after it, so one run of the
ordered directory holds every array nesting of one `path = value`, which a lax jsonpath search
would want.

### 42.2 Queries

`@>` extracts the query's `L` keys, a `C` key for each EMPTY container in it (a non-empty one is
implied by the paths below it), and an `R` key when the query is an array (which must not match a
raw scalar) or an empty object, and ANDs them. The AND is exact unless one array element of the
query contributes two or more keys: `{"a": [{"b": 1, "c": 2}]}` must find both in the SAME element
of the row's `a`, and `{"a": [{"b": 1}, {"c": 2}]}` has the same keys. Then, and when a key was
hashed, extractQuery answers `LION_SEARCH_MODE_LOSSY`, a search mode of lion's own beside GIN's:
`lion_extract_query()` calls the query not exact, and `lion_extract_query_superset()` builds the
same AND with LION_QMODE_LOSSY, which every caller already rechecks (§17, "Literal queries through
the superset"). Duplicate query keys are dropped.

`?` is one `E` key, `?|` their OR and `?&` their AND, NULL array elements skipped as
`jsonb_exists_any()`/`_all()` skip them; `?| '{}'` and `?| '{NULL}'` select nothing, and `?& '{}'`
every document, which no key names, so it answers GIN_SEARCH_MODE_ALL.

Every document has at least one key (`R`, or a raw scalar's `L`), so nothing goes to the EMPTY
entry.

### 42.3 Elsewhere

- `lion_match_index()` let an index with no collation match a clause with one (`doc ? 'k'`: the
  text operand has the default collation), which is the planner's own `IndexCollMatchesExprColl()`.
- lionvalidate() accepts the pre-18 `hashvarlena` for a multi-key class's bytea keys, as it does
  for a scalar bytea class.
- `LION_STRAT_IS_MULTI()` replaces the 2 .. 5 range checks; `doc @> ANY (array)` and `doc ? ANY
  (array)` reach the count pushdown's OR like the other multi-key operators.

### 42.4 Size and speed

On synthetic corpora (1M documents each, PostgreSQL 18; a catalog of low-cardinality fields, an
event log with ids, timestamps and short text, orders with arrays of item objects): 15 to 21 keys
per document; the index 1.0 to 1.4 times GIN jsonb_ops and 1.5 to 1.9 times jsonb_path_ops; a
serial build 1.5 to 2.7 times faster than jsonb_ops and from 1.4 times slower to 1.5 times faster
than jsonb_path_ops, and with three workers faster than either. Counts over `@>`, `?`, `?|` and
`?&` were 25 to 500 times faster than through GIN, and twice as fast for one matching 4 rows
(GIN rechecks every `@>` in the heap; the count pushdown reads no heap on all-visible pages), and
the lossy `{"items": [{"sku": .., "qty": ..}]}` 17 times, rechecking only the rows its keys select.

### 42.5 Tests

`jsonb_contains.sql`: random documents (nested objects and arrays, raw scalars, empty containers,
numbers written several ways, NULL) and random queries, half of them pruned copies of a document,
through bitmap scans, plain index scans and the count pushdown with the query a literal and a
parameter, against a sequential scan, GIN jsonb_ops and jsonb_path_ops, before and after updates
and deletes; fixed edge cases; keys over 2000 bytes; the plans. Disabling the lossy answer makes it
fail.

### 42.6 A field equal to a string (2026-10-20)

`(doc ->> 'k') = 'v'` is the usual spelling of "field k is v", and no operator of the class: the
count pushdown left it to the heap in a WHERE, and declined a count with it in a FILTER, whose
conditions have to be answered from posting sets (§10, "Filtered counts").  It is the same test as
`doc @> '{"k": "v"}'` when v is a string no other JSON value prints as.  `->>` gives the text of
the field's value: a string's own characters, a number's digits, `true` or `false`, a container's
JSON text, and NULL for a JSON null, for a missing key and for a document that is no object; the
containment holds exactly where the document is an object whose field k is the string v (`{"k":
["v"]}` and `[{"k": "v"}]` contain no such field, and their `->>` is no `v` either).  So the two
agree on every row, NULL counting as false as it does in a WHERE and a FILTER, when:

- `=` is texteq() under a deterministic collation, which compares the characters themselves;
- the key and v are constants (text or varchar), so that v can be looked at when planning;
- v is the text of no number - numeric_in() refuses it, which also turns away `NaN`, `Infinity`
  and padded digits, though no JSON number prints as those -, is neither `true` nor `false`, and
  starts with neither `{` nor `[`, as every container's text does.

`lion_jsonb_field_eq()` (lion_plan_match.c) builds the containment - the same expression as `->>`'s
operand, pg_catalog's `@>`, and v as a JSON string under the key, escaped by escape_json() - and
`lion_analyze_leaf()` analyses that in the clause's place, as the multi-key clause the posting sets
answer exactly (§42.2: one `L` key, whose array marks keep `{"k": ["v"]}` apart); the plan and its
EXPLAIN show the containment.  Not under a `NOT`, whose `->>` is NULL where the containment is
false, and not as `<>`, which the planner makes of `NOT (... = ...)`.  A value that is a parameter,
`IN (...)`, `doc -> 'k' = '"v"'` and a nondeterministic collation stay the heap's.  The estimate is
core's, of the `->>` expression.  An expression index on `(doc ->> 'k')` is an expression column
first (§41), and answers the clause as one.

Tests: `jsonb_fieldeq.sql`: documents whose field is the string, a number, a boolean, null, an
array or object holding the string, strings that print like those, other cases and padding,
escapes in the key and the value, top-level arrays and scalars, nested fields, NULL documents;
every spelling taken and every one declined, in a WHERE, a FILTER with `doc IS NOT NULL AND doc ?
'k'` beside it, an OR, a GROUP BY and a generic plan, against the pushdown off.

### 42.7 Not done

- **Multi-leaf array elements exactly**: store each leaf's outermost array-element ordinal as a
  per-(key, row) payload, as positions are (§17), and keep candidates with an ordinal all the
  element's keys share.
- **jsonpath** ranges over the ordered `L` keys (§43.6).
- **More than 1000 query keys** answers every row; dropping keys from the AND would still be a
  superset.
- **Opclass options** to leave chosen paths or value types out, which keeps every query a
  superset.

## 43. jsonpath `@?` and `@@` through `jsonb_contains_ops` (lion_jsonb.c, 2026-10-09)

Strategies 15 (`jsonb @? jsonpath`) and 16 (`jsonb @@ jsonpath`) of `jsonb_contains_ops`, on the
keys of §42 unchanged. A jsonpath is never answered exactly: the index selects a superset, which
every caller rechecks, as GIN does for every jsonpath. `doc @? path` is `doc @@ exists (path)`.

### 43.1 What a jsonpath requires (`lion_jp_bool()`)

The query is a tree of AND and OR over key PREFIXES, true for at least the documents the jsonpath
is true for:

- **An accessor chain** (`lion_jp_chain()`) from `$`, or from `@` in a filter, is followed as the
  object key names it passes; array accessors (`[*]`, `[n]`, `[last]`) add none, since array
  levels are not part of a key's names, and lax mode's unwrapping of arrays only changes how many
  levels there are. `.*`, `.**` and item methods cut the chain: its items lie at or below the names
  so far. A chain that starts anywhere else (a variable, a literal, arithmetic) says nothing about
  the document.
- **`chain == scalar`** is the `L` keys that start with the names, `0x00` and the value, at any array
  levels. jsonpath compares strings by their bytes and numbers by value, which is what the `L` key
  stores. A cut chain only says something is under its names. The scalar is a bare literal: with
  an accessor after it (`$.a == "2".double()`) it stands for another value, and the chain is only
  required to yield an item.
- **A chain that must yield an item** (`exists (chain)`, either operand of `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`,
  `>=`, `starts with`, `like_regex`, and `@?`'s path) is the `L` and `C` keys that start with its
  names. The root (no names) is every document.
- **A filter** (`? (pred)`) adds what pred requires, with `@` at the chain so far: it passes only
  items pred is true for. When a chain's filters narrow, the chain is not also required to yield an
  item: the keys under its names are a union that costs more than it narrows (§43.4).
- **`&&`, `||`, `!`**: the AND or OR of the parts, NOT pushed down to the leaves. An AND keeps the
  parts that narrow; an OR needs both. Under a NOT, `exists` and comparisons narrow nothing
  (`$.a != 1` being false includes `$.a` being absent), and the operator flips: `!(a && b)` is an
  OR. GIN's jsonb_ops and jsonb_path_ops decide AND or OR from the operator alone, so they take
  `!(!($.a == 1) && $.a == 3)` as needing `$.a == 1` and miss every document where `$.a` is
  neither 1 nor 3, for which the jsonpath is true (PostgreSQL 18). Lion returns the sequential
  scan's rows there.
- **`is unknown`**, and anything else, narrows nothing.

### 43.2 Expanding the prefixes (`lion_query_expand()`, lion_multikey.c)

extractQuery returns the prefixes as keys with pmatch set, LION_SEARCH_MODE_LOSSY, and the tree in
extra_data[0], built of `LionKeyNode`s. `lion_extract_query_superset()` reads that tree only when the
column's extractQuery is `lion_jsonb_extract_query()` (GIN's own jsonb extractQuery leaves a tree of
another type there), and takes an index: the executor's callers pass theirs, and each prefix becomes
the OR of the index's keys that start with it, read off the ordered directory by
`lion_prefix_keys()`, which serves tsquery's `foo:*` too (§17, "Prefix lexemes") and now bytea
columns as well. A key a visible row has was in the directory before the walk, so the OR selects
every row the prefix does. A prefix no key starts with selects no row; one with more keys than the
query has left of its 1000 is every row; the tree is folded around both, and may come out NONE,
