LOSSY or ALL. The planner's callers pass no index, and each prefix stands for its OR as one key.

A key longer than `LION_MAX_KEY_SIZE` is stored as its hash (§42.1), which keeps no prefix. So a
prefix that could start a hashed key - every `L`/`C` prefix of a chain that must exist, and an
`L` prefix with a value when its length plus five bytes per array-level count could pass the limit -
is ORed with the prefix `H`, every hashed key.

In the count pushdown a jsonpath is always counted from the superset with a heap recheck
(`lion_locate_multikey()` takes the superset branch for it), so the planner takes it only where a
recheck is allowed: never under an OR. A literal one may come out ALL at run time as a parameter's
may, so it is no clause positive whatever its value (§17, "Prefix lexemes", the cap).

### 43.3 Elsewhere

- `lion_extract_query_superset()` takes the index; `lion_keynode_leaf()`/`_op()` are exported for
  lion_jsonb.c.
- `LION_STRAT_IS_MULTI()` covers 15 and 16; `LION_STRAT_IS_JSONPATH()` names them.

### 43.4 Speed

On the §42.4 corpora (PostgreSQL 18, best of five, each index alone; every count the same as
the other two indexes), counts over fifteen jsonpaths against GIN jsonb_ops and jsonb_path_ops:

| jsonpath | rows | jsonb_ops | jsonb_path_ops | lion |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `@@ '$.status == "active"'` | 250619 | 224 ms (1.3x) | 265 ms (1.6x) | 167 ms |
| `@@ '$.status == "draft" \|\| $.status == "paused"'` | 374094 | 340 ms (1.3x) | 355 ms (1.3x) | 266 ms |
| `@@ '$.tags[*] == "tag3"'` | 69551 | 125 ms (1.5x) | 112 ms (1.4x) | 82 ms |
| `@@ '$.type == "type1" && $.flags.b == true'` | 11101 | 113 ms (8.6x) | 30 ms (2.3x) | 13 ms |
| `@? '$.attrs ? (@.color == "c3" && @.size == "m")'` | 18315 | 60 ms (3.0x) | 42 ms (2.1x) | 20 ms |
| `@@ '$.kind == "k3"'` | 52596 | 78 ms (1.8x) | 57 ms (1.4x) | 42 ms |
| `@@ '$.kind == "k3" && $.user.country == "cc7"'` | 1073 | 25 ms (10x) | 3.6 ms (1.5x) | 2.5 ms |
| `@@ '$.payload.amount == 500'` | 4 | 0.42 ms (3.2x) | 0.08 ms (0.6x) | 0.13 ms |
| `@@ '$.customer == 123'` | 7 | 2.4 ms (22x) | 0.05 ms (0.5x) | 0.11 ms |
| `@@ '$.customer > 99990'` | 107 | 1032 ms (1.5x) | 1091 ms (1.6x) | 669 ms |
| `@? '$.gift'` (on 1000 rows) | 1000 | 943 ms (3400x) | 690 ms (2500x) | 0.28 ms |
| `@@ '$.gift.wrap == true'` | 1000 | 0.50 ms (1.4x) | 0.79 ms (2.1x) | 0.37 ms |
| `@? '$.items[*] ? (@.sku == "sku42" && @.qty == 3)'` | 76 | 13 ms (13x) | 2.1 ms (2.1x) | 0.97 ms |
| `@@ '$.items[*].sku == "sku42"'` | 714 | 8.3 ms (4.5x) | 1.1 ms (0.6x) | 1.8 ms |
| `@@ '$.shipping.method == "air"'` | 333711 | 382 ms (1.8x) | 293 ms (1.4x) | 214 ms |

Ratios are the GIN time over lion's. Every jsonpath count rechecks the heap, so the gap is
smaller than for `@>` (§42.4). Neither GIN index narrows a bare existence path (`$.gift`, on a
thousandth of the rows, cost them as much as a range over the whole table); lion reads it from
its `L`/`C` prefixes. The range (`$.customer > 99990`) narrows only to rows with the path, so
all three indexes read most of the table. A filter's chain (`$.attrs ? (...)`) is not also
required to exist when the filter narrows: that would be every key under its names, a union
costing more than it narrows (counting this filter took 91 ms with it). Lion is slower than
jsonb_path_ops, which hashes the path and value into one key, on point lookups of a few rows and
on `$.items[*].sku == "sku42"`, by under a millisecond.

### 43.5 Tests

`jsonb_path.sql`: random documents as in §42.5 against random jsonpaths (lax and strict; key,
array, wildcard and method accessors; filters; comparisons, `exists`, `starts with`, `like_regex`,
`&&`, `||`, `!`, `is unknown`), a third of them a path and value read off a document, through
bitmap scans, plain index scans and the count pushdown with the query a literal and a parameter,
against a sequential scan, before and after updates and deletes; fixed cases (lax unwrapping, raw
scalars, empty containers, numbers, the NOT case above); hashed keys; a path too common to expand;
`op ANY (array)`; the plans. Each of these makes it fail: deciding AND/OR from the operator alone,
pinning the array levels to zero, and leaving out the hashed keys.

### 43.6 Not done

- **Ranges** (`$.price > 10`) from the ordered `L` keys: needs an order-preserving number encoding
  in place of `numeric_normalize()`'s text. Today a range only requires its path to exist.
- **`.**` and `.*`** with the names after them: the names before the wildcard are all a key can
  say.
- **Hashed keys keeping a prefix** (`H` + the first bytes + the hash) would let a prefix find only
  its own hashed keys instead of all of them.

## 44. lionvec: nearest neighbours of pgvector's `vector` (pg_lion_vector; lion_vec.c, lion_vec_scan.c, lion_vec_math.c; 2026-10-14)

The shape is

    SELECT ... FROM t [WHERE <clauses lion indexes answer>] ORDER BY v <-> q LIMIT k

with `<->`, `<#>` or `<=>`, pgvector's L2, negative inner product and cosine distance. pgvector's
own indexes answer it from a graph (HNSW), whose every hop is a random read and which is fast only
while the graph - here 3.8 GB for 975,000 1536-dimension rows, as halfvec - is in memory, or from
k-means lists (IVFFlat), which hold every row's floats. Under a WHERE both filter AFTER the
search, so a selective filter leaves a LIMIT short or sends the scan on through most of the index.

lionvec is IVF over compact codes. The build partitions the rows by k-means; a scan reads the
partitions in the order of their centroids' distance to the query, and of each partition's rows
only a code of one bit a dimension - 224 bytes a 1536-dimension row, a twenty-seventh of its
floats - whose error bound decides which few rows are read in full. It stops once the next
centroid, less a margin, lies farther than the rows it has (§44.4), having read a few percent of
the rows; among those it returns rows in the exact order of their distances, unless a bound of
`pg_lion.vector_epsilon` standard deviations fails. Under a WHERE lion answers, it reads and
scores only the rows lion's set holds, and for a set of up to 2,000 rows, or of up to 1.5 a
partition, computes every member's distance outright (§44.6).

The codes are RaBitQ's (Gao and Long, SIGMOD 2024): a fixed random rotation makes every
coordinate of every vector look like an independent Gaussian, so that one bit a dimension - the
coordinate's sign - estimates an inner product with an error whose distribution is known whatever
the data, and so a bound on it that holds with a chosen probability. What is lion's here is the
rest: the bound and the partitions decide what a scan reads next (§44.4), the further bit-planes
and the heap are read only for the rows it cannot rule out, and a lion set restricts the whole
(§44.6).

The first format had no partitions: every scan read every row's code, in heap order, and the
answer was exact (96 ms for the ten nearest of 975,000 rows, §44.9). At the scale this is for, a
billion rows, that is 224 GB of codes a query. Format 2 (the same day) gave the exactness up for
partitions; a simulation over the benchmark's vectors chose their number and the margin (§44.9).
Format 3 SPILLS: every row is in two partitions, its nearest and a second chosen by SOAR (§44.3),
so that a row near a partition's edge is found from either side, for a second CODE item a row.

### 44.1 Packaging

The access method lives in pg_lion's library, which reads pgvector's on-disk `vector` itself (a
varlena of an int16 dimension count, two unused bytes and the floats: `LionVecPgVector`) and calls
pgvector's distance functions only through the operator class, so pg_lion loads, and its tests
run, without pgvector. A separate extension, `pg_lion_vector` (`requires = 'pg_lion, vector'`),
creates the AM and three operator classes for `vector` - `vector_l2_ops` (the default),
`vector_ip_ops` and `vector_cosine_ops` - each ONE ORDER BY operator, whose strategy number (1,
2, 3) is the index's metric; pgvector's objects are named through `@extschema:vector@`. The rest of
pg_lion sees four functions (lion_vec.h): `lion_vec_index()` and `lion_vec_relation()`, which tell
a lionvec index by its own routines (`amcostestimate`, `ambeginscan`), not its name, so that an AM
of that name another handler serves is never taken for one; `lion_vec_restrict()`; and
`lion_vec_scan_cost()`. The changes to lion's own code are `_PG_init()` calling `lion_vec_init()`
(the settings, the 8-bit tables, the kernels) and LionOrdered's (§44.6).

An operator class of one's own is checked as far as lionvec reads through it. Its input type must
be NAMED `vector` or `halfvec`, of length -1 (`lionvec_type_ok()`): the reader below takes every
datum for a varlena of pgvector's layout, and a class over `int` had it detoast an integer as a
pointer, a crash (a review found it, 2026-10-15). The index's open refuses any other type, and
`amvalidate` reports the class. Its ORDER BY operator must return `float8` or `float4`
(`lionvec_distance_type_ok()`), as `amvalidate` reports and a scan's start checks; the scan reads
each distance, and hands it back in `xs_orderbyvals`, in the operator's own type, as core's
`index_store_float8_orderby_distances()` does. Until that review a `float4` operator's distances
were read, and returned, as `float8`.

`halfvec` (2026-10-15; pgvector 0.7 and on: the same 8-byte header, then IEEE 754 binary16
halves) has the same three, `halfvec_l2_ops` (its default), `halfvec_ip_ops` and
`halfvec_cosine_ops`, over pgvector's `l2_distance`, `halfvec_negative_inner_product` and
`cosine_distance` of `halfvec`. The format does not change: the codes, the 8-bit codes and the
centroids are made from floats whatever the column holds, so a halfvec column's index is the size
of a vector column's, while the column is half its size. An index knows its type from its operator
class's input type, `rd_opcintype[0]`: a halfvec when that type is NAMED `halfvec` in `pg_type` (by
the syscache, for pgvector's OIDs differ from database to database), a vector otherwise. It is
looked up once an index open and kept in `LionVecInfo.half`, before `rd_amcache` is set, for the
lookup may take a lock whose invalidation would free the cache; the build looks it up too, before
there is a meta page. One reader turns either datum into floats, `lionvec_datum_floats()`: it
detoasts it and checks its length (`lionvec_datum_dim()`: the header, a count not below zero and
that many floats or halves, or `ERRCODE_DATA_CORRUPTED`), and returns a vector's floats where
they lie, or converts a halfvec's into the caller's array - the build's and an insert's, of the
index's dimensions - or, without one, a palloc'd one. A scan converts its query once a rescan; its
exact distances are pgvector's own functions of the datums (the ORDER BY operator's), so a row
read from the heap is never converted. The conversion is exact, every half being a float
(`lionvec_halves`, a kernel like the others, §44.3): the portable one assembles the float's
bits - the exponent rebiased, a subnormal normalized at its leading one, infinities kept and a
NaN made the quiet NaN of its payload - without a loop or a table, and F16C's VCVTPH2PS converts
eight halves at a time to the same bits. The errors name the type: `different halfvec dimensions
3 and 2`, and pgvector's `expected 3 dimensions, not 4` and `halfvec must have at least 1
dimension`. Measured on DBpedia (bench/results/2026-10-15-dbpedia-pg18/, "halfvec"): a halfvec
column's index probes the same partitions, reads the same pages and returns the same recall as the
`vector` column's; the exact path is 13 to 26% faster warm (4.6 against 5.5 us a member, half the
TOAST chunks) and reads 9% fewer pages cold, not half, because a 3 KB halfvec still takes a TOAST
page of its own for each of the scattered rows a narrow filter admits.

A column's dimensions come from its type modifier, or, for a type without one, from the first
vector the build or an insert meets (`lionvec_set_dims()`, under the meta page's lock, so that two
first inserts agree); a vector of other dimensions is pgvector's own error, `expected 3
dimensions, not 4`, and a query of other dimensions `different vector dimensions 3 and 2`. At most
`LIONVEC_MAX_DIM` dimensions, 8128 at 8K pages, as many whole 64-bit words as leave a REFINE item a
page; pgvector's HNSW and IVFFlat take 2000. Single-column, no INCLUDE, no search operators
(`amoptionalkey`: a query with no WHERE at all is the point), forward only (`amcanbackward =
false`: a SCROLL cursor gets a Material node), no bitmap scans. Scanned in parallel
(`amcanparallel`, with `amestimateparallelscan`, `aminitparallelscan` and `amparallelrescan`:
§44.4, "A parallel scan") and built in parallel (§44.12).

### 44.2 Format (lion_vec.h)

Block 0 is the meta page: magic, format version 5, metric, flags (`LIONVEC_META_SPILL`: the build
spilled, §44.3; `LIONVEC_META_LOCATOR`: it keeps a locator, §44.13), dims and the padded `dimsp` (a
multiple of 64), the rotation's seed, the MEAN chain's head, the PART chain's head and the
partitions' number, the heads and tails of the two chains of rows in no partition, the REFINE tail,
the partitions' SCALE (the rows' standard deviation about their centroids along one dimension, the
unit of the margin, §44.4), the build's row count, and the REGION chain's head and the regions'
number, appended in format 4 so that every earlier field keeps its offset (`lionvec_check_meta()`
holds `nregions > 0` to a valid head, and to no more than the partitions), and the locator's fields,
appended in format 5 (§44.13). Every page's special space carries its next block, its type,
`LIONVEC_PAGE_ID` and, on CODE pages, the least and greatest container key (§2) of the TIDs on it.

- **MEAN**: the indexed rows' mean, rotated, as floats over as many pages as it takes; written by
  the build and never changed. Absent (`mean_head` invalid) when there were no non-NULL rows.
- **PART**: one item a partition (`LionVecPart`), in order: its number, its CODE chain's head and
  tail, the items the build put in it (its rows and, spilling, other rows' copies), the greatest
  `|x|` of those rows and their mean `|x - c|^2` (an inner-product scan's bound, §44.4, which
  must hold for every row the chain holds, copies included), and its centroid, coded as a row is
  - its plane 1 here, its 8-bit codes in a REFINE item whose TID is (partition, 0), which no heap
  row's is (`LionVecCentTid()`). 248 bytes at 1536 dimensions, 32 a page: 62 pages for the
  benchmark's 1,974 partitions. Written by the build after the CODE chains; an insert changes
  only a tail. In an index of regions (below) the partitions are numbered region by region, so
  that each region's are one run of the chain.
- **REGION** (format 4): in an index of `LIONVEC_REGION_MIN` (64) partitions or more, one item a
  region of the centroids (`LionVecRegion`, §44.3), in order: its number, its run of partitions -
  the first and how many - the block and offset of the run's first PART item, and the region's
  centroid coded as a row is, plane 1 alone (its TID and REFINE item invalid, its `<x, mean>`
  zero): 248 bytes at 1536 dimensions, 32 a page, two pages for DBpedia's 53 regions and 16 for
  the 512 of `LIONVEC_MAX_PARTS`. A region k-means left without partitions is kept, with no run
  and no PART item, so that the count is always `ceil(sqrt(C))` and the beam an insert takes of
  them the build's. Written by the build after the PART chain, never changed. An insert reads
  the chain and then only the runs of the regions it picks; it checks that the regions number
  from 0, that their runs follow one another and cover the partitions, and that each PART item
  of a run is that run's next partition, reading on along the PART chain from the item the region
  names (`lionvec_insert_read_regions()`, `_read_run()`), and any of it amiss is an
  `ERRCODE_INDEX_CORRUPTED` error, as every item's length, place and line pointer are checked
  against its page (`lionvec_item_ok()`). An index of fewer partitions, one or none included,
  has no REGION chain (an invalid head, `nregions` 0), and an insert reads the whole PART chain.
  A scan reads no REGION page (§44.3, "Regions").
- **CODE**: one item a row, 32 bytes of header - TID, flags (`LIONVEC_NULL`, `LIONVEC_ZERO`: a
  cosine zero vector, `LIONVEC_SPILL`: a copy), `|x|`, `alpha1`, `<x, mean>`, the REFINE item's
  block and offset, plane 1's popcount - and plane 1, `dimsp / 64` words: 224 bytes at 1536
  dimensions, 35 a page. A NULL row or a cosine zero vector is the header alone. In an index that
  spills, every other row has a second item, its COPY, in its second partition's chain: the
  primary's every byte - the REFINE item's place among them, so that there is one REFINE item a
  row, never two - but for `LIONVEC_SPILL`. A chain a partition, which the build writes in one
  run of blocks, in heap order (§44.5), so that a probe reads it sequentially and each page covers
  a narrow range of heap blocks; every partition has a page, even an empty one, for inserts to
  append to. Then two chains of rows in no partition: the REST chain, of every row of an index
  built without partitions (an empty table's, §44.3), and the NULL chain, of the NULL rows and the
  cosine zero vectors, which no distance orders.
- **REFINE**: one item a non-NULL row or a centroid, 16 bytes of header (TID, `nloc`, `alpha8`,
  `|r|`) and `dimsp` 8-bit codes: 1552 bytes at 1536 dimensions, five a page. Read only for the rows
  plane 1 cannot rule out and for the centroids a scan comes to. In an index that keeps a locator
  over vectors wide enough, every item ends with a slot for its row's place in TOAST (§44.13), 20
  bytes at 1536 dimensions, five a page still.
- **LOC** and **LOCDIR** (format 5): in an index whose vectors may lie in TOAST, an entry a row
  whose vector does - its TID, its value's id and its chunks' places - in heap order, and a
  directory of those pages (§44.13).

So an index of n rows of d dimensions is about n (d / 8 + 36) bytes of CODE pages, twice that when
it spills, and n (d + 20) of REFINE pages - 1.7 GB for the benchmark's 975,000 rows of 1536
without spill (225 MB of it CODE pages), 1.9 GB with it - and C (d + 1.2 d / 8 + 70) of
centroids. A scan reads the PART chain, 500 KB there, and the CODE pages of the partitions it
probes, each twice as long when the index spills.

Format 4 had no locator and no REFINE slots. Format 3 had no REGION chain, and its partitions
were numbered as k-means left them. This pg_lion refuses both as it refuses format 2
(`lionvec_check_meta()`: "has format version 4 ... REINDEX it"), since the extension has no
release to migrate from. Format 2 had no copies and no flags in its meta page.

Format 1 (§44 above) had one CODE chain, every row in heap order, and a DIR chain of each CODE
page's least and greatest TID, by which a filtered scan read only the pages that could hold a
member. With partitions a filter's members are spread over every partition, the build's order is by
partition first, and a filtered scan of more members than the exact path takes (§44.6) probes
partitions as an unfiltered one does, so the directory went; the page's container keys still skip a
page that holds no member (§44.6).

### 44.3 Codes and partitions (lion_vec_math.c)

- **The rotation**: three rounds, each flipping the signs of a pseudo-random half of the
  coordinates (`pg_prng` from the meta page's seed: the same on every platform) and applying the
  normalized Walsh-Hadamard transform; when `dimsp` is not a power of two, two windows of the
  largest power of two below it, one at each end, overlapping, each after its own signs. Every
  step is orthogonal, so distances and inner products are unchanged. A vector is padded with zeros
  to `dimsp`, scaled to unit length first for cosine, and rotated; the rotation's signs and the
  mean are kept per backend in `rd_amcache` (`lionvec_get_info()`, which hands out a copy, since a
  relcache invalidation - possible whenever a lock is taken, a TOAST fetch's included - frees it).
- **Centring**: the stored vector is x = rotated - mean. Any fixed mean is correct (inserts use the
  build's); a near one makes |x| small and the bounds, which scale with it, tight.
- **Plane 1**: the sign bits of x, and `alpha1 = <sign(x) / sqrt(dimsp), x / |x|>`, about 0.8.
- **The 8-bit codes**: `x_i sqrt(dimsp) / |x|`, a standard Gaussian, in uniform steps of 1/32 over
  [-4, 4), clipped beyond (one coordinate in 16,000); r is the vector of the steps' middles and
  `alpha8 = <r / |r|, x / |x|>`. Uniform steps beat equal-probability steps by eight times in
  squared error, those being as wide in the tails as the tails are long.
- **The query** (`lionvec_query_init()`): rotated and centred as the rows are, giving qc, and for
  plane 1 quantized to four bits a dimension, uniformly over its own range, held as four bit-planes
  interleaved with plane 1's words, so that `<sign(x), qc>` is `2 sum_j 2^j popcount(bits & plane_j)`
  rescaled, less `sum(qc)` (the kernels below).
- **The estimate and its error**: `<x, qc>` is estimated as `|x| <c, qc> / (|c| alpha)`, c the
  code's vector. Its error is the part of x / |x| the code misses, `sqrt(1 - alpha^2)` long and,
  after the rotation, pointing nowhere in particular, times qc: a Gaussian of standard deviation
  `|qc| sqrt(1 - alpha^2) / (alpha sqrt(dimsp - 1))`, plus, for plane 1, the query's own rounding,
  `Delta^2 / 12` a dimension. A bound of epsilon of those either side holds with the Gaussian's
  probability. The 8-bit codes' deviation is about 1/70 of plane 1's, and their bound is `2 eps`
  wide (`LIONVEC_EPS8`): still far the tighter, and its failures all but vanish (§44.10).
- **The key** a scan orders by is the distance up to a constant of the query: `|x|^2 - 2 <x, qc>`
  for L2, `-<x, mean> - <x, qc>` for inner product and cosine (`lionvec_key_bounds()`); an exact
  distance d has key `d^2 - |qc|^2` for L2, `d + <mean, q>` for IP and `d + <mean, q> - 1` for cosine
  (`lionvec_key_exact()`). A bound that overflows to NaN is taken as no bound, (-inf, inf).
- **Partitions** (`lionvec_build_centroids()`, `lionvec_kmeans()`). The build's first heap scan
  takes a SAMPLE as it computes the mean: reservoir sampling (Vitter's algorithm R) from a
  generator seeded alike every build, so that the same rows make the same partitions, of as many
  rows as half of `maintenance_work_mem` holds as 8-bit codes (rotated, not centred - the mean is
  not known yet - a percent off the floats, which k-means does not notice), at most 2^24
  (`LIONVEC_SAMPLE_MAX`; 2^20 until the regions, below). The
  number of partitions C (`lionvec_parts()`, lion_vec_math.h) is the `partitions` reloption's, or
  else 1 below 10,000 rows and `8 sqrt(n)` above (`LIONVEC_PARTS_PER_ROOT`: 8,000 for a million
  rows, 2,715 for DBpedia's 115,186), at most a sixteenth of the sample, never more than its rows,
  and 0 for an empty table.
  It was `2 sqrt(n)` (1,974 for the benchmark's 975,000) until DBpedia (§44.9): partitions a
  quarter the size read 1.55 to 1.78 times fewer rows for a recall in the numpy model, and on the
  index 1.5 times fewer CODE pages for 0.95 of the true ten, which is the direction a billion rows
  needs (§44.11), though at 115,186 rows no faster. The sixteenth means the default needs a sample
  of `128 sqrt(n)` rows, 1,540 bytes each at 1536 dimensions, so `maintenance_work_mem` of 2 x 1,540
  x 128 sqrt(n) bytes: 376 MB for a million rows. The default 64 MB holds 21,788 rows, a sixteenth
  of them 1,361 partitions, which a table of 28,986 such rows outgrows: a build whose sample has
  rows for fewer partitions than a sample of every row would make fails, at the first row that
  makes it so, naming the `maintenance_work_mem` that would hold enough, unless
  `pg_lion.vector_build_sample` is `allow` (§44.8). 1 GB holds 348,617, 44 a partition at a
  million rows, about the 42 the numpy model trained on with every row, and enough to 7,418,133
  rows; every row of a million takes 2.9 GB. A sample row is `dimsp + 4` bytes (its
  codes and its scale), so the cap of 2^24 rows is 25.8 GB at 1536 dimensions, reached at a
  `maintenance_work_mem` of 52 GB; it is 64 rows a partition at `LIONVEC_MAX_PARTS` (262,144, §44.8),
  and the sixteenth binds only past 2^20 partitions, so the default is `8 sqrt(n)` up to that
  ceiling, which it reaches at 1.07 billion rows. A billion rows want 252,982 partitions, at least
  4.05 million sample rows (6.2 GB, a `maintenance_work_mem` of 12.5 GB, 11,890 MB as the
  build's error rounds it) to be given them, and
  the cap's 2^24, 66 a partition, with 52 GB. (The cap was 2^20 rows, 3 GB, and the ceiling 65,536
  partitions, which then held every table of more than 67 million rows - a billion's 15,000 rows a
  partition.) **k-means' share** of the sample is at most 128 rows a partition
  (`LIONVEC_SAMPLE_PER_PART_MAX`) and never fewer than 65,536 rows (`LIONVEC_SAMPLE_MIN`;
  `lionvec_kmeans_rows()`): when the reservoir holds more than that, the partitions are still
  counted from all of it, and k-means is given a uniformly random 128 C of its rows, or 65,536,
  whichever is more (`lionvec_subsample()`: a partial Fisher-Yates shuffle of the slots from a
  seed of its own, `LIONVEC_SEED_SUBSAMPLE`,
  the slots kept sorted and the rows moved down in place, so that they keep the reservoir's order,
  in which k-means' update sums them, and the build is the same every time), before k-means and
  before a parallel build copies the sample into shared memory, which then holds those rows alone
  (`lionvec_build_subsample()`). An iteration costs its rows, and past some rows a partition more
  of them move the centroids less than their iterations do (FAISS warns below 39 and cuts at
  256). 64 was too few: on DBpedia in 679 partitions, where 64 a partition keep 43,456 of the
  115,386 rows and 128 keep 86,912, the margin of 3 found 0.891, 0.900 and 0.906 of the true ten
  over three draws (seeds of the cut) at 64, against 0.909 with every row, and 0.916, 0.920 and
  0.915 at 128; at 8 both were within the draws' spread of every row's 0.984 (0.980 to 0.982 at
  64, 0.981 to 0.985 at 128), and in 1,358 partitions 64 gave 0.918 and 0.979 against 0.917 and
  0.982. At the default `8 sqrt(n)` the cut is 1,024 `sqrt(n)` rows, past the floor from 4,096
  rows and every row up to a million, so it falls only on a larger table whose sample holds more:
  none at a `maintenance_work_mem` of 1 GB (348,617 rows at 1536 dimensions), and at 52 GB's 2^24,
  the rows of a table of between a million and 268 million rows past 1,024 `sqrt(n)`; or on fewer
  partitions than the default, on a table of more than 65,536 rows. The floor is for the tables
  below it: k-means over 65,536 rows is seconds at most, so a cut saves little there, and such a
  table is then built from every row it sampled whatever its partitions, as it was before the cut,
  which the regression tests' expected outputs - the partitions a query probes, the pages it
  reads, for tables of 3,000 to 10,000 rows in 20 to 50 partitions - rest on (vector_filter.sql's
  400,000 rows in 20 partitions are cut, to 65,536).
  Lloyd's k-means then runs over the sample, in the
  rotated space (which changes no distance), from C distinct sample rows the seed picks, for ten
  iterations or until no row moves; spherical for cosine, whose rows and so centroids are of unit
  length, so that nearest by L2 is nearest by angle too. A row's nearest centroid is found among
  the candidates plane 1 leaves (`lionvec_candidates()`: each centroid coded as a row, a bound of
  `LIONVEC_ASSIGN_EPS` = 4 standard deviations on its distance, and the centroids whose lower bound
  is under the least upper bound), by their exact distance; about ten candidates of 200 at 320
  dimensions and more, so that k-means costs a popcount scan of the centroids a row and a few float
  distances - of the centroids of the row's regions alone at 64 partitions or more (below,
  "Regions"). A centroid left with no rows takes half of the largest's (FAISS's way). The
  centroids are then coded as rows are, against the mean. Every loop of it - the centroids'
  coding, the assignment, the means, the splits - checks for interrupts once an item
  (`LIONVEC_CHECK_INTERRUPTS()` in `lionvec_kmeans_codes()`, `_assign()` and `_update()`, the
  steps a parallel build's leader and workers run too, §44.12; nothing in the unit tests' build), so that a cancel,
  `statement_timeout` or shutdown ends a build in k-means within one item's work. Until a review
  found it (2026-10-15) none did, and a build was deaf to all three until k-means ended: days at the
  `partitions` reloption's old ceiling of a million. Measured on 500,000 rows of 16 dimensions,
  `maintenance_work_mem` 1 GB, 60,000 partitions (the heap scans take 8 s): before, the build ran
  on past 150 s of a 60 s `statement_timeout` and a cancel, and took `kill -9`; after, it stops at
  10.02 s of a 10 s one and 60.01 s of a 60 s one. The coding of the FINAL centroids after
  k-means, each one's REFINE item put as it is coded (`lionvec_build_centroids()`), checks once a
  centroid as well since the 2026-10-18 review; it had no check, which at `LIONVEC_MAX_PARTS` =
  262,144 partitions of many dimensions is seconds. The second heap scan, which finds each row's
  partitions (below) and so costs as much as an iteration of k-means over every row, was deaf too,
  for another reason found measuring the first: the build kept the REFINE page it was filling
  locked from row to row, and a content lock holds off interrupts. It now keeps the page pinned
  and locks it only to add an item (`lionvec_build_put_refine()`, as a parallel build's workers do,
  §44.12); no other backend reads the index yet. Measured on 200,000 rows of 256 dimensions, 1,800 partitions, `maintenance_work_mem`
  64 MB (k-means about 8 minutes): a cancel early in the second scan took 78 s before, the scan's
  whole length (the build 569 s), and 0.013 s after.
- **Assignment.** The build's second scan puts each row in the partition of the centroid nearest
  it by L2: of the candidates plane 1 leaves, by the centroids' 8-bit codes, whose error is about a
  seventieth of plane 1's (`lionvec_build_nearest()`); an insert does the same from the PART chain
  and the candidates' REFINE items (`lionvec_insert_nearest()`). An insert keeps, as it reads the
  PART chain, only the partitions plane 1 cannot rule out so far (`lionvec_cands_add()`, the
  streaming form of `lionvec_candidates_n()`: the m least upper bounds met, and every partition
  whose lower bound is under the m-th), and drops those the bound has since passed whenever they
  fill an array that starts at 64 and doubles only when more than half stay: 40 bytes a candidate,
  where it kept every partition's codes and bounds, about 250 bytes a partition at 1536 dimensions,
  16 MB an insert at 65,536 partitions and 192 MB at the reloption's old ceiling (a review found
  it, 2026-10-15). The candidates are the batch function's, as the unit tests check; an insert's
  memory at 1536 dimensions went from 539 KB to 224 KB at 1,250 partitions and from 1.54 MB to 359
  KB at 5,000 (356 and 364 KB at 125). The root of the rows' mean
  squared distance from their centroids, over the dimensions, is the meta page's scale; each
  partition's own mean squared distance and its longest row go in its PART item (§44.4's inner
  product). Both k-means and the assignment cost a plane-1 estimate of every centroid for every
  row, so the build grew as the rows times the partitions, `n^1.5` at the default: 19 minutes for
  the benchmark's 975,000 rows in 1,974 partitions, where format 1 took 98 seconds (§44.9,
  §44.11). DBpedia's 115,186 rows took 159 s in 678 partitions and 347 s in 2,715, about 96 s of
  it the rest of the build and 0.09 s a partition; at `8 sqrt(n)` the benchmark's 975,000 rows, in
  7,899, would take about four times its 19 minutes (not measured), and 86 minutes for a million
  rows in 8,000 were measured on another machine. Regions (below) make it `(beam + 1) sqrt(C)`
  estimates a row rather than C, and the second pass, a spilling build's, `(16 + 1) sqrt(C)`.
  Ten iterations are not fewer
  than four times the partitions want: numpy's spherical k-means over DBpedia's rows moved 0.8% of
  them in the tenth iteration at 2,715 centroids and 1.9% at 678, and its rows' mean cosine to their
  centroid was within 0.18% (0.36% at 678) of thirty iterations'. At low dimensions, where plane 1
  leaves most centroids as candidates (61 of 200 at 64 dimensions), the cost is nearer the rows
  times the partitions' exact distances: vector_filter.sql's 40,000 rows of 64 dimensions take 42 s
  in their default 1,600 partitions, 12 s in the 400 of `2 sqrt(n)`.
- **Regions** (`lionvec_regions_make()`, `lionvec_route()`, format 4, 2026-10-16). C centroids,
  when there are `LIONVEC_REGION_MIN` (64) or more, are gathered into G = `ceil(sqrt(C))` regions
  (`lionvec_region_count()`: 53 for DBpedia's 2,715 or 2,717, 512 at `LIONVEC_MAX_PARTS`) by
  k-means over the centroids - their 8-bit codes the sample, as the rows' are, `LIONVEC_REGION_ITERS` (5)
  iterations from G of them the seed picks (`LIONVEC_REGION_SEED`, one past the rows'), spherical
  for cosine as the rows' k-means is - and then each centroid into the region whose centroid is
  nearest it after the last update, found as k-means finds a row's. Its members are listed in
  ascending order (a counting sort, `first[]` and `member[]`); a region left with no members is
  kept, so that G is a function of C alone. A row is routed (`lionvec_route()`) by a plane-1
  estimate of its squared distance from each region's centroid, coded against the rows' mean as a
  row is (`lionvec_region_key()`); the `beam` nearest with members are taken, least key first, ties
  to the lower region, and then the next nearest until they hold the m centroids the row wants
  (`lionvec_regions_pick()`), sorted ascending, so that their members come in the centroids'
  order. Its candidates are then found among those members alone, by the rule over every centroid
  (`lionvec_candidates_among()`, `lionvec_candidates_n()`'s over a list of indices), and its
  nearest, and SOAR's second, among them as before. A row costs G + beam C / G estimates, about
  `(beam + 1) sqrt(C)`, where it cost C: some 310 rather than 2,717 in DBpedia's k-means and 870
  in its second pass, more where the regions are uneven (theirs held 16 to 141 centroids, whose
  squares summed to 65 a centroid where 53 even regions' would have to 51). The candidates
  include every centroid the full rule makes one that is in the beam's regions, but not only
  those: the m-th least upper bound among fewer centroids may be larger, which admits more (the
  unit tests count it as a rate). A row whose nearest centroid lies in no
  region of its beam goes to the nearest that does; the partition's spread and longest row, which
  the scan's bounds come from, are of the rows it holds, so a scan finds it there all the same,
  as it would a row placed by a centroid that moved.
  - **Where.** In k-means, each iteration's centroids are regrouped before its rows are assigned
    (`lionvec_kmeans()`, and a parallel build's leader before it posts the iteration, §44.12),
    from the same seed each time, so that the same rows make the same centroids and regions; the
    update is unchanged. For the second pass the final centroids are regrouped once and the
    partitions RENUMBERED region by region (`lionvec_build_renumber()`: the centroids, their codes,
    floats and plane 1 permuted in place, the regions' members rewritten as runs), so that each
    region's partitions are one run of the PART chain, which its REGION item names (§44.2); the
    renumbering changes no centroid, and the build routes by the renumbered regions, so a row's
    candidates come in ascending partition order whether the build or an insert finds them. An
    insert reads the REGION chain, keys every region, takes the build's beam (the same G and m)
    and reads those regions' runs alone (`lionvec_insert_read_regions()`); vector.sql checks that
    copies of rows inserted afterwards go to the originals' partitions and spill partitions. A
    scan reads no REGION page and ranks every centroid, as before: in the simulation that chose
    the regions, ranking partitions through their regions read a third more rows for a recall.
  - **The beam** is a constant, by what it is asked for: `LIONVEC_BEAM` (5) regions for a row's
    nearest alone (k-means, and the second pass and inserts of an index that does not spill),
    `LIONVEC_BEAM_SOAR` (16) for its nine nearest (`LIONVEC_SOAR_CANDS` + 1: the second pass of
    an index that spills, and its inserts), never more than G (`lionvec_region_beam()`). A share
    of G, as the first design had it (`ceil(G / 12)`, at least 4), would let a row's cost grow as
    C, and the measurements did not ask for one: on DBpedia (§44.9, "Regions") 5 found the
    partition exact assignment would have for 98.8% of the rows in 53 regions and 99.5% in 100,
    and 16 the copy's for 99.5% in 27, 98.6% in 53 and 97.9% in 100, at a recall within the
    sample's own spread of exact assignment's. A row's copy wants the larger beam: SOAR picks it
    from the nine nearest, which lie farther out, and 5 found it for 88% of the rows in 100
    regions, 13 for 96.95%.
- **Spill** (`lionvec_soar_second()`, the `spill` reloption, on by default). A row's true
  neighbours lie mostly in its own partition, but a row near the edge of its partition has
  neighbours in the next one too, and a query near such a row may probe one and not the other. An
  index that spills puts each row in a second partition as well, by SOAR's rule (Sun et al., "SOAR:
  Improved Indexing for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search", NeurIPS 2023): of the eight centroids
  next nearest the row after its own (`LIONVEC_SOAR_CANDS`), the one that minimizes `|x - c|^2 +
  lambda <r, x - c>^2 / |r|^2`, r = x - c1 the row's residual from its own centroid c1, lambda = 1
  (`LIONVEC_SOAR_LAMBDA`). The second term charges a partition whose residual x - c points the way
  r does: a scan passes c1's partition by when r points at the query, the row lying much nearer the
  query than c1 does (§44.4's margin), and a partition whose residual points the same way is passed
  by for the same reason. Eight candidates rather than every centroid cost no more than the
  assignment does already: they are those plane 1 cannot rule out of the nine nearest
  (`lionvec_candidates_n()`, the ninth least upper bound in place of the least; ten or so of 200 at
  320 dimensions and more, as before, a hundred at 64), ranked by their 8-bit codes, the first
  being the row's partition as before. Two partitions or more give two candidates or more - every
  bound having lo <= hi, as it does when the centroids' lengths are numbers no less than zero,
  which `lionvec_part_at()` checks, so that fewer is corruption - and so a row always has a second;
  one partition gives no copies, and the build records whether it spilled in the meta page's flags.
  The build compares the row with the centroids' floats, kept centred alongside their codes; an
  insert, whose floats are gone, decodes the candidates' 8-bit codes (`lionvec_decode8()`: `|x|
  alpha8 y / |y|`, y the code's vector, the projection of x on it, an error of `|x| sqrt(1 -
  alpha8^2)`, about a percent of `|x|`) and chooses among those, reading each candidate's REFINE
  item once, for its estimate, and keeping its codes. The floats, C dimsp of them, which the
  k-means held already, are kept to the end of the second scan: 12 MB for the benchmark's 1,974
  partitions of 1536 dimensions. Over clustered vectors at 64, 384 and 1536 dimensions (the unit
  tests, §44.10), SOAR chose a partition other than the second nearest for 25-29% of rows, the
  cosine squared of the copy's residual with r fell from 0.34-0.38 to 0.26-0.32, and decoded
  centroids chose as the floats did for 97 to 98% of rows, the rest within a percent of the least
  cost. The scale counts each row once, from its own partition, so that the margin means what it
  meant; a partition's spread and longest row are over everything its chain holds, copies included,
  since §44.4's bound must hold for each of them.
- **Kernels** (`lionvec_kernels_init()`, from `lion_vec_init()`). What a scan and a build spend
  their arithmetic on: plane 1's popcounts against the query's planes, for each of a query's
  centroids and each row a probe reads, and in k-means for each centroid for each sample row each
  iteration; the 8-bit codes' sum `<r, qc>`, for each centroid and row refined; k-means' exact
  distances (`lionvec_l2sq`); the rotation; and a halfvec's conversion (§44.1), once a row a build
  or an insert reads and once a query. Each has a portable kernel and, from x86-64 GCC 5
  and clang 6, kernels compiled with `__attribute__((target))`, of which the best set the CPU runs
  is chosen at load, as lion_container.c chooses its own (§3): **POPCNT**, plane 1 a word at a
  time; **AVX2**, plane 1 a word's four planes in one vector against the row's word broadcast,
  each byte counted with VPSHUFB and the bytes summed by VPSADBW every 31 words, the sums four
  doubles at a time in four vectors, and the rotation's signs and butterflies eight floats at a
  time, the strides under 8 by permutes inside a vector, and where the CPU has F16C, which its own
  `__builtin_cpu_supports("f16c")` checks (a name GCC knows from 11 and clang from 18; before
  them, as in the JIT's bitcode an older clang compiles, the portable conversion stays), a
  halfvec's halves eight at a time by VCVTPH2PS; and **AVX-512**, AVX2's with plane 1
  counted by VPOPCNTDQ (Ice Lake, Zen 4 and on; GCC and clang from 8), a word's four planes in one
  instruction on a 256-bit vector. AVX-512 is taken for VPOPCNTDQ alone: AVX-512BW's VPSHUFB
  counted plane 1 only a sixth faster than AVX2's, and the 8-bit sum eight doubles at a time less
  than a tenth faster in cache, where a scan waits on the codes' cache lines more (§44.9,
  "Kernels"), so no 512-bit instruction runs, for which some cores lower their clock. `make
  LION_NO_SIMD=1` builds the portable set alone.
  Every set returns what the portable one does, to the bit, so that on any CPU a scan refines the
  same rows and probes the same partitions, a build makes the same partitions and an insert picks
  the same one. Plane 1's are integer counts. The sums are in double, of terms each kernel
  computes with the same operations - a code's reconstruction `-4 + (c + 1/2) / 32` is computed
  rather than looked up, which vectorizes, and is exact, a multiple of 1/64 under 4, as is its
  product with a float - into 16 partial sums (`LIONVEC_LANES`), the i-th term into partial i mod
  16, added in a fixed tree (`lionvec_lanes_sum()`); the portable kernels add so too, which moved
  their rounding from the plain sum's by an ulp or so: DBpedia's index, rebuilt, gave the same
  recall, partitions, candidates and pages as before at every setting. lion_vec_math.c is compiled
  with `-ffp-contract=off`, for GCC and clang would otherwise fuse a multiply and an add wherever
  the target has fused multiply-adds (aarch64, x86-64-v3, `-march=native`) and round `l2sq`'s
  terms once where the other kernels round them twice. The rotation's butterflies are the portable ones' additions and subtractions, of the same
  operands. The halves' conversion is exact either way; VCVTPH2PS, which MXCSR's DAZ and FTZ do not
  touch, keeps a subnormal half and makes a NaN the quiet NaN of its payload, as the portable one
  does. The unit tests force each set (§44.10).
  `lionvec_query_init()` keeps its sums in locals and builds each word's four planes in registers,
  without a branch: adding into the query's own fields, which every store to qc and the planes
  might overwrite, and a branch on each bit of each code, which the CPU cannot predict, made it 45
  us a row at 1536 dimensions, 16% of a build; it takes 12, and gives the same planes to the bit.
  **2026-10-26: the choice and plane 1 come from §50.** lionvec no longer chooses its own set. Every
  kernel in lion_vec_math.c dispatches at each call on `lion_simd_current()`, the extension's one
  choice (§50), which picks on every CPU the set `lionvec_kernels_init()` picked, by the same
  `__builtin_cpu_supports()` tests - AVX-512 (AVX2 with AVX-512F, VL and VPOPCNTDQ), else AVX2, else
  POPCNT, else portable - where function pointers set at load were; `lionvec_kernels_init()` now
  only resolves the choice and asks `lion_simd_f16c()` once, and the AVX2 and AVX-512 sets convert
  halves with F16C where it says the build knows it and the CPU has it. The build's tests are
  lion_planes.h's: `LION_HAVE_X86_SIMD`, `LION_TARGET()` and `LION_HAVE_X86_F16C` for
  `LIONVEC_HAVE_X86`, `LIONVEC_TARGET()` and `LIONVEC_HAVE_F16C`, which tested the same compilers;
  `LIONVEC_HAVE_AVX512` went with the one AVX-512 kernel there was, and no macro of lionvec's own is
  left. **From §50:** plane 1 is `lion_planes_dot_interleaved(bits, planes, nwords, 4)`, that
  module's pass of constant stride for four interleaved planes in each implementation, which
  `lionvec_plane_dot()`, now an inline function of lion_vec_math.h, calls; lionvec's own portable,
  POPCNT, AVX2 and AVX-512 plane-1 kernels are deleted. **Here still:** the 8-bit sum, `l2sq`, the
  rotation and the halves, each portable and AVX2 (the halves F16C), the AVX-512 set running the
  AVX2 ones; and `lionvec_query_init()`'s planes, built in registers as above, which §50's scatter
  reproduces to the bit but would need the codes in an array first. The unit tests force a set with
  `lionvec_kernel_force()` as before, its `LIONVEC_KERNELS_*` numbers now `lion_simd_force()` of the
  implementation of that number, which moves §50's and the container library's kernels with
  lionvec's (`lionvec_kernels_init()` restores the best). vec_test passes with the same 119,295
  checks (119,262 without the x86-64 kernels), every statistic it prints the same to the digit, and
  an index of 100,000 random unit vectors of 1536 dimensions, rebuilt under each build, is the same
  28,020 pages to the byte but their LSNs. Measured on §50's machine (Emerald Rapids, AVX-512 with
  VPOPCNTDQ, four cores shared with other builds; gcc 13.3, -O2, PostgreSQL 16), before / after, ns:
  `lionvec_plane_dot()` at 1536 dimensions in a harness linked as vec_test is, pinned to a core, the
  median of eight alternated runs of the median of 31 rounds: portable 136 / 133, POPCNT 30.4 /
  30.1, AVX2 25.4 / 26.7, AVX-512 16.6 / 12.9; and `lionvec_estimate1()` around it 140 / 136, 46.1 /
  43.8, 35.2 / 35.7, 21.3 / 18.9. That is after one fix in §50 ("Kernels"): with the portable pass
  inlined into `lion_planes_dot_interleaved()`, every call saved six registers and grew a frame
  before jumping to its kernel, and AVX2's estimate took 39.2 against 36.5. A server whose flags
  have link-time optimization, as Ubuntu's packages' do (`-flto=auto`, which PGXS builds the
  extension with), inlines the dispatch into `lionvec_estimate1()`: a load of the choice and a
  direct call, where the pointer was an indirect one. End to end, eight queries `ORDER BY embedding
  <=> $1 LIMIT 10` on that table's `vector_cosine_ops` index, warm, under `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING
  OFF)`, the two builds alternated over 20 sessions of seven rounds each, 140 runs of each query a
  build: the queries' medians 33.1 - 67.9 ms before and 32.7 - 66.3 after, the geometric mean of
  their ratios 0.983, within the spread between sessions (a tenth). Such a query probes 581
  partitions, estimates some 40,000 candidates by plane 1 and refines 16,000, so plane 1 is about 2%
  of it. Its index's build (`REINDEX`, whose k-means and assignment estimate their candidate
  centroids by plane 1), alternated, took 142.9 and 141.5 s before and 138.4 and 139.7 after.
  **2026-10-27: the 8-bit sum in integers (`lionvec_dot8()`).** What §44.14 found worth doing
  instead of planes: `lionvec_estimate8()` no longer sums `recon8[c_i] qc_i` in double
  (`lionvec_sum8()`, 16 lanes, the AVX2 kernel four doubles at a time) but takes the codes against
  the query rounded to 16-bit integers once a scan, in `lionvec_query_init()`: `w_i = round((qc_i
  - mid) / delta)` with `mid = (max + min) / 2` and `delta = (max - min) / 65534` over qc's own
  range (plane 1's quantization is over the same range, in 15 steps), so that every w_i is within
  +-32767, kept with `sum(w)` and the rounding's variance `e^2 / dimsp` (`qw`, `qmid`, `qwdelta`,
  `qwsum`, `varq8`; `qw0` below). The kernel computes `sum(c_i w_i)` and `sum(c_i)` exactly in
  integers: portably in sixteen 32-bit lanes over blocks of 64 runs of 16, widened to 64 bits a
  block (a product is under 2^23, so 64 fit a lane with room), and under AVX2 sixteen codes a step
  widened to 16 bits and multiplied in pairs by VPMADDWD into eight 32-bit lanes, widened every 64
  steps, the bytes summed by VPSADBW; the POPCNT set runs the portable one and the AVX-512 set
  AVX2's, as for the other kernels. Then

      <r_8, q^> = (-4 + 1/64) (dimsp mid + delta sum(w)) + (1/32) (mid sum(c) + delta sum(c w))

  for the rounded query q^ - the codes' reconstructions being `(-4 + 1/64) + c / 32` - of which the
  first term is the query's alone (`qw0`, once a query), and the estimate is what it was of that
  sum; its error adds the rounding's variance under the root, `sqrt(var1 (1 - alpha8^2) + varq8)`,
  as plane 1's adds `varq`. The rounding is a 65,534th of the range a step, so `varq8` is some
  `delta^2 / 12`, a hundred-thousandth of the codes' own variance at 1536 dimensions, and the
  coverage test's calibration holds: its printed shares of rows outside 2 standard deviations
  moved by one in the fourth decimal (0.0404 to 0.0403 at 100 dimensions under L2, 0.0414 to
  0.0415 at 1536), nothing outside 6. The integer sums are the same in every implementation by
  construction, whatever order each adds in, and the double arithmetic after them is the same
  code of the same inputs under `-ffp-contract=off`, so every set still estimates the same bytes
  (`test_kernels_agree()`). k-means' queries, one a sample row an iteration, are not rounded
  (`qw` NULL): they never reach the codes; a scan's, the build's assignment pass's (once a row) and
  an insert's are. `lionvec_sum8()` stays as the reference the unit test checks the estimate
  against (and `vecplanes_eval`'s comparison row); no scan or build runs it. Tested in
  `test_kernels()`, `test_estimate8()` and `test_query_rounding()` (§44.10): the kernel against
  a plain integer loop at every dimsp from 64 to 8128 from unaligned pointers, over codes and
  weights at and mixed between their extremes, every set the portable one's; the rounding's
  every property; and the estimate against the serial sum over the rounded query (to 1e-9),
  within the rounding's reach of the floats' (`lionvec_sum8()`'s, 0.04 of that reach at most),
  its error as stated, every set the portable set's bytes. vec_test passes 119,449 checks
  (119,395 without the x86-64 kernels; 119,295 and 119,262 before), under ASan and UBSan too,
  and mutants of the kernel (an oversized block, a dropped lane or half of the byte sum, `floor`
  for `rint`, 65,535 steps, the wrong constant, the variance over dimsp - 1 or left out of the
  error) each fail it. Measured on this tree's machine - a 4-vCPU VM of a Xeon at 2.1 GHz with
  AVX-512 and VPOPCNTDQ, gcc 13.3, PostgreSQL 16.15 - in `vecplanes_eval --costs` (§44.14's
  harness, at `-O1` as the unit tests are built; ns a refine at 1536 dimensions, warm / from a
  24 MB pool / the lines flushed, pinned to a core, one run of both rows), `lionvec_sum8()`
  368 / 523 / 1,500 with AVX2, 365 / 511 / 1,500 with AVX-512 and 1,005 / 1,167 / 2,107
  portably; `lionvec_dot8()` 78 / 241 / 1,136, 75 / 242 / 1,100 and 274 / 439 / 1,406 (271 /
  438 / 1,384 with POPCNT): 4.7 times faster warm, 2.2 from the pool, 1.3 flushed. The
  prototype's `idot16` is 57 / 205 / 1,083: the byte sum's VPSADBW shares the shuffle port with
  the widening, 20 ns warm; a rounding grid through zero would need no `sum(c)`, for a step up
  to twice as wide, and is not done. In a scan (`bench/results/2026-10-27-lionvec-dot8/`):
  100,000 random unit vectors of 1536 dimensions in TOAST, `vector_cosine_ops` at the defaults,
  the index built once by the old library (104 s) and read by both, 50 held-out queries `ORDER
  BY embedding <=> q LIMIT 10`, everything in 4 GB of shared buffers and prewarmed, the two
  libraries alternated over 4 sessions of 5 rounds each of every query: the sessions' medians of
  the queries' medians 42.8 - 47.0 ms before and 35.7 - 39.2 after (45.7 and 36.9 at their
  medians), and each query's time under the new library over its time under the old 0.81 at the
  median of the 200 pairs, quartiles 0.78 and 0.85; each query probes 547.8 partitions and
  refines 14,957 rows on average under both (4 of the 50 queries' candidates or refines differ
  by a few: 16 rows more refined in 748,000, one partition more probed in 27,000, the bounds
  having moved by the rounding's variance), and recall is 0.632 for every query under both, row
  for row. That is about the 11 to 13% §44.14 expected of random vectors, and a little more: the
  sums were a quarter of their query there, and this machine's memory is slower against its
  cores. DBpedia was not on this machine; §44.14's arithmetic put the kernel at 5% of its warm
  query, whose sums are a tenth of it. No format change: the codes are read as they are.

### 44.4 The scan (lion_vec_scan.c)

Two priority queues. The PARTITION queue holds every partition, by the key (§44.3) its centroid's
codes bound from below, less the MARGIN: how much nearer than its centroid a partition's rows are
taken to come. The ROW queue holds rows, by a lower bound on their keys. Whichever queue's least
entry is less is worked; at equal keys, the row's:

- a partition known from its centroid's plane 1 (every partition starts so, `lv_read_parts()`
  having read the PART chain): read the centroid's REFINE item and put it back by its 8-bit codes;
- a partition known from its codes: PROBE it - read its CODE chain and put its rows in the row
  queue by plane 1's bounds;
- a row known from plane 1: read its REFINE item and put it back at the lower bound of its 8-bit
  codes (which replaces plane 1's rather than tightening it: keeping the larger of the two would
  keep plane 1's failures too);
- a row known from its codes: fetch it from the heap, compute its distance with the operator's own
  function on `FormIndexDatum()`'s value (so an expression index computes its expression), and put
  it back at its exact key;
- a row known exactly: nothing left in the row queue, nor in a partition whose turn has not come,
  is taken to be nearer; return it, its distance in `xs_orderbyvals` and `xs_recheckorderby =
  false`;
- REST: probe every partition probed so far again, for four times as many rows, skipping the rows
  returned already.

The REST chain is probed first, before either queue is worked: it holds every row of an index built
without partitions, and nothing otherwise. At equal keys the better-known entry comes first (a row
known exactly before REST or a bound at its key), then by distance and TID, so ties come out the
same from run to run.

**Probes.** A probe computes the key bounds [lo, hi] of each of its rows. The scan keeps the L
smallest upper bounds of the rows probed so far in a max-heap; their largest, tau, is a key at
least L rows lie within, so a row whose lo exceeds tau cannot be among the next L, and only the
rows with `lo <= tau` go into the row queue. One REST entry, at the least lo of those left out,
stands for them. L is `pg_lion.vector_batch` (100), or the LIMIT the scan is told when that is
more ("A known LIMIT" below), until the first REST, and four times as many after each. A LIMIT k
query thus probes the partitions whose centroids, less the margin, lie nearer than its k-th row,
refines about the rows plane 1 cannot tell from the k-th, and fetches about k and a few.

**The margin** (`lv_margin()`) is `pg_lion.vector_margin` (3) standard deviations of the rows about
their centroids along one dimension, the meta page's scale: a row is nearer the query than its
centroid by the part of its offset from the centroid that points at the query, and that part's
spread, `|x - c| / sqrt(d)` for a random direction, shrinks with the dimensions as a partition's
rows come to lie ever more nearly at one distance from any query. For L2, whose key is the squared
distance less a constant, the margin comes off the distance (`lv_part_key()`); for cosine, off the
key; for inner product, see below. It is one number for every partition: a constant margin did as
well as any scaled by a partition's own radius in the simulation (§44.9), as the rows farthest
toward a query lie about as far out in a small partition as in a large one when one k-means made
them. A row whose partition's turn does not come before the LIMIT is met is missed; that is the
scan's approximation, and the margin trades it against the partitions read.

**The pause.** The margin alone leaves a tail: unfiltered at a margin of 2, the partitions a query
probed had a median of 74, a mean of 143 and a maximum of 1,430 of the 1,974 (§44.9). A query whose
ten nearest lie far from every centroid finds many centroids within its tenth row's key less the
margin, and probes them all, though few hold a row nearer than those it has. So the scan counts the
rows it scores since one last entered the least upper bounds of the rows it is after, and once
those are in hand and the count reaches `pg_lion.vector_patience` (30) units - a unit the rows an
average partition would hold were there `2 sqrt(n)` of them, n the rows of the build (the meta
page's count): `sqrt(n) / 2` rows, or under a restriction twice that share of the members
(`lv_patience_unit()`) - it PAUSES (`lv_probe_part()`). The rows it is after are a TIER: besides
the L least upper bounds it keeps the K least for K = 10, 20, 40 and so on below L (`LvTier`), and
the next row's tier is the least K past the rows the pass has returned, or L. Paused on a tier, it
takes those K as found and probes no partition until it has returned them or the next row lies past
the K-th upper bound; then the next tier, whose count has run all along, decides the next pause. A
REST, which starts a batch of four times the rows, ends a pause too.
Paused, the scan still returns rows in order; a row nearer than those a pause returned, in a
partition not probed yet, is skipped when it is found, as one the margin leaves till too late is.
The pause trades those rows against the tail: in the numpy model (vtoy's `patience.py`), at 975,000
rows in 1,950 partitions, a patience of 20 partitions reached 0.98 recall reading a mean of 28,000
rows a query (95th percentile 75,000), where the margin alone needed 57,000 (227,000).

How a pause ends was found by its failures. Ended when the row queue was empty, it returned every
row the probes had kept below tau, and tau, the L-th least UPPER bound, lies past many more than L
rows: a restricted scan pausing at once (vector_filter.sql's, a patience of one partition's members) returned 1,255 rows
of a LIMIT 2000 over 9,000 members, the other 7,745 skipped as out of order. Ended only once the
next row lay past tau, it filled the LIMIT but still returned rows far past the L nearest, and a
LIMIT 1000 on the benchmark got 0.955 of its true rows; ended after L rows too, 0.983, against
0.980 for a LIMIT 10. Counting a restricted scan's patience in members rather than rows lets a
filter pause as an unfiltered scan does; counted in rows, a 1% filter never paused.

The tiers came from the local million-row benchmark (2026-10-16), where a query's 95th percentile
took three to four times its median. Counted against L alone (`pg_lion.vector_batch`, 100), a LIMIT
10 went on probing while rows entered the 100 nearest, which it would never return. On DBpedia's
115,186 rows, LIMIT 10 at a margin of 8: 200 partitions at the median and 401 at the 95th
percentile for 0.986 of the ten nearest (4.8 and 9.2 ms); by tiers, 159 and 254 for 0.985 (3.8 and
5.7 ms). A smaller L instead (`vector_batch = 10`) did as well for a LIMIT 10 and cost a LIMIT 100
2.5 times as much, its RESTs reading every chain again; by tiers a LIMIT 100 pauses at its own
100, as it did, but returns its first ten at the first tier's pause and loses a row it finds later
that belonged among them: 0.9908 at a margin of 8 for 336 partitions, against 0.9900 for 273. A
filter's members come a few to a partition, and a tier of ten fills and stalls sooner than one of
100: with the same unit, DBpedia's 1% filter, probed (`vector_exact_rows = 0`), fell from 0.969 of
the ten nearest at the default margin to 0.939; with twice the unit, 0.961, probing 368 partitions
at the median against 530. At each recall a filter now probes fewer partitions than it did: 0.9925
at 1% for 820 against 908, 0.9935 at 10% for 360 against 448.

**A known LIMIT** (2026-10-16). A pause on a tier ends once it has returned that tier's K rows,
and probing resumes for the rows the query still wants; a member it then finds, in a partition not
probed yet, nearer than rows already returned is skipped. A LIMIT 10 is stopped by its Limit at
the first pause and loses nothing so; a LIMIT 100 paused at 10, 20, 40, 80 and L's 100 in turn,
each pause ending by count, and lost what it found after each (the ten "returned at the first
tier's pause" above). Through LionOrdered on DBpedia's 115,186 rows (`vector_exact_rows = 0`, so
that the 1% filter probes too), at a patience of 30, a LIMIT 100 found 0.9884 of its hundred
nearest under a 3% filter at a margin of 8, against 0.9997 never pausing, and 0.9845 against
0.9999 under 1%; and at that margin it returned the plain scan's rows (an Index Scan with a
Filter) for 24 to 58% of the queries. A smaller LIMIT was to pause where it does, not a larger
one at every tier on its way. So LionOrdered hands the scan
the rows its query level's LIMIT takes, OFFSET included, when the planner knows them (§44.6,
`lion_vec_scan_limit()`), and the scan keeps no tier below them (`lv_reset_rows()`): a LIMIT 100
at the default L has none and pauses on L alone, whose rows the LIMIT takes whole, as before the
tiers; a LIMIT 50 first pauses at 80; a LIMIT of 1 to 10 keeps every tier, `LV_TIER_MIN` being the
least. On the same 200 queries (`bench/results/2026-10-16-lionvec-limit`) a LIMIT 100 at a
patience of 30 now pauses once a query rather than five times, skips 0.01 rows a query where it
skipped up to 0.97, and finds 0.9942, 0.9940 and 0.9941 of its hundred nearest at a margin of 8
under 10%, 3% and 1% (0.9913, 0.9884 and 0.9845 before), 0.9982 to 0.9988 at 16 (0.9963 to
0.9974) and 0.9679 to 0.9823 at 3 (0.9677 to 0.9727), probing the same partitions and reading the
same pages to within three, in the same time. With the pause off nothing changes, and a LIMIT 10
is the same row for row and count for count at every filter, margin and patience measured. What is
left of the gap to the pause off is the members in partitions the pause leaves unprobed, the
pause's trade; at 3% and a margin of 8 LionOrdered now returns the plain scan's rows for 57% of
the queries (39% before), the plain scan probing twice the partitions for 0.9987. A LIMIT the
scan is not told keeps every tier: none, a generic plan's Param, one under grouping, aggregates,
DISTINCT or a window, and every LIMIT of the plain scan, which core's Index Scan runs and no plan
data reaches - a filter lion cannot index, or none, whose LIMIT 100 is the 0.9908 above.

A LIMIT past L paused on L by count all the same, then found the rest in further passes, each REST
probing every chain probed so far again for four times the rows: at a patience of 30 a LIMIT 1000
under 10% and 3% filters made 2.5 and 2.75 passes a query, read 11,800 to 21,800 CODE pages and
found 0.9840 to 0.9998 of its thousand nearest at margins of 3 to 16 (0.9838 to 0.9997 with every
tier). So a scan told its LIMIT makes it L when it is more (`lv_start()`), up to an eighth of the
rows `work_mem` holds, where REST stops growing L too (`lv_cap()`; about 10,900 rows at the default
4 MB, past which it RESTs as before): the LIMIT 1000 makes one pass and pauses at most on its
thousand, reads 5,300 to 7,900 pages and finds 0.9863 to 1.0000 - at a margin of 8, 0.9997 under
10% and 0.9999 under 3% (0.9987 and 0.9983) from 6,816 and 7,793 pages (19,251 and 21,729), in 75
and 67 ms (142 and 137). With the pause off it returns the same rows, every query, from 2.2 to 2.8
times fewer pages. LIMITs of 10 and 100 are untouched, L being 100 already; and L at most an
eighth of `work_mem`'s rows keeps the queue's bound `work_mem`'s (`lv_cap()` is never under four
L's).

The patience grows with the margin past twice its default (`lv_patience_scale()`: by `margin / 6`
at the default). A larger margin asks for more of the nearest rows, and a patience that stayed put
held the recall to what the scan had found by then: 0.9935 of the ten nearest at any margin from 12
(0.9865 with the tiers). In step, the margin alone reaches 0.9975 at 24 (0.999 of a LIMIT 100's at
32); up to twice the default the margin stops a scan first, and the patience only its tail.

The unit was the average partition's own rows, the rows or members over the partitions, until
the default went from `2 sqrt(n)` partitions to `8 sqrt(n)` (§44.3). Then a patience of 30 paused
after a quarter of the rows, and on DBpedia held the unfiltered recall to 0.966 at any margin in
2,715 partitions, where 678 reached 0.988 (§44.9). Counted in the rows of `2 sqrt(n)` partitions,
whatever their number, the pause is where it was at the old default, and the `partitions`
reloption no longer moves it: 30 in 2,715 partitions now pauses where 120 did. The unit takes n
from the meta page's rows as of the build rather than from the partitions, and is at least one
row. In an index that spills (§44.3), each row is in two partitions and the probes count items,
so the unit is doubled for the copies.

**Inner product** takes one more step. An L2 row nearer the query than its centroid by its
offset's projection is so only by that projection less `|x - c|^2 / 2` (`|q - x|^2 = |q - c|^2 -
2 <q - c, x - c> + |x - c|^2`), and a cosine row likewise on the sphere; the margin is calibrated
against that. An inner product's row gains all of `<q, x - c>`, so a partition of rows of mixed
lengths keeps its answers - the rows that stick out farthest along q - beyond any such margin:
vector_filter.sql's ten clusters, of rows 2.4 to 3.3 long, got 0.61 of their ten nearest at
margins 0 and 2 alike and all of them only at 4. So `lionvec_lift_key()` lifts each partition's
rows by one more coordinate, `sqrt(M^2 - |x|^2)`, M the partition's greatest `|x|` (its PART
item's), which puts them at M from the origin, where the nearest to the unit query `(q / |q|, 0)`
are those of the greatest `<q, x>` (Bachrach and others, RecSys 2014). Their centroid then lies
inside that sphere by the rows' spread, their mean `|x - c|^2` (the PART item's too), at squared
distance `1 + M^2 - spread - 2 <q / |q|, c>`, and the margin comes off that distance as off L2's.
On unit vectors this is L2's ranking for the unit query; on the test's clusters it finds all ten
from a margin of 1. Each partition's own M, rather than the table's, keeps one long row from
widening every partition's margin. An insert longer than its partition's M is lifted to no
height, and its bound is the looser for it until REINDEX. The unit tests check the algebra: at
a margin of the lifted rows' greatest distance from their lifted centroid, the bound holds for
every row and query (the triangle inequality there).

**Strict order.** When a bound fails, a row turns up after rows farther than it were returned. It
is skipped (`nskipped` in the DEBUG1 line), so the scan's output is always in order: a failure
costs recall, never order, and the executor never needs to recheck.

**Memory.** The row queue is capped at `work_mem` (`sizeof(LvItem)` each, never under four
batches' worth). When a probe reaches the cap it drops the rows tau has since passed by, and if
that is not enough, CUTS: the half with the least lower bounds stay, the cut is the least bound of
those that went, and the probes keep only rows below it until the next REST; a REST at the cut
stands for the rest. Rows AT the cut stay - REST comes out after every row at its key - so a scan
of a million equal vectors returns `cap / 2` of them rather than none. After a REST, L is `min(4
L, max(L, cap / 8))`.

**Progress.** A hash keyed by TID keeps what the scan has learnt of each row across RESTs: its
codes' bounds once refined, its exact key once fetched, and GONE once returned or found missing.
A probe starts a row from that, not from plane 1 again. Without it a pass cut short by `work_mem`
whose kept rows all refined past the cut was made again, the same, for ever - the rows came back
from plane 1 below the cut, refined past it, and the cut's REST came out first (found by
vector.sql's `work_mem = 64kB`, `vector_batch = 1` case, 2026-10-14). With it, every REST moves at
least one row up a level or out.

**Copies.** In an index that spills a row has two CODE items, in two partitions' chains, and a scan
may probe both. Each must be met once a PASS - from the start or a REST to the next REST - or a row
would be refined, fetched or returned twice, and would stand twice among the L least upper bounds,
making tau too small and the pause too early. So the progress hash also records each row a pass
ENTERS - whose lower bound is within tau and below the cut, so that it goes into the L least upper
bounds and the row queue - and the pass's number (`lv_enter()`); the row's other item, met later in
the same pass, is skipped and counted (`ncopies`, the DEBUG1 line's last field, `N copies
skipped`). The first met wins: the other has the same bounds, being the same bytes, and tau and the
cut only fall within a pass, so it could do no more than the first did. A row left out of the pass
(`lo > tau`) is not entered, and its other item is left out too, for the same reason; the REST that
stands for them starts a new pass, in which each row is entered once again. A row returned is GONE
in every pass. A row that leaves the pass unworked - dropped by `lv_shrink()` or a cut, left out on
the second look at tau after its upper bound went in, or still queued at a REST - is forgotten if
the hash knows nothing more of it (`lv_forget()`): its other item is then left out as it was, tau
and the cut only falling within a pass. So the entries that say only that a row entered are the row
queue's own rows, within its `work_mem` cap, and the rest are the rows refined, fetched or
returned, as without spill. Kept, they would grow to every row within tau of every pass, orders of
magnitude past `work_mem` in a deep scan under a small one (a review found it). An assert build
checks at each REST that none is left. A probe of an index that spills looks every row up, even in
a pass whose hash was empty when it began, so that a TID a corrupted chain holds twice is skipped
as a copy rather than returned twice. The patience counts items, which the probes see, so a
partition's worth is twice the rows over the partitions; restricted, it is twice the members over
the partitions, the members themselves counted once, from the filter. A walk (NULL or cosine zero
query, or no ORDER BY) reads each partition's chain and skips its copies, so that it returns each
row once.

**The hash's bound** (2026-10-15, after a review found the hash unbounded). The GONE entries stay
for the scan's life, so the hash grew with every row returned: a scan with no LIMIT over a hundred
million rows would hold gigabytes, past any `work_mem`, and fail in palloc where a sort would
spill. It is now held to `hash_mem`, as a hash join's table is: as many entries as the largest of
simplehash's power-of-two arrays within it holds below its fill of 0.9 (`lv_seen_most()`), 48
bytes each; the PLANE1 entries, the row queue's own, come with its cap and are counted apart.
When an entry would not fit, `lv_seen_evict()` walks the hash, in three tiers:

- the entries a probe no longer needs: those of rows whose PLANE-1 upper bound, kept in the entry
  (`hi1`, carried in the queue's items from the probe), lies below the key of the row returned
  last. The scan's order is strict, so no such row can be returned again, and from that walk on a
  probe drops a row whose upper bound lies below that key, as the hash would have - and a refine
  or a fetch one whose codes or distance put it there, which the hash then keeps. Nothing is
  lost: the probe tells those rows by plane 1 alone, as it first read them. (A row whose plane-1
  bound fails so, not yet returned, is lost, as one the margin leaves till too late is.) This is
  the review's own suggestion made exact: the rows returned are dropped as the scan moves past
  them, as far as plane 1 can tell them from the rest.
- if that freed less than a quarter of the hash, the rows behind the last that plane 1 cannot
  tell: returned at a lesser distance, or known by their codes or distance to lie nearer. A probe
  meets them again and refines (or fetches) them once more, to find them behind again;
- and if that is still less than a quarter, what it knows of the rows ahead (CODES8, EXACT).

The second and third lose knowledge, and bring back the livelock that knowledge prevents (above):
so after four passes that lost knowledge since the scan was last done with a row, it stops
(`lv_may_probe()`); passes that lose nothing in between do not reset that count, since they may
only win back what the last one lost (vector.sql's scan at 64 kB made 65,000 passes for 20 rows
when they did). A walk is allowed once a quarter of what the hash may hold has come in since the
last, which pays for it; when none is, or a walk frees no room, a row's codes or distance are not
kept, and a row returned must be, so the scan stops after it. In an index that spills, an entry
lost also lets the row's other item enter its pass, so that the queue may hold the row twice;
whichever comes out second finds the row returned, or behind, and is dropped. A scan that cannot
go on fails the query by default, `lionvec scan of "i" outgrew hash_mem after N rows`, an ERROR
whose HINT names `work_mem`, `hash_mem_multiplier`, a sort, a LIMIT and
`pg_lion.vector_overflow` (§44.8). Set to `stop`, that ends the scan instead: it returns no more
rows and raises a NOTICE, `lionvec scan of "i" stopped after N rows, what it knew of its rows
having outgrown hash_mem`; what it returned is in order, each row once, the nearest it found.
The ERROR is the default (chosen 2026-10-16) so that a query that asked for every row never gets
fewer without failing; pgvector's iterative scans end without a word. The DEBUG1 line
counts the walks and those that lost knowledge. How far a scan gets depends on how well plane 1
tells rows apart, so on the dimensions and the data. Measured with `stop`, no LIMIT, `work_mem`
4 MB and so `hash_mem` 8 MB (117,964 entries) unless said, one row of the table as the query:

- 3,006 rows of 40 dimensions (vector.sql's), at 128 kB and `hash_mem_multiplier` 1 (1,843
  entries): every row, in order, the first tier alone making room.
- 2,000,000 rows of 16 dimensions, where plane 1 tells rows apart worst: before, every row, the
  scan's memory 165 MB, 81 s; after, it stops after 31,250 rows, 30 MB, 2.4 s; at 16 MB after
  88,212; at 64 MB every row, 241 MB (its queue's cap and the hash both grow with it), 33 s.
- 200,000 rows of 256 dimensions in 100 clusters of 2,000, uniform noise about each centre, so
  that the other 198,000 rows lie at distances within a few percent of each other, inside plane
  1's bound: before, 199,994 rows (6 out of order), 25 MB, 1.9 s, each row refined once; after,
  it stops after 14,912 rows, 18 MB, 2.0 s, having refined 604,286 (five walks, each losing
  knowledge); at 8 MB every row as before, 36 MB, 2.1 s, no walk. The rows a scan must know of at
  once to return the next is the table here, and the hash holds 59% of it.

A LIMIT of 10 or 1,000 over the last, 200 queries, costs what it did before (2.8 and 5.3 ms a
query either way, within the noise of runs). pgvector's iterative scans bound theirs the same
way, and tighter: HNSW's ends, without a word, at `hnsw.max_scan_tuples` (20,000) rows or
`work_mem` times `hnsw.scan_mem_multiplier` (1). The bound is read once, as the scan starts
(`seenmost`), so that `lv_remember()` costs no more than it did: a new entry with room is one
insert, and only a full hash looks a row up first.

**NULLs and zeros.** NULL rows come last, with NULL distances, from the NULL chain; before them,
in a cosine index, the zero vectors, whose distance is NaN (float8 sorts NaN after every number,
as the sequential scan's sort does), from the same chain. A NULL query returns every row of every
chain with a NULL distance; a cosine zero query every non-NULL row with NaN, then the NULLs; an
index with no vector yet only its NULLs. A walk copies a page's TIDs out under the page's lock, so
a VACUUM between two calls cannot make one come back twice. A scan without an ORDER BY, which the
planner never makes (its cost is infinite, and from PostgreSQL 18, which weighs disabled nodes
before costs, it carries two disabled nodes, as pgvector's do: without them it beat a sequential scan
disabled by `enable_seqscan = off`, and a count(*) failed as an index-only scan, found by the
insert spec of §44.10), walks every row.

**Prefetch** (2026-10-16). A cold scan waits on its reads one at a time: a probe reads a partition's
CODE chain a page after another, a refine a REFINE page, an exact distance a heap page and its
vector's TOAST pages, and none starts before the one before it is in. While
`pg_lion.vector_prefetch` is `fadvise` (§44.8: the default on 16, and what its `on` was until
2026-10-17; from 17 the scan reads through streams instead, "Read streams" below) the scan asks for
the pages it will read next before it reads them, through `PrefetchBuffer()`: as many ahead as the
relation's tablespace's `effective_io_concurrency`, to `LIONVEC_PREFETCH_MAX` (64), `so->ipf` pages
of the index and `so->hpf` of the heap, 0 asking for none (`lv_start_prefetch()`).
`PrefetchBuffer()` pins nothing and is `posix_fadvise()` under it on 16 to 19 alike, whatever 18's
`io_method`: the kernel reads the pages into its cache meanwhile, and the scan's `ReadBuffer()`
finds them there. It is a hint, never a read, so the rows a scan returns and their order are the
same with it on or off, and so is every count of the DEBUG1 line but the two it adds,
`N pages prefetched (M not in shared buffers)`, M the pages `PrefetchBuffer()` did not find in
shared buffers, which the kernel may still hold. It asks for:

- the rest of a chain the build wrote. The build writes each partition's CODE chain in blocks one
  after another, and its PART item counts its items, so its first `lionvec_chain_pages()` pages at
  `lionvec_page_items()` items a page (`so->pnrows`, kept by `lv_read_parts()` beside the heads)
  lie from its head on: reading block b of that run a probe asks for those to b + dist
  (`lionvec_prefetch_end()`), and once a page's next is not b + 1 for no more of the chain, the
  pages inserts appended lying a page here and there. The PART chain, which every scan reads
