  whole, likewise, its pages counted from the partitions', and a walk's chains for as long as each
  runs on block after block; not a probe's of the REST chain, whose length nothing records.
- the queues' next pages: the REFINE pages of the centroids at the top of the partition queue
  (`LV_CENT1`) and of the rows at the top of the row queue (`LV_PLANE1`), and the heap blocks of the
  rows whose exact distances come next (`LV_CODES8`). Of a queue's first `LV_PF_TOP(dist)` = 4 dist
  + 1 entries, which hold its least (a binary heap's first levels), the dist least at the level
  (`lionvec_least()`), after `lv_read_parts()`, after each probe, and again once half as many
  entries at that level as the last look chose have come out, so that what was asked for stays
  about dist ahead (`lv_prefetch_due()`). Of the row queue only the rows the scan works before its
  next probe, keyed below the next partition's key or the end of a pause if later
  (`lv_prefetch_bound()`): a look at the least 64 rows after every probe asked for 2,941 REFINE
  pages of a DBpedia scan that refined 97 rows. An entry asks once at a level (`pf`, cleared when it
  moves on), however many looks find it near the top, and a table of the 128 blocks of each
  relation last asked for, by hash, keeps a page that several entries share - five centroids'
  REFINE items to a page at 1536 dimensions - from being asked for again.
- the exact path's members (`lv_exact()`), in TID order, each one's heap block dist members
  before its fetch, a block's members asking once.

The heap is asked for only when it is the heap access method's, whose TIDs name its blocks, and
its vectors lie in its pages (`lv_vector_inline()`): stored `PLAIN` or `MAIN`, or small enough,
within the larger of `TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD` and the table's `toast_tuple_target` (both 2,032 bytes
at 8K pages unless the table sets the target: 506 dimensions of `vector`, 1,012 of `halfvec`; under
`toast_tuple_target = 8160`, every vector an index takes). The heap moves a row's values to TOAST
only once the row is past the threshold, and only until it is within the target. Until 2026-10-17
the threshold alone decided, so a table loaded under a raised target - the DBpedia benchmark's,
`KNN_INLINE` - had its vectors in its pages and none of them asked for. Past both pgvector's
`EXTERNAL` storage puts a vector in TOAST, which a fetch reaches through the TOAST index, the heap
page the least of what it reads; asked for alone, on DBpedia's
1536 dimensions, the heap pages bought nothing, the exact path cold taking 113 ms a query under
the 1% filter against 109 without. Reading a toasted vector's chunks ahead needs its TOAST
pointer, from the heap tuple, first, or the chunks' places kept in the index, which an index of
vectors that may lie in TOAST keeps (§44.13): its exact path streams them, and its rerank asks for
a row's first chunk page with its heap page.

Measured (§44.9, "Prefetch and parallel scans"): cold, each query alone after a restart with the
page cache dropped, a serial scan at a margin of 3 took 17.4 ms against 21.2 without (its wait on
reads, by `track_io_timing`, 11.4 ms against 17.7, for 410 pages from the kernel), at a margin of 8
32.4 against 49.4 (20.6 against 41.9, for 972 pages), and the exact path over vectors kept in the
heap, under a 1% filter, 33.5 against 70.6 (11.0 against 64.8, for 1,213 pages). Warm, every page in
shared buffers, an ask is a lookup of a page that is there already, 4 to 9% of a scan when every
page was asked for (2.39 ms against 2.29 at a margin of 3, 5.51 against 5.06 at 8). So the scan
watches what its asks of each relation find (`LionAsk`, lion_readahead.h): after `LION_ASK_WARM`
(32) asks in a row that found their page in shared buffers it lets the next `LION_ASK_DORMANT` (256)
asks pass unasked, then asks again. A cold relation is asked for all along, a warm one a ninth as
often (a margin-8 scan asks for 65 pages rather than 880), and one warm in parts loses at most 256
asks at a time; the PART chain, which every scan reads and so is warm whatever else is, does not
count. Warm it then costs about 2%: 2.33 ms against 2.29 at a margin of 3 and 4.99 against 4.91 at
8. While a relation's asks rest, the looks into the queues for them rest too (2026-10-27), as they
do while a stream rests ("Read streams" below): on 16 a look read up to 257 entries of its queue and
chose its asks only for `lion_ask()` to let them pass, 5.6% of a warm DBpedia query by perf and 6%
of a random vector's. So a look whose every ask would pass - the index's, or the heap's and, of a
row placed in TOAST, the TOAST relation's too - is let pass and chooses nothing, which has the next
entry out at its level bring the next; each such entry counts one against the rest, the ask the look
would have made for it, so the rest ends after 256 of them as it did after 256 asks, and the first
look after it asks for all it chooses, a resting look having marked nothing. It asks a little more
that way, 93 pages a warm DBpedia query against 80 and 2,346 against 1,876 on random vectors, and
looks 450 ns less a refine ("The refine's reads" below).

**Read streams** (2026-10-17; lion_readahead.c, lion_readahead_ring.c). From PostgreSQL 17 a scan
reads the pages it expects through core's read stream (`read_stream_begin_relation()`) instead of
asking the kernel for them: `pg_lion.vector_prefetch = stream`, the default there (§44.8). The
stream reads them into shared buffers itself - adjacent blocks in one read of up to
`io_combine_limit`, on 18 by an I/O worker or io_uring as `io_method` says, under `io_method = sync`
and on 17 by `preadv()` after `posix_fadvise()` advice - and hands the scan each buffer pinned, so a
page read ahead lands in shared buffers rather than the kernel's cache, and is looked up once.
Core's stream, as 17's and 18's read_stream.c have it, reads only the blocks its callback names, in
the order named, and calls the callback only from `read_stream_next_buffer()`, as its consumer
pulls: it looks ahead to a distance that starts at one block (a full I/O's, `io_combine_limit`,
under `READ_STREAM_FULL`), doubles each time the consumer waits on a read and falls by one at each
block found in shared buffers; once the callback names no block the stream gives nothing more until
`read_stream_reset()`, which starts it again from one block ahead. It cannot be paused, and it
starts no read before its consumer's first pull. A scan's reads fit that only in part. It knows the
run of the chain it is reading, and in a REST pass the chains it will probe; past those it predicts
(the REFINE pages at the top of its queues, the next partition's chain) and reads out of the order
it predicted, some pages never, some it never predicted, as its queues reorder under the rows and
partitions coming in.

`lion_readahead.c` sits between, through a ring of the blocks the reader expects
(`lion_readahead_ring.c`, frontend-safe, unit-tested against a model of core's stream in
test/unit/readahead_test.c). The reader pushes a block, urgent - the rest of the run it is reading -
or predicted; the stream's callback takes urgent blocks first, then predicted ones, then what the
reader's refill pushes when it is asked for a block and none is pending, and with nothing names
none, which ends the stream. A read takes its block from wherever it is: held, pulled from the
stream already by a read of a later block, its pin handed over; given to the stream, which is pulled
up to it, the blocks before it held for their own reads; pending, moved to the front, and the stream
started again if it had ended - once it holds nothing, which a restart releases; tracked nowhere,
read apart (`ReadBuffer()`), unless the stream is idle with blocks pending, which the read then sets
going. Held and given blocks are pins, at most the ring's limit: a block given when the ring is full
pushes out the oldest held one, released unread, and with every pin a given one the callback names
none. A stream that ended is begun anew with `READ_STREAM_FULL`, a full I/O ahead, if it read
anything in since it last started, and reset, which costs less, if it found every block in shared
buffers (`lion_readahead_op_restart()`). And a stream rests as the asks do, seeing its reads rather
than guessing from `PrefetchBuffer()`: after `LION_ASK_WARM` (32) reads in a row that read nothing
in, it pushes nothing and refills nothing for the next `LION_ASK_DORMANT` (256) reads, which are
`ReadBuffer()`'s, or until one reads a block in (`lion_readahead_dormant()`), and the scan skips its
looks into the queues meanwhile. A reader that knows its whole list in order needs none of that:
`lion_readahead_begin_list()` is a plain stream over it, from a full I/O ahead, holding as many pins
as core's own limits allow (`GetPinLimit()`), as a bitmap heap scan's does. It rests too, blind as
the asks are: after 32 blocks in a row it read nothing in for, its callback names none, the stream
ends once it has handed out what it was named - however many rests that lasts, a stream far ahead
holding hundreds - and the reads left of the rest are the reader's own (`lion_readahead_next()`
returns those blocks unpinned), after which the stream is reset and goes on from the list's next
block - a warm block it hands out being a lookup and a pin that the reader's own read repeats. Where
a stream is not wanted, or on 16, the same calls ask the kernel (`lion_ask()`) and read with
`ReadBuffer()`, or only read: the fallback for lion's readers as for lionvec's. Every pin is the
current resource owner's, so an error releases them with its transaction, subtransaction or portal.

A lionvec scan has three streams of the index, in its own context, kept from one rescan to the next
and reset - every pin released, every block forgotten - at each rescan, at each change of phase (the
walks after the queues) and when it stops (`lv_readahead_reset()`): `so->chains`, the PART chain,
each probe's run of its chain, pushed urgent `so->ipf` pages ahead, its first page too
(`lv_run_start()`), REST's chains and the walks'; `so->crefs`, the centroids' REFINE pages; and
`so->rrefs`, the rows'. Each holds up to twice `so->ipf` pins, at least `LION_READAHEAD_MIN_PINS`
(4), and no more than an `LV_RA_SHARE`th (an eighth) of the backend's fair share of shared buffers
(`lion_pin_fair_share()`: `GetPinLimit()` on 18, the same arithmetic on 17), reading half its pins
ahead; a pool that leaves a stream fewer than 4 has the scan ask the kernel instead. The queues'
looks (`lv_prefetch_queue()`) push their pages in the order of their keys, which is the order a
stream reads them in, and a stream that wants a page with none pending looks into its queue at once
(`lv_crefs_refill()`, `lv_rrefs_refill()`), rather than once half the last look is read, so that it
does not end. Between REST passes the chains' refill predicts the partitions to probe next
(`lv_chains_refill()`): of the partition queue's top, the least centroid known by its 8-bit codes
whose chain was not pushed yet, a chain at a time to `so->ipf` pages ahead, one another process has
claimed passed over. A chain it predicts and the scan does not probe - its LIMIT met, a centroid
refined after coming first - is read for nothing and released unread; without the prediction each
probe's stream ended with its run and started again from one block, and cold scans took 1.3 to 2.3
times as long (§44.9).

The heap's pages are another matter. The rows' heap blocks for their exact distances (`LV_CODES8`)
are asked of the kernel in every mode (`lv_prefetch_heap()`): a stream's pins on them would stay
from one `amgettuple()` call to the next, between which the executor runs anything, and the fetch
prunes a page only when its own pin is the backend's only one (`heap_page_prune_opt()`,
`ConditionalLockBufferForCleanup()`), which a stream's would not be. The exact path reads its heap
blocks inside one call (`lv_exact()`): there a list stream over the members' blocks, each block
taken from it at its first member and its pin dropped before the fetch pins it again, and the stream
ended before the call returns. The index's streams do hold pins between calls - the pages they read
ahead - which nothing waits on: lionvec's VACUUM takes no cleanup lock and never recycles a page
(§44.5), its WAL is generic WAL, whose redo on a standby takes none either, and the scan holds no
lock between calls. A parallel scan's participants each have their own. The DEBUG1 line names what
the streams did: `N pages streamed (M read in), A read apart, W streamed unread, R restarts` - the
reads they served and the pages of those they read into shared buffers, the reads no stream was
given (unpredicted, or made while resting), the pages they read ahead and released unread, and the
times one ended and started again - and the heap's asks as
`H heap pages prefetched (X not in shared buffers)`. On 16, `stream` is accepted and is `fadvise`.

**The refine's reads** (2026-10-27). A refine reads one REFINE item - a row's (`lv_refine()`) or a
centroid's (`lv_refine_part()`): `lion_readahead_read()`, which on 16 is `ReadBuffer()`, the share
lock, `lionvec_check_page()`, `lionvec_refine_at()` and `lionvec_estimate8()` over its codes - and
warm, every page in shared buffers, a row's took 2.6 us on DBpedia at 1536 dimensions, 1.0 of them
in the estimate (the timing of 2026-10-26 found 3,125 ns, 1,810 of them from the read through the
item's checks). A shared-buffer hit does not cost that; a chain of cache misses does, each waiting
for the one before it. Timing each step twice over, the second time on the same inputs a moment
later (temporary `rdtsc` instrumentation, each timestamp behind `lfence`, so that a step waits for
its own loads), gives the instructions' cost as the repeat and the misses' as the difference. On 4
KB pages, first and repeat, ns a row: `ReadBuffer()` 871 and 92 - the buffer table is a chained
hash, and its segment, its element and then the buffer's descriptor are read one after another,
three misses, two thirds of the step in `hash_search_with_hash_value()` and a quarter in
`PinBuffer()` by perf; the lock 40 and 41; `lionvec_check_page()` 789 and 28 - the page header, then
the special space where its `pd_special` points, on the page's other 4 KB half, two more misses in a
row, each a TLB miss as well; `lionvec_refine_at()` 180 and 34 - the line pointer lies in the
header's line, the item's first line is the miss; and `lionvec_estimate8()` 986 and 396 - 24 lines
of codes read in order, which the hardware prefetcher catches only after the first few. A centroid's
refine (245, 168, 98 and 681) is cheaper only because its 543 pages come up query after query and
stay in the cache. The rest of the list it was not: a query's rows share no REFINE page - 85 refines
read 85 pages, none the one before it, and even a random-vector query's 13,400 refines read 10,180
pages, 0.45 of them the one before - so refining a page's rows together, or keeping its pin from one
refine to the next, would save nothing (centroids do share, 118 refines on 62 pages, 1.7 of them
consecutive: not worth a pin cache); and the checks cost 28 ns once their lines are there. Huge
pages take the TLB misses out of all of it, the buffer table's and the descriptors' lines included:
a row's refine 3,480 to 3,110 ns serialized, a DBpedia query 6% faster and a random-vector one 11%,
so `huge_pages = on` is worth recommending for a warm index - a setting, not a change.

What the scan can change is the order of the misses: it asks for the lines before it needs them
(`lion_prefetch()`, lion_compat.h: `__builtin_prefetch`, which reads nothing, waits for nothing and
never faults), so that they run together. Once the buffer is pinned and before it is locked, both
refines prefetch the page header and the special space, whose place on a lionvec page is fixed
(`BLCKSZ - MAXALIGN(sizeof(LionVecPageOpaqueData))`), nothing of the page read before the lock; and
`lionvec_refine_at()`, once the line pointer has given it the item and its length is checked,
prefetches every line of the item before it reads the header (`lion_prefetch_range()`, a macro: GCC
13 deletes a function that only prefetches), so that the header's miss and the codes' overlap and
the estimate finds its codes on the way. The chain after the pin is then the header and the special
space together, then the item, in place of four misses and the prefetcher's run-up: serialized, a
row's refine on DBpedia 3,590 to 2,950 ns, the check 843 to 100, the estimate 911 to 488 and the
lock 40 to 472, where the two lines' misses now land (a locked instruction waits for them). The
buffer table's three misses stay: the lookup is core's, an extension cannot prefetch into it, and
the pages being distinct no refine shares one. The look into the queues before a refine
(`lv_prefetch_due()`) was the other cost, 450 to 540 ns of a row's refine on DBpedia and 5.6% of a
warm query by perf, mostly to choose asks that then rested: it rests with the asks now ("Prefetch"
above), 47 ns. Measured (§44.9, "The refine's reads"): warm, the same rows in the same order, a
DBpedia query 1.151 to 1.071 ms and a random-vector query 50.7 to 39.7 ms on 4 KB pages, 1.083 to
0.976 and 45.2 to 33.9 on huge pages; cold, the same reads and the same time.

**A parallel scan** (2026-10-16). `amcanparallel`: with `pg_lion.vector_parallel_scan` on (off by
default since 2026-10-17, the measurements below finding it slower everywhere; off, `lo_knn_partial()`
drops a lionvec order's partial paths), an unfiltered `ORDER BY` of the distance may be
a Parallel Index Scan under a Gather Merge (§44.7 prices it; a filtered one stays serial, below).
Each participant - every worker, and the leader unless `parallel_leader_participation` is off -
runs the whole scan above on its own: it reads the meta page and the PART chain, ranks every
centroid, and keeps its own queues, tau, tiers, pause and progress hash, returning its rows in the
order of their distances, each with its distance in `xs_orderbyvals`, which Gather Merge merges
into one order. What the participants share is whose each chain is. `LvShared`, in the area core
gives the access method after the `ParallelIndexScanDesc` (at `ps_offset`, `ps_offset_am` from 18),
holds a claim bit a chain - partition p's bit p, then the REST chain's and the NULL chain's - and a
participant probes a partition only if its `pg_atomic_fetch_or_u32()` found the bit clear
(`lv_claim()`, in `lv_probe_part()`), and drops one another has claimed as it comes out of its
queue (`lv_claimed()`), before reading the centroid's REFINE item, counting it neither among its
probes nor in `so->probed`. The bits are `LIONVEC_MAX_PARTS` + 2, 32 KB, the most `check_meta()`
allows, as before 18 the estimate cannot see the index. So each partition is probed by one
participant and each of its rows returned by that one, in that one's order, and the merged order is
in distance as the serial scan's is: a row leaves its participant when nothing in that
participant's queues, nor in a partition it may still claim, is nearer by the bounds, and the other
participants' rows reach Gather Merge in their own order. The REST chain is the first participant's
to reach `lv_start()`, and a REST pass probes again the chains its participant probed, for four
times the rows. The walks claim chain by chain the same way (`lv_walk_claim()`), so a walk through
the index returns every row once; the NULL chain is claimed once a scan, by the first walk to reach
it, and that participant walks both its zero vectors and its NULLs, whose NaN and NULL distances
sort after every other participant's rows. `amparallelrescan`, which core calls with no worker
running, clears the area. A restricted scan (LionOrdered's, §44.6) is never parallel, which
`lv_start()` asserts: LionOrdered's paths are not partial, and under `pg_lion.vector_postfilter`
`exact` or `error` a partial path that a Filter would follow is removed as the serial one is
(§44.7).

In an index that spills (§44.3) a row's two items lie in two partitions, which two participants
may claim, each then finding the row. So `LvShared` holds the rows returned as well, an
open-addressed set of 32,768 TIDs (256 KB), each slot set once by a compare-and-swap from zero:
the participant that records a row first returns it and the other drops it (`lv_take_row()`; `rows
another returned` in its DEBUG1 line, 3 to 7 a query on DBpedia). A row that finds none of its 32
slots free nor its own is returned through its own item and not its copy - one partition holds a
row's own item, and one participant that partition - so it never comes out twice, whatever the
set holds, and is missed only where no participant probes its own partition.

The stop rules stay each participant's own, over the partitions it claimed and the rows it found.
A row's place in its participant's order needs nothing else, and a bound shared between the
participants - the least tau of all, so that one stops where another's rows already lie nearer
than its next partition, as the serial scan stops on all of its rows - would put a heap of upper
bounds that every probe updates between them, and make one participant's pause hang on the
others' rows. The hope was that each participant, scoring about a share of the rows and finding a
share of the nearest, would pause where the serial scan does in its own count, so that together
they probe about what it probes. They do not: its rows are its own partitions' and so lie
farther, which carries the margin farther down the order, and the patience is a count of rows,
which a participant scores at the serial scan's rate. On DBpedia at a margin of 3 each of two
participants probed 29 partitions and each of four 33, where the serial scan probed 36, so
together 1.6 and 3.7 times its partitions - and they found more of the nearest rows for it, 0.935
and 0.9515 of the ten nearest against 0.919. To that recall the serial scan, at a wider margin,
probes 1.24 times fewer partitions than two participants (at a margin of about 3.7) and 2.0
times fewer than four (4.6), and as many times fewer CODE pages; at a margin of 8 two
participants' 0.994 cost 1.03 times the serial scan's partitions for it (at about 15), and four's
0.996 lies past the serial scan's best measured (0.9945 at 16, from 382 partitions to their 791).
That is the ratio a shared bound would win back, which §44.11 leaves to it.

The executor runs the workers ahead of the leader. A worker does not wait to be asked: it runs
its scan and puts each row in its tuple queue until the queue is full or the leader ends the
query, while Gather Merge waits first for a row from every participant and then takes the least
of their heads. So under a LIMIT 10 the participants together returned 17.3 rows a query with two
participants and 36.8 with four, against the serial scan's 11 (the query's own row is filtered
out), and computed 24.3 and 54.2 exact distances against 11.8: the executor's model, not the
scan's, which cannot know how many rows the leader will take. And the first row waits for the
slowest participant's first, each having ranked every centroid and probed to its own rules, and
for the workers' start, about 10 ms a query here: warm, under `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, VERBOSE)`, the
Gather Merge's first row came at a median of 12.1 ms with one worker and 14.7 with three, where
each worker's own first row came 1.6 and 2.1 ms into its scan and the serial scan's 0.6 ms into
its (an assert-enabled build, pg_lion preloaded, pgvector loaded by each worker). The parallel
scans took 5 and 8 times as long as the serial one (§44.9).

### 44.5 Concurrency, WAL and VACUUM

- **Insert** (`lionvec_append()`): under the meta page's exclusive lock, which serializes inserts,
  the row's partition is found (§44.3), its REFINE item goes on the REFINE tail and its CODE item
  on its chain's tail - its partition's, the REST chain's in an index without partitions, or the
  NULL chain's - each extended with a new page when full; in an index that spills, its copy then
  goes on its second partition's tail (§44.3). A generic WAL record a step, as one takes at most
  four buffers: the REFINE item with the meta page, whose REFINE tail it may move; then the CODE
  item, its page, any new one, and the PART item or the meta page that holds the chain's tail when
  the tail moves; then the copy, as the CODE item. A crash after the first leaves a REFINE item
  nothing points at, which costs its space and nothing else. A crash after the second leaves a row
  without its copy: it is still in its nearest partition, and only a scan that would have found it
  through the copy alone misses it - recall, for that row only, until REINDEX; no scan returns a
  wrong row, nor one twice. Scans and VACUUM lock one page at a time and never the meta page with another, so the
  order meta, REFINE, CODE, PART, then the copy's CODE and PART, each record's pages released
  before the next record's are locked, cannot deadlock against them. A probe follows
  the chain to its end as it then stands, so it may meet rows inserted since its snapshot; the heap
  fetch drops them. Every row a scan's snapshot sees had its items appended before that snapshot
  was taken, so none is missed. An insert reads the whole PART chain, 60 pages for 1,975
  partitions, and the REFINE items of its candidates.
- **Build**: two heap scans. The first computes the mean (its rows normalized for cosine) and
  takes the sample, from which k-means finds the centroids (§44.3), whose REFINE items are the
  first written; it fails the build at the first row with which the rows so far want more
  partitions than the sample has rows for (`pg_lion.vector_build_sample`, §44.8). The second
  writes each row's REFINE item in place and puts its CODE item into a tuplesort
  (`maintenance_work_mem`) keyed by its group - its partition, then the REST and NULL chains - and
  its TID, from which the CODE chains are written in one run of blocks, each group
  starting a page, and each partition's count, spread and longest row summed in that order; then
  the PART chain, then the meta page. In an index that
  spills the sort holds two items a row, the copy under its second partition's group, so it is
  twice the size and spills to disk at half the rows; the meta page's row count counts each row
  once, the PART items' counts every item. The whole range is
  WAL-logged at the end (`log_newpage_range()`). Neither scan joins a synchronized scan
  (`allow_sync = false`), which could start part-way through the heap: the sample must be the same
  from build to build, and the second scan's REFINE items then lie in heap order, as each
  partition's CODE items do whatever order the rows came in, being sorted by TID. Built in
  parallel from PostgreSQL 16 (§44.12); progress is reported for the second scan. `CREATE INDEX
  CONCURRENTLY` and
  `REINDEX` work as for any AM. An unlogged index's init fork is the meta page and empty REST and
  NULL chains.
- **VACUUM** (`lionvecbulkdelete()`): walks every CODE chain (`lionvec_chain_heads()`: the
  partitions' from the PART chain, then REST and NULL), removing the dead rows' items
  (`PageIndexMultiDelete()`), and collects their REFINE locations, in `maintenance_work_mem`, which
  it then removes a REFINE page at a time in block order, each checked by TID first, with
  `PageIndexTupleDeleteNoCompact()`: the line pointers stay, so the other rows' CODE items still
  point right. A crash between the two steps leaves REFINE items nothing points at, which the next
  VACUUM does not find; they cost space and nothing else. In an index that spills a dead row's two
  items go as their chains are walked, and its REFINE location is taken from its primary alone, so
  that it is removed once; the row is counted once, by its primary, in the rows removed and the
  index's rows. When the locations fill `maintenance_work_mem` mid-walk they are removed then, and
  a copy in a chain not walked yet may point a while at a REFINE item gone or reused; a scan that
  meets it finds no item with its TID and takes the row as gone, which it is. A crash part-way
  leaves copies of rows whose primaries went; the heap's line pointers stay dead until a VACUUM
  completes, so the next one removes them. The bulk-delete callback is asked of a copy's TID as of
  its primary's: twice the lookups in lazy VACUUM's dead-TID store, and twice the TIDs in
  `validate_index()`'s sort under `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, whose merge with the heap skips a
  TID it has passed, so the duplicate costs a sort entry and nothing else. Pages are never
  recycled; the centroids' REFINE items, which no CODE item names, are never removed.
- **A scan against VACUUM.** A scan copies what it needs of a CODE item (the REFINE location among
  it) into its queue and holds no lock between rows; through read streams (§44.4, "Read streams")
  it holds pins of the index pages they read ahead, which VACUUM, taking no cleanup lock, does not
  wait for, and never one of the heap's. VACUUM may remove the REFINE item before the scan reads it,
  and an insert may reuse the slot: `lionvec_refine_at()` returns the item only if its TID is the
  row's, and the scan treats a missing one as a row gone, which it is - VACUUM removes only rows
  dead to every snapshot. A reused slot with the same TID (the heap reused the TID too) holds a row
  inserted after the scan's snapshot, which the heap fetch drops. A row the scan returns it has just
  found visible to its snapshot, so VACUUM cannot have removed it, and the executor's own fetch finds
  it. A centroid's REFINE item missing is corruption.
- **Serializable**: `ampredlocks = false`, so a reader takes a predicate lock on the whole index
  (`index_beginscan()`), and an insert checks it.
- **`old_snapshot_threshold`** (PostgreSQL 16 only; 17 removed it): with it set VACUUM may remove
  rows a snapshot older than the threshold still sees - their CODE and REFINE items with them - so
  "VACUUM removes only rows dead to every snapshot" above does not hold. Core's access methods turn
  that into "snapshot too old" by testing every page they read (`TestForOldSnapshot()`); lionvec
  tests none, and the heap fetch it returns rows through (`table_index_fetch_tuple()`, 16's
  `heap_hot_search_buffer()`) none either, so such a snapshot's nearest neighbours would come back
  short without a word: on a 16 server at a threshold of one minute, a REPEATABLE READ transaction
  counted 2,000 rows through a lionvec scan, another deleted 500 of them and VACUUMed a minute and
  a half later (`tuples: 500 removed`), and the same scan in the same transaction counted 1,500,
  where a sequential scan raised "snapshot too old". As lion is (§9), lionvec is not read while the
  threshold is set: `lionveccostestimate()` adds `disable_cost` to every order, so a sort of the
  rows wins; `lion_ordered_set_rel_pathlist()` raises no `pg_lion.vector_postfilter = error` for a
  filtered order, which no lionvec scan answers then; and what reaches one anyway, a plan with
  every other path disabled, is `ERRCODE_FEATURE_NOT_SUPPORTED` in `lv_start()`, at the scan's
  first amgettuple (the snapshot is not known in ambeginscan) and before it reads a page, in each
  process of a parallel scan. Inserts, VACUUM and builds are not refused.
- **Format checks**: every page's type and id before anything on it is read; every CODE item's
  length against its flags and `dimsp`, its flags against each other (a copy is neither NULL nor
  zero), and a copy anywhere but a partition's chain of an index that spills; the meta page's flags
  (none unknown, and spill only with two partitions or more); every REFINE item's length, and a
  centroid's alpha8 and code length finite; every PART item's length, flags and blocks, its
  centroid's length, its longest row and its spread finite and not negative and its alpha1 finite
  (a negative length makes a bound whose lower end lies past its upper, and the ranking of an
  insert's candidates come up short, which is checked too), and the PART chain's numbering against
  the meta page's count; chain cycles (`lionvec_chain_step()`); the meta page's fields. Each is
  ERRCODE_INDEX_CORRUPTED, never a crash. Every page's header is within the bounds
  `PageAddItemExtended()` PANICs outside of (`lionvec_check_page()`, §3, 2026-10-18). And an insert,
  which holds the meta page from its first page to its last, refuses a block it is about to read
  that names the meta page - a chain end or `refine_tail` on the meta page, a PART item's tail or
  centroid, a REGION item's run, a chain's next link - as it refuses a LOC tail that is also the
  LOCDIR tail and a partition's tail that is its PART page, BEFORE the lock
  (`lionvec_insert_readbuf()`): a buffer content lock is not reentrant, and the second one waited
  for this very backend with interrupts held off, which only a restart of the server ended
  (`test/sql/vector_corrupt_records.sql`). Every REFINE item lies inside its page's data, as a PART
  or REGION item must (`lionvec_item_ok()`): `lionvec_refine_at()` checks its line pointer's offset
  against `pd_upper` and its end against `pd_special` after its length and before the item's first
  prefetch or read, where an offset past the page - up to 32,767 - had a scan read the item from
  whatever memory follows it (the same file, 2026-10-27).

### 44.6 Filtered nearest neighbours (LionOrdered, lion_ordered.c)

§30's node walks an ordered index path filtered by lion's TID set. A lionvec index's order by
distance qualifies as an ordered path when it has one ORDER BY clause, no index clauses, a forward
direction and is not hypothetical (`lo_knn_path()`), and is paired with each lion access of the
relation as a B-tree's is. The plan differs from §30's in four places:

- **The set is built at once** (`LO_FLAG_BUILD`), never lazily: the scan needs every member before
  its first row. The ORDER BY clause goes in a sixth `custom_exprs` list (`LO_EXPR_ORDERBYS`), and
  the executor builds its scan key with `ExecIndexBuildScanKeys(isorderby = true)`, its run-time
  key (a Param query vector, a correlated subquery's) among the node's others, re-evaluated on
  rescan. EXPLAIN shows it as `Order By`.
- **The set is handed to the scan** after every `index_rescan()` (`lion_vec_restrict()`: its
  container keys, ascending, and its containers), and with it the rows the query takes
  (`lion_vec_scan_limit()`): `root->limit_tuples` as the plan recorded it (`LO_PRIV_LIMIT`), the
  LIMIT of the node's query level and its OFFSET, or -1 where the planner did not know them - no
  LIMIT, a generic plan's Param, grouping, aggregates, DISTINCT or a window above it. The scan
  keeps no tier of its pause below them, and makes them L when they are more, to an eighth of
  `work_mem`'s rows (§44.4, "A known LIMIT"). They say where to pause and what to gather, not how
  many rows to return: a residual filter or a join that takes fewer rows than the scan returns
  gets more, from probing resumed, and REST. The scan counts the members and then does one of
  two things:
  - **No more than `pg_lion.vector_exact_rows` (2,000) members, or than
    `pg_lion.vector_exact_per_partition` (1.5) a partition if that is more**
    (`lionvec_exact_limit()`): it fetches every member
    from the heap, computes its distance with the operator's function, sorts them (NaN last, then
    by TID) and returns them in order (`lv_exact()`), reading no CODE page. A member not visible,
    or whose vector is NULL, is left for the NULL walk, a cosine zero vector (NaN) for the zero
    walk. This is the exact answer, at a heap fetch a member; it replaces probing where the
    members are so thin over the partitions that most partitions hold none or one and the nearest
    member lies past many - in the simulation a 0.1% filter of 975,000 rows needed a fifth of the
    index probed for 0.95 recall.
  - **More**: it probes as an unfiltered scan does (§44.4), at the same margin, its patience
    counted in members. The k-th nearest member lies farther out, past more centroids within the
    margin, and the pause ends those probes. Before the pause counted members the margin was
    narrowed instead, by 1.3 standard deviations for each tenfold the members thinned the rows by
    (in the simulation the margin a recall needed fell about that much a tenfold) and then 1.8;
    with the pause, narrowing cost recall and saved no time - on the benchmark, through
    LionOrdered, narrowed by 1.8, 0.975, 0.974, 0.970 and 0.952 of the ten nearest under filters
    of 10%, 3%, 1% and 0.3%, and not narrowed 0.981, 0.980, 0.981 and 0.965, in the same time at
    each (27 ms at 1%). A probe skips a CODE page whose container keys hold no member, and every
    row not a member before it is estimated; a refine, a fetch and a return happen only for
    members.

  A set past `hash_mem` is in the node's arena (§30.4, "Spilling"), a mapped temporary file,
  and the scan probes it there as it probes one in memory: the containers are the same, at
  addresses that do not move. *(Until 2026-10-19 such a set had degraded to NULL containers,
  meaning every TID of that key's blocks, which the scan took whole and the node rechecked.)*
- **No fetch-and-sort switch**: the pathkeys are a distance, not columns a sort could take over.
- **No values from the index**: heap mode always.

**Which path** (`lionvec_exact_limit()`, 2026-10-16). The exact path costs a heap fetch and a
distance a member, as many as the members whatever the index. Probing costs partitions and CODE
pages: the k-th nearest member lies past more centroids the thinner the members, and a probe reads a
partition's CODE pages - skipping those whose container keys hold no member - for the members among
them, so where they are about one a partition each probe reads a page or two for one member, and the
pause, counted in members, comes late. What decides is the members a partition, which a count of
members does not follow from one index to another. With a flat 2,000, a million rows' 1% filter
(10,063 members in 7,999 partitions, 1.26 a partition) probed for 0.956 to 0.98 of the ten nearest
in 13 to 20 ms, where every member's distance took 11 ms for all ten; raised to the 12,000 that
takes it, the count would have made DBpedia's 10% filter exact too (11,377 members in 2,715
partitions, 4.2 a partition: 26 ms, against 8.5 to 13 ms probed for 0.956 to 0.994). Warm, the two
crossed at two to three members a partition on both data sets; cold, the exact path is a random heap
read a member, and on DBpedia's 115,186 rows crossed at 1,200 to 1,800 members, under one a
partition (§44.9). So the scan computes every member's distance when the members are no more than
`pg_lion.vector_exact_rows` (2,000: near where the cold costs crossed, whatever the partitions) or
`pg_lion.vector_exact_per_partition` (1.5, below the warm crossing) times the partitions, whichever
is more, and the cost (§44.7) asks the same of the same meta page, so that the planner prices the
path the scan will take.

The node's early stop - every member met - ends the scan without the probes that would find
nothing. Since the restricted scan returns members only, a LIMIT is never left short by the filter.

**Cost** (`lo_cost_knn()`): the lion lookups and the set as `lo_cost()` prices them, plus
`lion_vec_scan_cost()` for the members (§44.7) as start-up; then per member, at worst, a random
page (none where the exact path read the row's heap page before its first row, §44.7, "Exact path
pricing"), an index tuple, a probe and a tuple, its quals and the target. On 20,000 rows of 200
dimensions (format 1) the planner chose a sort of the lion bitmap scan's rows for a filter keeping
1% of them, the node from 3% to 30%, and the plain lionvec scan with a Filter from 60%, where most
rows pass and the set costs more than the rows it saves.

**Filter at the fetch: tried and removed (2026-10-19).** For a day (2026-10-18) LionOrdered had a
second flavour over a lionvec order, for wide filters, where the set is most of the query (845 ms
of 850 to 1,050 at 10% on the 50M-row benchmark, §44.7, "The set's pieces"): it built no set and
handed the scan the lion clauses instead, which the scan tested on the heap tuple of each row it
fetched for its exact distance, dropping a row that failed; the planner offered both flavours and
kept the cheaper. Measured by the maintainer at 50M rows, it was removed, and the set is the one
way the node restricts a lionvec scan:
- **its results depended on the plan.** Knowing a row's membership only at its heap fetch, the
  filter's scan counted its patience, its tiers and its refine threshold over every row, scaled by
  the planner's estimate of the filter's share, where the set's counts members. The two agreed at
  `pg_lion.vector_patience = 0` only: with the pause on, a 3% filter at a margin of 12 had a
  recall of 0.997 through the filter and 0.980 through the set, and a 1% filter at a margin of 6
  0.967 and 0.943, so a query's recall moved with the flavour its costs chose.
- **its tail grew sharply with the margin.** Every row it fetched to test was a random read of a
  130 GB heap: at a margin of 12 its slowest queries took 14 to 37 s, the set's 1.4 s at most.

The invariant: for a query's rows not to depend on its plan, the scan must know which rows are
members where it walks, before it scores them - as the set tells it, by container key - and a heap
row, read after the walk has counted it, cannot.

**Post-filtering (2026-10-16).** A lionvec scan under a `Filter` is another search than the
restricted scan, not the same one with the rejected rows left out. The scan ends a pause, and moves
the frontier behind which it skips a late row, on the rows it *returns* (`lionvecgettuple()`:
`pauseleft` and `passret` count every row returned, the tiers step on `passret`, and `lastdist` is
the last row's distance); the executor applies the Filter after `amgettuple`, and nothing of it
comes back to the AM. The restricted scan returns members only. So under a selective filter the
plain scan's pauses end by count on rows the Filter throws away and its probes resume, as if it
hardly paused, while its frontier runs past members it has not found yet. On the 1M-row DBpedia
set (200 queries, LIMIT 10), at 1%, a margin of 8 and the default patience of 30, the plain scan
returned 0.993 of the true ten for 29,075 pages and 17.6 pauses a query, LionOrdered 0.980 for
3,483 pages and 0.98 pauses, the same rows for 85.5% of the queries; with the pause off and a margin of
3, where both probe the same partitions, the plain plan is the lower, 0.960 against 0.966, from the
members it skipped behind a frontier that non-members had moved (21 a query against 0.1). Same
settings, other rows: the plan decided the answer, which it must not.

So a lionvec order a Filter would follow is not a plan (`pg_lion.vector_postfilter`, §44.8, at
`error`, its default since 2026-10-17, or `exact`). LionOrdered's `set_rel_pathlist_hook` takes it
out of the relation's path list before core's `set_cheapest()` (`lo_knn_take()`) whenever the
relation has a clause the scan would leave to its Filter: a restriction clause that is not
pseudoconstant (a gating Result tests those once), for a partial index not implied by its
predicate - such an index, whose predicate implies every clause, stays the filter's order - and
not the index's own (`lo_knn_own()`, 2026-10-17): a clause of the columns the index's key reads
alone, the vector's (`v IS NOT NULL`, a distance bound `v <-> q < 0.5`), rejects the NULL vectors
the scan returns last, or rows by the distance it returns them in, and so leaves the rows before
them as they were; it filters the scan's rows under every setting. Core's sequential scan, which a
cheaper order may have made `add_path()` discard, is offered again. The node still walks the order,
and over a lion side only if that side answers every clause but the index's own: the node's own
Filter would reject members the scan had returned just as the plain scan's does. Core's lion
accesses are a bitmap scan's, which leaves an index whose bitmap costs more than the rows it saves
to the heap scan's Filter (`choose_bitmap_and()`: `tag < 50` beside `cat IN (1, 2)`), so when none
of them answers every clause the node ANDs the access answering most of the clauses left, among
core's and each lion index's alone, until one does (`lo_knn_cover()`), and the price decides as for
any lion side. A filter lion indexes answer thus always goes through LionOrdered (unless
`pg_lion.enable_ordered_scan` is off, or the set would not fit `hash_mem`); any other fails at plan
time under `error`, EXPLAIN included, naming the clauses no lion index answers, and under `exact` is
planned exactly, by a sort of the filter's rows over a sequential, bitmap or B-tree scan
(`WHERE id = 5 ORDER BY v <-> q LIMIT 1` sorts the one row the primary key finds). The approximate
answer is then asked for in so many words:

    SELECT ... FROM (SELECT ..., embedding <=> $1 AS d FROM t [WHERE <clauses lion answers>]
                     ORDER BY d LIMIT 1000) s
     WHERE <the other clauses> ORDER BY d LIMIT 10;

The planner pushes no clause below a LIMIT, so the inner scan is unfiltered or restricted through
LionOrdered, and how far it reads, 1,000 rows here, is the query's to say. `allow` plans as before:
the plain scan with a Filter and LionOrdered with one compete on cost, which is what the planner
chose from 60% above and at 10% and 3% in §44.7 and §44.9. What the rule does not reach: a set
with a lossy lion clause has its rows rechecked by the node,
which filters members the scan returned; a join's clause filters an ordered scan of one side
(a nested loop over it) and is no restriction of that relation; and a distance bound few rows pass
leaves a LIMIT unfilled, so the scan reads on to its end, as pgvector's do.

**Row-level security (2026-10-17).** lionvec refuses it. A policy is a restriction no lion index
answers, on a table the node does not scan (§30.1), so under `error` every lionvec query of a role a
policy filters would fail, with a `WHERE` or without, and so would the subquery, whose scan the
policy filters too. `lionvec_refuse_rls()` builds no lionvec index on a table with row-level
security enabled, or on a partition of one, and fails at plan time, under every
`pg_lion.vector_postfilter` and for the owner too, a query that a lionvec index of such a table
could order; any other query of the table is planned as ever. A table that inherits from one with
row-level security (`INHERITS`, not a partition) is not looked at: under `error` the parent's
policies fail a lionvec query of the child through the parent, as any filter LionOrdered cannot
take does.

**The default, `error` (2026-10-17).** `exact` was the default for a day; from 2026-10-17 it is
`error`, so that a query whose filter lion cannot answer says which answer it wants: the
subquery's approximate one, or `exact`'s sort, which reads every row that passes the filter. What
the default fails, by `lo_knn_take()`'s rule unchanged, is every lionvec order under a restriction
clause no lion index answers and no partial lionvec index's predicate implies, however cheap the
exact plan: a key's `id = 5` (or `id = $1` in a generic plan); a volatile clause
(`random() < 0.1`); a correlated outer column's clause in a LATERAL subquery (`note = q.note`); a
plain view's WHERE; in a partition, the parent's clause on the partition key, which every row of
the partition passes (core keeps it as the partition's Filter); and on PostgreSQL 16, `IS NOT NULL`
on a NOT NULL column other than the vector, which 17 and later drop when planning. A partial
lionvec index whose predicate implies one clause is no way round another that lion answers:
LionOrdered's set must answer every clause, the predicate's too, so
`WHERE note = 'n1' AND tag < 50` over an index `WHERE note = 'n1'` and a lion index on `tag` fails,
the error naming `note = 'n1'`. What it does not fail: no WHERE; a pseudoconstant one (`WHERE $1`,
`WHERE current_user = 'app'`); a WHERE proven false; the vector column's own clauses
(`v IS NOT NULL`, a distance bound), alone, through the plain scan's Filter, or beside a filter lion
answers, through LionOrdered's (2026-10-17: they failed for a few hours before); a filter lion indexes answer (through
LionOrdered, which a generic plan's `cat = $1` and a LATERAL subquery's `cat = q.cat` reach too); a
join's clause; a filter of a CTE or of a security-barrier view's subquery (the order is then above
it, a sort); and a lionvec order an HNSW index's path has already beaten in `add_path()`, which is
then the plan, with its Filter, as pgvector's.

### 44.7 Costs (lionveccostestimate())

Start-up is the cost of the first row, which is most of a scan's. A restriction the exact path takes
(§44.6: `lionvec_exact_limit()` of the meta page's partitions, as the scan asks it) costs a member
an index tuple, a row's estimate and the ORDER BY's function, and the pages the scan will read, as
core prices the sort of the lion bitmap scan's rows it competes with ("Exact path pricing", below;
until 2026-10-18 a random page a member). Otherwise:
every centroid's estimate (`LIONVEC_ROW_OPS`, 2 `cpu_operator_cost`: the popcounts and a square
root); the share of the rows a scan probes; a random page a probed partition and the CODE pages'
share of the index (by the recorded dimensions, or 1536 before any) read sequentially; `0.1
cpu_index_tuple_cost` a row walked and `LIONVEC_ROW_OPS` a member scored; and a batch's refines and
exact distances, a random page and an index tuple each. The share probed is `LIONVEC_PROBE_PAUSED`
(0.46) `C^(-1/3)` and, under a filter keeping a share s, `s^(-LIONVEC_PROBE_SEL_PAUSED)` (0.27)
times as much, at most all: the power of C the simulation's, the rest the benchmark's at the
default margin and patience, where scans probed 3.9% of the 1,974 partitions unfiltered and 6.3%,
8.9%, 12% and 18% through LionOrdered under filters of 10%, 3%, 1% and 0.3% (the fit gives 3.6%,
6.8%, 9.3%, 12.5% and 17%). With `pg_lion.vector_patience = 0` it is `LIONVEC_PROBE_SHARE` (0.92)
`C^(-1/3)` and `s^(-LIONVEC_PROBE_SEL)` (0.2), the benchmark's at a margin of 2 before the pause,
when a filter narrowed the margin (§44.6); the same margin unnarrowed probes more. On DBpedia's
text-embedding-3-large rows (§44.9) the share fell from 678 to 2,715 partitions as `C^(-1/3)` says,
within 25% of the model's level under filters and at under half of it unfiltered, where a margin of
3 stops early on that data; the constants were left as they are. In an index that spills, by the
meta page's flags (§44.3), the CODE pages' share is of two CODE items a row to one REFINE item, a
partition's rows walked are twice its rows, and the share probed is `LIONVEC_SPILL_PROBES` (0.93)
times as much: at the same margin such a scan probed 91 to 94% of the partitions a scan without
did (§44.9). That is one data set, and the costs do not see what spill buys, the recall.

Each further row adds a refine and a fetch at worst and a share of the start-up over
`pg_lion.vector_batch`: the farther rows lie past more partitions, and the planner prices a LIMIT
under a Filter as LIMIT over the filter's selectivity rows of the scan. Without pauses the share is
`LIONVEC_DEEPER` (1), a scan of the benchmark's index having probed 7.3% of the partitions for 10
rows, 23% for 100 and 61% for 1,000 at a margin of 2. With them it is `LIONVEC_DEEPER_PAUSED`
(0.06): the same scans probed 4.1%, 4.6% and 50%, the first batch coming from the rows a scan holds
when it pauses and the deeper ones much as without, which one share a batch cannot follow; 0.06
prices the first batches right. The charge is what keeps a plain scan, walking past every row a 1%
filter rejects, from looking as cheap as LionOrdered reading the members alone: charged a refine
and a fetch a row and no more, the two tied at 1% and the planner's pick ran 7 times slower (202
ms to 30). Before the pause, with the full charge, the planner picked the plain scan at 30% and 10%
(15 and 30 ms, LionOrdered 196 and 82) and LionOrdered at 3% and 1% (40 and 26 ms). With pauses it
picks the plain scan down to 3% (9 ms at 30% against LionOrdered's 206, 15 at 10% against 81, 32
at 3% against 41) and LionOrdered at 1% (24 ms against the plain scan's 256, whose 1,000 rows 0.06
prices low); at 0.3% and below it sorts the bitmap scan's rows (27 ms, LionOrdered 27). A path with
no ORDER BY costs infinity. Selectivity 1, correlation 0.

Until 2026-10-18 ("Exact path pricing", below) the exact path was priced at a random page a member,
the price of its cold run, a random heap read a member (§44.9), and four to six times the probes' at
the filters `pg_lion.vector_exact_per_partition` newly sends down it (3.6 and 5.7 times below). The
plain scan with a `Filter`, priced low under a selective filter (LIMIT / selectivity rows at 0.06 of
a batch's start-up each, above; the million-row follow-up's problem 1), then comes out cheapest: on
DBpedia's 115,186 rows in 2,715 partitions (§44.9), at 2% and 3% the planner's estimate was 5,248
and 3,954 for the plain scan, 9,183 and 13,829 for LionOrdered's exact path, 8,735 and 12,800 for
the sort of the bitmap scan's rows, where LionOrdered probing had been 2,552 and 2,426 - so its plan
there went from LionOrdered probing (warm, 0.964 of the ten nearest in 8.7 and 9.0 ms at the default
margin) to the plain scan (0.960 in 16.9 ms, 0.957 in 10.8 ms), where LionOrdered, forced, is exact
in 4.2 and 7.8 ms and the sort exact in 2.9 and 4.6. The cost follows the scan, as it must for the
planner to compare what will run; what is wrong is the plain scan's price, which the follow-up's
problem 1 is to fix. Until then `pg_lion.enable_plain_scan = off` with `enable_sort = off` and
`pg_lion.pushdown_margin = 1000` takes LionOrdered, and `pg_lion.enable_plain_scan = off` alone the
sort, both exact there (`enable_indexscan = off` disables LionOrdered with the plain scan, §39).
**2026-10-16**: under a restriction the plain scan is no longer a candidate (§44.6,
"Post-filtering"), so the comparison of it with LionOrdered that this charge decides arises only
under `pg_lion.vector_postfilter = allow`. On the 1M-row DBpedia set, at `random_page_cost` 1.1,
it priced the plain scan under the 1% filter at 5,030 against LionOrdered's 5,915 and the planner
took it, 32 ms at a margin of 2 against LionOrdered's 14 (FOLLOWUP.md's Problem 1: a scan that a
Filter un-pauses by count, 17.6 times a query there, pays about a whole start-up's probes for each
further hundred rows, measured at 115,000 rows, not 0.06 of one); there the filter is now
LionOrdered's or a sort's with no constant changed. `LIONVEC_DEEPER_PAUSED` still prices an
unfiltered scan's deeper batches, and the plain scan under `allow`.

**The set's pieces** (2026-10-18). Until then `lo_cost_knn()` priced the set as `lo_cost()` does for
a B-tree's walk (§30.3): the lion access's own cost - a summary entry a bucket - and
`cpu_operator_cost` a container key, nothing a member, so the 50M-row benchmark's 10% set, 1,220
summary entries and 260,417 keys built in 845 ms, cost 650. Both now add the pieces the set gathers
(`lo_set_pieces()`): each leaf's source hands the set a container for each entry it reads at each
container key that entry's rows reach, so they cost

    min(members, entries x keys) x LO_PIECE_TUPLES x cpu_tuple_cost

with `entries` from `lion_cost_path_entries()` (lion_amcost.c, summed over a BitmapAnd's or
BitmapOr's leaves): for a key column's range, `lion_cost_ranges_entries()`'s - a summary a bucket it
covers whole, and the keys at its ends, or without summaries every key between its bounds; for an
equality list longer than a batch (`lion_scan_list_batch()`), a LIST source, its elements; else one;
a leaf's most of any column. A 10% equality on a column the heap is ordered by brings a piece a key;
a range over a unique column a piece a member. A piece was first `LO_PROBE_TUPLES` (2)
`cpu_tuple_cost`s, the walk's 170 ns an entry, which the 50M build's 5M pieces came to (845 ms); at
5M rows the same filter's 500,000 members took 44 to 48 ms, 1.36 members a piece, 90 ns a member.
Since the pieces are gathered by key (2026-10-19, §30.4) the 2M emulation's take 105 ns each where
they took 278, so a piece is `LO_PIECE_TUPLES` (1) `cpu_tuple_cost`, 85 ns on the walk's scale: a
little under the measurement, where a tie should fall, the set's answer being the one that does not
move with the plan. To be measured again at 50M rows.

**Exact path pricing (2026-10-18).** Under the default `pg_lion.vector_postfilter` the exact
path's one competitor is core's sort of the lion bitmap scan's rows under the LIMIT, and it was
still priced against the plain scan, above: a random page, an index tuple and `LIONVEC_ROW_OPS`
`cpu_operator_cost` a member, and in `lo_cost_knn()`'s run another random page a row returned.
Core prices the sort's input as `cost_bitmap_heap_scan()` does: the heap pages the rows lie on,
each read once in block order - Mackert and Lohman's 2Tn / (2T + n) of a table of T pages for n
rows, rounded up and at most T (`compute_bitmap_pages()`, one loop) - each at `random_page_cost`
less (`random_page_cost` - `seq_page_cost`) x sqrt(pages / T), a single page at `random_page_cost`;
a tuple and the ORDER BY's expression a row (pgvector's distance at COST 100, §44.11: 0.25); the
sort; and never the detoasting of a vector, its TOAST pages read one at a time through the TOAST
index after the row's heap page. With the vectors in TOAST the exact path reads those same TOAST
pages by their places (§44.13), through a stream, and no heap page but those of the rows it returns,
yet was charged the most: on 200,000 rows of 1536 dimensions in TOAST (1,728 heap pages) at
`random_page_cost` 1.1, a 1% filter (1,944 members) was planned as the sort, at 1,852, over
LionOrdered at 2,207, and ran in 37 ms warm against LionOrdered's 8 (less the query vector's 10 ms
InitPlan). The exact path's start-up for n members (`lionvec_exact_cost()`) is now

    ORDER BY start-up + n x (cpu_index_tuple_cost + LIONVEC_ROW_OPS x cpu_operator_cost
                             + ORDER BY per row) + pages

the ORDER BY's costs `cost_qual_eval()`'s of the path's `indexorderbys`, which the sort's input pays
a row the same, and its pages as the scan will read them, which `lionvec_reads_placed()` tells the
planner as it tells `lv_start_toast()` (a heap table, the index keeping a locator over the heap's
TOAST relation, `pg_lion.vector_toast_direct` on, a vector of at most `LIONVEC_LOC_MAXRUNS`
chunks; the scan's MVCC snapshot is the one thing the planner cannot ask, and under 16's
`old_snapshot_threshold` no lionvec order is read at all, §9). With P(n, T) the bitmap heap scan's
page price above (`lionvec_pages_in_order()`):

- **by place**: P(n, L) + D x `seq_page_cost`, at the index's tablespace's costs, with L the LOC
  pages (the index's rows over 291, a page's one-run entries, `LIONVEC_LOC_SIZE(1)`, rounded up)
  and D the LOCDIR's (L over 407), and no page of the heap or of TOAST a member. Both plans read a
  member's TOAST pages and core prices them for neither: charged to the exact path alone, even at
  `seq_page_cost` a member, they would keep the sort the plan at 0.3% to 3% below (476.61 + 286 =
  762.61 against the sort's 679.31, 675.19 + 966 = 1,641.19 against 1,186.02, 1,238.59 + 2,885 =
  4,123.59 against 1,754.46), where LionOrdered runs 2.0 to 2.7 times faster warm. A row returned
  still costs a random heap page in `lo_cost_knn()`'s run, its check (`lv_check_placed()`).
- **from the heap** (the vectors inline, or the locator not used): P(n, the heap's pages), at the
  heap's tablespace's costs, the pages the bitmap heap scan reads for the same rows, and nothing
  more a row returned, whose page the scan read before its first (`lion_vec_scan_cost()`'s
  `*fetch`, 0 here, which `lo_cost_knn()` charges a row in place of the random page it charged
  every row).

P is `compute_bitmap_pages()`'s count and not `index_pages_fetched()`'s, whose re-reads past the
table's share of `effective_cache_size` are an index scan's, its rows in the index's order: the
exact path reads its pages once each in block order, as the bitmap scan does. The probing branches
are unchanged. On vecbench's 100,000 rows of 1536 dimensions (a uniform `u` under a lion index;
cosine distance at COST 100; `random_page_cost` 4; a lionvec index of 2,530 partitions, so an exact
limit of 3,795 members; in TOAST 834 heap pages, 100,000 TOAST pages and 344 LOC pages, inline
100,000 heap pages), LIMIT 10, the Limit's estimate before and after, the plan picked, and the two
plans' times - the scans themselves unchanged - in ms, medians of 5 warm and of 3 cold (the server
restarted, the OS's page cache kept):

| vectors | filter | members | LionOrdered before | after | sort | plan before | after | warm, node / sort | cold, node / sort |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TOAST | 0.3% | 286 | 1,217.87 | 476.61 | 679.31 | sort | LionOrdered | 1.03 / 2.05 | 5.48 / 7.07 |
| TOAST | 1% | 966 | 3,952.69 | 675.19 | 1,186.02 | sort | LionOrdered | 2.43 / 5.11 | 12.87 / 19.38 |
| TOAST | 3% | 2,885 | 11,712.34 | 1,238.59 | 1,754.46 | sort | LionOrdered | 5.62 / 15.38 | 27.32 / 45.07 |
| TOAST | 10% (probing) | 9,990 | 2,139.91 | 2,139.91 | 3,975.46 | LionOrdered | LionOrdered | 10.82 / 49.42 | 37.12 / 116.44 |
| inline | 0.3% | 310 | 1,298.50 | 1,284.22 | 1,288.27 | LionOrdered | sort, then LionOrdered leaned | 0.65 / 0.58 | 3.00 / 2.63 |
| inline | 1% | 1,034 | 4,228.78 | 4,114.14 | 4,133.83 | sort | sort, then LionOrdered leaned | 1.75 / 1.83 | 8.34 / 11.19 |
| inline | 3% | 3,020 | 12,267.29 | 11,266.11 | 11,332.36 | sort | sort, then LionOrdered leaned | 3.98 / 5.37 | 23.96 / 24.83 |
| inline | 10% (probing) | 10,143 | 2,157.84 | 2,157.84 | 32,814.98 | LionOrdered | LionOrdered | 13.00 / 17.83 | 52.30 / 90.16 |

In TOAST the exact path is now the plan wherever it is taken, 2.0 to 2.7 times faster than the sort
warm and 1.3 to 1.65 times cold. Inline the two plans read the same heap pages and are priced within
1% of each other, near enough for the planner's 1% fuzz to decide (the sort, as before at 1% and 3%,
and at 0.3%, running in 0.88 to 1.35 times the node's time) until the lean below. At `random_page_cost` 1.1 the node
is the plan at all six (in TOAST 305.83, 628.79 and 1,163.19 against the sort's 346.50, 914.17 and
1,708.06; inline
429.48, 1,415.34 and 4,072.35 against 433.53, 1,435.04 and 4,138.60). The benchmark's vectors are
one vector repeated (its generator's InitPlan): the exact path and the sort compute every member's
distance whatever they are, so their rows stand; the probing rows show only that their prices did
not move. On vector_toast.sql's 3,000 rows of 1536 dimensions with a kilobyte of text each (§44.10),
a 1% filter (30 members) costs the node 66.65 against the sort's 105.94 in TOAST, where it cost
167.15 (0.15 ms against 0.16), and 125.71 against 123.55 inline, where it cost 167.21: the sort is
the plan there and runs in 0.06 ms against the node's 0.16, a tenth of a millisecond of the node's
own start that no price follows. vector_filter.sql's 1,200 members on some 850 of vfb's 1,482
inline pages cost the node 1,781.98 against the sort's 1,807.57, where they cost 4,761.08, the two
running alike.

**Leaned (2026-10-19).** The exact path's start-up is then divided by `LIONVEC_EXACT_LEAN`, 1.2:
it is planned wherever its price is within 1.2 times the sort's, the maintainer's preference for
the exact path at the margins over a sort that runs about as fast - no sort, no `hash_mem`, the rows
in order from the first - where the near-ties above went to the sort. On the 100,000 rows above the
node is now the plan at all six exact-path cases: in TOAST 406.33, 575.83 and 1,056.07 against the
sort's 679.31, 1,186.02 and 1,754.46; inline 1,072.75, 3,435.52 and 9,407.94 against 1,288.27,
4,133.83 and 11,332.36, where it runs in 1.12, 0.96 and 0.74 times the sort's time warm. On
vector_toast.sql's 3,000 rows the inline node costs 104.76 against the sort's 123.55 and is the
plan, 0.16 ms against the sort's 0.06, the tenth of a millisecond above; vfb's 1,200 members cost
the node 1,484.98 against the sort's 1,807.57. The probing branches are not leaned: the sort's
competitor there is priced on its own terms (above), and the exact path alone was the near-tie.

**A parallel scan** (2026-10-16; §44.4). `cost_index()` asks `lionveccostestimate()` for the
index's cost before it counts the path's workers, and of the result divides only its own CPU part
by the parallel divisor, so a partial path came out at about the serial scan's price.
`lion_ordered_set_rel_pathlist()`, the `set_rel_pathlist_hook`, which runs before core makes its
Gather paths, takes each partial lionvec path out of the relation's partial paths and offers it
again (`lo_knn_partial()`, so that `add_partial_path()` orders and prunes them by the cost they now
have) at `lion_vec_parallel_cost()`'s: the ranking of every centroid, `nparts` x
`LIONVEC_ROW_OPS` x `cpu_operator_cost`, which every participant pays, in full; the rest of the
start-up and every row after it over the divisor - costsize.c's `get_parallel_divisor()`, which
is static there and so copied (`lionvec_parallel_divisor()`): the workers, and while the leader
takes part 1 less 0.3 a worker, none from four workers on. On DBpedia's 2,717 partitions at
`random_page_cost` 1.1 the serial start-up is 584.79, of which the ranking is 2,717 x 2 x 0.0025 =
13.585: with two workers (a divisor of 2.4) a partial path starts at 13.585 + 571.205 / 2.4 =
251.59, with three (3.1) at 197.84, as EXPLAIN shows. Gather Merge adds `parallel_setup_cost`
(1,000) and `parallel_tuple_cost` (0.1) a row, so at the default costs no parallel scan of this
index is chosen, its setup alone costing more than the serial scan's start-up - and rightly, the
parallel scans having run 4 to 8 times slower (§44.9). The workers are core's,
`compute_parallel_worker()`'s: from `*indexPages`, which is the CODE pages a scan reads, against
`min_parallel_index_scan_size` (512 kB), and from the heap pages the rows' fetches would read,
against `min_parallel_table_scan_size` (8 MB) - DBpedia's heap is 768 pages, its vectors in TOAST,
and gets none without lowering it - unless the table's `parallel_workers` says how many, and at
most `max_parallel_workers_per_gather`. Under `pg_lion.vector_postfilter` `exact` or `error`
`lo_knn_take()` removes a partial path that a Filter would follow as it removes the serial one
(§44.6, "Post-filtering": a Gather Merge over a Parallel Index Scan with a Filter is the same
post-filter), with nothing to bring back for it, a partial sequential scan having no pathkeys it
could have lost to; LionOrdered's paths are serial.

### 44.8 Settings

- `pg_lion.vector_margin` (real, -10 to 1000, default 3): how much nearer than its centroid a
  partition's rows are taken to come, in standard deviations of the rows about their centroids
  along one dimension (§44.4). Larger probes more partitions and misses fewer rows; 100 probes,
  on any data a test has used, every partition that could hold a nearer row, and the regression
  tests set it so, with the pause off, to compare with a sort. Below zero probes a partition only
  once rows nearer than its centroid by that much are in hand. A filter no longer narrows it
  (§44.6). The default was 2 until the pause; with the pause, 3 took the benchmark's recall from
  0.964 to 0.979 for 1.3 ms (§44.9).
- `pg_lion.vector_patience` (int, 0 to 1,000,000, default 30): how many units of rows a scan
  scores without one entering the nearest rows it is after (its tier, §44.4) before it pauses, a
  unit `sqrt(n) / 2` rows, n the build's, the rows an average partition would hold in `2 sqrt(n)`
  partitions - under a lion filter twice that share of the members - whatever the partitions'
  number, and `margin / 6` times as many past a margin of 6; 0 never pauses, and then a filter's
  scan probes far more than the costs assume (§44.7). Smaller pauses sooner, probing fewer
  partitions and missing more rows. 30 is where the 975,000-row benchmark's tail ended, in its
  `2 sqrt(n)` partitions, where a unit is a partition's rows: at a margin of 3, 30 and 40 gave the
  same recall (0.979), 40 a 95th percentile a third longer.
- `pg_lion.vector_exact_rows` (int, 0 to 100,000,000, default 2,000): how many members a lion filter
  may admit for the scan to compute every member's distance from the heap, exactly, instead of
  probing (§44.6), whatever the partitions; 0 leaves the choice to
  `pg_lion.vector_exact_per_partition`. The exact path costs a heap fetch a member - at 1536
  dimensions a 6 KB vector, a page of its own in TOAST or inline, so 2,000 members are 12 MB - where
  a probe reads a few hundred to a thousand CODE pages (§44.9) but, under a filter that leaves most
  partitions empty, many for nothing: in the simulation a 0.1% filter of 975,000 rows probed a fifth
  of the index for 0.95. It is the floor under the ratio below, which matters in an index of fewer
  than 1,334 partitions, where 1.5 a partition is under 2,000: a probe's fixed costs (every centroid
  ranked, a thousand pages or more however thin the filter) are most of a scan there, and on
  DBpedia's 115,186 rows the probes took 7.4 ms for 0.953 of a 0.3% filter's ten nearest (345
  members, 0.13 a partition, 1,584 pages), the exact path 0.5 ms for all ten (§44.9). The default
  sat where the two cost about the same on the 975,000-row benchmark, and stays where they cost
  about the same cold, whatever the partitions: on DBpedia, a random heap read a member at 50 to 60
  us each, 1,204 members took 75 ms exact against 99 ms probed for 0.98, and 3,472 183 against 67.
  Raise it where storage is fast or exactness is wanted, lower it where the vectors are wide and the
  disk slow. The planner prices both (§44.7), so it may sort the filter's rows itself instead, as it
  did at 1% on DBpedia (§44.9), which is exact too; since 2026-10-18 the exact path is priced as
  that sort is (§44.7, "Exact path pricing"), and with DBpedia's vectors in TOAST, read by place,
  it should be the plan there (not measured).
- `pg_lion.vector_exact_per_partition` (real, 0 to 1,000,000, default 1.5): the members a lion
  filter may admit for each of the index's partitions, on average, for the scan to compute every
  member's distance instead of probing, however many members that is; the larger of it times the
  partitions and `pg_lion.vector_exact_rows` is the bound (`lionvec_exact_limit()`, which the scan
  and its cost both ask). 0 leaves the choice to `pg_lion.vector_exact_rows`. What decides between
  the two paths is how thinly the members spread (§44.6): at one or two a partition a probe finds
  about one member for the CODE pages it reads, and the pause, counted in members, comes late, while
  the exact path's heap fetches are as many as the members whatever the partitions. A flat count
  misfires across sizes: 10,063 members at a million rows, 1.26 a partition of 7,999, are faster
  exact; 11,377 at 115,186 rows, 4.2 a partition of 2,715, are faster probed. 1.5 sits below where
  the two crossed warm on both data sets, at two to three a partition (§44.9), for the exact path's
  cost cold, a random heap read a member where the probes read CODE chains a partition at a time: at
  1.28 a partition on DBpedia (its 3% filter) the exact path was 1.3 times faster warm than the
  probes for 0.98, and 2.7 times slower cold. It takes up to 12,000 members in a million rows' 7,999
  partitions (1% is 10,063) and 4,072 in the 115,186 rows' 2,715 (3% is 3,472), and leaves 3% of the
  million and 5% of the 115,186 to the probes. Raise it where the heap is in memory and exact
  answers are worth a few milliseconds more; lower it, or set it to 0, where cold reads dominate.
- `pg_lion.vector_overflow` (enum, `error` or `stop`, default `error`): what a scan does when what
  it knows of its rows outgrows `hash_mem` (§44.4, "The hash's bound"): fail the query, or end
  the scan at the rows it returned, with a NOTICE. Only a scan with no LIMIT, or a large one,
  over rows plane 1 cannot tell apart gets there.
- `pg_lion.vector_postfilter` (enum, `error`, `exact` or `allow`, default `error`; 2026-10-16, the
  default `exact` until 2026-10-17): whether a plan may apply a filter to the rows a lionvec scan
  returns (§44.6, "Post-filtering"). `error`: no plan does; a filter lion indexes answer goes
  through LionOrdered, over a set that answers every clause, and a query whose lionvec order would
  be filtered and that no LionOrdered path answers fails at plan time, EXPLAIN too, naming the
  clauses no lion index answers, and hinting at the subquery that filters an unfiltered or
  lion-filtered scan's first rows and at `exact` and `allow`. `exact`: the same, but such a query is
  planned exactly, a sort of the filter's rows. `allow`: the plain scan with a Filter, and
  LionOrdered with one, are plans chosen by cost, as before; for comparing plans and for §44.9's
  earlier measurements. `pg_lion.enable_ordered_scan = off` takes LionOrdered away, not the rule:
  under `error` or `exact` a filtered query then gets the error, or an exact plan. A pseudoconstant
  clause, tested once by a gating Result, one a partial lionvec index's predicate implies, and the
  index's own, of the vector column alone (`v IS NOT NULL`, a distance bound; 2026-10-17), are no
  filter here. A table with row-level security lionvec refuses under every value (§44.6,
  "Row-level security").
- `pg_lion.vector_build_sample` (enum, `error` or `allow`, default `error`; 2026-10-19): what a
  build does when its sample has rows for fewer partitions than the table's rows want - fewer than
  a sample of every row would make (`lionvec_parts_short()`, lion_vec_math.h). The build chooses
  its partitions from a reservoir of what half of `maintenance_work_mem` holds, and makes no more
  than the reservoir has rows for: 16 a partition it chooses by itself, one a partition the
  `partitions` option asks for (§44.3). Were that all, the partitions would follow a memory
  setting, unseen: at the default 64 MB a table of more than 28,985 rows of 1536 dimensions would
  get 1,361 partitions whatever its size - a billion rows, which want 252,982, 734,000 rows each -
  and a `partitions` of 30,000 over 40,000 rows 21,788, with only the DEBUG1 line to say so; and
  the partitions decide which rows a scan reads at a margin (§44.4), so the answers would follow it
  too. `error`: the build fails in its first pass, at the first row with which the rows counted so
  far want more partitions than the full reservoir has rows for. With the reservoir's size fixed, a
  count of rows that is short stays short as the rows grow - the partitions made stop at what the
  reservoir allows, and those wanted only grow - which the unit tests check over every count to
  200,000 and every 0.05% from there to 4 billion, so the table's rows would be short too and the
  error is never wrong; and it comes before the rest of the first pass, k-means and the second
  pass, the build's other 98% (§44.12): at 64 MB a billion rows of 1536 dimensions fail at the
  28,986th. A parallel build's first pass is the leader's alone, so it fails before its parallel
  context is set up. The message names the partitions wanted, those the sample has rows for, and
  the `maintenance_work_mem` whose reservoir would make them all - the rows
  `lionvec_parts_sample()` says, at `lionvec_sample_mem()`, rounded up to a megabyte; a kilobyte
  less than the unrounded figure is short (vector_build_sample.sql). For a pass that stops before
  the table's end those are for the rows it reckons the table holds (`lionvec_build_rows_about()`:
  the rows counted times the heap's blocks over those read, which it reads in order from the first,
  "About" in the message), so that the setting named is for the table and not for the rows read: on
  40,000 rows of 1536 dimensions at 64 MB the build failed in 1.0 s at the 28,986th row, reckoning
  39,954 and naming 76 MB, where building the 1,361 partitions took 10.2 s and the 1,600 at 76 MB
  11.7 s (75 MB failed, its sample having rows for 1,595). A table whose rows are not spread evenly
  over its blocks may be reckoned low, and then fails again at the setting named, later in the pass
  and reckoned better. `allow`: the partitions the sample has rows for, with a NOTICE that counts
  the rows and names the same `maintenance_work_mem`. Under neither does a build fail for what no
  memory changes: a table of fewer than 10,000 rows has one partition however few of them the
  sample holds, and a `partitions` above the table's rows wants as many as the rows, and is held to
  those alone. Nor for the reservoir's cap: 2^24 rows have 16 each for 2^20 partitions, four times
  `LIONVEC_MAX_PARTS` (a static assertion), so past 1.07 billion rows the build wants 262,144, the
  format's ceiling, whatever the memory.
- `pg_lion.vector_prefetch` (enum, `off`, `fadvise` or `stream`, default `stream` from 17 and
  `fadvise` on 16; 2026-10-17, a boolean from 2026-10-16, whose `on`, the default, and `off` it
  still takes): how a scan reads ahead the pages it will read next (§44.4, "Prefetch" and "Read
  streams"), as many ahead as the tablespace's `effective_io_concurrency` (a query's setting;
  `maintenance_io_concurrency` is not read), to 64; an `effective_io_concurrency` of 0 reads none
  ahead whatever it says. `stream` reads the index's pages, and the exact path's heap pages, through
  read streams into shared buffers; `fadvise` asks the kernel for them (`PrefetchBuffer()`), as `on`
  did; `off` reads each when it comes. On 16, which has no read streams, `stream` is `fadvise`, and
  `SHOW` says so. The rows' heap pages for their exact distances are asked of the kernel under
  `fadvise` and `stream` alike. The rows a scan returns, and their order, are the same under all
  three. On DBpedia (§44.9, "Read streams"), each query alone with its pages on the disk, under 18's
  `io_method = worker`, `stream` took a margin-8 scan to 43.2 ms against `fadvise`'s 47.6 and
  `off`'s 67.2, a 1% filter's probing to 62.0 against 82.8 and 100.9, and the exact path under it to
  53.3 against 58.9 and 108.3; a margin-3 scan, 346 pages, about even. With its pages in the
  kernel's cache, though, a stream's read is an I/O worker's or, under `io_uring`, a kernel
  thread's, where `ReadBuffer()` copies the page itself: `stream` cost 0 to 40% more than `fadvise`
  on the index's pages under `worker` and `io_uring` and 2 to 14% under `sync`, and on the exact
  path half the time under `worker`'s default 3 workers (1.17 times under 16) and one and a half to
  twice under `io_uring`. Warm, every page in shared buffers, `stream` costs 2 to 11% over `off` and
  `fadvise` within 5%. So `stream` where the index is read from the disk; `fadvise` where it lives
  in the kernel's cache and not in shared buffers, under `io_uring` above all; `off` where it lives
  in shared buffers.
- `pg_lion.vector_toast_direct` (boolean, default on; 2026-10-17): whether a scan of an index that
  keeps a locator reads vectors in TOAST by their chunks' places (§44.13) - the exact path's
  members through the locator, the rerank's rows through their REFINE items - every chunk checked,
  rather than through the heap tuple and the TOAST index. The rows returned, their order and their
  distances are the same either way, which the tests compare; inserts keep the places up whatever it
  says. Off is the way back should a place ever be wrong in a way the checks miss.
