- `pg_lion.vector_parallel_scan` (boolean, default off, 2026-10-17): whether a lionvec order gets
  partial paths at all (§44.4, "A parallel scan"); off because the parallel scan was slower than
  the serial one on every query measured.
- core's `max_parallel_workers_per_gather`, `parallel_setup_cost`, `parallel_tuple_cost`,
  `min_parallel_index_scan_size`, `min_parallel_table_scan_size` and the table's
  `parallel_workers`: with `pg_lion.vector_parallel_scan` on, whether an unfiltered scan runs in parallel, and in how many processes
  (§44.7, "A parallel scan"). At the defaults it does not: the setup costs more than a serial
  scan's start-up.
- `partitions` (reloption, 0 to 262,144, default 0; 1,000,000 until a review found the build at a
  million partitions days long and uncancellable, then 65,536 until the regions, §44.3): the
  partitions the build makes; 0 chooses by the rows' count, `8 sqrt(n)` above 10,000 rows, at
  most a sixteenth of a sample of every row (§44.3; `2 sqrt(n)` until DBpedia, §44.9); a build
  whose sample, what `maintenance_work_mem` holds, has too few rows for either fails
  (`pg_lion.vector_build_sample`, above). 262,144
  (`LIONVEC_MAX_PARTS`, 2^18) is what `8 sqrt(n)` gives at 1.07 billion rows. A partition number
  is an `int` everywhere, never 16 bits, and the sort's group (`LIONVEC_SORT_GROUP`, an int4)
  holds it with room for the two groups after the partitions. The build's arrays of the
  partitions (`lionvec_build_arrays()`) are outside `maintenance_work_mem`, in the parallel
  context's shared memory for a parallel build: the centroids' floats, C `dimsp` x 4 bytes, the
  8-bit codes and plane 1 in C (`dimsp` + `dimsp` / 8) bytes, a few words a partition more, the
  sample's assignment, 4 bytes a row, and the regions' arrays: 2.1 GB at 262,144 partitions of
  1536 dimensions, 1.6 GB of it the floats (403 MB at 65,536); the leader's region k-means works
  in another C `dimsp` bytes of codes, 403 MB there, and an insert in its candidates alone (§44.3).
  Read by the build alone, so a change takes a REINDEX.
  It does not move the pause: `pg_lion.vector_patience` counts the rows of `2 sqrt(n)` partitions,
  not of these (§44.4). When it counted these, on DBpedia a patience of 30 in 2,715 partitions held
  the unfiltered recall to 0.966 at any margin, where 120, the rows of 30 in 678 partitions,
  reached 0.993.
- `spill` (reloption, boolean, default on): whether the build puts each row in a second partition
  as well (§44.3), recorded in the meta page, which inserts then follow; with fewer than two
  partitions it does nothing. Read by the build alone, so a change takes a REINDEX. Off saves the
  copies' CODE pages - an index of 1536 dimensions a ninth smaller - and an insert's third WAL
  record, for less recall at each margin: on 115,000 embeddings, 0.84 of the ten nearest at the
  default against 0.92 (§44.9).
- `pg_lion.vector_epsilon` (real, 1 to 10, default 4): the bounds' width in standard deviations.
  Each plane-1 bound fails with the Gaussian's two-sided probability, 0.27% at 3, 0.006% at 4; a
  failure matters only for a row that belongs in the answer and is found too late, so the rate of
  queries with a miss is far lower. Wider bounds refine and fetch more rows. The default was 3 until
  the format-1 benchmark (§44.9): there one query in 100 under the 0.1% filter lost a row at 3, in
  each of three runs, and none of 400 at 4, which refines twice the rows for a few percent of the
  time.
- `pg_lion.vector_batch` (int, 1 to 100000, default 100): rows the probes gather candidates for
  before REST; each REST gathers four times as many, probing every partition probed so far again.
  It no longer sets where a LIMIT 10 pauses (the tiers do, §44.4), and a LIMIT past it that
  LionOrdered knows is L in its place, to an eighth of `work_mem`'s rows (§44.4, "A known LIMIT"),
  so it need not follow the LIMIT: it is L for the plain scan, a LIMIT the planner does not know,
  and one below it.
- `maintenance_work_mem`: half of it holds the build's sample (§44.3), and the CODE items' sort,
  two items a row when the index spills; a parallel build divides the sort's share among its
  processes, as core's builds do, and holds the sample once, in shared memory (§44.12). A sample
  row takes `dimsp + 4` bytes, 1,540 at 1536 dimensions, so the default partitions want 2 x 1,540
  x 16 `8 sqrt(n)` bytes, 376 MB at a million rows and 12.5 GB at a billion, a build given less
  failing (`pg_lion.vector_build_sample`, above), and k-means is given
  at most 128 a partition of it, never fewer than 65,536 rows (§44.3), 1.6 GB of sample at a
  million rows' 8,000 partitions (so 3.2 GB is the most a million rows can use); the reservoir
  stops at 2^24 rows, 25.8 GB, which 52 GB reaches. A parallel build's shared memory holds the
  sample after the cut, and the arrays above.
- `max_parallel_maintenance_workers` (core's, default 2) and the table's `parallel_workers`: the
  workers a build asks for, whatever the heap's size or `maintenance_work_mem` (§44.12).
- `work_mem` bounds a scan's row queue (§44.4).

### 44.9 Measured

**Data.** Qdrant's `dbpedia-openai-1M-1536-angular` set: 975,000 OpenAI ada-002 embeddings of
DBpedia entities, 1536 dimensions, unit length, in `items(id int, u float8, embedding
vector(1536))`, and the first 100 of its test queries; `u` is uniform in [0, 1) (seed 42) and
unrelated to the vectors, so `u < s` keeps a share s of the rows, with a lion index on it. The
ground truth is the exact top 10 by cosine, computed in numpy for each query and filter.
Against pgvector 0.8.6's HNSW on `embedding::halfvec(1536)` (m = 16, ef_construction = 64, as
pgvector's documentation builds it for 1536 dimensions) - lionvec indexes the `vector` itself.
PostgreSQL 16, 4 vCPUs (Xeon, 2.8 GHz; AVX-512 but no VPOPCNTDQ, so the POPCNT kernel), 16 GB,
`shared_buffers` 5 GB, `work_mem` 256 MB, `maintenance_work_mem` 1 GB, no parallel query, and
pgvector's three `vector` distance functions at `COST 100`, as lionvec's documentation asks
(§44.11). `bench/vector/knn.py`; the results are in `bench/results/2026-10-14-lionvec-partitions/`.

**Size and build.** lionvec 1,752 MB (225 MB of it the 28,810 CODE pages, 0.5 MB the PART chain),
HNSW 3,809 MB, the table 63 MB and its TOAST 7.6 GB. The default 1,974 partitions, k-means over a
sample of 348,617 rows (half of `maintenance_work_mem`): `REINDEX` took 18 min 58 s with the table
in the page cache, where the unpartitioned format took 98 s. Nearly all of it is the O(n C) of §44.3
- ten k-means iterations over the sample and the assignment of every row, each a plane-1 estimate
against every centroid and the exact distances of the few it cannot rule out.

**Warm** - every index, the table and its TOAST in memory (HNSW and the table in shared buffers,
the rest in the page cache, `pg_prewarm`; each method's queries run once untimed first); the
median of 100 queries, LIMIT 10, and the 95th percentile. Recall is the share of the true ten
returned. The plans are the planner's own: the plain lionvec scan with a `Filter` at 10%,
LionOrdered at 1%, and at 0.1% a sort of the lion bitmap scan's 953 rows, for either index.
lionvec at its defaults (margin 3, patience 30), at margins 2 and 4, and with the pause off:

| Filter | lionvec, defaults | margin 2 | margin 4 | no pause | HNSW, ef_search 40 | 100 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| none | 7.9 ms (p95 16), 0.979 | 6.6 (15), 0.964 | 9.1 (18), 0.983 | 14 (68), 0.984 | 4.7 (6.5), 0.900 | 8.1 (11), 0.954 |
| 10% | 13.5 (29), 0.978 | 15 (29), 0.974 | 15 (28), 0.979 | 60 (123), 0.996 | 8.7 (14), 0.931 | 8.0 (15), 0.939 |
| 1% | 24 (40), 0.981 | 27 (41), 0.981 | 27 (38), 0.981 | 109 (136), 1.000 | 37 (62), 0.947 | 41 (66), 0.950 |
| 0.1% | 9.9 (11), 1.000 | | | | 13 (18), 0.999 | |

HNSW under a filter is its iterative scan (`hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order`); without it,
at ef_search 40, it returned 3.9 of the ten rows at 10% (recall 0.393) and 0.4 at 1% (0.038).
Times vary between runs: HNSW at ef_search 100 took 6.2, 7.0 and 8.1 ms unfiltered in three, the
defaults 8.6, 8.4 and 7.9.

What the scans did, averaged over the 100 queries. Unfiltered, at margins 2, 3 and 4: 65, 77 and
86 partitions probed (3.3%, 3.9% and 4.3% of 1,974), 993, 1,171 and 1,295 CODE pages read, 0.5 to
0.8 pauses, about 120 rows refined and 10.5 fetched; with the pause off, 254 partitions and 3,856
pages. Under the 10% filter, through the plain scan, 99 to 104 partitions, 955 rows refined and 104
fetched (the filter keeps one row in ten of those returned); with the pause off, 725 partitions.
Under the 1% filter, through LionOrdered, 244 partitions at every margin - every query paused,
before the margin would have stopped it - 65 refined and 10.5 fetched; with the pause off, 1,511 of
the 1,974, why a filter's margin was narrowed before the pause (§44.6). No bound failed; 0 to 0.6
rows a query were skipped out of order.

The pause is what ends the tail. The partitions a query probed unfiltered: with it, a median of
68, a 95th percentile of 175 and at most 256; without it, 150, 837 and 1,664, a query's time
following them (correlation 0.84, at a margin of 2 before the pause). For that it gives up half a
point of recall unfiltered (0.984 to 0.979) and two under the 1% filter (1.000 to 0.981). A
patience of 40 gave the same recall as 30 at a margin of 3 (0.979) with a 95th percentile a third
longer (17.9 ms against 13.5, in an earlier run). By LIMIT, unfiltered over 40 queries: 4.1%, 4.6%
and 50% of the partitions probed for 10, 100 and 1,000 rows, recall 0.980, 0.975 and 0.983, in
10.5, 17 and 212 ms; with the pause off, 15%, 39% and 74%, 0.985, 0.997 and 0.999, in 17, 60 and
219 ms.

Before the pause, at a margin of 2 narrowed by 1.3 a tenfold under a filter
(`before-pause/`), lionvec took 8.5 ms (p95 37) for 0.968 unfiltered, 32 ms (96) for 0.989 at
10% and 31 ms (59) for 0.979 at 1%; margins 1 and 3 took 5.3 ms for 0.939 and 14 ms for 0.984
unfiltered. The unpartitioned format, which read every CODE page of the rows it scored and
returned the exact ten (no bound failed in 400 queries at ε = 4), took 96 ms unfiltered, 138 ms
at 10%, 34 ms at 1% and 6.6 ms at 0.1% (reading only the 965 CODE pages that held a member, by a
page directory this format no longer has). So partitions are 12 times faster unfiltered, 10
times at 10% and 1.4 times at 1%, and slower at 0.1%, where the planner now sorts the members'
rows fetched from the heap.

**Cold** - PostgreSQL restarted and the page cache dropped before each query; the median of 5:

| Filter | lionvec | HNSW, ef_search 40 (iterative under a filter) | unpartitioned |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| none | 85 ms (49 to 155) | 118 ms | 402 ms |
| 1% | 196 ms | 1,254 ms | 196 ms |
| 0.1% | 210 ms (planner: Sort of the filter's rows) | 251 ms (the same) | 112 ms |

Unfiltered, a cold query reads the PART chain and the CODE chains of the partitions it probes,
about 9 MB, where the unpartitioned format read all 218 MB; its time varies with the partitions a
query needs. Cold reads are noisy here: the first run of these five queries, straight after the
warm benchmark, took 779 ms unfiltered (one query 3.6 s) and HNSW's 1% 1,739 ms, and the next
76 ms and 1,244 ms. Interleaved, each query after its own restart, twelve queries took a median
of 89 ms at the defaults and 173 ms at the old ones (a margin of 2, no pause), reading 28 and
67 MB. Under the 1%
filter it reads lion's set and the probed partitions' CODE chains, where HNSW's iterative search
fetches row after row that fails the filter. At 0.1% the sort fetches 953 TOASTed vectors.

**Memory-capped** - a stream of queries with PostgreSQL in a memory cgroup of 1 or 2 GB (its
processes, `shared_buffers` of 128 MB, and the page cache its reads fill), which holds lionvec's
CODE pages but not HNSW's 3.8 GB. Each method after a restart with the page cache dropped, run with
rows of the table as queries until the cgroup is full and for 100 more, then timed on the 100 test
queries; the median, and the pages a query read from disk (the backend's `read_bytes`):

| Memory | Filter | lionvec | HNSW, ef_search 40 (iterative under a filter) | unpartitioned |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 GB | none | 19 ms, 100 pages | 51 ms, 767 pages | 157 ms, 100 pages |
| 1 GB | 1% | 28 ms, 0 pages | 691 ms, 9,229 pages | 31 ms, 0 pages |
| 2 GB | none | 13 ms, 41 pages | 41 ms, 672 pages | 161 ms, 25 pages |
| 2 GB | 1% | 30 ms, 0 pages | 465 ms, 7,853 pages | 29 ms, 0 pages |

What lionvec reads from disk are the CODE chains of partitions the stream had not yet probed, and
the REFINE items and vectors of the rows it refines and fetches; under the 1% filter the stream
never filled the cgroup (5,000 rows of the table as queries, and the members' working set still
fit). The pause cut the 95th percentile by a third here: 41 ms with 1 GB, 65 ms before it at a
margin of 2. The unpartitioned format read as few pages but scored every row, and most of its
time was most likely the CODE pages being copied into 128 MB of shared buffers on every pass,
which a scan of 4% of them mostly escapes. HNSW reads 650 to 800 random pages a query unfiltered, and 8,000 to
9,000 under the filter, of graph and of rows that fail it.

**Spill** (format 3, §44.3). The benchmark above is format 2's, which did not spill; spilling,
its index would have some 28,800 CODE pages more, about 1,980 MB. Measured since on a smaller set:
the first three of the 26 parquet shards of DBpedia entities embedded by OpenAI's
text-embedding-3-large at 1536 dimensions (`text-embedding-3-large-1536-embedding`), 115,386 rows,
200 of them held out at random (seed 0) as the queries, the ground truth their exact ten nearest
by cosine among the other 115,186. One cosine index in the default 678 partitions, built with
`spill` on and then off; PostgreSQL 16, 4 vCPUs (Xeon, 2.1 GHz, the POPCNT kernel),
`shared_buffers` 2 GB, everything in memory, no parallel query; LIMIT 10, the median of the 200
queries, and the DEBUG1 line's partitions probed and pages read, averaged. Queries all but never
paused: a patience of 0 gave the same figures at margins 0 to 4.

| | Spill | No spill |
|---|---|---|
| Build | 175 s | 157 s |
| Size | 235 MB, 6,912 CODE pages | 210 MB, 3,624 CODE pages |

| Margin | Spill: recall, partitions, pages, ms | No spill: recall, partitions, pages, ms |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.793, 4.5, 53, 2.0 | 0.710, 4.9, 30, 2.1 |
| 1 | 0.835, 6.4, 76, 2.0 | 0.757, 7.0, 42, 1.9 |
| 2 | 0.886, 9.4, 110, 2.4 | 0.808, 10.2, 60, 2.2 |
| 3 (default) | 0.919, 14.2, 164, 2.7 | 0.843, 15.3, 88, 2.1 |
| 4 | 0.946, 20.6, 237, 3.0 | 0.881, 21.9, 124, 2.3 |
| 5 | 0.962, 30.1, 342, 3.7 | 0.912, 32.0, 180, 3.0 |
| 6 | 0.975, 41.6, 468, 3.9 | 0.934, 45.4, 252, 3.2 |
| 8 | | 0.963, 81.2, 444, 4.2 |

At each margin spill found 0.065 to 0.083 more of the ten nearest, probing 91 to 94% as many
partitions (`LIONVEC_SPILL_PROBES`, §44.7) and reading 1.7 to 1.9 times the CODE pages, for up to
0.7 ms more. At each recall it probed less than half the partitions and read fewer pages: 0.919 at
a margin of 3 from 14 partitions and 164 pages in 2.7 ms, where without spill a margin of 5 gave
0.912 from 32 partitions and 180 pages in 3.0 ms; 0.962 at a margin of 5 from 30 partitions and
342 pages in 3.7 ms, where without it a margin of 8 gave 0.963 from 81 and 444 in 4.2 ms. A
spilling scan skipped 122 copies a query at a margin of 0 and 553 at 3, and fewer rows out of
order (0.38 a query at 3, against 0.65): a row near its partition's edge comes in time from the
partition beyond. Recall at
each margin is lower here than on the benchmark's set (0.84 without spill at the default, against
0.98): other embeddings, and an eighth of the rows. What this measures is the one setting against
the other; the benchmark's million rows spilling are still to be measured.

**Regions** (format 4, §44.3; 2026-10-16). The same 115,386 rows, every one of them indexed (so
the default is 2,717 partitions, in 53 regions), the same 200 query rows each kept out of its own
answer; cosine, spilling; PostgreSQL 18 (an assert build), 4 cores shared with other work,
`maintenance_work_mem` 2 GB, the table cached; recall of the true ten, the median and 95th
percentile of the 200 queries' times, after a pass to warm. Main, the build before the change,
ran on one cluster, the rest on a second of the same build and settings, where the change with
the regions and the cut switched off for the measurement ("every centroid") built main's index
again: the same recall, 0.913 and 0.9865, in 287.9 s against 291.6.

| 2,717 partitions | Main | Regions |
|---|---|---|
| Build, serial | 291.6 s | 108.2 s |
| Build, 3 workers and the leader | 84.9 s | 35.9 s |
| Size | 247.1 MB | 246.9 MB |
| Margin 3: recall, median, p95 | 0.913, 3.2 ms, 6.2 ms | 0.919, 3.3 ms, 6.5 ms |
| Margin 8 | 0.9865, 6.6 ms, 10.7 ms | 0.9845, 7.1 ms, 11.4 ms |

The parallel build's index answered as the serial one's (the same recall at both margins). In
679 partitions (27 regions), where the cut to 128 a partition keeps 86,912 of the rows, and in
10,000 (100 regions, no cut):

| | Every centroid, every row | Regions, and the cut |
|---|---|---|
| 679: build serial, 3 workers | 108.0 s, - | 62.7 s, 23.2 s |
| 679: margin 3, margin 8 | 0.909, 0.984 | 0.913, 0.980 |
| 10,000: build serial, 3 workers | -, 248.7 s | -, 65.0 s |
| 10,000: margin 3, margin 8 | 0.9285, 0.992 | 0.932, 0.989 |

The recall moves by as much from one draw of the sample to another: without regions, at 679
partitions, three draws of the cut to 128 gave 0.916, 0.920 and 0.915 at a margin of 3 and 0.981,
0.982 and 0.985 at 8, and the regions' k-means makes other centroids as another draw does. The
assignment's MATCH, the share of the rows whose partition (and, spilling, whose copy's partition)
the routed second pass chose as exact assignment over the same final centroids would, measures the
routing alone. With one beam for both passes, in 53 regions:

| Beam | Partition | Copy's partition | Margin 3 | Margin 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 94.8% | 67.9% | 0.8965 | 0.974 |
| 3 | 97.1% | 78.2% | 0.908 | 0.980 |
| 4 | 98.3% | 84.3% | 0.9115 | 0.983 |
| 6 | 99.1% | 90.5% | 0.911 | 0.984 |
| 8 | 99.5% | 93.7% | 0.9165 | 0.9825 |
| exact | 100% | 100% | 0.913 | 0.9865 |

A spilling row's copy wants more: SOAR picks it from the nine nearest, which lie farther out. With
k-means' beam at 5, the second pass's at 10, 13, 16 and 20 matched 99.78, 99.89, 99.94 and
99.97% of the partitions and 96.2, 97.8, 98.6 and 99.2% of the copies' in 53 regions (recall
0.9205 to 0.919 at 3, 0.985 to 0.9845 at 8: k-means' centroids decide it); 13 and 16 matched
96.95 and 97.9% of the copies' in 100 regions, and 7 and 10 93.1 and 96.6% in 27. Sixteen is the
least that held 97% at all three. With k-means routed at 5 and the second pass exact, the recall
was 0.9195 and 0.9845, and with k-means exact and the second pass at 5, 0.9095 and 0.984: neither
pass's routing moves it past the draws' spread. K-means' own beam, the second pass's at 16: 3 and
4 gave 0.914 and 0.9145 at a margin of 3 and 0.9815 at 8, half a hundredth under exact
assignment's 0.9865, and 5 gave 0.919 and 0.9845 (4 gave 0.914 and 0.9825 in 679 partitions,
against 0.909 and 0.984), so 5 is the least within 0.003 of it at both margins. The regions' own
k-means: 2, 5 and 10 iterations matched 98.6, 98.8 and 98.9% of the partitions at a beam of 5,
and 86.8, 88.1 and 88.4% of the copies' partitions, for 0.9145, 0.916 and 0.9135 at a margin of 3
and 0.981, 0.985 and 0.982 at 8; the regions held 16 to 141 centroids of 2,717 (6
to 58 of 679, 4 to 287 of 10,000), none empty. Build times with the match measured include an
exact assignment of every row besides, and are not given.

**Simulation.** Before the partitions were written, a numpy model of the scan chose their number
and the margin (vtoy's `ivf.py`, not in the tree): the benchmark's 975,000 vectors, k-means at
256, 1,024 and 4,096 partitions, the first 100 test queries, partitions taken nearest first by
their centroids less a margin, and the rows read until the ten nearest (under each filter) were
in hand. The rows of the partitions read, for 0.95 recall:

| Partitions | none | 10% | 1% | 0.1% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 256 | 50,800 (5.2%) | 51,700 | 90,200 | 272,000 |
| 1,024 | 27,800 (2.9%) | 31,900 | 67,300 | 207,000 |
| 4,096 | 16,600 (1.7%) | 20,300 | 46,500 | 160,000 |

The unfiltered share falls about as `C^(-1/3)` (0.26 `C^(-1/3)` is 4.1%, 2.6% and 1.6%), which is
`LIONVEC_PROBE_SHARE`; a filter keeping a share s reads about `s^(-0.3)` times as many, since its
nearest matching rows lie farther out. Ordering partitions by centroid less a margin scaled by each
partition's own radius (its largest or its rms distance to its centroid) read as many rows or more
at every recall, which is why the margin is one number. Spilling each row to its second-nearest
partition as well (SOAR's spill, chosen by the residual's angle) read 17% fewer rows at 4,096
partitions for twice the CODE items; SPANN's (a second partition within 10% or 25% of the
nearest's distance) read more. The margin a recall needed, in cosine units at 1,024 partitions:
0.010 for 0.95, 0.025 for 0.98, 0.035 for 0.99 unfiltered, about 0.016 less for each tenfold a
filter thins the rows, and about the same at 256 and 4,096 partitions; the rows' standard
deviation about their centroids along one dimension, σ, was 0.0122, so a margin of 2σ, the
default before the pause, is about 0.98 recall.

**Growth.** How the rows a scan reads grow with the table, in the same model (vtoy's `scale.py`):
random subsets of 60,938 and 243,750 of the 975,000 rows and all of them, k-means at `2 sqrt(n)`
partitions and at one per 500 rows, the 100 queries' true ten within each subset, and the margin
that reaches each recall chosen afresh at each size. The rows read, the mean over the queries, and
in brackets their median and 95th percentile:

| Rows | Partitions | 0.95 recall | 0.98 recall |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 60,938 | 493 (`2 sqrt(n)`) | 2,146 (1,262; 6,495) | 5,907 |
| 243,750 | 987 | 6,403 (3,518; 18,285) | 16,157 |
| 975,000 | 1,974 | 27,086 (13,122; 104,816) | 73,589 |
| 60,938 | 121 (n / 500) | 5,252 (3,480; 15,156) | 10,322 |
| 243,750 | 487 | 8,584 (4,588; 30,776) | 23,240 |
| 975,000 | 1,950 | 23,085 (10,934; 74,955) | 56,781 |

At `2 sqrt(n)` the partitions grow as the rows' root and the rows read grow almost as the rows
(n^0.91 at 0.95 recall): the probed share hardly falls. At 500 rows a partition they grow as n^0.53
(0.95) and n^0.61 (0.98), the partitions probed as n^0.53 too (10, 17 and 46 at 0.95). Taken that
far, a billion rows in two million partitions would read about 900,000 rows a query for 0.95 and
four million for 0.98 - 230 MB and 1 GB of CODE pages at the benchmark index's 242 bytes a row, from
some 1,900 and 8,000 partitions, against 5.6 and 14 MB at 975,000 rows; three sizes over a
sixteenfold range do not pin a power down a thousandfold further, so this is a direction, not a
forecast.

The mean is the tail's: the median query reads less than half the mean and the 95th percentile three
to four times it, as in the benchmark. Capping the partitions probed cuts the tail for little
recall. At 975,000 rows in 1,950 partitions, with the margin for 0.98: no cap, 0.981 and a mean of
56,781 rows (95th percentile 226,626); at most 10% of the partitions, 0.979 and 40,729 (102,971); at
most 5%, 0.971 and 28,612 (55,643) - more recall than the margin for 0.95 with no cap (about
0.956, 23,085 and 74,955) at a 95th percentile a quarter lower. At the smaller sizes a cap of 5% or
10% did the same.

A pause does better than a cap, and is what the scan does (§44.4). In the same model (vtoy's
`patience100.py`), the scan stopping once P partitions in a row have put nothing into its 100
nearest: at 975,000 rows in 1,950 partitions, with the margin for 0.98, P = 20 read a mean of
28,062 rows (95th percentile 74,986) and P = 40 38,740 (100,481), against 56,781 (226,626) with
neither, the cap of 5%'s rows at 0.98 recall rather than 0.971; at 243,750 rows in 487
partitions, P = 20 read 18,142 (48,213) against 23,240 (68,741). Between those two sizes the rows
read for 0.98 grew as n^0.32 with P = 20 and n^0.64 without - two sizes, so a direction only, but
the one that matters at a billion rows (§44.11).

**DBpedia.** The method again on a public set of another model's embeddings
(`bench/vector/knn_dbpedia.py`, `bench/results/2026-10-14-lionvec-dbpedia/`): shards 0-2 of
Qdrant's `dbpedia-entities-openai3-text-embedding-3-large-1536-1M`, 115,386 text-embedding-3-large
rows of 1536 dimensions, 200 of them held out as queries (the numpy model's `default_rng(0)`), the
true ten by cosine among the other 115,186, filters keeping 11,377, 3,472 and 1,204 rows (10%, 3%,
1%). PostgreSQL 16, pgvector 0.8.7, 4 vCPUs, every relation in 2 GB of shared buffers,
`maintenance_work_mem` 1 GB (the sample is every row); the server's median over 200 warm queries.
lionvec is 210 MB in 678 partitions (`2 sqrt(n)`) and 221 MB in 2,715 (`8 sqrt(n)`), built in 159 s
and 347 s; HNSW 450 MB, 187 s.

The margin does not carry over. At the defaults lionvec returned 0.843 of the true ten unfiltered,
in 1.1 ms, probing 15 of 678 partitions (88 CODE pages), where ada-002's got 0.979; 0.95 took a
margin of about 7 (2.4 ms) and 0.98 one of 11 (3.2 ms). HNSW took 1.9 ms for 0.951 at
`ef_search` 40 and 4.1 ms for 0.979 at 100. The margin a recall needs, in the rows' spread about
their centroids, is the embeddings' own.

In 2,715 partitions, at the same margin and patience, a scan probed 2.5 times the partitions and
read three quarters of the CODE pages (37 and 68 at a margin of 3) for 0.835, in 1.4 ms. Along the
margins, 0.95 took 234 CODE pages against 358 in 678 partitions - 1.5 times fewer, and about 5,700
rows scored against 11,000, 1.9 times fewer (the numpy model's 1.78) - but 2.9 ms against 2.4: each
query ranks four times the centroids, and a partition of 42 rows spans two 35-row pages, so a probe
reads 1.75 pages for 1.2 pages of rows. At a patience of 30 the finer partitions never reached 0.98
(0.966 at margins 12 and 16), as the patience then counted partitions' worth of rows, a quarter as
many there; at 120, the rows of 30 in 678 partitions, they did, in 566 pages against 578 and 4.5 ms
against 3.2. Counted since in the rows of `2 sqrt(n)` partitions (§44.4), a patience of 30 on the
same index gave the 120's recall in every row, and its partitions and pages to within 0.07 a query:
0.98 in 566 pages, 327 partitions and 4.1 ms. At this size the finer partitions buy pages and rows,
not time; the default changed for the rows a scan reads at a billion (§44.11), where the centroids
need an index of their own anyway. Under 10% the planner took the plain scan with a `Filter` at both
sizes (0.879 and 0.872 at a margin of 3, 5 to 8 ms); under 3% LionOrdered in 678 partitions (0.917,
5.0 ms) but a sort of the lion bitmap scan's 3,472 rows in 2,715 (exact, 20 ms, where LionOrdered
took 5.8 ms for 0.908), its estimate 2,034 against LionOrdered's 2,213, which charges a random page
for each partition probed, a number that grows as C^(2/3); under 1% a sort of the 1,204 rows (5.3
ms) and LionOrdered's exact path (5.6 ms) alike. HNSW's iterative scan took 10.7 ms at 3% (0.953)
and 26.7 ms at 1% (0.959); the planner sorted for it there too.

**Both** (`lionvec-p0-spill.json`: the defaults since, 2,715 partitions spilling, format 3, a
patience of 30 in the rows of `2 sqrt(n)` partitions; 356 s, 247 MB). At a margin of 3 the scan
returned 0.917 of the ten nearest from 35 partitions and 114 CODE pages in 1.6 ms, where the old
default gave 0.843 from 15 and 88 in 1.1 ms; 0.976 at 6 (111 partitions, 351 pages, 3.2 ms), 0.986
at 8 and 0.993 at 12 and 16, the finer partitions' ceiling. Along the margins, 0.95 took 203 CODE
pages, 63 partitions and 2.2 ms against the old default's 358, 65 and 2.4 and the finer partitions
alone's 310, 177 and 2.7; 0.98 464 pages, 148 partitions and 4.1 ms against 578, 106 and 3.2 and
566, 327 and 4.1. So the two together read 1.8 times fewer pages at 0.95 and 1.25 times fewer at
0.98 than the old default (about 7,100 and 16,200 items walked against 11,000 and 18,000 rows), in
the same time at 0.95 and 1.3 times longer at 0.98: the ranking of four times the centroids is a
fixed cost each query, and a partition's 84 items span 2.6 pages. The numpy model's 2.7 and 2.5
times fewer rows counted rows, not pages, and no copies. Under the filters, at 0.95 and 0.98, the
plain scan at 10% read 455 and 791 pages (7.0 and 8.9 ms) against 589 and none reached (0.969) in
678 partitions; LionOrdered at 3% 671 and 1,155 (6.0 and 8.3 ms) against 771 and 1,210 (5.6 and
7.1). The planner's plans are the finer partitions' (above): the plain scan with a `Filter` at 10%
(0.948 at a margin of 3), a sort of the lion bitmap scan's rows at 3% (exact, 15 to 21 ms, where
LionOrdered took 7.2 ms for 0.967) and at 1%. HNSW: 0.951 in 1.9 ms at `ef_search` 40, 0.979 in
4.1 ms at 100.

**Cold** (`cold.json`; the server restarted and the page cache dropped before each query, the
median of 7, the index above and HNSW's). Unfiltered, lionvec at a margin of 3 (0.917) read 478
pages in 22 ms, at 7 (0.95) 1,314 in 50 ms and at 12 (0.993) 1,378 in 61 ms; HNSW at `ef_search`
40 (0.951) 926 in 50 ms and at 100 (0.979) 1,918 in 106 ms. Under the 3% filter LionOrdered at a
margin of 3 (0.967) read 1,607 pages in 64 ms, where HNSW's iterative scan (0.953) read 5,365 in
293 ms and the planner's sort of the bitmap scan's rows (exact, for either index) 5,620 in 209 to
218 ms, every matching row's vector from TOAST; under 1% lionvec's exact path read 2,721 in 90 ms,
HNSW's iterative scan (0.959) 11,870 in 539 ms. So cold, lionvec reads what HNSW reads unfiltered
and three to four times less under a filter; on the million-row set it was 85 ms against 118
unfiltered and 196 against 1,254 at 1% (above), not re-measured with spill.

The share probed at a margin of 3, in 678 and 2,715 partitions: 2.2% and 1.4% unfiltered (§44.7's
`0.46 C^(-1/3)`: 5.2% and 3.3%), 8.1% and 4.8% through the plain scan at 10% (9.7% and 6.1%), 14.9%
and 10.3% through LionOrdered at 3% (13.5% and 8.5%). Between the sizes it fell by 1.4 to 1.7
times, the model's `C^(1/3)` 1.59; unfiltered it is under half the model's level because a margin of
3 stops this data's scans early, at 0.84 recall. So the constants stay.

**Kernels** (2026-10-15; the index above, on the same machine, whose Xeon has AVX-512 with
VPOPCNTDQ, so the AVX-512 set, §44.3). Timed by section with `rdtsc` (its own cost taken off), a
warm query at a margin of 3 spent 35% of its time in the arithmetic before them: plane 1's
estimates of the 2,715 centroids and 2,914 rows 15%, the 8-bit sums of 123 centroids and 88 rows
18% (1.8 us a call), the rotation and the query's planes 4%; the rest was the walk of 36
partitions' CODE pages around those estimates (28%), the PART chain's ranking (13%), the 11 heap
fetches with their exact distances (6%), the executor (7%) and the scan's queues. At a margin of 7
the arithmetic was 32% (the walk 47%); under LionOrdered at 3% 19% at either margin, most of it
the 8-bit sums of 800 and 1,600 centroids, the executor's filter a quarter at a margin of 3. The
build spent 59% of k-means in the candidates (plane 1 against every centroid), 24% in their exact
distances and 16% in the query's planes. Per call at 1536 dimensions, the library in a harness
(gcc -O2, the median of six), ns:

| call | before | POPCNT | AVX2 | AVX-512 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `lionvec_estimate1()` (plane 1) | 60 | 58 | 38 | 27 |
| `lionvec_estimate8()` (the 8-bit sum) | 1,170 | 1,055 | 386 | AVX2's |
| `lionvec_l2sq` | 1,100 | 955 | 270 | AVX2's |
| `lionvec_rotate()`, us | 35.0 | 34.1 | 6.2 | AVX2's |

"Before" is the POPCNT kernel and the plain sums (its `l2sq`, a static function, timed as a copy);
the portable set is POPCNT's with plane 1 counted without the instruction (164 ns); the query's
planes took 46 us before and take 12 with any set. End to end, the median execution time of the
200 queries, the median of eight runs alternating the builds, before and after: unfiltered 1.52
-> 1.18 ms at a margin of 3 (0.917) and 3.73 -> 2.98 at 7 (0.980); the plain scan at 10% 6.46 ->
5.29 and 9.38 -> 7.31; LionOrdered at 10% 7.74 -> 7.12 and 11.04 -> 10.01, at 3% 7.03 -> 6.21
(0.967) and 11.97 -> 10.54 (0.994); the exact path at 1% and the planner's sorts as before. Recall,
partitions, candidates and pages were the same at every setting. The arithmetic is now 21% of the
query at a margin of 3 and 10 to 11% under LionOrdered at 3%: in a scan a centroid's or row's 8-bit
estimate takes 0.6 to 1.3 us, against 0.39 in cache, waiting on its codes' 24 cache lines -
prefetching them took a third off a sum out of cache in a harness (1,083 -> 675 ns), not done -
and plane 1's estimates are 7% inside a walk of 42 to 66%. The build took 148 s against 348 (the
medians of three and two), the same index.

**The exact path or the probes, by members a partition** (2026-10-16; `knn_dbpedia.py exact` with
`KNN_EXACT_SELS` and `KNN_EXACT_MARGINS`, on main's build at 1c85107). DBpedia's 115,186 rows as
above, the vectors inline (`KNN_INLINE`: a row a heap page), the index of 2,715 partitions spilling,
every relation in 2 GB of shared buffers; 200 queries, LIMIT 10, through LionOrdered
(`enable_sort` off and the lionvec index's own scan out of the way, as `knn_dbpedia.py`'s `lo`
settings put it - §39, "Core's switches"), its exact path with `pg_lion.vector_exact_rows` past
every filter, its probes with it at 0 and the default patience. The server's median time, the
median of three runs' (two other builds shared the 4 cores), and the 95th percentile; recall and
pages, the same in every run. Probed at the default margin, at the margin nearest 0.98 of the ten
nearest and the one nearest 0.99:

| Filter | Members | A partition | Exact path | Probed, margin 3 | ... about 0.98 | ... about 0.99 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.3% | 345 | 0.13 | 0.5 ms (p95 0.7) | 0.9530, 1,584 pages, 7.4 ms (12.4) | 0.9825 (12), 2,597, 10.9 (18.0) | 0.9890 (16), 3,219, 13.7 (21.1) |
| 1% | 1,204 | 0.44 | 2.0 (2.7) | 0.9610, 1,172, 8.6 (13.2) | 0.9795 (8), 1,511, 10.0 (15.5) | 0.9925 (16), 2,644, 15.2 (23.6) |
| 2% | 2,288 | 0.84 | 4.2 (5.9) | 0.9640, 955, 8.2 (12.1) | 0.9795 (6), 1,100, 9.3 (14.3) | 0.9940 (12), 1,918, 12.9 (19.3) |
| 3% | 3,472 | 1.28 | 7.8 (9.4) | 0.9640, 790, 9.1 (14.0) | 0.9770 (4), 944, 9.9 (13.9) | 0.9895 (8), 1,319, 12.4 (18.4) |
| 5% | 5,760 | 2.12 | 8.9 (13.1) | 0.9610, 621, 7.5 (11.5) | 0.9750 (4), 803, 8.9 (12.9) | 0.9915 (8), 1,258, 11.0 (16.8) |
| 7% | 8,001 | 2.95 | 19.2 (24.4) | 0.9575, 521, 8.9 (12.6) | 0.9765 (4), 691, 10.8 (15.9) | 0.9880 (6), 926, 11.1 (16.7) |
| 10% | 11,377 | 4.19 | 26.4 (33.4) | 0.9560, 433, 8.5 (12.6) | 0.9740 (4), 593, 10.2 (14.7) | 0.9870 (6), 848, 11.5 (16.3) |

The exact path's time follows the members, 1.5 to 2.4 us each (a heap page in shared buffers and a
distance); the probes' hardly moves with the filter, 9 to 11 ms for 0.98, because the thinner the
members the more partitions they probe and pages they read for them - 1,584 pages at 0.3% against
433 at 10% for about 0.955. The two crossed warm at about two members a partition (5%: 8.9 ms
exact against 8.9 for 0.975), and at three (7%) the probes took 10.8 ms to the exact path's 19.2.
The planner's own exact plan, a sort of the lion bitmap scan's rows by distance, took 0.4, 1.5,
2.9, 4.6, 6.9, 17.5 and 24.7 ms: the same rows, read a page at a time by the bitmap heap scan,
without LionOrdered's set and a fetch a member through the index's scan.

Cold - the server restarted and the page cache dropped before each query, the median of seven, the
pages read from the kernel (`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`): the exact path read a heap page a member,
in 23 ms at 0.3% (346 pages), 75 ms at 1% (1,209), 183 ms at 3% (3,492) and 692 ms at 10% (11,402,
89 MB), 50 to 60 us a page; the probes, at the margins nearest 0.98 above, 99 ms at 1% (1,907
pages, margin 8), 67 ms at 3% (1,724, margin 4) and 71 ms at 10% (1,361, margin 4). Cold the two
crossed at 1,200 to 1,800 members, whatever the partitions.

At a million rows (the maintainer's measurement, 2026-10-15/16, `bench/results/followup-1m/`
FOLLOWUP.md, problem 4: 999,800 rows of the same embeddings in 7,999 partitions, vectors inline,
PostgreSQL 18 on a Ryzen 7 5700X3D): under 1%, 10,063 members, 1.26 a partition, a sort of the lion
index scan's rows - every member's distance, what the exact path computes - took about 11 ms warm
for all ten, where LionOrdered probed for 0.956 in about 13 ms and 0.98 in 19.6; under 3%, about
30,000 members, 3.75 a partition, LionOrdered took 21 and 28 ms for 0.95 and 0.98, where the exact
path, at the 1% filter's rate a member, would take about 33. Cold, LionOrdered took 331 ms at 1%
(a margin of 3); the exact path's 10,063 random heap reads (80 MB) were not measured, and their
cost was accepted.

Hence `pg_lion.vector_exact_per_partition` = 1.5 (§44.8): below the warm crossing of two to three
a partition at both sizes, so that 3% of the 115,186 rows (1.28) and 1% of the million (1.26) are
exact - for all ten, 1.3 and 1.8 times faster warm than the probes for 0.98, at the cold price
above - and 5% of the 115,186 (2.12) and 3% of the million (3.75) are probed. And
`pg_lion.vector_exact_rows` stays 2,000, near the cold crossing, for an index whose partitions are
too few for the ratio to say. Through the planner it does not show yet at 2% and 3% here, where
the exact path's price sends it to the plain scan with a `Filter` (§44.7).

**Prefetch and parallel scans** (2026-10-16; §44.4, "Prefetch" and "A parallel scan"). DBpedia's
115,386 rows as above in `dbp(id, v vector(1536))`, the cosine index of 2,717 partitions spilling
(format 4, 247 MB; its heap 768 pages, the vectors in TOAST); the 200 queries are rows of the table,
each kept out of its own answer by `WHERE id <> q` under `pg_lion.vector_postfilter = allow`, a
Filter over the scan, the truth the numpy ten nearest of the others. PostgreSQL 18.6 built with
assertions, pgvector 0.8.7, 4 vCPUs, 15 GB, `shared_buffers` 3 GB, `work_mem` 64 MB,
`effective_io_concurrency` 200 (so 64 pages ahead), `io_method` worker, `random_page_cost` 1.1,
`max_parallel_workers` 4; the disk a virtio device, about 55 us a page read cold. LIMIT 10;
participants 1 (serial), 2 (a worker and the leader) and 4 (three and the leader), the parallel
plans forced by `parallel_setup_cost`, `parallel_tuple_cost`, `min_parallel_index_scan_size` and
`min_parallel_table_scan_size` at 0. Warm: `pg_prewarm` of the index and the table, a first pass

Interpolated to the recall of each parallel scan at a margin of 3, the serial scan probes 47.1
partitions for two participants' 0.935 and 65.3 for four's 0.9515 (margins of about 3.7 and 4.6),
so the parallel scans probe 1.24 and 2.0 times as many and read as many times the CODE pages, and

REFINE pages for itself; at a margin of 8 two participants' 0.994 is 1.03 times the serial scan's
partitions at about 15 (1.29 times its pages), and four's 0.996 lies past the serial scan's best
measured, 0.9945 at 16 from 382 partitions to their 791. In time the parallel scans lose
everywhere: 4.3 and 6.4 times the serial scan's at the same recall at a margin of 3, 2.5 times
two participants' at 8. Each participant ranks all 2,717 centroids and probes to its own stop,
Gather Merge waits for the slowest one's first row, and the workers are started for each query,
about 10 ms before their first row (§44.4).

The planner, at its default costs with `max_parallel_workers_per_gather` 3: the serial scan,
584.79..599.57 for the LIMIT, also with `min_parallel_table_scan_size` 0 (without which the
768-page heap gets no workers); with `parallel_setup_cost` 0 as well, a Gather Merge of two
workers, 251.61, and of three with the tuple cost and `min_parallel_index_scan_size` 0 too,
197.88 (§44.7's arithmetic). So at the default costs it never picks the parallel scan, which is
what the times say.

page of this table, its raised `toast_tuple_target` not counted until a9a27c5), in three states:
`device`, the server restarted and the page cache dropped before each query, the configurations
taking turns query by query; `os`, the server restarted before each query with every relation in the

returned the same rows in the same order in every configuration, state and `io_method`. The server's
median ms over the 10 queries, and in brackets each query's `stream` time over its `fadvise` time,

| Device | off | worker (3): fadvise, stream | sync: fadvise, stream | io_uring: fadvise, stream |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| margin 3 | 25.3 | 20.9, 21.9 (1.12) | 20.8, 18.8 (0.94) | 19.1, 20.3 (1.04) |
| margin 8 | 67.2 | 47.6, 43.2 (0.93) | 48.1, 41.0 (0.79) | 46.4, 39.8 (0.86) |
| 10%, probed | 58.0 | 58.1, 46.8 (0.94) | 51.5, 41.7 (0.87) | 51.6, 47.9 (0.85) |
| 3%, probed | 95.9 | 72.9, 57.9 (0.79) | 76.9, 61.6 (0.79) | 76.0, 68.1 (0.87) |
| 1%, probed | 100.9 | 82.8, 62.0 (0.80) | 93.0, 72.2 (0.81) | 88.2, 72.9 (0.85) |
| 1%, exact | 108.3 | 58.9, 53.3 (0.90) | 56.1, 67.2 (1.17) | 64.9, 43.8 (0.66) |
| 3%, exact | 318.3 | 172.8, 151.6 (0.88) | 168.1, 158.2 (0.93) | 168.3, 111.8 (0.65) |

From the disk the streams are the faster on 18 of the 21, by 6 to 35% query by query; about even at
a margin of 3 (0.94 to 1.12), whose scan probes 29 partitions and reads 346 pages, too few for
reading ahead to pay much either way; and slower on the exact path at 1% under `sync`, where a
stream's reads are the backend's own `preadv()` after `posix_fadvise()` advice, much as `fadvise`'s
are (67.2 ms against 56.1). The exact path, a list known whole, gains most, its wait on reads all
but gone (under `worker` 3.5 ms against 19.3 at 1% and 5.6 against 54.4 at 3%): under io_uring its
3,472 heap pages took 112 ms against 168 asking the kernel and 318 with neither. Main's `on` asked
for the index's pages as `fadvise` does and for none of the heap's, so its exact path took `off`'s
time (115.5 ms at 1%). The streams read more pages: 402 against 346 at a margin of 3, 996 against
861 at 8 and 1,708 against 1,500 at 1% - chains the refill predicted that the scan did not probe,
its LIMIT met or a centroid coming first, released unread (64, 228 and 677 a query) - and the disk
read 4 to 19% more on the index's kinds (11.1 MB against 9.7 at a margin of 8 under `worker`). A
scan's streams ended and started again 35 to 72 times a query, each time a stream had nothing left
to read and the scan then read a page it had pushed.

With every page in the kernel's cache and none in shared buffers, a read is a copy of 8 kB, and
handing it to another thread costs more than it: under `io_method = worker` an I/O worker reads
every page a stream reads, and under io_uring PostgreSQL submits a buffered read with `IOSQE_ASYNC`
once more than four are in flight (method_io_uring.c), so the kernel's io-wq threads copy it;
`ReadBuffer()` copies it in the backend under every method.

| OS cache | off | worker (3): fadvise, stream | sync: fadvise, stream | io_uring: fadvise, stream |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| margin 3 | 6.3 | 6.4, 11.5 (1.40) | 7.3, 7.1 (1.02) | 8.2, 8.9 (1.31) |
| margin 8 | 18.2 | 17.9, 21.7 (1.18) | 19.8, 18.5 (1.11) | 16.9, 18.9 (1.22) |
| 10%, probed | 20.2 | 23.8, 23.6 (1.00) | 19.5, 21.5 (1.08) | 19.8, 30.4 (1.23) |
| 3%, probed | 28.0 | 26.1, 29.8 (1.10) | 28.3, 30.8 (1.14) | 27.0, 31.1 (1.19) |
| 1%, probed | 29.2 | 28.4, 26.5 (1.05) | 31.0, 31.1 (1.02) | 27.6, 36.4 (1.10) |
| 1%, exact | 18.4 | 19.1, 8.6 (0.44) | 19.8, 21.6 (1.10) | 22.3, 34.0 (1.54) |
| 3%, exact | 52.5 | 55.1, 23.2 (0.45) | 56.6, 61.4 (1.07) | 55.8, 107.9 (1.96) |

So from the kernel's cache the streams cost: 0 to 40% on the index's pages, whose reads a scan
mostly waits on one at a time, and on the exact path one and a half to twice the time under
io_uring, every copy a thread's hop, where under `worker` its many reads in flight, copied by three
workers at once, took half the time. Sixteen workers (`io_workers = 16`, `off`, `fadvise` and
`stream` only) read the disk faster still - the exact path 37.2 ms at 1% against 61.9 asking the
kernel, 99.5 at 3% against 170.0, a margin of 8 37.1 against 45.4 - and the kernel's cache slower,
sixteen processes on four CPUs: 10.9 ms against 6.2 at a margin of 3 (1.72), the exact path 1.17
times `fadvise`'s.

Warm, every page in shared buffers, each query against itself under the same build's `off` in one
session (`warm-rest3.json`, 20 queries, 5 runs each): `fadvise` 0.98 to 1.05, `stream` 1.02 to 1.11
(1.11 at a margin of 3, 1.07 at 8, 1.02 to 1.05 filtered and on the exact path); and a build whose
streams did not rest (r3, the ring's stream ever pushed and refilled, the list ever streamed), 1.06
to 1.15 against its own `off` (1.15 at a margin of 3, 1.13 at 8, 1.11 and 1.15 at 3 and 1%). The
rest roughly halves what a warm stream costs, as dormancy did the asks' (§44.4, "Prefetch"), so it
stays, for the streams too: of a warm margin-8 scan's 1,098 reads, 341 come from its streams and 758
are read apart, and of the exact path's 1,204 blocks at 1%, 165 come from its list's stream. The
matrices' warm runs, a session for each build and the configurations taking turns, agree: `stream`
over `fadvise` 0.93 to 1.04 under each method.

What the parts are worth, from smaller runs (5 queries, `io_method = worker`, device): without
predicting the next partitions' chains (`nopred`), each probe's stream ended with its run and
started again from one block, and a scan took 68.4 ms at a margin of 8 against 42.8, 146.9 at 1%
against 62.8, 65.5 at 10% against 49.6 and 31.7 at a margin of 3 against 19.3 (`ab-restart.json`); a
stream that ended reset rather than begun anew from a full I/O ahead (`r2`) took 62.7 ms at 10% and
25.4 at a margin of 3 against 49.6 and 19.3, and the same at 8 and at 1%. The exact path through the
ring, before the list stream, took 65.9 ms at 1% (its wait 45.4 ms), through a list stream 50.9
(3.2) and asking the kernel 57.8 (18.1); at 3% 163.8, 132.2 and 166.0 (`ab-list.json`); a list
stream without `READ_STREAM_FULL`, which starts one block ahead, 53.7 and 146.4.

The vectors in TOAST (`toast-worker-3.json`): pgvector keeps a `vector` of more than 506 dimensions
there unless told otherwise, so most tables of real embeddings do. The same rows loaded with
`KNN_INLINE=0` into another database - the heap 7.6 MB, its TOAST 900 MB - with an index of their
own (2,715 partitions, 247 MB), under `io_method = worker`, from the disk and warm. Nothing reads a
toasted vector ahead (§44.4, "Prefetch"; §44.11). The index's streams gained what they gained
inline: a margin-8 scan took 43.0 ms streaming, 47.7 asking the kernel and 57.9 reading as it went,
a 3% filter's probing 67.4, 81.2 and 97.4, a margin of 3 about even (29.5, 26.3 and 28.7). The
exact path at 1% read its 2,717 pages - the members' heap pages, the TOAST index's and the chunks -
one at a time under every setting, 157 to 168 ms, 135 to 146 of them waiting on reads, where the
inline table's, streamed, took 53; warm it took 11.2 ms against 4.6, detoasting 1,204 vectors.

**Vectors in TOAST read by place** (2026-10-17; §44.13, "Measured";
bench/results/2026-10-17-lionvec-toast-direct/): the same `dbpedia_toast`, its index REINDEXed as
format 5, under `pg_lion.vector_toast_direct` off and on. The exact path from the disk took 68.3 ms
at 1% against 179.7, reading 1,631 pages against 2,717 and waiting 12.7 ms against 152.7, and 158.6
at 3% against 457.2; warm 7.9 against 14.1 and 16.4 against 31.8. The probing kinds were 6 to 7%
faster from the disk and the same warm, and the inline table's queries took main's time.

By perf on the resting build, 4 KB pages, the look (`lv_prefetch_queue()`) is gone from a DBpedia

### 44.10 Tests

- **test/unit/vec_test.c** (`make unit`, and under ASan and UBSan with `SANITIZE=1`), against the
  arithmetic alone, with exact-size heap buffers: the 8-bit tables (evenly spaced and symmetric,
  each code the inverse of its step, extremes, infinities and NaN); the rotation at 64 to 8128
  dimensions (norms and inner products kept to 1e-5; the same signs from the same seed and others
  from another; one window and two; a basis vector spread out; rotated coordinates with the
  variance, kurtosis and tails of a Gaussian); `lionvec_prepare()` (padding, cosine scaling, zero
  vectors); the encoding (bits, popcount, both alphas, a row at the mean); the query's quantization
  and planes; every set of kernels the build and CPU have, forced in turn (§44.3, "Kernels"): plane
  1 against a bit-at-a-time count at 1 to 127 words, the 8-bit sum and `l2sq` against their sixteen
  partial sums added in the header's order and the rotation against the portable one's, all to the
  bit, at every dimsp from 64 to 8128, from unaligned pointers, over inputs of every scale, denormals
  and signed zeros, and end to end the same rotations, estimates and k-means as the portable set's
  (2026-10-27: and `lionvec_dot8()` against a plain integer loop, both its sums, at every dimsp
  from 64 to 8128 from unaligned pointers, over codes and 16-bit weights at and mixed between
  their extremes, every set the portable one's results; the query's rounding - every coordinate
  within half a step, the extremes at +-32767, the sums and the variance as stated, a constant
  query's zeros, and the same query but for the rounding with `qw` NULL; and the estimate: the
  affine formula against the serial sum over the rounded query to 1e-9, within the rounding's
  reach of the floats' estimate, its error as stated, and every set the portable set's bytes)
  (`test/unit/vec_test_nosimd` is the same program built with `-DLION_NO_SIMD`); the halves'
  conversion, the portable one against a reference computed in double from each half's fields,
  over all 65,536 halves (2,046 NaNs, each quiet with its payload), and each set's against the
  portable one's to the bit, over all of them and at every length 0 to 40 from offsets 0 to 7,
  with nothing written past the end; `lionvec_datum_dim()`'s bounds for both types (shorter than
  the header, a header alone, a byte short of the count's elements, negative counts); the key
  algebra against true distances; and
  the bounds' COVERAGE on clustered data at 100, 384 and 1536 dimensions for each metric: plane 1
  outside 1 sd 30 to 32% of the time (the Gaussian's 31.7%), outside 3 sd 0.16 to 0.29% (0.27%); the
  codes outside 2 sd about 4% (4.6%) and never outside 6 sd, in 24,000 row-query pairs each. A heavy
  tail would fail it. The partitions: `lionvec_candidates()` at 64, 320 and 1536 dimensions - at a
  wide bound the nearest centroid is always a candidate and every key within its bounds, at the
  build's bound it is missed at most once in 200, and the candidates are few (10 of 200 at 320
  dimensions and more); no centroids, and identical ones; `lionvec_lift_key()` over partitions of
  300 rows of 24 dimensions, of mixed lengths and of unit length - at a margin of the lifted rows'
  greatest distance from their lifted centroid it bounds every row's key for every query, on unit
  rows it is the L2 bound of the unit query, and it falls as the margin grows; and
  `lionvec_kmeans()`, plain and spherical - it converges, every row ends with its nearest centroid,
  every centroid is its rows' (normalized) mean to 1e-4, the same seed gives the same centroids, a
  zero mean gives the same as none, one centroid is the mean, as many as rows one row each, with
  eight centroids a cluster none mixes two clusters, and identical rows finish; and its steps
  (§44.12), each iteration's rows assigned in chunks of 1, 7, 32 and all, the chunks taken last
  first and alternating between two scratch areas, giving its centroids, assignment and iterations
  to the bit, for as many centroids as clusters and eight times as many. Spill:

### 44.11 Not done

- **A billion rows.** Partitions are what make one possible, and three things stood in the way.
  The build's k-means and assignment, and a scan's ranking, cost a plane-1 estimate of every
  centroid for every row or query: O(n C) and O(C); and the sample's cap of 2^20 rows, at 16 a
  partition, with the reloption's ceiling, held the default to 65,536 partitions (15,000 rows
  each at a billion). The build's are the regions' now (§44.3): O(n sqrt(C)), each row routed
  through about sqrt(C) region centroids and the members of 5 regions in k-means, 16 in a
  spilling second pass; and the cap is 2^24 rows and the ceiling 262,144 partitions, so that a
  billion rows get the default `8 sqrt(n)`, 252,982 partitions of 3,950 rows, given the
  `maintenance_work_mem` (12.5 GB at 1536 dimensions for the sixteen a partition the default
  needs, without which the build fails, 52 GB for the cap's 66, §44.8). At 503 regions of some 503 centroids that build is,
  by arithmetic (not measured), 16.8 million sample rows x 10 iterations x about 3,000 estimates
  for k-means, 5 x 10^11, and a billion rows x about 8,550 for the second pass, 8.6 x 10^12, where
  every centroid for every row was 4.2 x 10^13 and 2.5 x 10^14. DBpedia's 53 regions save less
  (2,717 estimates a row, against some 310 and 870), and its build went from 292 s to 108 s
  serially (§44.9). The old default, `2 sqrt(n)`, kept the
  partitions few but let the rows read grow almost as the rows (§44.9's growth: n^0.91). `8
  sqrt(n)` (§44.3) is four times finer, 125 rows a partition at a million rows, but still grows
  as the root: 4,000 rows a partition at a billion. The scan's step is still O(C): it ranks every
  centroid, a 65 MB PART chain a query at 262,144 partitions, where routing it through the
  regions read a third more rows for a recall in the simulation (§44.3). A large table wants
  partitions of a fixed few hundred rows - two million of them
  for a billion rows, which makes the scan's O(C) the whole cost, a 500 MB PART chain a query,
  and a build of 2.4 x 10^13 estimates even through 1,415 regions, unless an index over the
  centroids that a scan can use as well (regions with a better order than their centroids', or a
  small graph) ranks them by reading a few thousand. And even then, by the margin alone, the rows
  read grew as n^0.53 to n^0.61 at a fixed partition size: one to four million rows a query at a
  billion, 230 MB to 1 GB of CODE pages. With the pause (§44.4) they grew as n^0.32 between the
  model's two largest sizes, which taken that far is about 260,000 rows, 60 MB of CODE pages, a
  parallel scan's tens of milliseconds from memory (arithmetic on two sizes, not measured).
  Spill (§44.3) is the other lever on the rows read, measured so far at 115,000 rows (§44.9); the
  index over the centroids is still to be built.
- **The sample's rows** (§44.8, `pg_lion.vector_build_sample`). The build fails rather than make
  fewer partitions than its rows want, but which rows the reservoir draws, and so the centroids,
  still follow `maintenance_work_mem` wherever it holds fewer rows than the table has: another
  size of reservoir keeps other rows, and k-means is given 16 to 128 of them a partition as it
  holds more (§44.3). The answers at a margin follow the centroids. A reservoir of one size
  whatever the setting - k-means' 128 a partition, or every row - spilled to a temporary file past
  `maintenance_work_mem` as LionOrdered's set is (§30.4), would make the same centroids at every
  setting; at a billion rows of 1536 dimensions it is 32 million rows, 50 GB, and k-means reads
  it ten times.
- **What the parallel scan leaves** (§44.4, "A parallel scan"; 2026-10-16). LionOrdered stays
  serial: its lion set is one process's, and a parallel restricted scan would need the set shared
  or built in each participant, and a partial path of the node. The stop rules are each
  participant's own: on DBpedia two and four participants together probed 1.6 and 3.7 times the
  serial scan's partitions at a margin of 3, 1.24 and 2.0 times what the serial scan probes for
  the recall they returned, and two 1.03 times at a margin of 8 (§44.9). A bound shared through
  the parallel area - the participants' least tau, or their tiers' - would win that back, as might
  a participant's patience counted in its share of the rows; it is worth its shared state only
  where the probes, not the workers' start and Gather Merge's wait for every participant's first
  row, are what a parallel scan pays, which on DBpedia they were not. (The read stream this item
  once proposed in place of `PrefetchBuffer()` is §44.4's "Read streams", 2026-10-17; what it
  leaves is the next item.)
- **What reading ahead leaves** (§44.4, "Prefetch" and "Read streams"; 2026-10-17). A vector in
  TOAST is not read ahead at all, by the asks or the streams: its chunks are found through the TOAST
  index from the heap tuple's pointer, which reading them ahead would have to read first, a heap
  page and an index descent a row before its chunks could be named; pgvector stores a `vector` of
  more than 506 dimensions there unless its column says otherwise, so most tables of real embeddings
  read their exact distances' chunks one after another: on DBpedia so stored the exact path at 1%
  took 157 to 168 ms from the disk under every setting, against 53 with the vectors in the heap's
  pages and streamed (§44.9), while the index's streams gained what they gain inline. Reading the
  chunks ahead wants the heap tuples first - a stream over the members' heap blocks whose reader, a
  block ahead, reads their TOAST pointers and names the chunks' TOAST index pages and then their
  pages to a second stream - or the chunks' TIDs kept beside the index's own items, which §44.13
  built (2026-10-17): the locator for the exact path, a REFINE item's place for the rerank. The
  rows' heap pages for their exact distances are asked of the kernel under `stream` too, a stream's
  pins being unwelcome between `amgettuple()` calls (§44.4); a scan asked for 0 to 26 of them a
  query on DBpedia, fetching 10 or 11 rows for their distances, too few for a stream to be worth its
  pins.
  The executor's fetch of a returned row is a buffer hit, the scan having fetched it for its
  distance just before, so nothing is read ahead for it. From the kernel's cache a stream costs more
  than `ReadBuffer()` under 18's `worker` and `io_uring` (§44.8), core handing each read to an I/O
  worker or a kernel thread; a default by `io_method`, or a stream that stays away while its
  relation's reads are quick, is left. And lion's own readers do not stream: `lion_count`'s heap
  recheck reads its sorted blocks a `ReadBuffer()` at a time where it does not stream already, and a
  lion set's leaf walk asks for one right-link ahead. A list stream (`lion_readahead_begin_list()`)
  fits the first, a ring (`lion_readahead_begin()`) the second; the exact path's list stream, from
  the disk, took its 3,472 heap pages in 112 to 152 ms against 168 to 173 asking the kernel (§44.9).
- **sparsevec, bit.** The codes do not care where the floats came from; each needs an operator
  class and a reader for its format, as halfvec has (§44.1).
- **The double heap fetch.** Each returned row is fetched by the scan for its distance and again by
  the executor; the second is a buffer hit. An index-only distance would need the REFINE item to be
  exact, which it is not.
- **REFINE space.** VACUUM leaves REFINE line pointers and frees the space only for the tail page's
  inserts; a table with much churn grows until REINDEX. A drifting distribution does not make the
  index wrong - any mean is correct, and an insert goes to the nearest centroid there is - but
  loosens the bounds and unbalances the partitions until REINDEX recomputes both.
- **A small `work_mem` with loose bounds** (few dimensions, a large LIMIT) makes many RESTs, each
  probing again every partition probed so far; the DEBUG1 line shows them.
- **The planner underprices a sort by distance**, at pgvector's own costs. Its distance functions
  cost 1 (`procost`), and a 1536-dimension vector is stored out of line, so the planner sees an
  18-byte column and a cheap operator: sorting a filter's rows by distance looks cheaper than the
  lionvec scan, and was chosen at 548 ms over the scan's 136 ms for 97,000 rows, at 82 ms over 31
  for 9,700, and cold at 1,209 ms over 199 (format 1). Repricing core's Sort paths whose key is a
  lionvec distance would be new territory for lion's planner hooks, and is not planned. Instead
  lionvec's documentation has the functions its operator classes use (`l2_distance`,
  `vector_negative_inner_product` and `cosine_distance` of `vector`, and `l2_distance`,
  `halfvec_negative_inner_product` and `cosine_distance` of `halfvec` for a halfvec column) set
  to `COST 100` with the extension, and the benchmarks assume it. pg_dump does not keep the
  setting (an extension member's), and a pgvector update may reset it. `enable_sort = off` does
  the same for one query.
- **Choosing between lionvec and HNSW.** With both on one column, the planner takes HNSW for
  nearly every query, as pgvector prices an HNSW scan at almost nothing: on 200,000 random
  256-dimension rows, about 13 against lionvec's 3,100 unfiltered (format 1).
- **Progressive refinement from planes 2 to 8** (evaluated 2026-10-26, §44.14): the 8-bit codes
  kept as seven bit-planes, a refine reading them until its bound decides. On DBpedia it would stop
  at 3.2 planes a row and 4.0 a centroid, but the sums are a tenth of a warm query, reading the
  REFINE item costs a refine more than its sum, and an integer kernel over today's bytes takes as
  much off: not worth a format. That kernel, the codes against the query rounded to 16-bit
  integers (60 ns against 326 warm, 373 against 682 out of L2), is done: `lionvec_dot8()`,
  2026-10-27 (§44.3, "Kernels", with its measurement in a scan).

### 44.12 Parallel build (lion_vec.c, lion_vec_math.c; 2026-10-15)

A build's time is arithmetic, not reading: DBpedia's 115,186 rows of 1536 dimensions, in 2,715
partitions, took 134.2 s serially (PostgreSQL 18, 4 cores, the table cached) - the first pass
2.8 s, k-means 108.0 s, the second pass 23.1 s, the sort and the writing 0.4 s; another run took
124.8 s, the machine being shared. Both k-means' iterations and the second pass find, for each row
on its own, the nearest of the centroids by a plane-1 estimate of each (§44.3), so both are shared
out among processes. With 3 workers and the leader the same build took 37.8 s: the first pass
3.0 s, k-means 28.3 s, the second pass 6.2 s, the writing 0.4 s (38.2 s in another run); the
shared steps ran 3.8 and 3.7 times as fast on four processes. It runs on PostgreSQL 16
as well, counting its own workers rather than waiting for core's (below).

The regions (§44.3, 2026-10-16) cut the arithmetic of both shared steps, and the parallel build
keeps its share of what is left: on a 4-core machine shared with other work, where the build
before them took 291.6 s serially and 84.9 s with 3 workers (115,386 rows in 2,717 partitions),
it took 108.2 s and 35.9 s, 3.0 times as fast with the workers (§44.9, "Regions"). What the
leader does alone each iteration is the regions' k-means: C centroids into `sqrt(C)` regions, 5
iterations at C `sqrt(C)` estimates each, some tens of milliseconds here and, by arithmetic,
7 x 10^8 estimates at `LIONVEC_MAX_PARTS`, where an iteration over the 2^24 rows the sample can
hold is 5 x 10^10 shared among the processes.

- **The phases.** The first pass, the mean and the sample, stays serial, and with it the check that
  fails a build whose sample is too small for its partitions (§44.8), before the parallel
  context is set up: reservoir sampling draws
  the same rows only when it meets them in the same order, and it is a fiftieth of the time. With
  the partitions known, the leader sets up a parallel context (`lionvec_begin_parallel()`, the
  workers' entry `lionvec_parallel_build_main()`): a shared struct with a parallel heap scan from
  the first block (as a serial build's scans, `allow_sync = false`, §44.5), the sample, copied
  into it and the leader's own copy freed, so that it is held once, the arrays k-means and the
  assignment work in (`LionVecBuildArrays`: the centroids, their plane 1 and 8-bit codes, their
  floats, the sample's assignment and the mean, laid out by one function in the leader and in
  every worker, and kept in local memory by a serial build), a shared tuplesort, and the workers'
  WAL and buffer usage, which the leader adds to its own. It then posts the workers work, under a
  spinlock and a condition variable, and takes part in each itself:
  - KMEANS, each iteration: the leader codes the centroids (C rows, a moment), regroups them into
    their regions when there are 64 or more (`lionvec_regions_make()`, into the region arrays
    `LionVecBuildArrays` holds in shared memory beside the centroids', §44.3, "Regions") and
    posts the iteration; every process takes the sample's rows 32 at a time (`LIONVEC_KMEANS_CHUNK`) from an
    atomic counter, assigns each its nearest centroid in the shared assignment and counts the rows
    that moved; the leader waits for the last row, then moves the centroids to their rows' means,
    alone. The counter's high 32 bits are the iteration's, so that a process still finishing the
    last iteration takes none of this one's rows, and its compare-and-swap never runs past the end.
  - SCAN, once: the second pass over the parallel heap scan. Each process puts its rows' CODE items
    into its own run of the shared sort, with `maintenance_work_mem` divided among them as core's
    builds divide it, and their REFINE items on REFINE pages it extends the index by for itself;
    the leader merges the runs and writes the CODE chains, the PART chain, the REGION chain and
    the meta page, as a serial build does, ends the workers, and WAL-logs the index. Before it
    posts the pass the leader has made the final centroids' regions and renumbered the partitions
    region by region in the shared arrays, so that every process routes each row through the
    same regions, by the same numbers, as a serial build's second pass does.
- **A serial build's index.** lionvec_kmeans() is its steps run in a loop
  (`lionvec_kmeans_start()`, `_codes()`, with regions `lionvec_regions_make()`, `_assign()` over
  a range of rows, `_update()`): a row's assignment depends on the centroids, their regions and
  the row alone, the regions are made by one process (the leader, as a serial build makes them:
  the same k-means of the centroids from the same seed), and the update sums the rows in the
  sample's order in one process, so the centroids come out of a parallel build to the bit as out of
  a serial one, however the rows were shared out (the unit tests, §44.10, which route by chunks in
  two "processes" with scratch of their own; vector_parallel.sql's 100-partition indexes, whose
  meta page, PART and REGION items match a serial build's). A row's partitions, its
  own and its copy's, depend on the centroids and their regions alone. The CODE items' sort was keyed by the group
  and a count in scan order; it is keyed by the group and the TID now, so the merged runs come out
  in the order a serial build's scan made, and the partitions' counts, spreads and longest rows, and
  the meta page's scale, which the scan callback summed, are summed as the CODE chains are written,
  in the sort's order, so that the floating sums do not depend on which process met which row. What
  differs is where the rows' REFINE items lie: each process fills pages of its own, so their blocks,
  the REFINE locations in the CODE items, and the chains' blocks, laid after the REFINE pages, are
  not a serial build's. A scan reads the same codes in the same order either way, and gives the same
  answers: DBpedia's 200 queries returned the same ten rows through either at margins of 3 and 8.
- **How many workers** (`lionvec_build_workers()`): `max_parallel_maintenance_workers`, or the
  table's `parallel_workers` when it sets it, at most `max_parallel_maintenance_workers`, as for
  core's builds. Core's count (`plan_create_index_workers()`) would also size a build by the heap's
  main fork and by `maintenance_work_mem`. pgvector stores a vector of more than about 500
  dimensions out of line, in the TOAST table: DBpedia's main fork is 7.6 MB, under
  `min_parallel_table_scan_size`, and core gives its 115,186 rows none, though the build's cost is
  arithmetic over the rows, whatever their bytes. And core keeps 32 MB of `maintenance_work_mem` a
  process, which at the default 64 MB allows one worker, for its sorts; a lionvec build's processes
  share the sample, and each holds only its share of the sort, which spills (at 1 MB,
  vector_parallel.sql). So lionvec counts its own, and core's goes unused. (pgvector's HNSW build
  asks for `max_parallel_maintenance_workers` whatever the size too, but only once core's count is
  more than none.) None below 10,000 rows with a vector unless `parallel_workers` is set
  (`LIONVEC_MIN_AUTO_ROWS`, below which a build is one partition by default and quick); none for an
  index whose expressions or predicate are not parallel safe (`lionvec_build_parallel_safe()`,
  `is_parallel_safe()` as core asks it), for a temporary table, which workers cannot read, or with
  no partitions. 17's `amcanbuildparallel` is set, as the build is parallel; core then counts
  workers for its DEBUG1 line alone, and on 16, which counts only for btree, the build is parallel
  all the same. Either way core's line may say "serially" of a build lionvec's next line says it
  "built in parallel". If no worker starts, the leader undoes the parallel setup and builds
  serially.
- **Shared memory.** The sample, up to half of `maintenance_work_mem` (§44.3; 177 MB for DBpedia),
  and the arrays (the centroids' floats and codes, 22 MB there) are in the parallel context's DSM
  segment, sized before the workers start. Where `/dev/shm` is small - Docker's 64 MB unless
  `--shm-size` raises it - creating the segment fails, and so does the build, as pgvector's
  parallel HNSW build does, whose documentation says the same; the guide says it, and that
  `max_parallel_maintenance_workers = 0` builds serially. The sort's runs are in temporary files,
  as core's are.
- **Locks and cancel.** A worker opens the heap and index with the locks `index_build()` took for
  the leader, `ShareLock` and `AccessExclusiveLock`, or for `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`
  `ShareUpdateExclusiveLock` and `RowExclusiveLock`, and scans with the leader's snapshot - an MVCC
  one under CONCURRENTLY, else `SnapshotAny`, as `table_index_build_scan()` wants. The second pass
  used to hold its REFINE page's content lock from one row to the next; an LWLock holds off
  interrupts, so a cancel waited for the page to fill, and a worker's for the leader, whose
  condition-variable wait is where a worker's error reaches it. Each row's REFINE item now locks
  the page for itself, which costs nothing measurable, and a serial build's cancel is as prompt.

### 44.13 Vectors in TOAST: reading them by their chunks' places (the locator; format 5, 2026-10-17)

pgvector stores a `vector` of more than 506 dimensions (a `halfvec` of more than 1,012) in TOAST
unless the column or the table says otherwise (§44.4, "Prefetch"), so most tables of real
embeddings keep theirs there. A fetch of such a vector reads the row's heap page for its TOAST
pointer, descends the TOAST index on `(chunk_id, chunk_seq)` for its chunks, and reads their
pages: three random reads where an inline vector costs one, none of which can be named before the
one before it is in, so neither the asks nor the streams read them ahead (§44.11, "What reading
ahead leaves"). The exact path (§44.6) pays that a member: on DBpedia's 115,186 rows so stored
(`dbpedia_toast`, §44.9) the 1% filter's 1,204 members cost 158 ms from the disk (157 to 168 under
every setting, §44.11), 2,717 pages read one at a time - 708 heap pages, about 800 of the TOAST
index's 1,273 and 1,204 of chunks - and 11.4 ms warm, against 53 and 4.6 to 4.9 with the vectors
in the heap's pages and streamed. A probing scan fetches a dozen rows or so, each the same three
reads.

So an index whose vectors may lie in TOAST keeps where each row's chunks lie - the TOAST
relation's block and line pointer of each, as RUNS (below) - in two places: in a map from heap TID
to those places, the LOCATOR, which the exact path reads in heap order beside its members, and then
each member's chunks directly, a page a vector in the usual case, through a read stream over blocks
it knows whole; and, where the vectors leave room, in each row's REFINE item, which the probing
path's rerank has just read when it comes to fetch the row, and which then names the row's chunks'
page beside its heap page. A place is only ever a hint: every chunk read there is checked to be the
chunk it should be, anything else sends that row down the heap path, and a row read so is returned
only once its heap tuple, fetched under the scan's snapshot, shows the same value.

**What the prototype was worth** (before it was built: a throwaway C function outside the
repository, on the benchmark cluster - PostgreSQL 18.6 release, `io_method = worker`, 3 workers,
§44.9's settings; the 10 queries of `knn_readahead.py`'s `x1` and, for 5 of them, `x3`; the
medians). From the disk (the server restarted and the page cache dropped before each query) and
warm (every relation in shared buffers, 3 runs a query): `x1` as it ran, under EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,
BUFFERS); and the members' vectors read by their chunks' places (from `pg_column_toast_chunk_id()`
and the TOAST table's `ctid`s, computed beforehand), each chunk checked as `heap_fetch_toast_slice()`
checks it, the distances computed with pgvector's `cosine_distance()`, after a 400-page relation
read in order standing for the locator, and the ten nearest rows' heap tuples fetched and their
TOAST pointers compared with the values read. Every configuration returned the ten rows `x1` did.
`p` the pages read, `w` the wait on them (`track_io_timing`):

| | 1% (1,204 members), disk | warm | 3% (3,472 members), disk | warm |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the exact path then | 158.3 ms, 2,717 p, 137.6 w | 11.41 | 427.2 ms, 5,620 p, 370.7 w | 29.09 |
| by place, read one at a time | 124.1 ms, 1,614 p, 118.3 w | 3.98 | 336.4 ms, 3,882 p, 321.6 w | 11.58 |
| by place, asked of the kernel 64 ahead | 80.3 ms, 1,614 p, 28.9 w | 4.15 | | |
| by place, through read streams | 55.2 ms, 1,614 p, 10.1 w | 3.97 | 141.5 ms, 3,882 p, 13.4 w | 11.83 |
| the same function, heap fetch and detoast | 189.0 ms, 2,712 p, 158.2 w | 11.17 | 461.6 ms, 5,600 p, 379.2 w | 37.03 |
| ... the heap blocks streamed | 184.2 ms, 2,712 p, 146.4 w | 11.27 | | |
| inline, streamed (`mx-worker-3.json`) | 53.3 ms | 4.9 | 151.6 ms | 12.6 |

Streaming the members' heap blocks alone bought nothing (184 against 189 ms), as §44.4 found asking
for them; reading by place, streamed, made the toasted table's exact path as fast as the inline
table's. What the built scan does is under "Measured", below.

**Where a value's chunks lie.** A chunk holds `TOAST_MAX_CHUNK_SIZE` (1,996) bytes at 8K pages and
a page holds four, so a 1536-dimension vector (6,148 bytes) is three chunks and 160 bytes, four
tuples, which `toast_save_datum()` inserts one after another, each where the last went if it fits.
In `dbpedia_toast`, bulk loaded, every one of the 115,186 values has its four chunks on one page
of its own, at line pointers 1 to 4, and the TOAST blocks follow the heap's TIDs (correlation
0.99999), so the members' chunks come in ascending blocks. Elsewhere (a scratch cluster, 2,000 to
6,000 random rows each): 768 dimensions and `halfvec(1536)`, two chunks, all on one page; 1024
dimensions, three chunks (4,100 bytes), two values in three on one page and the third across two;
3072 dimensions, seven chunks, every value across two pages or three; 1536 dimensions from four
concurrent inserters, 70 to 74% on one page in one run of line pointers, 25 to 30% across two
pages, under 1% in three runs; and after half of 6,000 rows deleted at random and a VACUUM, the
3,000 values inserted into the holes all on one page each. So a value's place is a list of RUNS -
a block, a first line pointer, and how many chunks follow at consecutive line pointers - one in the
common case, two for a value across pages (`LionVecLocRun`, `lionvec_loc_runs()`, lion_vec_math.h,
which merges the consecutive line pointers of a block and nothing else).

#### What is stored where

- **The locator: the exact path's.** Its members come from a lion set, as heap TIDs in heap order,
  never from the index's items, so their places must be found by heap TID. One entry a row whose
  vector lies in TOAST, on pages of their own (below), read in heap order beside the sorted
  members - streamed, and only the pages whose heap blocks hold a member.
- **The REFINE item's place: the rerank's.** A row a probe reranks has had its REFINE item read
  just before, so a place there costs the rerank no read, and its TOAST page can be asked for with
  its heap page (§44.4, "Prefetch"). Every REFINE item of an index that keeps them ends with a slot
  (`LionVecRefineLoc`): the value's id and `refloc_runs` runs, `min(n, ceil(n / 4) + 1)` for a value
  of n chunks - 2 at 768, 1024 and 1536 dimensions and for `halfvec(1536)`, 3 at 3072 - of which the
  item's `nloc` (the header's former pad) are in use: 20 or 28 bytes, which leave every one of those
  widths its REFINE items a page (10, 7, 5 and 2). A centroid's item, and a row's whose vector has
  no place or whose place takes more runs than the slot holds (a 1536-dimension value across three
  pages), has `nloc` 0, and is reranked from the heap as before; every REFINE item of the index is
  then one size. Built in the same format as the locator, so that one REINDEX brings both.
- **Not in the CODE items.** Every probe reads every CODE item of a partition for a dozen fetches:
  12 to 20 bytes more an item would be 5 to 9% more CODE pages read by every scan, for a saving on
  a few rows.
- **Not the REFINE item's place in the locator, yet.** An exact path that bounded its members by
  their 8-bit codes and fetched only those that could make the top k would want each member's
  REFINE item, and the locator could carry its place (6 bytes). But a REFINE page holds five items
  and a 1% filter's members are scattered one to a page, the same count as their TOAST pages, so
  it pays only for wider vectors or with codes in the locator itself. An entry carries a flags
  byte, 0 now and checked so, so that a later format can add the place under a flag.

#### The format (format 5)

- **LOC pages** (`LIONVEC_PAGE_LOC`, 6): one item an entry (`LionVecLoc`): the heap TID; the
  number of runs (1 to the value's chunks); flags (0); the value's `va_valueid`; then the runs
  (`BlockNumber blk`, `OffsetNumber off`, `uint16 n`). 12 bytes and 8 a run: 24 with its MAXALIGN
  and 28 with its line pointer for one run, 291 a page; 36 for two runs, 226 a page. The value's
  length is not kept: an entry is made only for an uncompressed value of exactly the length the
  index's dimensions give (`8 + 4 dims` bytes for a `vector`, `8 + 2 dims` for a `halfvec`,
  `va_extsize` four less), so the chunks' number and lengths follow from `dims`, as core's checks
  have them (`lionvec_toast_extsize()`, `_nchunks()`, `_chunk_size()`). The special space's `minkey`
