  and `maxkey` are the least and greatest heap BLOCK of the page's entries, not container keys as
  on CODE pages.
- **LOCDIR pages** (`LIONVEC_PAGE_LOCDIR`, 7): one item a LOC page (`LionVecLocDir`: its block and
  the least and greatest heap block it has held an entry for), 12 bytes, 407 a page: one page for
  DBpedia, 9 for a million rows. The build's items come first, in heap order with disjoint ranges,
  filling `loc_bpages` pages from `loc_head` - consecutive blocks, which the build writes one after
  another - the STATIC LEVEL, `loc_built` items. On the same chain after them (on the static
  level's last page, and the pages after it) come the item of the LOC page the build leaves empty
  for inserts to append to (`lo` invalid and `hi` 0: no range yet), and those of the pages inserts
  add. Each LOCDIR page's special space holds the least and greatest heap block of its items'
  ranges. VACUUM narrows no range (below), so a range holds every entry the page has, and perhaps
  fewer.
- **REFINE items** end with the slot above in an index whose meta page gives `refloc_runs`, and
  their length is checked against it (`lionvec_refine_at()`: the item exactly `16 + dimsp + 4 + 8
  refloc_runs` bytes, `nloc` at most `refloc_runs`).
- **The meta page** appends, after `nregions` (format 4's last field, ending at byte 104): `loc_head`
  and `loc_dtail`, the LOCDIR chain's head and tail; `loc_tail`, the LOC page inserts append to;
  `toastrelid`, the heap's TOAST relation as the build found it; `loc_built` and `loc_bpages`, the
  static level's items and pages; `loc_root`, a level over the static one, `InvalidBlockNumber` and
  not read (below); `refloc_runs`, 0 when the REFINE items have no slot. `pd_lower` is 136. A flag,
  `LIONVEC_META_LOCATOR` (2), says the index keeps a locator, and `lionvec_check_meta()` holds the
  fields to it: all of the blocks valid with it, none without.

**A second level.** This version reads the LOCDIR whole on every exact-path query: one page for
DBpedia, 9 for a million rows (72 KB), 85 for ten million - and for a billion rows of 1536
dimensions in TOAST, 3.44 million LOC pages (27 GB) under 8,450 LOCDIR pages, 66 MB read for a
query whose members' entries lie on a few hundred LOC pages. Past some tens of millions of rows a
query should read only the LOCDIR pages whose ranges hold its members' blocks, and the static level
is laid out so that a later version can, with no change of format: its items are in heap order
with disjoint ranges, on `loc_bpages` consecutive blocks from `loc_head`, each page's special space
holding its items' least and greatest heap block, and `loc_built` says where it ends. So a later
version may

- search it: a binary search of the static level's pages by their special spaces, about
  `log2(loc_bpages)` reads (13 at a billion rows) for the first member's block, then onward through
  the members' sorted blocks, the pages they need and those a search passes; or
- write a level over it at build time: an item a static page (its block and its range), 21 pages
  of 407 for a billion rows' 8,450, named by `loc_root`.

Either reads, of the static level, only the pages whose ranges hold a member's block, and then the
items after `loc_built` - the tail's and the inserts' - whole, as this version does (they are
bounded by the inserts since the build, and by the append area's re-sort if it is built, below).
Neither changes a byte this version writes or a rule by which it reads: an index this version
built is searched as it is, `loc_root` left invalid; one a later version built with a root this
version reads whole, as it reads its own, since it never reads `loc_root` (nor checks it), the
root's pages lie on no chain it walks (scans and VACUUM walk the LOCDIR chain from `loc_head`, and
the LOC pages its items name), and inserts append past the static level, which neither a root nor
a search ever has to follow. The static level stays right as long as the index does: inserts never
touch its items, and VACUUM empties its pages' entries but narrows no range.

**Which rows have an entry**: those whose stored vector is on disk in TOAST
(`VARATT_IS_EXTERNAL_ONDISK`), uncompressed (`VARATT_EXTERNAL_IS_COMPRESSED` false, so `EXTENDED`
storage's pglz or lz4 values have none), of exactly the dimensions' length, in the heap's own TOAST
relation (`va_toastrelid`), and whose chunks the TOAST index finds as `heap_fetch_toast_slice()`
would - `chunk_seq` 0 to n - 1 once each, each `TOAST_MAX_CHUNK_SIZE` but the last - in at most n
runs (`lionvec_toast_value()`, `_ptr_ok()`, `_locate()`, lion_vec_loc.c). A NULL, a vector inline,
compressed, or anything else has no entry, and is read as it always was.

**Which indexes keep a locator** (`lionvec_build_locator_plan()`): an index of a plain column (not an
expression, whose values the build computes and no TOAST relation holds) of a heap-AM table that has
a TOAST relation, whose vectors may lie there - its storage `EXTERNAL` or `EXTENDED`, and its
vector past the larger of `TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD` and the table's `toast_tuple_target`
(`lionvec_vector_inline()`, §44.4's rule, moved to lion_vec.c to share) - or whose build met a row
whose vector did all the same (its REFINE items then without a slot). Of those, the REFINE items
carry their rows' places when the dimensions are known before the build's second pass and an item
with its slot fits a page. An index built over no rows (an empty table's, and `ambuildempty()`, an
unlogged table's init fork) decides by the plan alone, `dims` 0 taken to be past any threshold, and
writes an empty LOC page and LOCDIR page; its REFINE items have no slot, the dimensions being
unknown. Decided by the build, recorded in the meta page's flag, and kept until REINDEX. **An index
whose vectors lie inline - the DBpedia benchmark's own table, any table under `toast_tuple_target =
8160`, any column `PLAIN` or `MAIN`, any `vector` of 506 dimensions or fewer - keeps none: no page,
no work at insert, build or VACUUM, and the scan tests one flag.** A table that later toasts some of
its vectors (other wide columns can push even a short vector out) reads those rows as before.

#### The exact path (`lv_exact()`, `lv_exact_places()`)

When the scan starts (`lv_start_toast()`) it reads by place if the index keeps a locator,
`pg_lion.vector_toast_direct` is on (§44.8; off reads every row as before, which the tests compare
against), the heap is heap-AM and its TOAST relation the meta page's `toastrelid`, the dimensions
are known, and the snapshot is an MVCC one (on 16 under `old_snapshot_threshold` no scan gets
this far, below). It opens the TOAST relation once, with `AccessShareLock` as a detoast takes it -
held to the end of the transaction, which keeps the relation from being rewritten (`VACUUM FULL`)
or truncated under the scan - and counts its blocks then: a place at or past that count is never
read. Then:

1. The members, from the lion set, in TID order, as before.
2. The LOCDIR chain, whole (`lionvec_locdir_read()`), and of its items those whose range holds a
   member's heap block (`lionvec_loc_select()`: each item's range against the members' sorted,
   distinct blocks by a binary search); those LOC pages, in block order, through a list stream over
   the index (§44.4, "Read streams"; asked of the kernel or read plainly under `fadvise` and `off`,
   and on 16). A page of the static level only, its entries in TID order, is searched: each member
   between its first entry's TID and its last's found by a binary search of its entries
   (`lv_exact_page_sorted()`), about 9 of 291 read; a page an insert's item names, its entries in
   the order they came, is read whole, each entry looked up among the members by TID. An entry
   read is checked as every item is (`lionvec_loc_at()`: its length against its runs, its runs
   against the value's chunks and a page's line pointers, its TID and value id valid, its flags 0;
   `ERRCODE_INDEX_CORRUPTED` if not). A member met by two entries that differ takes neither. An
   entry out of order on a static page, which only damage leaves, can hide a member's from the
   search; that member is read from the heap. At 1% of DBpedia the 1,204 members' entries lie on
   all 394 LOC pages, 3 or so a page: reading each of the 115,186 entries and looking it up among
   the members cost a warm query 4 ms more than the search, 11.4 against 7.2 in one session.
3. The injection point `lionvec-exact-located`, where the isolation spec parks a scan.
4. The members with an entry, by their first chunk's place: one list stream over the TOAST
   relation (as far ahead as its tablespace's `effective_io_concurrency`, to 64) naming each run's
   block in turn (a block repeated in a row once), each member's chunks read from their pages under
   a share lock and checked (`lionvec_place_run()`, below), the vector assembled in one buffer, its
   header checked (`lv_value_ok()`: `lionvec_datum_dim()` the index's dimensions, its unused field
   zero), and its distance computed with the operator's function on that datum - the same bytes
   the heap fetch would have handed it. A member whose chunks fail any check joins the rest; a
   cosine zero vector, its distance NaN, is left to the zero walk, as the heap path leaves it.
5. The rest - no entry, a place past the end, or a failed check - as before: the heap fetch, its
   visibility, the detoast, their heap blocks streamed.
6. Every distance sorted as before (NaN last, then TID), and returned in order. A member read by
   place has had no heap fetch, so before it is returned the scan fetches its heap tuple under the
   scan's snapshot (the RETURN-TIME CHECK, `lv_check_placed()`): not visible, it is passed over, as
   the heap fetch passes it over; visible, its vector's TOAST pointer must name the value read
   (`va_valueid`, `va_toastrelid`; `lv_check_pointer()`), and if it does not the index has named
   another value for a live row, which no history below allows: `ERRCODE_INDEX_CORRUPTED`, never a
   wrong answer. The executor's own fetch of the row is then a buffer hit; the rows of a LIMIT 10
   cost ten heap reads, which the executor would make anyway.

The streams end before `lv_exact()` returns, so no TOAST or LOC page is pinned between
`amgettuple()` calls. Once more than half of a scan's reads by place have failed, after 64 of them
(a TOAST relation rewritten on its own, below), the scan reads by place no more (`lv_place_ok()`):
such a scan pays for 64 reads at most. The DEBUG1 line adds `N read by place (L locator pages, F
not), C checked`. Memory: an entry a member, the LOCDIR's items (12 bytes a LOC page), one vector.

**The checks of a chunk** (`lionvec_place_run()`) are `heap_fetch_toast_slice()`'s, each a fallback
where core raises an error, and those a place read directly needs besides: the page a heap page
(initialized, no special space); the line pointer within it and `LP_NORMAL`; its tuple visible to
the TOAST snapshot (`HeapTupleSatisfiesVisibility()` under `get_toast_snapshot()` from 18,
`init_toast_snapshot()` on 16 and 17, through lion_compat.h's `lion_toast_snapshot()`), as the TOAST
index's own fetch of it would require - a TOAST tuple is never updated, so the tuple at the line
pointer is the chunk, with no HOT chain to follow; a TOAST tuple's three columns, within the
tuple's own bytes; its `chunk_id` the entry's value id; its `chunk_seq` the one the run's place in
the entry says; `chunk_data` not NULL, not compressed or external (a plain or short varlena); and
its length `TOAST_MAX_CHUNK_SIZE`, or the remainder for the last. `HeapTupleSatisfiesVisibility()`
is heapam's, as core's own TOAST fetch is; master's move of index fetches into the table AM leaves
it.

#### The probing path's rerank (`lv_rerank_placed()`)

`lv_refine()` reads a row's REFINE item for its 8-bit codes; in an index whose items have a slot, a
row whose slot is in use is marked (`tp`) with the first block of its place (in the item's union
with plane 1's `<x, mean>`, which is done with by then). When the row comes near the top of the row
queue for its exact distance, `lv_prefetch_queue()` asks for its heap block, as before, and for that
TOAST block, both of the kernel (`PrefetchBuffer()`), under every `vector_prefetch` but `off`, as
many ahead as the larger of the two relations' tablespaces' `effective_io_concurrency`: a stream's
pins between `amgettuple()` calls are unwelcome, as for the heap pages (§44.4). The DEBUG1 line
adds `N TOAST pages prefetched (M not in shared buffers)`. Then, at the rerank: the REFINE item
read again for its slot (its page read a moment before; `lionvec_refine_at()` checks the TID, so an
item VACUUM removed and an insert reused gives none); the heap tuple fetched under the snapshot -
not visible, the row is done, and costs no TOAST read; visible, `lv_check_pointer()` holds its value
to the slot's, `ERRCODE_INDEX_CORRUPTED` otherwise; then the value read by its runs a block at a
time (`lionvec_place_read()`, every block within the count), its chunks checked as above and its
header by `lv_value_ok()`, and its distance computed. A read that fails detoasts the fetched row's
vector, as the heap path does, and counts toward `lv_place_ok()`. The heap fetch comes first, unlike
the exact path's, because every row the rerank reads needs its heap tuple anyway - its exact
distance decides whether it is returned, and most of a probe's dozen are - so the check costs
nothing more there, and what reading by place saves is the TOAST index's descent, a random read
that no ask could start before the heap page was in.

#### Why a place that checks is the right chunk

Two facts of core's, and one of the index's:

- **A visible row's value is present, where it was put.** A row's chunks are deleted only by the
  transaction that deletes the row or changes its vector, and removed only once that transaction is
  older than every snapshot's xmin; a scan that sees the row holds an xmin before it. A standby
  replays the removal only after cancelling, or waiting out, every query whose snapshot could see
  the row (`ResolveRecoveryConflictWithSnapshot()`), as it does for any heap tuple. A chunk tuple is
  never updated, and while it is there nothing moves it from its line pointer or gives the line
  pointer to another: pruning and defragmenting keep line pointers, and VACUUM frees one only once
  its tuple is gone. Only a rewrite of the TOAST relation on its own moves chunks (below), which the
  scan's lock holds off while it runs. So for a row the scan sees, the places its entry was made
  with hold its value's chunks, which pass every check.
- **A value id names one value among the chunks that can pass.** `toast_save_datum()` takes a new
  value's id from `GetNewOidWithIndex()`, which refuses an OID for which the TOAST index finds any
  tuple under `SnapshotAny` - dead, uncommitted or aborted alike ("SnapshotToast considers dead rows
  as active indefinitely", as catalog.c says) - and a value's chunks are in the TOAST index from
  their inserts until VACUUM has removed them, so no two values whose inserters committed or are
  running share an id. Core's own detoast depends on this, taking every tuple the index finds for
  the id under `SnapshotToast`, which passes every tuple whose inserter is not known to have
  aborted (`HeapTupleSatisfiesToast()`). So after a rewrite, which copies only those values'
  chunks, a chunk that checks is the one core's detoast of that value would return, wherever it now
  lies. A chunk an aborted inserter left behind passes `SnapshotToast` until its abort is hinted,
  and its id can be given out again after the OIDs wrap; but its row is not visible to any
  snapshot, which the return-time check finds, and no entry made later can take a present value's
  id.
- **An entry names its row's value.** It is written from the row's own stored datum - the build's
  from the tuple it scans, an insert's from the tuple the heap stored at its TID (below) - and that
  value is never changed in place: TOAST values are immutable; a HOT update cannot touch an indexed
  column and carries the same pointer (`toast_tuple_init()` keeps an unchanged external value's
  reference, and `heap_attr_equals()` compares the raw datums, so a HOT update's vector is the same
  pointer, `SET embedding = embedding` included); a non-HOT update makes a new TID with an entry of
  its own. The entry leaves with its TID: VACUUM removes it in the same `ambulkdelete()` as the
  row's CODE items, before the heap marks the TID unused, so a TID reused for another row never
  finds the old row's entry (a crash part-way leaves the TID LP_DEAD until a VACUUM completes, as
  for every index).

So a row the scan sees, read by place, has exactly the distance its heap fetch would give it, or
falls back. A row it does not see may read another value's bytes at a place that checks - its
value removed and its id given to a new one, which then happens to lie there - and is passed over
by the return-time check before it is returned; its distance only placed it in the sort. The
checks of the vector's header keep such bytes from reaching the operator's function as a vector of
other dimensions, which pgvector's functions would refuse with an error; they raise none for two
vectors of the same dimensions, whatever their floats. Through each history (each tested where
named, in `vector_toast.sql` unless said):

- **An UPDATE of another column**, HOT (the root TID keeps its entry, and every version the same
  pointer) or not (a new TID, a new entry, the same value); **`SET embedding = embedding`**, the
  same pointer, HOT; **an UPDATE that changes the vector**, a new value at a new TID, the old one's
  chunks deleted by it; **a DELETE and the rows inserted again**; **an INSERT ... SELECT** from the
  table itself, which the heap stores anew under new value ids. Each followed by the exact path and
  the probing path, direct reads on and off, the same rows, order and distances, no error.
- **An insert rolled back**: its rows are in the index and the locator and their chunks in TOAST,
  passing `SnapshotToast` until their inserter's abort is hinted; read by place, each is passed
  over by the return-time check, and once hinted, each read fails and falls back to a heap row
  that is not there (both in `vector_toast.sql`).
- **Pruning and defragmenting a TOAST page** (`heap_page_prune_opt()`, `PageRepairFragmentation()`)
  move tuples' bytes within the page and keep their line pointers; the place still names the
  tuple. A pruned chunk is LP_DEAD and fails the check. Both need a cleanup lock, which the
  reader's pin and share lock hold off while it copies a chunk.
- **VACUUM of the TOAST relation reusing line pointers** (`VACUUM (PROCESS_MAIN false)`, and
  autovacuum, which processes a TOAST table on its own: the common way an entry goes stale): a
  value whose row is dead is removed, its line pointers made unused and given to the next chunks
  inserted on that page, while the heap row and its index entries stay. The new tuple's `chunk_id`
  differs - or, its id given out again since, is that value's, whose row is not the scan's - and the
  row is dead either way. Tested with rows inserted into the space after, and in the isolation spec
  with a scan parked between its entries and its chunks.
- **VACUUM FULL or CLUSTER of the table**, and every ALTER TABLE that rewrites it (a column's type,
  `SET ACCESS METHOD`, `SET LOGGED`/`UNLOGGED`, a volatile default) write a new heap and TOAST
  relation and rebuild every index (`reindex_relation()`), the locator with it. `ALTER TABLE ...
  SET TABLESPACE` copies both block for block, every place kept (not tested). `SET STORAGE`, `SET
  COMPRESSION` and `SET (toast_tuple_target)` move no stored value; the rows they store otherwise
  later go as before (`SET STORAGE PLAIN` is tested).
- **VACUUM FULL of the TOAST relation alone** (`VACUUM FULL pg_toast.pg_toast_N`, which a superuser
  may run) rewrites its chunks to new places and keeps their value ids and the heap: every place
  may be stale, and each read by place either checks - the same value's chunk, by the second fact -
  or falls back. The scan stops trying after its first 64 (above); a REINDEX makes the locator
  whole. The meta page's `toastrelid` does not see it (the relation keeps its OID), nor would its
  relfilenode, which `SET TABLESPACE` changes too, with every place kept. Tested, and on a standby
  (test/recovery, phase 5).
- **REINDEX** builds the locator anew; `REINDEX` of the TOAST index moves no chunk.
- **pg_upgrade** keeps relfilenodes (15 on), TOAST relations' OIDs, the value ids in the pointers,
  and every TID, and refuses a cluster of another `TOAST_MAX_CHUNK_SIZE` (pg_control): the
  locator stays right, as the index's other pages do.
- **Standbys** replay the locator's generic WAL to the same pages, and the conflict rule above
  keeps a query from seeing a removal its snapshot could see; a stale place on a standby is stale as
  on the primary (test/recovery, phase 5).
- **OID wraparound of value ids**: the second fact; an id repeats only for a value no longer
  present, or for an aborted inserter's chunk whose row no snapshot sees.
- **A speculative insertion** that lost (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`) leaves an index entry, a
  locator entry among them, and chunks whose xmin is made invalid, which `SnapshotToast` refuses:
  the read falls back, and the heap fetch finds the row dead.
- **CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY**: the build as below, and `validate_index()`'s inserts, whose TID is
  a HOT chain's root that a later version may follow with another value: such a row has no entry
  (`lionvec_stored_pointer()` takes only a tuple that ends its chain, as an insert's does).
- **`old_snapshot_threshold`** (16 only; 17 removed it): a TOAST value a snapshot older than the
  threshold sees may be removed, and core's fetch then fails with "snapshot too old" on the TOAST
  index's pages, which a read by place does not read. With it set no lionvec index is read at all
  (§9, "old_snapshot_threshold"; §44.5): the scan refuses before it starts, so there is nothing to
  read by place and no case of its own here. (Until 2026-10-18 the scan ran and only read every
  vector through the table instead - which the threshold made no more right, VACUUM's early
  horizon removing the CODE items of rows such a snapshot sees.)
- **Serializable transactions**: a member read by place and not returned has no heap fetch, and so
  no SIREAD lock on its tuple, where the heap fetch takes one. lionvec takes a predicate lock on the
  whole index (`ampredlocks = false`, §44.5), which every insert into it checks, and a change of a
  member's vector is a non-HOT update and so an insert into the index; a delete of a member not
  returned does not change what the query returned. A row returned is fetched, and locked, by the
  return-time check, and a row the rerank reads by place is fetched before it is read. No isolation
  spec shows it (an open question below).

#### Build (and parallel build)

The build's callback has the row's stored datum (`FormIndexDatum()` over the tuple the scan read),
a TOAST pointer for a toasted vector. For a row that qualifies, `lionvec_toast_locate()` scans the
TOAST index for its value id as `heap_fetch_toast_slice()` does (`toast_open_indexes()`, the valid
index, `systable_beginscan_ordered()` under the TOAST snapshot), takes each chunk tuple's `t_self`
with its checks, and makes the runs; the entry goes into the build's sort as one more group, after
the NULL chain's (`LIONVEC_SORT_LOC_GROUP`, nparts + 2), keyed by its TID, and its place into the
row's REFINE item's slot when it fits. The rows' vectors are detoasted as before (one more descent
of the TOAST index a row, its pages just read). After the CODE chains the build writes the group's
entries to LOC pages in heap order, one run of blocks, each page's range in its special space
(`lionvec_loc_writer_*()`); then the empty LOC page inserts append to; then the LOCDIR, an item a
page, the static level first; the meta page records them, `loc_built`, `loc_bpages`, `toastrelid`,
`refloc_runs` and the flag. `log_newpage_range()` covers them with the rest. A parallel build's
workers do the same into the shared sort (each opening the TOAST relation and its indexes with
`AccessShareLock`, as a detoast does), and the leader's merge writes them in heap order: the
locator comes out of a parallel build as out of a serial one, page for page (tested). Rows the
build passes over as dead have no entry; RECENTLY_DEAD and in-progress ones do, their values being
present. DEBUG1 says `a locator of N rows in TOAST, its refine items with their places` (or
`without places`).

#### Inserts

An executor's insert hands `aminsert()` the vector before TOAST took it (`heap_insert()` toasts a
copy, and the slot keeps the original), and an `INSERT ... SELECT` of another row's vector hands it
that row's pointer while the heap detoasts it and stores it anew under another id. So an index that
keeps a locator reads the row's tuple at `ht_ctid` - just written by this transaction, its page in
shared buffers, under a share lock - for the pointer the heap stored (`lionvec_stored_pointer()`;
the tuple must be `LP_NORMAL` and the end of its chain), finds its chunks through the TOAST index
as the build does, and compares their bytes with the value it was handed, detoasted: the same, or
no entry (`lionvec_insert_locate()`). All of that before the meta page is locked. Under the meta
page's lock, the REFINE item (with the place in its slot), the CODE item and its copy go in as
before, then the injection point `lionvec-insert-unlocated`, then the entry
(`lionvec_loc_append()`): on the tail LOC page, the tail's LOCDIR item - the last of the chain -
widened to its heap block, one generic WAL record of the two pages; when the tail is full, a new LOC
page with the entry, its LOCDIR item on the chain's last page, and the meta page naming it the tail,
in one record; and when that LOCDIR page is full too, a new one after it, in the same record: four
pages at most, which a generic WAL record takes. A crash before the entry's record leaves a row
without an entry, which reads as before; the entry is the last thing written, so it never names a
row whose items are not in (test/recovery, phase 5, crashes an insert parked there).

**The append area.** Inserts append in arrival order, not heap order, so a page they fill covers
the heap blocks they landed in: a narrow range for a table that grows at its end, a wide one under
updates that move rows (a non-HOT update is an insert at a new TID, its vector the same value) or
inserts into space VACUUM freed. A query reads every LOC page whose range holds a member's block,
so a wide range is read by most queries. The cost is bounded by the inserts since the build: an
update of 10% of DBpedia's rows would be 40 LOC pages more a query, a millisecond or two from the
disk. A re-sort by VACUUM - the pages inserts added, but the tail, gathered once they are more than
a few and their ranges overlap, sorted by TID and written back over the same pages in order, their
LOCDIR items narrowed - is not built (an open question below).

#### VACUUM

`lionvecbulkdelete()` walks the LOC pages after the CODE chains (`lionvec_vacuum_locs()`: the LOCDIR
items sorted by block, each LOC page under an exclusive lock), removing the entries of dead TIDs
(`PageIndexMultiDelete()`, a generic WAL record a page that loses any), the bulk-delete callback
asked once a row more. It narrows no range: a reader passing a page over by a range that is too
wide loses nothing, but one too narrow would miss entries an insert adds while it runs, and nothing
gains by the work. Pages are never recycled (§44.5): a page emptied stays in the LOCDIR, and an
insert reuses no free space but the tail's, as CODE and REFINE pages do until REINDEX (§44.11,
"REFINE space"). A crash part-way leaves entries of TIDs still LP_DEAD, which the next VACUUM
removes. A REFINE item, and its slot, goes when the CODE items that point at it do, as before, so a
crash part-way can leave a REFINE item no CODE item points at; nothing reads it (§44.5).

#### WAL

Generic WAL, as every write of lionvec's, in both of lion's modes: lionvec writes no record of the
custom resource manager's, which `installcheck-rmgr` runs it under all the same. The recovery
harness's phase 5 (test/recovery/README.md) builds a table of 768-dimension vectors in TOAST,
runs a write load of inserts, updates HOT and not, of the vector and of other columns, deletes,
rollbacks and `INSERT ... SELECT`, beside VACUUMs of the table and of its TOAST relation alone,
under `wal_consistency_checking = 'generic'`; kills the server three times in the middle of it, the
last with a VACUUM in flight, and once with an insert parked at `lionvec-insert-unlocated`; and
after each recovery, and on a hot standby under the same load and after a `VACUUM FULL` of the
TOAST relation alone, reads the locator off the pages with `pageinspect` and checks it against the
heap and the TOAST relation (no entry names a value other than its TID's tuple stores; every row
the snapshot sees whose vector is in TOAST has an entry of its value, where its chunks are; a REFINE
item's place is its row's entry's), and the exact and probing paths' rows, order and distances with
direct reads on and off and a sort's.

#### Format 5

The meta page's fields are appended, every earlier one at its offset, the page types are new, and
the REFINE item's slot is past its codes, its `nloc` in the former pad. A format-4 index is refused
with the REINDEX hint, as format 3 is: there is no release to migrate from
(`vector_toast_corrupt.sql` makes a meta page format 4's, and a REINDEX brings it back).

#### Measured

`bench/results/2026-10-17-lionvec-toast-direct/`: `knn_readahead.py` on `dbpedia_toast` (above;
the heap 7.6 MB, its TOAST 900 MB), its index REINDEXed by this version - format 5, a locator and
REFINE places - under `pg_lion.vector_toast_direct` off and on, on the prototype's cluster and
settings (§44.9; `io_method = worker`, 3 workers); the 10 queries of each kind from the disk (the
server restarted and the page cache dropped before each query) and warm (every relation in shared
buffers, 5 runs a query). The median ms, `off / on`, and in brackets the median of each query's on
over its off:

| Query | Disk | Warm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| unfiltered, margin 3 | 30.5 / 27.2 (0.94) | 2.6 / 2.6 (0.96) |
| unfiltered, margin 8 | 53.7 / 44.8 (0.93) | 6.2 / 6.3 (0.99) |
| 3%, probed | 70.8 / 63.9 (0.93) | 10.2 / 10.0 (0.99) |
| 1%, exact | 179.7 / 68.3 (0.38) | 14.1 / 7.9 (0.55) |
| 3%, exact | 457.2 / 158.6 (0.34) | 31.8 / 16.4 (0.52) |

The exact path at 1% read 1,631 pages where it had read 2,717 - the LOCDIR page, 394 LOC pages (the
members' entries lie on all but two of the 396), the 1,204 vectors' pages, the 10 rows' heap pages
and 22 of the TOAST index's (below) - and waited 12.7 ms on them, not 152.7; at 3% 3,915 pages, not
5,620, and 12.2 ms of waiting, not 395.9: within 12 ms of the inline table's exact path at 1% (56.2
ms the same morning, its rows' heap pages streamed) and level with it at 3% (158.3), and within 13
and 17 ms of the prototype's (55.2 and 141.5, a 400-page stand-in for the locator, no entry
checked). Warm, the exact path took a little over half its time (7.9 ms against 14.1, and 16.4
against 31.8; inline 4.3 and 11.5, the prototype 4.0 and 11.6, its members given it): the TOAST
index's descents saved, a page a vector, every chunk still checked.

The probing kinds read each row they rerank by its REFINE item's place - 10 a query, none failing,
the return-time check finding each row's value its own - asking the kernel for the chunks' page
beside the row's heap page where they ask for the heap's (1 and 16 asks at margins 3 and 8): 6 to 7%
faster from the disk, query by query, but no fewer pages read (429 against 430 at a margin of 3).
The query's own projection detoasts each row returned, through the TOAST index, after the scan,
whichever way the scan read it: the plan's index scan computes `embedding <=> q` for the `ORDER
BY`'s column, which no index scan can hand it (below, "Open questions"). That costs the exact path
too: the 10 rows' TOAST index descents, 22 of its 1,631 pages. Warm, the probing kinds took the same
time (0.96 to 0.99). Every query returned the same rows in the same order under both settings, with
the recall the inline table's.

On the inline table (`dbpedia`, whose index keeps no locator, read by this version and by main at
1be037c) the queries took main's time: from the disk each query's over main's 0.90 to 1.07 by
kind (the medians; `inline-worker-3.json`), and warm, in eight sessions taking turns between the
two libraries, 0.97 to 1.00 (quartiles 0.95 to 1.06; `inline-warm-alternating.json`). Runs of one
session a library had made it look 0.79 to 1.59, by which library ran first.

#### Costs

- **Size**: an entry of 28 bytes a row with its vector in TOAST (36 across two pages), about 0.45%
  of a 1536-dimension vector's 6.2 KB of TOAST; the LOCDIR 0.25% of that; the REFINE slot no page
  at the widths above. On DBpedia, REINDEXed: 396 LOC pages of entries, the inserts' empty tail
  and one LOCDIR page, 3,260,416 bytes - 1.26% of the 258,949,120 the index took as format 4 -
  and the REFINE pages the same 23,581, five items a page with their 20-byte slots as without.
- **Build**: a TOAST index lookup a row, its pages just read by the detoast; the sort holds a
  tuple more a row, of 20 to 30 bytes, beside its CODE item's 224 at 1536 dimensions. DBpedia's
  serial REINDEX took 131.0 s, main's 137.1 (one run each): the lookups are lost in the build.
- **Insert**: a heap page, a TOAST index descent and the chunks' pages, all in shared buffers, the
  value compared, and one generic WAL record of the LOC tail's and the LOCDIR page's changes.
  Measured (`knn_toast_insert.py`: 5,000 rows of DBpedia's by `INSERT ... SELECT` into 20,000
  under a fresh index, its vectors in TOAST): 121 bytes more WAL a row, the REFINE slot's 20 among
  them (50.79 MB against main's 50.19, +1.2%), and 2,275 ms against 2,211 (medians of 8, taking
  turns; each pair's ratio 0.83 to 1.13, their median 1.00), the spread of the runs wider than the
  difference. `pg_lion.vector_toast_direct` does not change what an insert does: an index keeps
  its locator up whatever the setting.
- **VACUUM**: the LOC pages walked and the callback asked once a row more.
- **The exact path**: the LOCDIR, the LOC pages with members, and a TOAST page a vector, streamed,
  and a heap page a row returned; memory as above.
- **The rerank**: the REFINE item read again (a buffer hit), and the TOAST index descent saved.
- **Inline tables: nothing** - no locator, and one flag tested by the scan; measured, main's time
  (above).

The cost model (§44.7) prices the exact path at a random page a member, which a vector read by
place is; it priced the toasted table's two to three pages a member as one before. Nothing in it
changes, and `pg_lion.vector_exact_rows` - set where the exact path and probing cost the same
cold, on the inline table - may be worth raising for toasted tables. **2026-10-18**: read by place,
a member now costs no page but its share of the LOC pages, the sort it competes with paying for
the same TOAST pages nothing either (§44.7, "Exact path pricing").

#### Tests

- Regression, `vector_toast.sql`: a table of 1536-dimension vectors in TOAST, some NULL - the
  build's locator checked entry by entry against the heap and the TOAST relation (`tt_check()`,
  reading LOC and REFINE pages with `pageinspect`), what the scans read with every page in shared
  buffers (the DEBUG1 counts), and every `vector_prefetch` the same rows; then each of the
  histories above, each followed by the exact path and the probing path with direct reads on and
  off, compared row for row, order and distance (`tt_cmp()`), none raising an error; the TOAST
  relation vacuumed alone and rewritten alone, the fallbacks counted; VACUUM, and REINDEX making
  every place right again. Then 768, 1024 and 3072 dimensions and a `halfvec(1536)`, values in one
  run, across two pages and across three, a REFINE slot of three runs; rows of every kind under
  cosine (NULLs, zero vectors, compressed, inline, in TOAST) and an expression index (no locator);
  a parallel build's locator the same as a serial one's, page for page; indexes that keep none (short
  vectors, `toast_tuple_target`), and an unlogged table's init fork. Then (2026-10-18) 3,000 rows
  with a kilobyte of text each under a 1% filter: LionOrdered's exact path, reading by place, the
  plan in TOAST (§44.7, "Exact path pricing"), and priced within a tenth of 1 / 1.2 of the sort (the lean of 2026-10-19)
  reading from the heap (`pg_lion.vector_toast_direct` off) and inline, where it is the plan too.
- Regression, `vector_toast_corrupt.sql` (17 on, `pg_buffercache_evict()`): pages damaged on disk -
  a LOC entry's run past the TOAST relation's end, on another value's page, at a line pointer the
  page lacks, naming a value no row stores: each falls back; a LOC entry naming another row's value
  and place: the return-time check's `ERRCODE_INDEX_CORRUPTED`; an entry that is not one (flags,
  runs miscounted): `ERRCODE_INDEX_CORRUPTED`; a REFINE item's place wrong: the rerank falls back;
  naming another value: the error; and a format-4 index, refused until a REINDEX.
- Isolation, `lionvec_toast_scan.spec`: an exact-path scan parked at `lionvec-exact-located` while
  rows are deleted, the TOAST relation vacuumed alone and new rows take the freed places, its rows
  compared with a sort under the same snapshot and its lock on the TOAST relation shown held to its
  transaction's end; and a probing cursor parked with places queued while the table is vacuumed
  and its REFINE items, heap TIDs and TOAST space are taken again.
- Recovery: phase 5, above.
- Unit (`test/unit/vec_test.c`): the chunks a vector takes at each width and their sizes, the runs a
  REFINE slot holds, runs made from chunk places against a model, a run list's checks, and the LOC
  pages chosen for a scan's members against a brute-force model.

#### Open questions

- The append area's re-sort (above): now, or once an update-heavy measurement asks for it?
- The second level (above): a binary search of the static level or a level over it, and from how
  many rows - neither needs a format change.
- Serializable: a member read by place and not returned takes no tuple SIREAD lock; the index-wide
  predicate lock covers a change of its vector (an insert into the index), and a delete changes
  nothing the query returned. Argued, not shown: a spec of a serializable pair would show the
  read-write conflict still found.
- An option not to keep a locator (a reloption read by the build), for a table whose vectors lie in
  TOAST but whose queries never take the exact path - the locator then costs its pages and inserts
  their entries for nothing but the rerank.
- The rows returned are detoasted once more by the query's projection: the index scan's target list
  computes `embedding <=> q` for the `ORDER BY`, which the executor never takes from
  `xs_orderbyvals` (only a recheck reads them). Ten rows a query, a TOAST index descent each and its
  chunk page, after the scan - 22 of the exact path's 1,631 pages from the disk, whose chunk pages
  it has just read. The scan has every one of the values in hand; handing them to the projection
  would need the planner's help (a target list naming the scan's distance), not the index's.

### 44.14 Progressive refinement from planes 2 to 8 (evaluated 2026-10-26; not done)

The idea: keep a row's 8-bit codes (§44.3) as seven more bit-planes, planes 2 to 8 of each code,
most significant first - plane 1 being the code's top bit, the sign - so that a refine reads plane
2, bounds the row by the codes' top two bits, and stops as soon as that bound puts the row past
the k-th; else reads plane 3; and so on, plane 8 being the codes as a refine reads them today
(§44.4), 1,536 bytes at 1536 dimensions. It was evaluated before the format was touched, with a
frontend prototype on lionvec's own encoder (`test/unit/vecplanes_eval.c`, `make vecplanes-eval`;
not in `make unit`), on DBpedia's rows and on vec_test's kinds of data, and with the scan's refines
timed on a server. **The format is not changed**: on DBpedia a refine does stop early, but the
8-bit sums are a tenth of a warm query, the larger part of a refine is reading its REFINE item,
which planes do not shorten, and a kernel over today's bytes takes about as much off as the
planes would, with no new format. That kernel is built (2026-10-27, `lionvec_dot8()`; §44.3,
"Kernels"), and the sums it replaced are kept as the unit test's reference, nothing else.

**The estimator.** The top m bits of a code c leave 2^(8-m) steps; their middle is

    r_m(c) = -4 + (c_m + 2^(7-m)) / 32 = (-4 + 2^(2-m)) + sum over p <= m of 2^(3-p) b_p(c)

c_m the code with its 8 - m low bits cleared and b_p its plane-p bit, so that r_8 is
`lionvec_recon8[]` and r_1 is 2 sign(c), and r_m is linear in the planes: for any v,

    <r_m, v> = (-4 + 2^(2-m)) sum(v) + sum over p <= m of 2^(3-p) S_p(v)

S_p(v) the sum of v over the dimensions plane p has set - one more S_p a plane. The estimate is
§44.3's with r_m for the code's vector, `|x| <r_m, qc> / (|r_m| alpha_m)` with
`alpha_m = <r_m / |r_m|, x / |x|>`, and its error, by the same argument (the part of x / |x| that
r_m misses, sqrt(1 - alpha_m^2) long, points nowhere in particular after the rotation), a Gaussian
of standard deviation

    |x| / alpha_m * sqrt(|qc|^2 (1 - alpha_m^2) / (dimsp - 1) + varq)

varq the query's own rounding a dimension, `e^2 / dimsp`, as plane 1's (§44.3), when the S_p come
from a quantized query, and 0 when they come from its floats; a bound of epsilon of those either
side holds with the Gaussian's probability, whatever the data. Each prefix needs its own alpha_m
and |r_m| a row, both computed by the build from x: six pairs more than the REFINE item holds
(alpha8 and |r| are m = 8's), 48 bytes. For a standard Gaussian coordinate (numerical
integration) alpha_m is 0.7979, 0.8681, 0.9607, 0.9897, 0.9974, 0.99935, 0.99983, 0.99996 for
m = 1 .. 8, the relative error `sqrt(1 - alpha_m^2) / alpha_m` 0.756, 0.572, 0.289, 0.144, 0.072,
0.036, 0.018, 0.0094: near plane 1's at two planes, a fifth of it at four, an eightieth at eight,
halving a plane from three on. The rows' own, measured on 2,000 clustered rows of 1536
dimensions, are those to the third digit (0.79763, 0.86831, ..., 0.99996). Over every pair of
those rows and 12 queries the bound was outside 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations for 0.295 - 0.308,
0.037 - 0.045 and 0.0016 - 0.0028 of them at every m from 2 to 8, floats or quantized, against
the Gaussian's 0.317, 0.046 and 0.0027 (the same at 384 dimensions); eight planes' estimate from
the S_p was `lionvec_estimate8()`'s to the bit, and the codes' top bit was the sign bit in all
3,072,000 dimensions. (A zero coordinate, or a negative one that rounds into code 128, would
differ; a format would make the encoder give the top bit the sign's.)

**Its sums: popcounts, not masked floats.** S_p from the floats is a masked sum of dimsp floats a
plane, in double in 16 lanes as `lionvec_sum8()`'s; the prototype's portable, AVX2 (a mask, compare
and AND) and AVX-512VL (a masked add, 256 bits) versions agree to the bit, and a plane takes 245 ns
with AVX-512, 432 with AVX2 and 1,820 portably at 1536 dimensions warm, against the whole 8-bit
sum's 326, 406 and 890: a plane costs most of what all eight do, and the planes cost more than the
bytes they save. From the query quantized to 8 bits a dimension over its own range, as 8 interleaved
planes (plane 1's quantization, four bits wider), S_p is `qlo popcount(P_p) + qdelta
lion_planes_dot_interleaved(P_p, Q, dimsp / 64, 8)`: integer counts in every implementation, and the
rest a few operations in double, as deterministic as `lionvec_estimate1()` under
`-ffp-contract=off`. 32 ns a plane with AVX-512, 56 with AVX2. Its rounding adds about three
quarters of the codes' own variance at plane 8, a sixth at plane 7 and next to nothing below, and
the bound, which counts it, stays as calibrated (the ranges above are the quantized sums' as well as
the floats'). No new kernel: the weighted sum of k = 8 interleaved planes is lion_planes.c's general
pass.

**The planes a refine needs.** A best-first scan refines a row, or a centroid less the margin,
whenever its lower bound lies below the key the scan stops at, about the k-th row's; so a
progressive refine reads planes 2 to m until the prefix's lower bound passes that key, or all
seven, and a row whose plane-1 lower bound passes it is never refined. The prototype keys every
row against the query exactly, takes the tenth least key as the stopping key, and for each row and
centroid that plane 1 leaves below it records the first plane whose bound passes it: the bound
`LIONVEC_EPS8(eps)` wide at every plane, as the codes' is ("2 eps"), or eps wide at planes 2 to 7,
as plane 1's ("eps"), eps the default 4; the S_p quantized. Partitions are k-means' (three
iterations over a strided sample of at most 32,768 rows, exact distances, spherical for cosine) at
the default `8 sqrt(n)`, no spill, and the centroids' bound comes off the margin of 3 as the scan's
does (`lv_part_key()`). DBpedia is §44.9's text-embedding-3-large set, its 115,186 rows and 200
held-out queries as `knn_dbpedia.py` holds them out, cosine; vec_test's kinds are 20,000 rows and
40 queries of 1536 dimensions, cosine: "clusters" `make_clusters()`'s 12 centres, "random"
isotropic Gaussian rows (random unit vectors), "tight" 200 centres with each row 0.4 of a
centre's length from its own. "Refined" is the mean a query, "past today" the share the 8-bit
codes put past the stopping key, then the share past by planes 2 - 3, 2 - 4, 2 - 5 and 2 - 6, and
the planes and bytes a refine reads on average, at 2 eps and at eps:

| data | refined | past today | by 3 / 4 / 5 / 6 (2 eps) | planes, bytes (2 eps) | planes, bytes (eps) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DBpedia, every row | 87.9 | 88.0% | 48.9 / 76.3 / 83.8 / 86.4% | 3.17, 609 | 2.32, 446 |
| DBpedia, rows of the 27.1 partitions probed | 63.1 | 86.2% | 45.1 / 73.5 / 81.4 / 84.3% | 3.30, 634 | 2.47, 474 |
| DBpedia, centroids (2,715) | 98.9 | 72.6% | 31.3 / 56.7 / 65.9 / 69.8% | 4.05, 777 | 3.34, 641 |
| clusters, rows | 1,667 | 99.0% | 0.1 / 26.4 / 81.6 / 95.5% | 3.98, 765 | 2.97, 570 |
| clusters, centroids (1,131) | 94.0 | 0.2% | 0 / 0 / 0 / 0% | 7.00, 1,344 | 7.00, 1,343 |
| random, rows | 8,687 | 99.9% | 62.4 / 96.0 / 99.2 / 99.7% | 2.43, 466 | 1.50, 288 |
| random, centroids | 1,128 | 33.9% | 0.4 / 6.7 / 17.8 / 26.1% | 6.18, 1,187 | 5.83, 1,119 |
| tight, rows | 101 | 80.0% | 0 / 0 / 2.0 / 33.4% | 6.00, 1,152 | 5.17, 992 |
| tight, centroids | 5.8 | 0% | 0 / 0 / 0 / 0% | 7.00, 1,344 | 7.00, 1,344 |

So on DBpedia a refine does stop early: half the rows at plane 3, three quarters by plane 4, a
centroid at four planes on average, 40 to 51% of the codes' bytes (the 12% of rows that are fetched,
and the 27% of centroids probed, read all seven). The model is near what the scan does: on the
server below it refined 85 rows and 119 centroids a query and probed 35 partitions, so that 70% of
the centroids it refined were passed by (§44.9's 2026-10-15 count: 88 rows, 123 centroids, 36
partitions); the model refines 88 rows - 63 in the 27 partitions a margin alone probes, with no
spill - and 99 centroids, 73% passed by. The floats' S_p give the same shares to a tenth of a point.
Synthetic data brackets it: random vectors, whose distances plane 1 hardly tells apart, stop at
plane 3; tight clusters, whose refined rows are the cluster's own and nearly as near as the tenth,
at 6; and where the margin is wide against the centroids' spread (clusters, tight) a refined
centroid is a probed one and reads everything. At 384 dimensions the shares are within two points of
these; L2 on the clusters, 3.98 planes, the same.

**What a refine's sums cost**, ns at 1536 dimensions, warm (one row again and again), from a pool
of 16,384 rows (24 MB of each layout: past a core's 2 MB of L2, within the L3) one at a time in a
random order, and with the lines it reads flushed first (`clflush`), the median of 9 rounds, on
the Emerald Rapids of §50 pinned to a core; "bytes, 16-bit query" is the comparison below:

| | AVX-512 | AVX2 | POPCNT | portable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `lionvec_sum8()` | 326 / 682 / 1,399 | 406 / 767 / 1,535 | 888 / 1,312 / 1,867 | 890 / 1,142 / 1,803 |
| planes 2 - 3, quantized | 58 / 230 / 609 | 109 / 332 / 652 | 184 / 349 / 675 | 552 / 757 / 955 |
| planes 2 - 4 | 86 / 328 / 698 | 161 / 441 / 774 | 276 / 477 / 1,102 | 828 / 1,078 / 1,317 |
| planes 2 - 8 | 227 / 572 / 1,028 | 386 / 729 / 1,420 | 657 / 921 / 1,506 | 1,965 / 2,216 / 2,554 |
| bytes, 16-bit query | 60 / 373 / 747 | 60 / 323 / 912 | 442 / 673 / 1,561 | 509 / 718 / 1,691 |

Weighted by DBpedia's planes, a row's sums would take 95 / 313 / 737 ns with AVX-512 where they
take 326 / 682 / 1,399, a centroid's 124 / 370 / 819; with AVX2 172 / 439 / 842 and
220 / 510 / 983 against 406 / 767 / 1,535.

**How much of a scan that is.** Timed inside the scan (a build of this tree with `clock_gettime()`
around `lv_refine()`, `lv_refine_part()` and their parts, not kept), PostgreSQL 16, 2 GB of shared
buffers, every relation prewarmed, AVX-512, LIMIT 10 at the defaults (margin 3, patience 30, spill),
two or three rounds after a warming one. DBpedia's 115,186 rows, 2,715 partitions: a query took 1.44
ms at the median and refined 85.2 rows and 118.5 centroids (35.1 partitions probed, 10.8 rows
fetched). The rows' refines were 15.8% of its time and their sums 5.0%; the centroids' 11.9% and
6.1%. A row's refine took 3,125 ns: 108 looking into the queue for what to read ahead, **1,810
reading its REFINE item** (the read, the lock, the page's and the item's checks), 988 the sum and 66
after; a centroid's 1,697, its sum 866. On 100,000 random unit vectors of 1536 dimensions (50
queries) a query took 57 to 67 ms, refined 14,082 rows and 2,413 centroids, and the rows' refines
were 63 to 65% of it, their sums 22 to 25%: 2,982 ns a refine, of which 1,474 reading the item and
1,039 the sum.

So progressive planes would take 5 to 5.5% off a warm DBpedia query (about half of the sums'
11.1%, at the pool's ratios or the flushed ones) and 13 to 16% off the random vectors' - before
anything a real scan would add: the scan does not know the stopping key until it stops, so a
refine must stop against what it knows (the next key in its queues, or the tier's k-th least
upper bound, §44.4), and a row put back with planes unread costs another 1.5 to 1.8 us reading its
item if it comes back, which the model does not charge; nor its partial sum and planes read,
which a queue item, held to 48 bytes, has no room for. Cold,
nothing: a REFINE page is read whole whatever part of an item a refine looks at.

**Why not.**

- A kernel over the codes as they are takes nearly as much. Against the query rounded to 16-bit
  integers, `sum c_i w_i` is exact in integers in every implementation - the same to the bit by
  construction, as plane 1's counts are - and <r_8, q> an affine function of it, `sum(c_i)` and
  `sum(w_i)`; the rounding, a 65,534th of the query's range, adds a hundred-thousandth of the
  codes' own variance. With AVX2's `VPMADDWD` (the prototype's) it takes 60 / 373 / 747 ns
  against the planes' 95 - 124 / 313 - 370 / 737 - 819 on DBpedia with AVX-512: better warm, as
  good from the pool and flushed; and with AVX2 60 / 323 / 912 against 172 - 220 / 439 - 510 /
  842 - 983. That is 5% off a DBpedia query (the sums at 0.53 - 0.55 of their time from the pool
  or flushed) and 11 to 13% off the random vectors', leaving the planes at most half a point
  beyond it on DBpedia and two or three on random vectors - for a new format. **2026-10-27**:
  that kernel is `lionvec_dot8()` (§44.3, "Kernels"), VPMADDWD under AVX2 as the prototype's,
  the AVX-512 set running it too, and the portable one in sixteen 32-bit lanes; measured in a
  scan there.
- What a refine costs most is not its sum. Reading the REFINE item is 1.8 us of a row's 3.1;
  fewer bytes of the item leave it as it is.
- The format would cost: 48 bytes a row of alpha_m and |r_m|; a second quantization of the query
  (8 planes, 1.5 KB at 1536 dimensions); plane 1 against that query as well - the CODE item's
  plane 1 is gone by the time a row is refined, so either a pass over it at every probe for the
  rows a probe keeps, or plane 1 again in the REFINE item, which takes the most dimensions from
  8128 to 8064; a row's planes read and partial sum in its queue item and its progress entry; a
  refine stopping against a key it does not know (above); and the build, inserts (SOAR's decoded
  centroids, §44.3), VACUUM's checks, `lion_index_verify()` and the SQL diagnostics reading planes
  where they read bytes - for a few percent, and for data like DBpedia's.

**When to look again**: if reading a REFINE item became cheap enough that the sums were most of a
refine (refines batched by page, say, or the codes nearer the queue), the bytes a refine reads
would be what it waits on, and planes stop at 40 to 51% of them on DBpedia; or for vectors
whose distances plane 1 tells apart as badly as random ones', where rows' refines are two thirds
of a query and planes stop at 30% of the bytes. The 16-bit integer kernel for `lionvec_sum8()`
was the change worth making now: made on 2026-10-27, as `lionvec_dot8()`, and measured in a scan
(§44.3, "Kernels").

**The prototype** (`test/unit/vecplanes_eval.c`): part 1 the prefixes' alphas and the bounds'
calibration on clustered rows, part 2 the planes needed on vec_test's three kinds at 384 and 1536
dimensions (and L2 at 1536), part 3 the costs (`--costs` alone); `--file ROWS QUERIES DIMS` runs
part 2 on raw float4 vectors, cosine - DBpedia's here, written from the shards as
`knn_dbpedia.py` reads them, the 200 queries of `np.random.default_rng(0).choice(115386, 200,
replace=False)` apart. It checks that eight planes are the floats' estimate (`lionvec_sum8()`'s, to 1e-6 of its error; 2026-10-27: and `lionvec_estimate8()`'s but for its query's rounding, within that rounding's reach, 5e-3 of the error at most), that its masked
sums and integer dot agree with their portable forms to the bit, and that the bounds are
calibrated (at most 0.40 outside 1 standard deviation and 0.006 outside 3), and exits 1 if not;
it runs in a few minutes, DBpedia's file in five (its k-means most of it). Its kernels are the
evaluation's own, not lionvec's; the flushed column needs the x86-64 build (`clflush`).

## 45. Partial indexes in the count pushdown (2026-10-19)

Every lookup the count planner made skipped partial lion indexes: `lion_find_roaring_index()` and
`lion_match_index()` took the first valid, NON-PARTIAL index on a column. A workload whose queries
all carry the same few dense filters - three boolean or low-cardinality columns that keep most of
the table, beside the filters and the GROUP BY that change from query to query - gained nothing
from a partial index on those filters, `CREATE INDEX ... USING lion (g, c1, c2) WHERE f1 AND f2 =
'a' AND f3 = 'n'`, whose sets hold only the rows the defaults keep: the count read the whole index
and intersected the defaults' sets, each nearly the table, into every count. Now a count whose
restrictions imply a partial lion index's predicate may read that index and leave out the
restrictions the predicate implies, as core leaves them out of a partial index scan's
`indrestrictinfo` - wherever every row the count can reach is one the predicate holds for.
lion_plan_partial.c holds the rule; the planner's lookups, the cost and EXPLAIN take the index as
they take any.

### 45.1 Held to the predicate's rows

Let Ω be the rows a partial index P holds: the table's rows its predicate is TRUE for. A set read
from P for a clause c holds the rows of Ω that c selects - it agrees with c inside Ω and is empty
outside it - and a restriction left out because the predicate implies it is TRUE inside Ω. Inside
Ω the count therefore computes the query exactly. It goes wrong only by counting a row OUTSIDE Ω,
where nothing it read from P says anything, and that happens wherever the rows a count adds up do
not come from one of P's sets:

- the restrictions are left out and the rest is read from a whole index: `WHERE f1 AND f2 = 'a'
  AND f3 = 'n' AND y = 2`, P on the three without `y`: `y = 2` from the whole index counts every
  row with y = 2;
- a set of P's is subtracted, not intersected: `a = 1 AND x <> 3` with P `WHERE x IS NOT NULL`
  reading `x`. `<>` is the rows of the other sources less `x = 3` and less the NULL entry (§35);
  P has no NULL entry, so the rows with a = 1 and x NULL - for which `x <> 3` is NULL - are
  counted;
- the count of every row (§14, §35) or a complement (§35, "Complements in an OR") taken from a
  whole index;
- a multi-key query known only at run time (§17), or a literal one with a prefix too common to
  expand, which may turn out to narrow nothing, and a count with nothing that narrows is the heap
  scan of `lion_count_scan_filtered()`: every row.

So the rule, checked per relation counted - the table, or each leaf partition with its own
partial index - and per RUN of the count (the WHERE's, run 0, and each filtered count's, §10
"Filtered counts"): a run that reads P, or any run at all when restrictions were left out, must be
HELD to Ω by one of

- **P's entries driving it**: a driving column read from P - a GROUP BY column's walk (§10, §20),
  the decoded walk's columns (§34: a row outside Ω has no value in P's column and is in no
  combination), the column a `count(DISTINCT)` walks (§26), the column a sum over every row walks
  (§14, §35), the FK-side join's fact group (§27). Every count of the run is ANDed with one of P's
  entries, which hold Ω's rows only;
- **a positive clause of the run read from P**, outside any OR: an equality (the FK-side join's
  lookup of a key among them, §27), an IN list, `IS NULL`
  (P's NULL entry holds Ω's NULL rows), a range taken as a source (§32) - each a set ANDed into
  every count of the run;
- **an OR** with no complement leaf, each of whose arms the partition keeps has such a leaf.

Never a multi-key clause (above), a negated one - `<>`, `IS NOT NULL`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, a
`NOT` of a multi-key query - which subtracts, or an OR with a complement arm, which counts rows
outside a set. A clause the partition's bounds leave out (§16) reads no index there and holds
nothing. And a sum over every row drives a filtered count's run only when the run has no source
of its own: one that has (an equality, a list, `IS NULL`, an OR of no range and no complement
arm) is counted as an intersection, not by the walk (`lion_count_runs()`,
`lion_run_has_plain_source()`), and needs a hold of its own.

`lion_partial_anchored()` checks it once the targets are collected (`lion_count_path_targets()`,
`lion_fkjoin_setup()`); false declines the attempt, and the plan made with whole indexes stands.
So does a relation counted that the scope holds no index for, when restrictions were left out:
they are left out only where every relation of the scope has one, and that relation's rows outside
the predicates would be counted.
An attempt that reads no partial index and leaves nothing out is declined too: it is that plan
again. The rule is a planning rule only: the executor counts what the plan names, as it always
did.

### 45.2 Planning: one attempt per candidate

- **Candidates** (`lion_partial_find()`): for each relation counted, its valid partial lion
  indexes (not hypothetical: they have no entries) whose predicate its restrictions imply -
  `predicate_implied_by(indpred, baserestrictinfo, false)`, core's own proof
  (`check_index_predicates()`), with, for a leaf partition, its partition constraint, which every
  row of it satisfies. Join clauses prove nothing about the rows a count reads. The smallest first,
  by the index's rows.
- **The attempts** (`lion_try_count_path()`): the count path is planned with whole indexes, as
  before, and then once for each rank up to `LION_PARTIAL_TRIES` (3): each relation reads its
  rank'th candidate, or whole indexes alone where it has none at that rank. `add_path()` keeps the
  cheapest; on an exact tie the whole-index plan, made first, stays.
- **The scope** (`lion_partial_enter()`, `lion_partial_leave()`, left in a `PG_FINALLY` as the
  expression columns' scope is, §41): `lion_find_roaring_index()` and `lion_match_index()` try the
  relation's scope index first and then whole indexes; no other partial index is read.
  `lion_vcol_collect()` takes the scope index's expressions too, so a partial expression index
  answers its expression (`exprindex.sql`).
- **Leaving restrictions out** (`lion_partial_drops()`, in `lion_count_path_where()` before a
  clause is numbered, so nothing downstream sees it): a restriction is left out when every relation
  counted has a scope index whose predicate implies it (mapped onto each partition's columns), it
  holds no mutable function and no subquery (core keeps those in `indrestrictinfo` too), and it
  names no column the query prints outside its aggregates - the target list and HAVING - other
  than a GROUP BY column: a column a restriction pins is printed from the key the index stored
  (§10), which needs the restriction. A restriction left out is not a source, is not priced, and
  EXPLAIN lists it. Only the WHERE's restrictions: a `FILTER` condition is never left out.
- **count(col)** (`lion_count_path_pred_nonnull()`): a column the predicate proves non-NULL
  (`col IS NOT NULL` implied) counts every row, as a NOT NULL column does (§10): the query implies
  the predicate, so every row the count reaches has the column.
- **The sum over every row** (§14, §35): `lion_count_all_driver()` prefers a column of the scope
  index, so that the walk holds the count; among those, as before, the fewest entries.

### 45.3 What the change leaves as it was (the audit)

- **Every "every row"**: the count of every row and the sum over all of a column's entries (§14,
  §35) hold the count only when P drives them; the NULL entry and `IS NULL` read from P hold it
  (Ω's NULL rows); negated sources and complements (§35), `<>` among them, never hold it, whatever
  index they read; a `count(DISTINCT)`'s existence tests (§26) are driven by its column's entries,
  and held when that column is P's; residual clauses (§10) are tested on the heap rows the other
  sources select, which are Ω's once the run is held. Each case is in `countpartial.sql`.
- **Uniqueness proofs** stay non-partial: `count(DISTINCT pk)` as `count(*)` (§26) and the FK-side
  join's dimension key (§27) still need a whole unique btree index.
- **The visibility interlock** (§9): a partial lion index's entries are written and removed by the
  same paths as a whole one's, and a TID from it is judged visible the same way. A HOT update
  cannot move a row into or out of Ω behind the index's back: lion is not a summarizing access
  method, so the columns of its predicate block HOT (`RelationGetIndexAttrBitmap()`), and a
  visible version reached through a P's TID satisfies the predicate.
- **Top k** (§36): an entry's TID count still bounds its group's count: the rows counted are in
  the entry.
- **reltuples** (§18): the one fix. ambuild reported the postings it wrote - one a key column, one
  an element - as `index_tuples`, so a partial index's `reltuples`, which the planner sizes it by
  (`estimate_rel_size()`), was a multiple of its rows until the first VACUUM or ANALYZE. The build
  now reports the rows it added (`lion_spool_nrows()`), serial and parallel, as VACUUM does.
- **Estimates**: n_distinct from the directory (§33), the selectivity hooks and the facet counts
  (§7) still read whole indexes only: a partial index's keys are not the column's.
- **EXECUTE** (§10, "Privileges"): `lion_replaced_functions()` walks every restriction, left out or
  not, so a function the query calls is still checked.
- **Generic plans**: a Param proves no predicate that needs a constant, so a generic plan of `st =
  $1` reads the whole index; a strict clause on a Param does prove `col IS NOT NULL`, for every
  value of the Param, and `x > $1` may read a partial index `WHERE x IS NOT NULL`.

### 45.4 Cost

The model prices a partial index by its own sizes (lion_plan_cost.c):

- `lion_index_rows()`: the rows the index holds - the table's for a whole index; for a partial one
  `idx->tuples` (its `reltuples`, rows since 45.3), or the table's rows times the predicate's
  selectivity where it has none yet, as core prices a partial index scan;
- a clause's set (`lion_cost_set_clause()`): its members are the index's rows times the clause's
  share of them, `sel(pred AND clause) / sel(pred)` (`lion_index_clause_share()`), and its
  containers and pages follow from those;
- a group's rows in the walk, the pairs of two GROUP BY columns and the decoded walk's columns:
  the index's rows over the column's entries.

What the model gains is the work the plan no longer does: the restrictions left out are not
sources, and the sets left are smaller. There is no bias toward the partial index beyond that.

### 45.5 The plan and EXPLAIN

custom_private member 22, `LION_PRIV_PARTIAL` (shape 27): NIL, or a list of two - the OIDs of the
partial indexes the count reads, and the restrictions left out, deparsed, as String nodes. TLKINDS
moves to 23, the members are 24, the magic is 0x5242491b; the codec checks the list's shape and
its OIDs. Only EXPLAIN reads it: the targets name their indexes, partial or not, as before.

EXPLAIN names a partial index among the `Lion Indexes` as it names any (`pc_p1.a (a = 3)`), prints
the restrictions left out under `Implied by Index Predicate`, and for a partitioned table, whose
`Lion Indexes` line names no index, the leaves' partial indexes under `Partial Indexes`:

```
 Custom Scan (LionCount)
   Lion Indexes: pc_p1.g (g), pc_p1.b (b = 3)
   Implied by Index Predicate: act, (st = 'on'::text), (kind = 'k0'::text)
   Group Key: g
```

`pg_lion.enable_count_partial` (on) turns the attempts off: the count reads whole indexes only.

### 45.6 Measured

4,000,000 rows of a synthetic table (`f1` boolean, true in 93% of rows; `f2`, `'a'` in 90%; `f3`,
`'n'` in 92%; together 77%), `g` of 50 values, `c1` of 10, `c2` of 1,000, `c3` of 5; a whole index
`(f1, f2, f3, g, c1, c2, c3)` and a partial one `(g, c1, c2, c3) WHERE f1 AND f2 = 'a' AND f3 = 'n'`
(51 and 36 MB), `VACUUM (FREEZE, ANALYZE)`, no parallel workers, the release build, warm cache;
the best of seven `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs, every query with the three defaults in its WHERE:

| query (beside the defaults)                     | whole index: containers, ms | partial index: containers, ms | chosen  |
|-------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------|-------------------------------|---------|
| `count(*) ... AND c1 = 3`                       | 1,840, 0.47                 | 460, 0.20                     | partial |
| `count(*) ... AND c1 = 3 AND c3 = 2`            | 2,300, 0.57                 | 920, 0.49                     | partial |
| `count(*) ... AND c2 IN (5, 50, 500)`           | 2,760, 0.48                 | 1,380, 0.07                   | partial |
| `count(*) ... AND c2 < 100`                     | 183,922, 27.9               | 45,935, 2.4                   | partial |
| `g, count(*) ... GROUP BY g`                    | 25,300, 5.8                 | 23,000, 3.0                   | partial |
| `g, count(*) ... AND c1 = 3 GROUP BY g`         | 25,760, 7.0                 | 24,380, 5.7                   | partial |
| `c1, c3, count(*) ... GROUP BY c1, c3`          | 8,740, 28.9                 | 6,900, 22.3                   | partial |
| `count(DISTINCT c2) ... AND c1 = 3`             | 9,272, 3.0                  | 4,732, 1.7                    | partial |
| three counts, two `FILTER`s                     | 5,060, 1.3                  | 3,220, 0.85                   | partial |
| `count(*)` (the defaults alone)                 | 1,380, 0.33                 | 2,300, 0.54                   | partial |
| `count(*) ... AND c1 <> 3`                      | 1,840, 0.44                 | 4,600, 2.4                    | partial |

With a third of the heap's pages not all-visible (10,000 rows updated), where both plans recheck
the same rows in the heap: `c1 = 3` 7.4 against 7.1 ms, the `IN` list 1.7 against 1.5, `GROUP BY
g` 110 against 89, the range 79 against 43.

The last two rows were the model's, not the index's: the count of every row of P is a sum over the
fewest-entry column's entries (`c3`'s five, 2,300 containers), which the model priced at a third
of intersecting the three dense sets (1,380) though it took 1.6 times as long; and the subtraction
of a `<>` from each of those entries was not priced at all - nor over a whole index, where
`count(*) WHERE c1 <> 3` cost what `count(*)` costs (§35) - so the partial plan, which subtracts
per entry, was taken where the whole index's one merge is five times faster. Both are priced now
(§10, "Dense sources": the sum's pages by the bytes its sets take, the AND of dense sets by their
words, negated sources where the merges subtract them), and the whole index is taken for both.
Measured again on a table of the same shape (4M rows on 25,478 pages, 399 container keys; the two
indexes 42 and 35 MB), medians of nine runs, the plans chosen by the library before that change
and after it; the times are the plans' as they are now:

| query (beside the defaults)                     | whole index, ms | partial index, ms | chosen before | chosen now |
|-------------------------------------------------|-----------------|-------------------|---------------|------------|
| `count(*) ... AND c1 = 3`                       | 0.42            | 0.16              | partial       | partial    |
| `count(*) ... AND c1 = 3 AND c3 = 2`            | 0.47            | 0.33              | partial       | partial    |
| `count(*) ... AND c2 IN (5, 50, 500)`           | 0.41            | 0.06              | partial       | partial    |
| `count(*) ... AND c2 < 100`                     | 22.6            | 2.1               | partial       | partial    |
| `g, count(*) ... GROUP BY g`                    | 5.5             | 2.9               | partial       | partial    |
| `g, count(*) ... AND c1 = 3 GROUP BY g`         | 6.4             | 4.9               | partial       | partial    |
| `c1, c3, count(*) ... GROUP BY c1, c3`          | 11.1            | 15.3              | partial       | partial    |
| `count(DISTINCT c2) ... AND c1 = 3`             | 3.0             | 1.6               | partial       | partial    |
| three counts, two `FILTER`s                     | 0.96            | 0.66              | partial       | partial    |
| `count(*)` (the defaults alone)                 | 0.30            | 0.47              | partial       | whole      |
| `count(*) ... AND c1 <> 3`                      | 0.40            | 1.60              | partial       | whole      |
| `count(*) ... AND c2 <> 7 AND c1 <> 3`          | 0.49            | 1.90              | partial       | whole      |

The GROUP BY of two columns keeps the partial index, which is now the slower of the two: the whole
index's plan of it took 30.4 ms before and takes 11.1, the partial index's 24.1 and 15.3 (45.8).

With two parallel workers allowed, the whole index's GROUP BY with `c1 = 3` runs in parallel (§10,
"A GROUP BY in parallel") and the partial index's does not (45.8), and the partial plan is still
chosen: 6.0 ms against 5.1 serially on the second table, and as much with `c1 = 3 AND c3 = 2`.
`GROUP BY g` alone, whose whole-index plan went parallel and took 10.7 ms against 3.1 on the
first, stays serial over both indexes now that its serial price no longer overstates it (§10,
"Dense sources"): 5.9 ms against 3.0.

### 45.7 Tests

`test/sql/countpartial.sql` compares every query, as a multiset both ways round, with a sequential
scan with the pushdown off, on random data with deleted rows and rows moved into and out of the
predicates on pages the visibility map no longer vouches for, and prints the custom scans, the
indexes read and the restrictions left out: a predicate the restrictions match, one stronger
restrictions imply (`x > 20` under `WHERE x > 10`) and one they do not; a predicate on indexed
columns and on a column no index has; a predicate that is a `<>`, implied by an IN list; NULLs,
`<>`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, `NOT IN`, complement ORs, ORs across the partial and the whole index, a
multi-key clause; GROUP BY one, two and three columns (the decoded walk mixing the partial and
the whole index), by the predicate's own column, by a column a restriction pins (printed and
not), HAVING, the top k, `coalesce`, `SELECT DISTINCT`; filtered counts beside a sum over every
row; `count(col)` the predicate proves non-NULL; `count(DISTINCT)`; residual clauses; generic and
custom plans of prepared statements; the FK-side join, inner, outer, semi and anti, with the
partial index on the fact side and a partial lion index on the dimension; a partitioned table
with partial indexes on the parent and one on a single partition; EXPLAIN, and the setting off;
and, with the whole index dropped, the partial index's sums over every row and its subtractions
from every entry, which the model leaves to the whole index's merge where there is one (45.6).
`exprindex.sql`: a partial expression index whose predicate the query implies answers, one whose
predicate it does not imply declines.

### 45.8 Not done

- **One partial index a relation an attempt**, three attempts at most: two partial indexes are
  never read in one count (one for the GROUP BY column, another for a clause), nor a partial index
  beyond the third smallest a relation has.
- **`FILTER` conditions are never left out**, only the WHERE's restrictions.
- **The FK-side join's dimension** is an ordinary plan (§27), whose scans read a partial index as
  core plans them (`LionOrdered` over `pcd_region` in the test); the rule above applies to the fact
  side.
- **Uniqueness proofs** (45.3).
- **A GROUP BY whose WHERE is left with a single source** after the restrictions go is priced as a
  merge per group rather than one collection of the WHERE (§10, "WHERE Sets Collected"); on 30,000
  rows that prices the whole index's four-source WHERE, collected once, below the partial index's
  one set, which on four million rows it no longer does.
- **The GROUP BY of two columns** (45.6) over the partial index is priced at 1,438 units for
  15.3 ms, 94 a millisecond, and the whole index's at 3,687 for 11.1: a GROUP BY's own work is
  priced below its time (§10, "Dense sources"), the pairs' most; and `c1`'s 774 rows a container
  key lie just past the 768 above which a build writes a NARROW of three words a block rather than
  an ARRAY, so 1,700 of its 3,990 containers are ARRAYs, which the model takes for NARROWs.
- **A parallel GROUP BY** (§10) needs a WHERE that is collected - two sources or more, or a union
  - and a positive one: a partial index that leaves one source or none after the restrictions go
  is counted serially, against the whole index's parallel plan (45.6).
- **Estimates** still come from the table's statistics (45.3).

## 46. The dimension by probe (`LionProbeJoin`, lion_probejoin.c; 2026-10-23)

The shape is

    SELECT CASE WHEN d.region IN ('north', 'east') THEN 'ne'
                WHEN d.tier = 1 THEN 't1' ELSE 'other' END AS k,
           f.channel, count(*)
      FROM fact f JOIN dim d ON f.dim_id = d.id
     WHERE d.active AND d.tier < 4
       AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM blocked b WHERE b.dim_id = f.dim_id)
     GROUP BY 1, 2

- a GROUP BY over a join of a fact table to a dimension by the dimension's primary key, its keys
CASE or boolean expressions over the dimension's lion-indexed columns, perhaps beside the fact's
own columns; `count(*)`; a WHERE on the dimension its lion indexes answer; perhaps a NOT EXISTS over
a small table keyed by the dimension's key; and no lion index on the fact. Nothing of lion's so far
took it: the FK-side join (§27) reads the fact's rows from a lion index on its key; a count by
cells (§10, "Counts by cells") counts one table; the nested loop's probe (§40.10) needs a B-tree
that covers what the query reads of the dimension, and the group keys read the lion-indexed
columns themselves. Core's plan is a nested loop over the fact's rows into the dimension's primary
key - an Index Scan a fact row, the dimension row fetched from the heap for the Filter and for the
group keys' columns - and on a production dimension of 87 GB that was two million random heap
pages, 140 s cold. A hash join reads the dimension's WHERE whole, which is most of that heap.

    HashAggregate
      Group Key: CASE WHEN ((d.region = ANY ('{north,east}'::text[]))) THEN 'ne'::text WHEN ((d.tier = 1)) THEN 't1'::text ELSE 'other'::text END, f.channel
      ->  Custom Scan (LionProbeJoin) on dim d
            Probe Index: dim_pkey
            Probe Cond: (d.id = f.dim_id)
            Lion Cond: (d.active AND (d.tier < 4))
            Lion Indexes: dim_active, dim_region_tier
            Cell Predicates: (d.region = ANY ('{north,east}'::text[])), (d.tier = 1)
            Cell Indexes: dim_region_tier
            Anti Join Cond: (b.dim_id = f.dim_id)
            ->  Seq Scan on fact f
            ->  Seq Scan on blocked b

`LionProbeJoin` takes the join and the group keys' predicates; core's Agg does the rest. For each
fact row, read from core's own path of the fact, it looks the key up in the dimension's primary
key, tests the TID found against lion sets of the dimension built once before the first row - the
WHERE's, and the LABELS that give each column the predicates read its outcome - asks the visibility
map, and emits the fact's columns and each predicate's truth. The heap is read for a page the map
does not call all-visible, and for every row found when the WHERE's set is inexact, to recheck the
WHERE on the heap tuple (`Rows Removed by Lion Recheck`). The group keys are computed above the
node from those truths, `setrefs.c` matching each predicate inside them to the node's column for it
(`LION_TL_CELLPRED`, as §10's cells are matched).

- **What qualifies** (`lion_fkjoin_recognize_probe()`, `pj_try_shape()`). At the GROUP BY of a
  join rel (`lion_create_upper_paths()`, `UPPERREL_GROUP_AGG`, no grouping sets, no set-returning
  target): an inner join of exactly two tables, either way round, joined by exactly one clause, a
  strict equality of plain Vars whose dimension side is the one column of a unique B-tree
  (`lion_column_unique_index()`) and whose operator is an equality of that B-tree's family (the
  probe's operator is the family's member for the fact column's type); no placeholder, no
  pseudoconstant clause, no LATERAL reference. The dimension is a plain heap table, not a parent,
  not the query's result relation, with no security quals or barrier clauses and no TABLESAMPLE,
  and every one of its restriction clauses is answered by a lion access with nothing left to a
  filter (`lion_ordered_where_access()`, below), or it has none. The grouping input target - what
  the node emits - holds expressions each of the fact's columns alone or of the dimension's alone,
  none volatile, with no SubPlan and no placeholder; the dimension's are functions of predicates
