610 fetches in all and no key rejected; the join with a fact and a dimension lion clause besides,
its set the AND of both; with nothing forced core's plan for product 7 - the key table, then the
key's lion index - and the split folded for product 3. A key set of repeated keys and NULLs; two key
sets, an IN on the fact's key and an EXISTS on the dimension's, two leaves; an empty one; the whole
join without a LIMIT; a LATERAL rescan whose key set is built and handed again for each of three
rows (`Key Set Builds: 3`); a key updated and a row inserted in the transaction before the query.
Not folded: a partial lion index of the key whose predicate the query does not imply, and folded
into where it does; a key table of `bigint` keys, no key set; `pg_lion.enable_key_set_fold` off.
Section 6, the key tested on the index tuple: with no lion index of the key and the B-tree `(rank
DESC) INCLUDE (fk)`, the split under product 7's key set walks the same 18,275 entries and fetches
55, 18,043 keys rejected unfetched - the other 177 entries NULL keys, turned away uncounted - and
with nothing forced the split is the plan, for product 3 too; repeated keys and NULLs, two key sets,
a LATERAL rescan; a key updated, a row inserted and rows of the set's keys updated HOT in the
transaction; and the key a key column, `(rank DESC, fk)`.
test/isolation/keyset_index_tuple_serializable.spec: the write skew of a row whose key an update
moves into the key set, after the join turned its entry away unfetched, ends in a serialization
failure in either order of the commits. ordjoin.sql's B-tree `fact_grp_score` holds the key
(`INCLUDE (fk)`), so its key sets are tested on the index tuple too: 191 heap fetches where there
were 19,944, 2,750 where there were 82,302.

### 47.9 Measured (2026-10-23; PostgreSQL 17, the dev cluster - a VM of four cores, `shared_buffers` 2 GB; warm and cold; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF))

A 5,000,000-row fact table (554 MB; its key uniform over the dimension, every 101st NULL; `score`
uncorrelated with the heap) with a B-tree `(score DESC) INCLUDE (fk, id)` (193 MB) and lion
indexes on an eight-value int `chan` and a text array `tags`, one of four a's and one of nine b's;
a 200,000-row dimension of 576-byte payloads (120 MB, a 4.4 MB primary key) with lion indexes on a
ten-value `kind`, a hundred-value `lvl`, a bool `flag` and a five-value `region`; a 20,000-row key
table. The query is `SELECT f.id, f.score, f.amount, d.pk, d.region FROM bfact f JOIN bdim d ON
f.fk = d.pk WHERE ... ORDER BY f.score DESC LIMIT 20`, `amount` in no index, so that the fact's
walk is in heap mode; without it the walk is index-only. "Walked" is the node's `Index Entries
Walked`. Warm: every table and index in shared buffers, the median of seven runs after one. Cold:
`effective_cache_size = 400MB`, which the tables and B-trees, about 870 MB, are twice, as a
50-million-row fact table is twice the default 4 GB; the cluster restarted and the kernel's page
cache dropped before each run, the median of three. "Planned" is the plan with nothing forced, at
the default 4 GB and at 400 MB; the node's time where it was not planned is with
`pg_lion.pushdown_margin = 1000`. Core's cold time is the plan with the node off, which for the
medium pages, the key set's and the deep one is core's nested loop over lion's LionOrdered walk of
the fact and a Memoize.

| page | WHERE | walked | core's plan | warm: core | the node | planned, 4 GB | planned, 400 MB | cold: core | the node |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| dense | `f.chan = 3 AND d.region = 'north'` | 720 | nested loop, Memoize | 0.88 ms | 1.67 ms | core | node | 45.0 ms | 17.6 ms |
| dense | `f.tags @> '{a1}' AND d.region = 'north'` | 491 | nested loop | 1.03 ms | 1.82 ms | core | core | 36.1 ms | 15.8 ms |
| dense | `f.chan = 3 AND d.lvl < 50` | 248 | nested loop | 0.59 ms | 7.61 ms | core | core | 18.1 ms | 19.4 ms |
| dense, a key set | the first, `AND f.fk IN (SELECT k FROM bwatch WHERE active)` | 2,829 | nested loops | 2.42 ms | 3.43 ms | core | node | 29.1 ms | 28.6 ms |
| medium | `f.chan = 3 AND d.lvl = 3 AND d.flag` | 26,257 | nested loop | 34.0 ms | 11.6 ms | core | node | 343 ms | 195 ms |
| medium | `f.tags @> '{a1}' AND d.lvl = 3 AND d.flag` | 9,595 | nested loop | 11.6 ms | 6.9 ms | core | node | 244 ms | 159 ms |
| medium, index-only | `f.chan = 3 AND d.lvl = 3 AND d.flag` | 26,257 | nested loop | 31.7 ms | 9.0 ms | node | node | 190 ms | 39.0 ms |
| the dimension's only, index-only | `d.lvl = 3 AND d.flag` | 3,902 | nested loop, Index Only Scan | 6.9 ms | 5.1 ms | core | node | 189 ms | 27.8 ms |
| dense, OFFSET 2000 | `f.chan = 3 AND d.region = 'north'` | 81,388 | nested loop | 101 ms | 49 ms | core | node | 893 ms | 599 ms |
| sparse | `f.tags @> '{a1}' AND f.tags @> '{b2}' AND d.lvl = 3 AND d.kind = 3` | 730,643 | hash join, Sort | 67.8 ms | 173 ms | core | core | 534 ms | 1,184 ms |

Where the page is neither dense nor sparse the node runs 1.4 to 3.5 times faster than core's nested
loop, which fetches every fact row the walk meets to test the fact's filter and reads the
dimension's heap row of every key it keeps: the node fetches a member's row, and the dimension's of
a member's key, one dimension row in about a hundred descents here. The index-only walk takes the
fact's heap out (0 heap fetches, 9.0 against 11.6 ms). A deep page gains as much, 2.1 times. Where
the page is dense core reads a few hundred fact rows and about a hundred dimension rows, and the
node pays its sets: the scalar ones lazily, each built after 64 keys by §30.4's heap-order rule
(1,109 and 241 containers, about a millisecond), the multi-key fact set at once; a range on the
dimension (`lvl < 50`, fifty posting lists) is always built at once, 7 ms; a key set's table is read
whole first, a Seq Scan of 20,000 rows. Where it is sparse the walk meets 730,000 entries for twenty
rows, and core's hash join of the two sets and its sort is 2.6 times faster.

Warm, at the default 4 GB, the planner takes the node for the medium index-only page (9.5 ms, timed
again, against 31.7) and keeps core's plan elsewhere: rightly where the page is dense or sparse,
wrongly for the other medium pages, the dimension's only and the deep one. The fact set's build
(§47.3: `chan = 3`'s 3,772 now about 960) and core's Memoize (§39, "A Memoize under a LIMIT") are
corrected. Per row kept, the two prices of the fact's heap agree: the node's fetches are Mackert and
Lohman's over the walk's 625,000 members and the table's 70,900 pages, about 0.45 a fetch, and
core's Index Scan fetches all five million rows of its walk over the same pages, about 0.06 a fetch,
eight to a member. The medium scalar page: the node 1,150..818,180 for 4,129 rows before the
Memoize's scale of 0.715, its Limit 5,110; core's loop 0.9..587,688 for the same rows, its Limit
2,847, and 3,982 with the hits its 3,030 calls meet where core counted 70% of them. The node's run
under the LIMIT, 3,960, is now core's corrected 3,982; what is left is its startup, the sets'
builds, 1,150, against core's fact heap, which Mackert and Lohman price at the whole walk's share
(§47.7, "The fact heap under a LIMIT"). The multi-key page's set is built at once (2,600 of
startup); the deep page comes to 11,040 against 9,594; and the dimension's only page ties, 235.2
against 235.3, where add_path() keeps the loop's lower startup. A descent of the node's is
`btcostestimate()`'s, `(tree_height + 1) * 50` operator costs and its comparisons, 0.39; core's
probe, the same index scan under the Memoize, was priced 0.19 on its hit ratio over the whole walk.
The dense page `f.chan = 3 AND d.region = 'north'`: the node 1,280..861,590 for 123,747 rows, its
Limit 1,420, its sets' builds most of it; core's loop over a Memoize, its Limit 95.8.

Cold, the planner takes the node for every medium page, the dimension's only, the deep page, the
dense scalar page and the key set's, and each flip is right: the medium pages 1.8, 1.5 and 4.9 times
faster than the plan without the node, the dimension's only 6.8 times (27.8 against 189 ms), the
deep page 1.5 times (599 against 893 ms), the dense scalar page 2.6 times, the key set's a tie. The
deep page's competitor is core's loop over lion's LionOrdered walk, weighed with that walk's reads
(§47.3): 42,317, which its Memoize's hits under the LIMIT bring to 68,059, against the node's 52,452
before the cold reads' 0.96, 31,306 in the loop's units. Core's plan stays, rightly, for the sparse
page (534 against 1,184 ms) and the dense range (18.1 against 19.4 ms); and wrongly for the dense
multi-key page (36 against 16 ms): core's loop at 944 under the LIMIT, 1,264 with its Memoize's
hits, against the node's 3,219, most of it the multi-key set built at once, of which the cold reads
take 0.54. Not measured: other majors.

### 47.10 Alone under the LIMIT (`oj_alone()`, `oj_limit_share()`, 2026-10-24)

What the LIMIT gives the node - the share of the walk it takes (§47.3: each side's set lazy or at
once, the competitor's Memoize under the LIMIT, the cold reads over that share) and the split's
shape (§48.3) - it gives only where the node is alone under the LIMIT: where the rows the LIMIT
counts are the node's, one to one, or about.

**The rule** (`oj_alone()`, asked once for each join rel in `oj_add_paths()`, the answer in
`OjJoin.alone`). After `reduce_outer_joins()`, which makes a left join whose inner side a strict
WHERE clause reads an inner join, and a left join under `IS NULL` of its key an anti join:

- every other table of the query level is on the inner side of a left join or an anti join that
  the join rel is not inside. A left join returns each of the node's rows; an anti join drops those
  it matches, and is taken to match few, the exclusions a NOT EXISTS lists. A table joined by an
  inner, semi or full join, or by none, is not;
- the join rel is on no special join's inner side but its own key sets' semi joins
  (`oj_special_ok()`);
- every clause that reaches past the join rel (its `joininfo`) is an outer join's own ON clause
  (not `is_pushed_down`), or is evaluated within the inner side of such a left or anti join, where
  it filters only that side; a WHERE clause on an inner side's columns carries the outer join's
  relid and is neither. No equivalence class joins the join rel to another table (a class with a
  constant makes no join clause);
- the query level asks nothing more of the rows: no HAVING, no set-returning function in its
  target, which may return no row for one, and no WITH TIES.

Grouping, aggregates, DISTINCT and windows leave `root->limit_tuples` at -1, so there is no share
to take; row marks are declined (§47.1). A Sort or Incremental Sort above for the rest of the ORDER
BY is core's, priced from the node's own start-up, total and rows. The key sets are inside the
join rel (§47.6), so a table folded into one filters nothing above it. `lo_limit()`'s other
conditions (§30.4) are its hard stop's and not a price's: a LIMIT of a Param is priced at core's
guess, as core's own plans are, and the order past the node's is the sort's above.

**Not alone**, the share is 1 (`oj_limit_share()`): the sets are chosen for the whole walk (at once
where it is long, §47.4), the competitor's Memoize gets no correction for the LIMIT
(`lion_memoize_limit_extra()` adds nothing at a share of 1), the cold reads are weighed over the
whole walk, and the path's start-up is its total (`oj_add_path()`), so that core's Limit, which
takes `startup + (total - startup) * n / rows` of its input, pays all of it. The split is priced
as without a LIMIT, every arm, its start-up its total too (`os_cost()`, §48.3). Both are still
offered. At the price of the walk to its end the node is taken only where core's plans cost more:
where they sort a large join for the page, or run a subquery for each row of a large first group
of the ORDER BY. The walk then costs at most what it was priced at, wherever the page's rows are.

**Why core's estimate is no price under a LIMIT.** Core prices a join or a clause above the node by
the share of rows it expects through, `sel`, spread evenly over the rows beneath, and its Limit
takes `n / (rows * sel)` of everything below: the walk is priced at the entries it takes to meet
`n` survivors at that density. Under an ordered walk the survivors are where what the filter keeps
falls in the walk's order, and nothing in the statistics says where that is: a small table's keys
among the fact rows the walk meets last, a side table's flagged rows those of the lowest scores, a
key table of the dimension rows of one value of the split's column. Where they come late the walk
runs on, possibly to its end - every entry fetched, descended and joined above - priced at a few
hundred. The page of the tests (§47.8) is this: core takes the filters above the walk to pass some
3,000 of its rows, ten do, and the walk's two arms run to their ends for them. Core's own plans
for it are a filter first and a sort, which read what they read whatever the order; core's ordered
nested loops under a LIMIT carry the same estimate, and it is theirs.

**What is pessimistic.** A filter above that is spread over the walk as core takes it would let the
walk stop early, and the node is priced as if it would not: a selective clause on a side table's
column that is not correlated with the score is priced as the whole walk, and core's plan is taken
(the measurements below: 968 ms against 37 ms for the walk). So is an inner join that drops no row,
a foreign key's to the referenced table's key with the fact's key NOT NULL.

**What it still takes on trust.** An anti join that drops many rows is taken to drop few. And the
joins above the node are core's, priced at core's density: not alone under a clause on a LATERAL
subquery that core cannot pull up (its LIMIT 1), the split is taken at the price of its whole walk,
under core's plans, which sort the whole of the flag's first value and run the subquery for each of
its rows; the nested loop of the subquery above the split takes the LIMIT's share of its own run,
and the tests' page of that shape runs 195 ms against core's 105 to 150.

**What the key sets take back** (§47.6). A table folded into a key set is inside the node: its
rejections are the node's, an entry of the fact's walk and a hash probe each, before any descent,
and it filters nothing above. The page's small key table was kept out of §47.6 for two reasons,
both lifted:

- *its key unique only with its primary key's other columns pinned* - `ib (fk, kind)` under `kind
  = 2` - which `lion_column_is_unique()`, a unique B-tree of the key alone, does not prove:
  `oj_keyset_unique()` takes a unique B-tree whose other columns the table's own restriction
  clauses pin to a constant each, the key set holding only those rows' keys;
- *its key in the join rel's target*, which the query does not read: a LATERAL subquery on the key,
  which a strict WHERE clause made an inner join, joins the key's class above the join rel, and core
  makes every member of the class available there, the key set's among them. Where nothing outside
  the class needs the key, its type has image equality and the class's equality is the type's
  default, the node fills the column with the fact's key (§47.6).

Not lifted:

- *a key that repeats* - `kind IN (2, 3)`, which pins nothing: each fact row would have to come out
  once for each of the key's rows, a count a hash set does not hold;
- *a column of the table read*, even one its clauses pin to a constant. The node could fill a
  pinned column with its constant as it fills the key; that would fold the page's side table -
  `s.level` read and pinned to `'high'` by the WHERE clause, its key unique with its other columns
  pinned - into a key set, and make the page's own shape alone, under the key set's estimate, which
  is the one that fails there (below);
- a second join clause, a key of another type, a key in the target whose type lacks image equality,
  a set past `work_mem` (§47.7), and a join rel core never forms as the rest joined to the key set
  of the highest relid (§47.2), as GEQO, or a join order the collapse limits keep, may not.

**What a key set leaves.** Its share of the walk is still core's estimate: its keys are taken to be
`setrows / dim.tuples` of the dimension's rows, spread evenly over the walk and over the split's
arms (§47.3, §48.3 "Independence"). Where they are not - the slice holding forty of kind 2's keys,
or a key table of `flag = false` rows under a split led by `flag DESC` - the walk runs to its end
as it would under the join above, but each entry it rejects is an index entry and a hash probe,
not a fetch, a descent, a dimension heap read and a join: 2.3 seconds where the join above took 20
and core's plan, the key table first, under one (below). Bounded by the walk, not by the page.

**Measured** (2026-10-24; PostgreSQL 17, §47.9's cluster and tables, warm: every table and index in
shared buffers, the median of five runs after one; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF)). §47.9's tables
with an index on the fact's key, `bfact (fk)`, as the page's own fact has one, and three tables of
the page's shape: `bib (fk, kind, since)`, primary key `(fk, kind)`, kind 3 the keys of 12,000
`flag = false` rows, kind 1 4,000 keys spread over all; `bsig (fk, day, level)`, primary key `(fk,
day)`, `'high'` for a tenth of the keys, spread; `bsup (fk, reason)`, every 50th key. The page is
`SELECT d.pk, d.flag, d.region, f.id, f.score[, s.level] FROM bdim d JOIN bfact f ON f.fk = d.pk
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT s.* FROM bsig s WHERE s.fk = f.fk AND s.day = 3) s ON true [JOIN bib ON
bib.fk = d.pk AND bib.kind = K] LEFT JOIN bsup ON bsup.fk = d.pk AND bsup.reason = 1 WHERE bsup.fk
IS NULL [AND s.level = 'high'] ORDER BY d.flag DESC, f.score DESC, f.id LIMIT 100`, the walk
index-only. "Taken under any LIMIT" is the same build without `oj_alone()` and the two key set
rules above. Core's plan, with the node off, is the key table or the side table first, the fact by
its key and a Sort, but for the dense page's, a Sort over the hash joins of the whole fact.

| page | above the node | taken under any LIMIT | §47.10 | core's plan |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| the page | `bib` kind 3, `s.level = 'high'`, `s.level` read | split, 19,884 ms (5,019,060 walked, 4,969,363 descents) | core's, 151 ms | 149 ms |
| the side table's clause alone | `s.level = 'high'`, read | split, 37.4 ms (1,807 walked) | core's, 968 ms | 983 ms |
| the same, `s` not read | `s.level = 'high'` | split, 36.1 ms | split, key set `bsig`, 47.7 ms | 954 ms |
| the key table alone | `bib` kind 3 | split, 20,116 ms (4,952,137 descents) | split, key set `bib`, 2,344 ms (5,001,659 walked, 297,188 descents) | 767 to 867 ms |
| the page, `s` not read | `bib` kind 3, `s.level = 'high'` | split, 18,189 ms | split, key sets `bib` and `bsig`, 1,597 ms (5,019,060 walked) | 151 ms |
| dense, a key set | `bib` kind 1 | split, 78.4 ms (7,681 descents) | split, key set `bib`, 10.4 ms (165 descents) | 359 to 385 ms |
| dense | the left join and the anti join | split, 8.8 ms (170 walked) | split, 9.2 ms | 6,452 ms |

The page goes to core's plan, 130 times faster; the dense pages keep the split, 35 to 700 times
faster than core's; the dense page with the key table gains the key set, 7.5 times. The side
table's clause alone is the rule's pessimism: spread as core takes it, it costs the walk 26 times
over. Read, the side table stays a join above; not read, it is a key set (its key unique with
`day` pinned) and the split is taken, 47.7 ms. The key table alone, and the page with the side
table not read, are a key set's estimate: 8.6 and 11 times faster than the join above, about 3 and
11 times slower than core's plan. Ordered by the score alone, the page is core's either way (50 and
54 ms). Not measured: cold, other majors.

## 48. An ORDER BY led by the dimension: the join an arm at a time (LionOrderedSplit, lion_ordjoin.c, 2026-10-24)

The shape is §47's with the ORDER BY led by a column of the dimension:

    SELECT f.id, f.score, d.pk, d.flag
      FROM fact f JOIN dim d ON f.fk = d.pk
     WHERE f.grp = 2 AND f.tags @> '{a1}' AND d.lvl < 30
     ORDER BY d.flag DESC, f.score DESC NULLS LAST, f.id LIMIT 20

asks for the fact's best rows among the flagged dimension rows first, then among the rest. No B-tree
of the fact gives that order, so §47's walk is not offered (§47.1, "The order"), and core has one
plan: the hash join of the two sets' bitmap heap scans, every joined row sorted for the first
twenty: 7,525 rows here, and on §48.8's tables 625,000 fact rows read for twenty. But the leading
column has few values, and lion holds each value's rows as an entry of its directory, in the
column's order (§30.11). Among the rows of one value the ORDER BY is the fact's walk: §47's join
with the dimension narrowed to that value's rows returns them in the order wanted, and run for each
value in turn, in the ORDER BY's order, the joins' rows one after another are the query's.

    Limit
      ->  Incremental Sort
            Sort Key: d.flag DESC, f.score DESC NULLS LAST, f.id
            Presorted Key: d.flag, f.score
            ->  Custom Scan (LionOrderedSplit)
                  Split By: dim_flag (flag, backward, nulls first)
                  Arms Max: 8
                  ->  Custom Scan (LionOrderedJoin)
                        Ordered By: fact_grp_score
                        Index Cond: (f.grp = 2)
                        Lion Cond: (f.tags @> '{a1}'::text[])
                        Lion Indexes: fact_tags
                        Dimension: dim d via dim_pkey
                        Dimension Lion Cond: (d.lvl < 30)
                        Dimension Lion Indexes: dim_lvl

`LionOrderedSplit` is the join rel's CustomScan over one LionOrderedJoin, its child. It walks the
column's lion entries in the ORDER BY's direction with §30.11's walk, the NULL entry where NULLS
FIRST or LAST puts it; for each entry - an arm - it narrows the child's dimension to the entry's
rows, the entry's TIDs ANDed with the dimension's own set, and runs the child from the start of its
walk; past the arm's last row, the next entry is the next arm. The dimension's set is made once and
kept, as is the fact's; only the fact's walk restarts. Core puts the rest above it: the Limit, and
an Incremental Sort for what the ORDER BY has past the walk - here `f.id`, which `fact_grp_score`
does not hold.

### 48.1 What qualifies (`os_split_of()`)

- **The join.** Everything §47.1 asks of the join, its sides and the query - one key join to a
  unique B-tree, each side a table LionOrdered may scan, the target, no row marks - with its key
  sets (§47.6); what §47.1 declines the split declines (`FOR SHARE OF d`, a `LEFT JOIN`). Neither
  side needs a lion clause and no key set is needed: the arm's narrowed set is a set of the
  dimension's.
- **The column** (`lion_ordered_column_order()`, lion_ordered.c; `lo_column_gives()`, the rule of
  §30.11's walk of a table's own column). The ORDER BY's first sort key is of an equivalence class
  that holds a column of the dimension; the column is a plain column, not an expression of it
  (`d.kind % 2`); a key column of a lion index, ordered and scalar - not multikey - of the column's
  type, under the column's collation; its comparison its type's default B-tree comparison; and its
  pathkey in that order of the sort key's class and operator family: another family (`USING ~<~`) or
  another collation (`COLLATE "POSIX"`) is declined. A partial index qualifies only where the query
  implies its predicate. The walk gives either direction and either place for NULLs.
- **The fact's order** (`lion_ordered_orders_for()`, lion_ordered.c). The rest of the ORDER BY leads
  with the order of a B-tree of the fact, at least its first key; an Incremental Sort above sorts
  what follows. Core builds no ordered path of the fact for an order the query's does not lead with
  (`truncate_useless_pathkeys()` finds the B-tree's pathkeys useless), so the paths are built on a
  scratch copy of the fact that sees only its B-trees, with `root->query_pathkeys` and
  `root->sort_pathkeys` both the rest of the ORDER BY while `create_index_paths()` runs: it judges
  an order by the one or the other, depending on the major. An order that holds the column's own
  class (a fact column the WHERE equates with it) is passed over.
- **The arms** (`os_arms()`, §48.3). At most `pg_lion.ordered_split_max` (8; 0 offers no split)
  are expected: the column's distinct values, and its NULL entry where the walk takes it. A column
  whose distinct count is a default is declined. The cap is the planner's alone: at run time every
  entry of the column is an arm, however many.

### 48.2 Planner (`os_add_paths()`, `os_add_path()`, `os_plan_path()`)

`oj_add_paths()` asks `os_split_of()` for each join §47.2 recognizes - two tables, or two and their
key sets - before it takes the join's own orders. For each order of the fact (§48.1), each of the
fact's lion accesses and each of the dimension's, paired as §47.2 pairs them, one path is priced
(§48.3) and handed to `add_path()`; the competitor of each order (`oj_competitor()`, §47.3) is
found at the split's pathkeys before the first path is added. Where a column of the fact is in the
column's class the join's own paths are offered too, and `add_path()` keeps what it keeps.

- The path's pathkeys are the column's sort key and then the order's pathkeys, as far as they give
  the rest of the ORDER BY; its target is the join rel's; it is unparameterized and not
  parallel-safe, and `enable_indexscan = off` disables it (`lion_path_core_switches()`,
  `LION_CORE_INDEXSCAN`) as it does the join's.
- Its one child (`custom_paths`) is the arms' LionOrderedJoin, built as §47.2 builds the join's
  path (`oj_join_path()`): its pathkeys the order's alone, its rows and price an arm's - the arms'
  rows divided by their count, the first arm's start-up and the mean arm's run - and its fact's
  side weighted for its lazy set by the arms the LIMIT takes (§48.3).
- The NULL entry's place (`os_nulls()`) is where the sort key puts NULLs, or nowhere when a
  restriction clause of the dimension is strict in the column (`find_nonnullable_vars()`: `kind IS
  NOT NULL`, `kind IN (2, 7)`), which no NULL passes.

The plan (`os_plan_path()`) is a CustomScan with `scanrelid` 0 over the child, whose
`custom_scan_tlist` is the child's target list; the split's target is projected over it
(`CUSTOMPATH_SUPPORT_PROJECTION`). `custom_private` is positional behind a marker: the column as
its lion index numbers it, whether the walk is backward, the NULL entry's place
(`LION_ORDER_NULLS_*`), the cap the plan was made under, and the index.

### 48.3 Cost (`os_arms()`, `os_cost()`)

**The arms.** With `nd` the column's distinct values (`get_variable_numdistinct()`: lion's count of
the column's entries where it has one, §33, ANALYZE's otherwise), ANALYZE's MCV list and its null
fraction:

- an arm for each of `max(ceil(nd), MCVs)` values, and one for the NULL entry where the walk takes
  it and the column has NULLs;
- a most common value's arm has its frequency, `freq`. The list is sorted by the type's B-tree
  comparison under the column's collation and taken in the walk's direction; the values past it
  share what is left of the rows, `1 - nullfrac - Σ freq`, evenly, and are taken after it; the NULL
  arm has `nullfrac`, first or last. The list is used only where `statistic_proc_security_check()`
  lets the comparison run on the column's statistics, as core's estimators ask (the user may read
  the column, or the comparison is leakproof); elsewhere every value shares `1 - nullfrac` evenly,
  the split priced less well rather than refused;
- arm i's share of the rows the dimension's quals pass is `share_i = freq_i / Σ freq` over the arms
  walked.

**An arm** is priced as §47.3 prices the join (`oj_cost()`, its competitor's Memoize and the cold
reads with it), the dimension's set taken to hold `share_i` of what it holds: the members, their
heap reads and the rows out are scaled by it, and each descent's TID is tested against a set even
where the dimension has no lion access, since the narrowed set is one. Each arm's walk starts at the
start of the fact's order, and the LIMIT's share of it is the share its own rows give.

**The arms in order.** The first arm's start-up is paid once: the sets' builds, the key sets', and
the column walk's descent, two `random_page_cost` (§30.11). Each later arm restarts the fact's walk
with a descent of its B-tree, `(tree_height + 1) * 50` operator costs and a random page. Each arm
reads its entry first (`os_entry_cost()`): `LION_RANGE_UNION_ENTRY_COST`, two `cpu_operator_cost` a
TID - handed out, gathered into the arm's set - and the entry's TIDs' pages, two bytes a row, at
`seq_page_cost`; and it holds its narrowed set beside the dimension's, within `hash_mem` and past it
in the arena (§48.4, "The arm's memory"), so it pays what the two sets take past `hash_mem` together
less what the dimension's alone takes, which the set's build has paid, at `lo_spill_cost()`'s price
(§30.3, §30.4 "Spilling"). The arm's set holds `share_i` of the dimension's set's members, or
without a set of the dimension the entry's rows, `freq_i` of the table, its bytes
`lion_ordered_set_bytes()`'s (`lo_set_bytes()` over at most a container for each
`LION_BLOCKS_PER_CONTAINER` pages); the arms' sets are given back one after another, so each arm is
priced against the dimension's set alone. With `out_i` the rows of arm i, `run_i` its price past its
start-up, and `S` the first arm's start-up with the walk's descent, the price of the LIMIT's `n`
rows (`limit_tuples`, the OFFSET's with the count's) is

    C(n) = S + Σ (entry_i + restart_i + run_i)  over the arms before m
             + entry_m + restart_m + run_m * (n - Σ out_i over the arms before m) / out_m

with `m` the first arm whose rows, added to those before it, reach `n` (the first arm has no
restart).

**The shape.** Core's Limit takes `startup + (total - startup) * n / rows` of its input. The path's
start-up is `S` and the first arm's entry, its rows `R` the arms' sum, and its total
`startup + (C(n) - startup) * R / n`, at which the Limit's price is `C(n)`. Without a LIMIT, or
with one the arms are not expected to meet, the total is every arm's. Where the split is not alone
under the LIMIT (§47.10: a join or a clause above it filters) nothing is shaped: `n` is taken as no
LIMIT, the fact's set weighed by every arm, and the start-up is the total, every arm's, which
core's Limit pays whole; the child's start-up is its own total too. Both are divided by
`pg_lion.pushdown_margin`, as the join's are.

**The sides' sets** (§47.4). The fact's is weighed for its lazy set by the arms up to `m`, their
shares of its walk summed - two whole arms weigh 2. The dimension's is built at once under a split,
whatever its weight (§48.4, "Built at once"), and `oj_cost()` prices its build whole, as it does
for the join. Key sets folded into the fact's set (§47.6) are priced in it as for the join (§47.3),
once: the set is kept from arm to arm, the key sets built once; and each arm's run, not folded,
carries the pages of the fetches its key sets reject at the arm's own share (§47.3).

**Where the price and the run part:**

- *Independence.* The dimension's quals are taken to pass the same share of each value's rows -
  `share_i` of the rows they pass are arm i's - which a correlation of the quals and the column
  breaks: the LIMIT may be met in another arm than the priced one.
- *The values past the MCV list* are priced after it, evenly; the walk meets them in their place.
  ANALYZE keeps every value it samples of a column of a few values in the list, so only a value its
  sample missed, a rare one, is misplaced.
- *The shape is for core's Limit.* It is exact where the Limit is right above the split. An
  Incremental Sort between them is priced by core from the split's start-up, total and rows, and
  hands the Limit a price near `C(n)`. A plan that reads every row of the split below the Limit -
  the split as a hash join's inner side - takes a total that is the LIMIT's price stretched over `R`
  rows, not every arm's, and may be under it or over.
- *An arm that returns fewer rows than priced walks further*: an entry whose dimension rows no fact
  row of the set joins walks the whole fact, or until the fact's walk has met every member of its
  set (§30.4's early stop).
- *An entry whose rows are all dead*, or invisible to the snapshot, still has members of the
  dimension's set: its arm runs and returns nothing. Only an entry with no member is passed over.
- *A filter above the split*, a join or a clause that drops rows of the arms: §47.10 prices the
  split at every arm. A key set filters inside it, and its keys are taken to be spread over the
  arms as the dimension's quals are; a key set of one arm's rows walks the others to their ends
  (§47.10, "What a key set leaves") - folded into the fact's set (§47.6), each to the last member
  of the set, or to the switch.

### 48.4 Execution (`os_begin()`, `os_exec()`, `os_next_arm()`, `os_rescan()`; `lion_ordered_narrow_begin()`, `_add()`, `_end()`, lion_ordered.c)

- **Begin.** The `custom_private` shape is checked; the child is initialised without
  `EXEC_FLAG_BACKWARD` or `EXEC_FLAG_MARK` - the split supports neither, and core puts a Material
  above it for a scroll cursor - and must be a LionOrderedJoin, whose dimension's side, the probe,
  is what the arms narrow. The column's lion index is opened.
- **An arm** (`os_next_arm()`). The column's walk begins with the first arm
  (`lion_order_walk_begin()`: the column, no bounds, the direction, the NULL entry's place). For
  each entry: the child is rescanned first, when it has run since its last rescan or a Param of the
  split's has changed; then `lion_ordered_narrow_begin()` on the probe, `lion_ordered_narrow_add()`
  for each of the entry's TIDs, and `lion_ordered_narrow_end()`, which returns the narrowed set's
  members. An entry with none is passed over (`Entries Skipped`), the child's rescan, which reads
  nothing, not repeated for the next; otherwise the child runs, and its rows are the split's until
  it returns none. The walk has read the next entry's first TID, and holds no pin or lock while the
  arm runs (§30.11).
- **The narrowing.** `narrow_begin` gives back the last arm's narrowed set, then makes the
  dimension's set unless it has it - built at once (below) - a changed Param of its lion quals
  making it again first. The narrowed set is built from the entry's TIDs a container key at a time,
  as they come in heap order (§30.11), each key's together, and each container is ANDed
  (`lion_container_and()`) with the dimension's set's container of the key; without a set the
  container is kept whole. While an arm runs, the probe tests a descent's TID against the narrowed
  set alone, a subset of the dimension's. A container key below the one before it would be an entry
  out of heap order, which only damage makes: `ERRCODE_INDEX_CORRUPTED`.
- **The arm's memory.** The narrowed set's containers and its directory are the set's memory
  (`lo_set_push()`, `lo_set_alloc()`): charged against `hash_mem` with the dimension's set, and in
  its arena past it (§30.4, "Spilling") - neither held without bound nor a reason to decline the
  plan. It matters most without a set of the dimension, where an arm's set is its entry whole: on a
  dimension of hundreds of millions of rows, a value of a column of a few holds tens of millions of
  TIDs, tens to hundreds of MB of containers, held for as long as the arm runs. Hence the order in
  `narrow_begin`. The last arm's set is given back first (`lo_set_drop()`): its bytes in memory to
  the charge, its blocks in the arena to the arena's free lists, where the next arm's take them, and
  the spill is put back as the set's build left it, so that an arm past `hash_mem` does not send the
  next, which may fit, to the file. Then the set: its build after a changed Param lets go of all of
  the set's memory and the arena's before it starts (`lo_set_reset()`), and of the arm's set with
  it. Then the new arm's set, charged on top of the set's. The node's end lets go of what is left
  with the set. EXPLAIN ANALYZE counts the arms whose set had bytes in the arena, and the most of
  one there (§48.5); the arena's bytes the node holds are counted for that (`arenabytes`), added at
  each block `lo_set_alloc()` takes there and taken off at each it gives back, since the arena's own
  measure (`lion_arena_used()`) is the file's high-water mark, which blocks taken again from the
  free lists do not raise.
- **Built at once.** Under a split the dimension's set is built at once, whatever the weight its
  plan carries (§48.3). Each arm ANDs its entry with the set at every container key the entry has,
  which for a column of a few values is most of them, so a lazy set would evaluate nearly every key
  before the first arm's first descent; its memo would sit outside `hash_mem` while the arm runs;
  and its conversion to a built set in the middle of an arm (`lo_lazy_convert()`) would reset the
  set's memory, the arm's set with it. `oj_cost()` prices the dimension's build whole either way.
- **The fact's side** is the child's (§47.4): its rescan restarts its walk and keeps its set, which
  no Param reaches (§30.4).
- **A row.** The child's row is copied into the scan slot and the split's target projected; the
  child does not touch its slot until it is asked for its next row.
- **Correctness.** The column is scalar, not multikey: each row version is under exactly one of its
  entries (§30.11), the NULL entry holding the NULLs, so the arms divide the join's rows by the
  column's value, and each arm's rows in the fact walk's order are a run of the query's order. The
  narrowed set is a subset of the dimension's set, so an arm returns only rows the join returns,
  and every row the join returns is in the arm of its dimension row's value: the walk reads the
  index, not the statistics, so a value ANALYZE never saw is an entry in its place, and a row
  inserted earlier in the same transaction is in the index. An update of the column is not HOT and
  puts the new version's TID under the new value: the arm of the old value meets the old version's
  TID, which a snapshot that sees the new version does not see, and the arm of the new value the
  new one. A TID met under two entries is a slot reused after the walk passed it, its row invisible
  to the snapshot (§30.11).
- **Rescans** (`os_rescan()`). The column's walk ends, and begins again at the next arm. A changed
  Param is handed to the child, whose rescan at the next arm hands it to its sides (§47.4) before
  the entry is narrowed: `narrow_begin` consumes the probe's with a rescan of it, which drops the
  dimension's set when its lion quals use the Param, and makes the set for the new value, once; the
  arm's descents find no Param left to rescan for. Rescanned after the narrowing instead, the child
  would hand the Param to the probe again, and its first descent would drop the set and build it a
  second time. Each side keeps its set unless its lion quals use the Param; a key set is kept
  unless its plan does.

### 48.5 EXPLAIN (`os_explain()`)

`Split By: <index> (<column>[, backward][, nulls first|nulls last])`, the column's walk as planned,
with no NULLs placement where a clause is strict in the column, and `Arms Max: N`, the cap the plan
was made under; under ANALYZE, `Arms Run` and `Entries Skipped`, the entries with no member of the
dimension's set; and, where any arm's narrowed set had bytes in the arena (§48.4, "The arm's
memory"), `Arm Sets Spilled: <arms>, <N> kB`, those arms and the most bytes of one there - what the
dimension's set itself spilled is its own line's. The child is printed beneath it once, as a
LionOrderedJoin with its own lines (§47.5), its counters summed over the arms and its loops theirs;
its `Dimension Lion Set` is the dimension's set, not an arm's.

### 48.6 Not done

- **An ORDER BY of the column alone** (`ORDER BY d.flag DESC LIMIT 20`): an arm needs an order of
  the fact to walk, and here any would do. Core's plan stays.
- **Two columns of the dimension leading** (`ORDER BY d.flag, d.kind, f.score`): arms of the first
  column only, and the fact's order then does not lead the rest, so no split. An arm for each pair
  of entries, the two ANDed, is not built.
- **Arms at once.** The arms run one after another; none is run ahead, merged or in parallel, and
  the split is not parallel (§47.7).
- **A cap at run time.** None: a column with more entries than planned - values inserted since
  ANALYZE - runs every one.
- **A multikey column**, whose rows are under several entries: declined.
- **Arms a key set passes over**, and a switch from a slow arm to the filter first: §47.7 - the
  switch is the fetch-and-sort's where the key sets are folded into the fact's set (§47.6).

### 48.7 Tests

test/sql/ordjoin.sql, section 13, on §47.8's tables and a nullable copy of the dimension (`dimn`:
every 11th `flag`, 13th `kind` and 17th `tier` NULL, `kind` four values and `tier` three, each with
a lion index). Each query is run through the split and through core's plan with the node off and the
answers compared row by row, in order; `oj()` says `LionOrderedSplit`. `d.flag` leading, DESC and
ASC: the split with nothing forced for a page in the first arm, an OFFSET into the second (`Arms
Run: 2`), and the whole join without a LIMIT (7,525 rows); a trailing `d.lvl` sorted by the
Incremental Sort; `d.kind` leading, ten values, declined at the default cap and split at
`ordered_split_max = 10`, and `kind IN (2, 7)` passing over the two entries above 7 (`Entries
Skipped: 2`). On the copy: NULLS FIRST and LAST, DESC and ASC; a text column, `tier`; `kind IS NOT
NULL`, whose walk takes no NULL entry (`Split By: dimn_kind (kind)`); a value inserted after ANALYZE
(`kind` 9, `tier` 'zinc') and one inserted in the same transaction before the query (`kind` -1,
`tier` 'aluminium'), each returned in its place. A key set built once for two arms (`Key Set Builds:
1`); a LATERAL subquery rescanned for each outer row, the dimension's set made again for each value
once however many arms the row runs (seven rows of two arms each: `7 builds`), and one that passes
over entries between rescans (`d.kind IN (x.x, x.x + 4)`); a generic plan's Param. Arms past a 64 kB
`hash_mem`, on a dimension of 640,000 narrow rows (`dimbig`, 55 containers): without a set of the
dimension, each arm's set the entry whole (`Arm Sets Spilled: 2, 21 kB`); with `d.lvl < 4`, the set
in memory and the arm's past it (`1, 23 kB`); with `d.lvl < 5`, the set spilled too and the arms'
sets in the arena whole; and a LATERAL subquery whose set, rebuilt for each of seven outer rows,
lets go of the arms' with its own (`7 builds`, `8, 83 kB`). Declined: another operator family,
another collation, an expression of the column, `FOR SHARE OF d`, a LEFT JOIN, `ordered_split_max` 1
and 0, and `enable_ordered_join` off (core's Sort over a Hash Join). test/sql/ordjoin_alone.sql
(§47.8) tests the split alone and not alone under the LIMIT (§47.10).

### 48.8 Measured (2026-10-24; PostgreSQL 17, §47.9's cluster and tables; warm and cold; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF))

`SELECT f.id, f.score, f.amount, d.pk, d.region FROM bfact f JOIN bdim d ON f.fk = d.pk WHERE ...
ORDER BY <the column>, f.score DESC LIMIT 20` on §47.9's 5,000,000-row fact table and
200,000-row dimension. Warm: the median of seven runs after one. Cold: `effective_cache_size =
400MB`, the cluster restarted and the kernel's page cache dropped before each run, the median of
three; the reads are EXPLAIN's shared buffers read. "Planned" is the plan with nothing forced, at
the default 4 GB and at 400 MB. Core's plan, with `pg_lion.enable_ordered_join` off, is in each
case a Sort over the hash join of the two sets' bitmap heap scans. "Walked" is the child's `Index
Entries Walked`; every page below took one arm.

| page | WHERE | ORDER BY | walked | warm: core | the split | cold: core | the split | planned, 4 GB / 400 MB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| dense | `f.chan = 3 AND d.region = 'north'` | `d.flag DESC` | 1,282 | 243 ms | 3.3 ms | 1,488 ms (86,490 reads) | 23.9 ms (532) | split / split |
| dense | the same | `d.flag` | 1,770 | 243 ms | 3.1 ms | 1,350 ms | 30.6 ms | split / split |
| dense, five values | `f.chan = 3 AND d.lvl < 50` | `d.region` | 1,079 | 323 ms | 8.2 ms | 1,473 ms | 29.0 ms | split / split |
| medium | `f.chan = 3 AND d.lvl = 3` | `d.flag DESC` | 26,257 | 167 ms | 12.7 ms | 805 ms (72,973 reads) | 208 ms (4,085) | split / split |
| medium | the same | `d.flag` | 32,336 | 192 ms | 13.2 ms | 757 ms | 218 ms | split / split |
| sparse | `f.tags @> '{a1}' AND f.tags @> '{b2}' AND d.lvl = 3 AND d.kind = 3` | `d.flag DESC` | 1,187,000 | 61.5 ms | 265 ms | | | core / core |

Core reads every row of both sets, joins them and sorts the join for twenty: `chan = 3` is 625,000
fact rows. The split's first arm fills each dense and medium page, its walk §47's for that value:
the medium `d.flag DESC` page's arm is §47.9's medium page (`d.lvl = 3 AND d.flag`), the same 26,257
entries, in about the same time (12.7 against 11.6 ms). Warm the split is 13 to 78 times faster
than core's plan, cold 3.5 to 62 times, and the planner takes it for each of those pages at both
sizes: its Limit 2,197 against core's 104,372 for the dense `d.flag DESC` page, 5,785 against
90,083 for the medium. It keeps core's plan for the sparse page, rightly: the arm walks 1.19 million
entries for its twenty rows, 4.3 times slower than core's plan, and is priced 128,890 warm and
190,970 cold against 77,161. Not measured: other majors.

## 49. A lion path's own price, and the heap probe (2026-10-25)

§39 prices a lion path against the cheapest core plan it meets: its own price times that plan's
rate, divided by that plan's cold reads, scaled by the rows that plan's probes of a skewed key meet
and by its Memoize's hits under a LIMIT. Each correction reads the competitor's plan, so each new
shape of core plan needs a new reading (§39's "The join that reads the dimension" is the latest),
and a path's price moves with a plan it is not part of. This section starts replacing that with a
rule: **a lion path is priced by the work it does, in core's units, and core's plans by core.**

- **Its own work, itemized.** No factor comes from another path.
- **What it shares with core, at core's prices.** Heap pages through `index_pages_fetched()` and the
  tablespace's page costs, a B-tree descent through the index's `amcostestimate`, a row at
  `cpu_tuple_cost`, quals at `cost_qual_eval()`. A table read cold is core's to price, through
  `effective_cache_size` and the tablespace's `random_page_cost`, and then it is priced so for every
  plan alike.
- **What is lion's alone, at its constants** (§31), fitted in core's units.
- **One set of row estimates.** What lion knows better than core (n_distinct, §33; the rows of an
  intersection, `pg_lion.enable_rows_correction`) goes to every path or to none.
- **Scans that core composes.** Where lion can offer a path of a relation that core's join search
  combines - the inner side of a nested loop, under a Memoize, a semi, anti or left join - its price
  meets core's alternative for the same relation and parameterization in `add_path()`, both made by
  the same formulas, and nothing needs to read the plan around it.

### The switch (`pg_lion.competitor_pricing`)

On by default, §39 as it was. Off, `lion_competitor_of()` finds the competitor's kind (for the margin,
which stays a policy) and takes nothing else from it: rate 1, no nested loop's or bitmap heap scan's
cold reads (`lion_competitor_bitmap_cold()`, `lion_units_scan_cold()`), no Memoize scale, and
LionOrderedJoin weighs no competitor of its own (`oj_cost()`). A skewed key's rows
(`lion_skew_param_factor()`, `lion_skew_clauses_factor()`) are core's: lion's paths, the AM's scans
and the competitors are all priced at core's rows per key. Off is the ablation of §39 in one
setting; the next step is to run the private workload and the matrix with it off, and keep only what
moves a plan to a faster one.

**On the fixtures' shapes at scale** (2026-10-26; PostgreSQL 18.6 release, the shared VM of four
cores, `shared_buffers` 1 GB, `work_mem` 64 MB, `effective_cache_size` 4 GB; `bench/calib/joins.sql`
and `joins.py` through `matrix.py`). A 4,000,000-row dimension of 1,563 MB with probejoin.sql's,
ordjoin.sql's and heapprobe.sql's lion columns, all-visible; an 8,000,000-row fact of 833 MB, two
rows a key, walked by §47.9's `(score DESC) INCLUDE (fk, id)` and by a B-tree of a rank without the
key; key sets of 1,000 and 80,000 keys; competitor_cold.sql's dimension at 8,000,000 rows, not
vacuumed. 48 queries of §40.10's, §46's, §47's, §47.6's, §48's and §49's shapes and
competitor_cold.sql's, each planned at the four settings of this switch and
`pg_lion.enable_heap_probe` and timed with every plan core's and lion's forced arms make. Warm, the
tables in the kernel's cache but not in `shared_buffers`: medians of seven runs, interleaved, and a
second run of five that made the same choices. Cold - before each run `matrix.py --cold` ran a
script that stopped the server (`pg_ctl stop`), ran `sync`, dropped each file of the database's
directory from the kernel's cache (`posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED)`) and started the server -
medians of three, 27 of the queries, planned at `effective_cache_size` 4 GB and 256 MB. Cold this disk reads
1.5 GB/s in sequence and a random page in about 70 us.

With the switch off, two warm choices change, both to slower plans: LionProbeJoin under a NOT
EXISTS of 150,000 keys, priced at its own 596,693 against the hash anti join's 323,929 where the hash
join's rate, 0.5, had it at 319,902 (2,021 ms against 879 warm); and LionOrderedJoin's medium page,
which without the Memoize under a LIMIT loses to core's loop, 5,917 against 5,573 (44.0 against 14.0
ms warm, 1,304 against 330 cold). At `effective_cache_size` 256 MB two more: a bitmap heap scan's
cold reads had taken LionBtreeScan's covering walk under the hash join, 795 ms cold against the
bitmap heap scan's 1,751; and a nested loop's cold reads had taken the dense page's LionOrderedJoin,
34.5 against 75.9 ms. Off took one plan to a faster one, and only cold with the planner told the
tables were cached: the same LionProbeJoin, 4,113 ms cold against the hash join's 2,343, which reads
its 1.2 GB in sequence. Off costs the warm matrix 1.2 s and the cold one at 256 MB 1.0 s, and moves
nothing faster that the planner was told the truth about. So four of §39's corrections still earn
their place: the hash join's rate, the Memoize under a LIMIT, and a bitmap heap scan's and a nested
loop's cold reads; the switch stays on until each is priced as work. The skew factors and the rates
other than the hash join's moved nothing here (no key of these tables is skewed, and no count
competes with a hash aggregate); whether they earn theirs is the private workload's to say.

### The heap probe (`pg_lion.enable_heap_probe`)

§40.10's probe is index-only: a nested loop's inner `LionBtreeScan` descends a covering B-tree to the
outer row's key and tests the entry against the relation's lion set. It declined the heap mode as "a
plan that loses to core's wherever the set does not" reject most rows. That is a judgement for the
price, and the price can make it: in heap mode the probe is core's parameterized Index Scan of the
same B-tree with the lion test in place of the Filter, the heap row fetched for a member alone. Its
fetches are a subset of the Index Scan's, priced by the same formula (`lo_cost()` with `loops`), so
its price is lower by the rejected rows' pages and quals and higher by the set's build, spread over
the scans (§40.10), and an entry's test. Where the B-tree does not cover what the scan must return,
`lo_set_rel_pathlist()` takes its parameterized paths alone (`lo_btree_paths()`; its unparameterized
walk would read every member's row) and offers each paired lion access in heap mode: `iocols` NIL,
no `LO_FLAG_INDEXONLY`; the executor's heap fetch, recheck and EvalPlanQual are §30's. It needs
`enable_indexscan`. This is the shape LionProbeJoin (§46) and LionOrderedJoin's dimension (§47)
each build inside a join of their own; as a path of the relation, core composes it with any join.

**The probe's members over the loop.** `lo_cost()` counted a probe's members and their pages a scan
at a time, each clamped to one: a set that passes one key in a hundred was charged a heap fetch and a
page an outer row - core's Index Scan's - plus its own test, and lost to it everywhere. A key finds
its entry in every scan and the set passes a share of them, so a probe's members are now counted over
all of the loop's scans and shared out (`fetched`, `candidates`), and a scan that fetches less than a
row reads that share of a page (`pages_corr`). The index-only probes are priced by the same counts.
In competitor_cold.sql three plans moved to LionProbeJoin, whose probe is priced the same way
(`lion_ordered_probe_price()`): the anti join's nested loop at ten times the cache with the cold
charge at 0, and the Memoize loop in the cache and at ten times it uncharged. Warm, on PostgreSQL 18.6
(release), medians of nine over three rounds: the anti join ties (node 1.54 to 1.89 ms, loop 1.46 to
1.92), and the Memoize query runs faster through the node (5.22 to 5.67 against 5.79 to 7.00).

**Measured** (heapprobe.sql's tables: a 100,000-row dimension on 2,619 pages, 200,000 fact rows;
PostgreSQL 18.6 release, warm, hash and merge joins off, `pg_lion.competitor_pricing` off; medians of
five to seven runs on a shared VM whose runs vary by a third, so a difference below that is a tie):

| outer rows | the set passes | heap probe | core's Index Scan | the planner takes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3,585 | 0.7% | 6.9 ms | 11.1 ms | the probe |
| 3,585 | 10% | 7.3 to 10.5 | 10.6 | the probe |
| 40,000 | 10% | 65.9 | 80.2 | core's, at a price 1.8% below the probe's ("The probe's own work", below) |
| 200,000 | 10% | 267 | 406 | core's, at a price 1% below the probe's |
| 4,000 | 100% | 12.3 | 13.0 | core's (the set rejects nothing) |
| 200,000 | 100% | 388 | 376 | core's |
| 3 | 7% | | | core's (the build is not paid back) |

With 200,000 outer rows over a 2,619-page table both plans read every page about once, which is all
`index_pages_fetched()` charges them, and each heap fetch past that is a `cpu_tuple_cost`: the 180,000
fetches the probe saves, about 0.7 us each here, are priced at a hundredth of a unit, and the two come
out within 1%. That is core's price of a cached heap fetch, which core's own plans take too; by this
section's rule the probe takes it as well, and the near tie goes to core's plan. Where the pages are
not all read - fewer outer rows, a larger table, a cold one at its `random_page_cost` - the fetches
the probe saves are pages, and its price shows them.

**At scale** (the fixtures of "The switch", above). On, the loops of the table above move to the
probe and run faster on the 200,000-page dimension: 39,600 outer rows 1.1 to 1.8 times warm and 1.6
to 2.9 times cold, 3,960 tied warm and 1.5 times faster cold; at 198,000 the probe is priced 2% over
the hash join and runs 1.4 times faster warm, 2.0 cold. Core's hash join over the dimension's bitmap
heap scan in competitor_cold.sql's subquery, 784 to 860 ms warm, gives way to the probe under a
Memoize, 118 to 139 (cold the hash join is 12% faster). Under a LIMIT the probe loses: on
LionOrderedJoin's medium page core's ordered loop over a Memoize of the probe is priced 3,635 against
the node's 5,475 and runs 3.1 times slower warm, 3.7 times cold, because the probe's set - 14,990 to
build - is spread over the 883,021 scans the whole loop would make, of which the LIMIT charges 2,403,
while it is built whole at the first (`loops * expected >= LO_SWITCH_MIN_WALK`, from the whole
loop's rows). The dense page and the medium page index-only lose the same way, 2.8 to 3.3 times; the
sparse page, 5.6 times, to core's price of the outer Index Scan's cached fetches, which the probe's
lower inner price exposes. On, the warm matrix comes out level with the default, the cold one 3.8 s
worse at 4 GB and 6.7 s better at 256 MB: the probe stays off until its set under a LIMIT is priced as
it is built.

### Calibration (`bench/calib/ops.py`)

A lion constant is a multiple of a core cost setting; what multiple is set by the core operation the
lion operation stands in for. Core's plans do not run at one rate. On PostgreSQL 18.6 (release), on
the shared VM above, a cached sequential scan's quals take 4.9 to 5.5 ns a `cpu_operator_cost` - the
slope of its time over the number of `a <> -k` quals a row - and a nested loop of cached Index Scans
12 to 15 ns: core prices a descent and a heap fetch at less of their time than a qual. A lion
operation that competes with one of them is priced at that one's rate - its time over core's price
of it - so that the planner weighs the two as their times weigh. Priced at the sequential scan's
rate, a probe's few hundred nanoseconds cost two and a half times what core charges for the same
time in the Index Scan the probe replaces. A ratio measured on one machine carries to another far
better than a rate of cost units a millisecond, which is the machine's. This is not §39's rates: a
constant is fitted once, offline, against the core operation its own shape replaces, and no price
reads the plan it meets.

`bench/calib/ops.py` checks the measurements into the tree. It prints the sequential scan's rate for
comparison; its first lion operation is the probe: the heap probe over a set that passes every row,
against core's Index Scan of the same B-tree with no filter - the same descents and fetches - as the
slopes of their times and of core's price over 50,000, 100,000 and 200,000 outer rows, so that the
set's build stays out; of a unique key (`calib_ops_dim`) and of a key of eight entries on one page
(`calib_ops_many`), which apportion the probe's own work between the scan and the entry.

**The probe's own work.** Under callgrind (a single-user backend, 10,000 and 30,000 outer rows, with
the cache and branch simulators, the difference over 20,000) a scan of the probe runs no more
instructions than core's Index Scan, but 134 instruction cache misses to core's 69: the node's code -
`lo_next()`, `lo_rescan()`, the set's lookup - runs beside core's between one outer row and the next,
and the two no longer fit the first-level cache. An entry costs about 370 instructions more: the
set's lookup, two binary searches - the container key's (`lo_set_find()`, 96 instructions and 1.6
mispredicted branches an entry) and the member's in its container (`lion_container_contains()`, 110
and 1.4) - and the node's projection of its target into a slot of its own (about 110 with its
bookkeeping), where core's Index Scan returns the heap tuple through a physical target list. The
key's search now starts within what sorted, distinct keys allow - an index no further from either end
than the key is from that end's key - so a set with a container at every key of its range, as a set
of a share of most blocks' rows has, finds it with no search: one run before measured an entry at 93
ns over core's, seven after at 31 to 107 (median 49).

Over those seven runs, at the Index Scan's rate, an outer row of a unique key costs the probe 14 to 29
`cpu_operator_cost`s more than core's (median 20), one of eight entries 40 to 70 (median 51): an entry
4.4, a scan 15.6. They are two settings: `pg_lion.probe_entry_cost` (4.5), charged by `lo_cost()` for
each entry an index parameterized by the outer row walks, in place of the walk's `LO_PROBE_TUPLES`
(a probe marks nothing), and `pg_lion.probe_rescan_cost` (16), charged a scan of LionBtreeScan's
probe. A probe of a unique key was charged 9 an entry and nothing a scan, and is now charged 20.5.
LionProbeJoin's probes (`lion_ordered_probe_price()`) take the entry's price; a scan of them is the
join's own loop, not a node's rescan, and is not measured.

**The descent is startup.** `lo_cost()` puts the B-tree's descent in the walk's run, so LionBtreeScan's
probe offered `add_path()` a first row at 0.00 against core's Index Scan's 0.29 - for the same
descent - and, its total within `add_path()`'s 1% of core's, won on it: at 40,000 outer rows the plan
above was the probe's at a price 1.8% above core's. The probe's path now takes the descent as its
startup, as `cost_index()` has an Index Scan's (`ipath`'s startup, in `lo_set_rel_pathlist()`). The
walks keep it in their run - one descent beside a set's build - and `lion_ordered_probe_price()`,
which takes a probe's price as its total less its startup, the build, keeps it in the probe's price.

**What it costs.** Priced so, the probe keeps the 3,585-row loop of the table above and loses the
40,000-row one to core's Index Scan, at a price 1.8% below the probe's - re-timed, the probe 70.5 ms
against core's 77.9 - and the 196,000-row one (359 against 419). The probe's saving is heap fetches
of cached pages, which core prices at an Index Scan's entry and its fetch, `cpu_index_tuple_cost` +
`cpu_operator_cost` + `cpu_tuple_cost`: 7 `cpu_operator_cost`s, about 95 ns at the Index Scan's rate,
against about 300 ns measured for each row past the first of a key's eight on one page (the
`calib_ops_many` loop), and more for a row on a page of its own. A probe that saves most of them wins
by more than its price says, and the near ties go to core's plan. That is core's price of a cached
fetch, which every core plan takes too; by this section's rule the probe takes it as well, and how
lion's plans fare against core's on a warm machine rests on core's page costs as the deployment sets
them.

**The probe's projection** (2026-10-26). Core's Index Scan under a plain nested loop returns the heap tuple it fetched, through a physical
target list, and the loop's own projection reads what it needs from it; the probe projected its
target into a slot of its own first. Core gives a CustomPath no physical target list
(`use_physical_tlist()`: "the custom path creator can set up the path's pathtarget that way"), and
a pathtarget of the relation's columns cannot be the probe path's own: `PlanCustomPath` is not told
whether its parent needs an exact target list (an Append's child) or a small one (a Memoize's,
which caches the rows) - the flags `create_scan_plan()` reads. The parent is known one level up:
`create_nestloop_plan()` asks its inner side for no particular list. So the join hook
(`lion_ordered_join_probes()`) gives each nested loop core made whose inner side is a probe a copy
of the probe whose pathtarget is the relation's columns (`lo_physical_target()`, under
`use_physical_tlist()`'s conditions: a plain table of the query, no system column, whole-row Var or
placeholder wanted of it; and none of its columns dropped or missing from older tuples, which
`tlist_matches_tupdesc()` would project anyway). Its plan's target list then matches the scan
tuple, and `ExecAssignScanProjectionInfo()` leaves the node no projection: heap mode returns the
buffer's heap tuple, index-only mode the virtual tuple it fills from the index tuple - the columns
the index does not hold NULL, which nothing above reads, since the loop reads the relation's
target alone. A Memoize's or an Append's probe keeps the relation's target, and its projection.
The path's width is the relation's row, which no nested loop's price reads. `EXPLAIN VERBOSE`
shows the probe's `Output` as every column of the relation, as it shows a core scan's physical
target list.

Under callgrind (§49's harness, the difference of 30,000 and 10,000 outer rows), an outer row of a
key of eight entries took the probe 23,157 instructions, 145 instruction cache misses and 37
mispredicted indirect branches - the expression interpreter's dispatch - against core's Index
Scan's 20,150, 75 and 4; returning its scan tuple, 22,274, 135 and 8. An entry is 110 instructions
and 3.6 mispredicted branches cheaper; a unique key's outer row 106 instructions and 8 cache
misses. Timed (`ops.py`, seven runs on the VM shared with another benchmark, load 2), the probe
over core's Index Scan came to 21.6 `cpu_operator_cost`s an outer row of a unique key (-3 to 58)
and 58 of eight entries (39 to 81), against 20 and 51 before: the runs spread wider than the
saving, so `probe_entry_cost` and `probe_rescan_cost` stay at 4.5 and 16 until a quiet machine
measures it.

**Not done.**

- *Column values from the sets.* A query that reads a low-cardinality lion column of the dimension
  still fetches the row for it; the probe could return its value from the column's per-value sets,
  as LionProbeJoin's labels give a predicate's truth, and be covering for it.
- *The comparison on the private workload* with the switch off, for the skew factors and the rates
  other than the hash join's, which the fixtures do not reach ("The switch", above).
- *LionProbeJoin's scan*: its overhead over core's nested loop, which `probe_rescan_cost` does not
  price.
- *The harness's next operations* - the set's build a container (`lo_build_excess()`'s
  `LO_BUILD_PIECE_TIDS` is a correction of §30.3's price, not a measurement of its own), a
  container's AND, a count - each against the core operation it stands in for, at that operation's
  rate.
- *A probe's set under a LIMIT* ("At scale", above): priced the LIMIT's share of its build, built
  whole at the first scan. LionOrderedJoin's dimension side, the same probe, prices its build in the
  startup and builds it lazily while the LIMIT's share of its descents is under 10,000 (§47.3,
  §47.4). Deciding lazy or at once at run time, as §30.4's lazy set does, and pricing a scan at the
  lesser of a lazy lookup and the build's share, is right for any share of the loop a LIMIT runs.
- *LionProbeJoin's competitor under the heap probe*: where the probe's loop takes the join, every
  path of the upper rel has a lion path inside, `lion_competitor_path()` finds none, and the node's
  rate rises from 0.5 to 1 - its price doubled (65,055 to 129,373) for nothing of its own: one more
  reason the rates are to be priced as work.
- *LionOrderedJoin's rejected fetches* (§47.3, `ks.noinc.*`): priced at the LIMIT's own pages where
  core's loop doing the same fetches is priced its share of the whole walk's - 18,897 against 1,158
  for 5,000 fetches, the node running 1.7 to 2.2 times faster than the loop chosen. By this section's
  rule the two are to be priced alike.

**Tests.** test/sql/heapprobe.sql: every query through the heap probe and through core's plan,
answers compared - an inner join, a left join, a Memoize chosen at the prices, an ORDER BY the loop
keeps, a residual filter, `FOR SHARE` of the dimension, rows updated after the VACUUM - and the
choice at the prices between the probe and core's Index Scan. costrates.sql: with the switch off no
rate moves a count, a GROUP BY, an FK-side join or a semi or anti join, each at its reference price.
competitor_cold.sql: with the switch off LionProbeJoin's price at ten times the cache is its price
with no cold charge.

## 50. Bit-plane arithmetic (`lion_planes.[ch]`, 2026-10-26)

n values of nbits bits each are nbits **bit-planes**: plane j holds bit j of every value, bit i of
its word w being bit j of value 64 w + i. A set of rows F, as a bit vector over the same rows, then
weighs the values it selects as

    sum over i in F of x_i  =  sum over j of 2^j popcount(F AND plane_j)

Two parts of lion compute that sum. lionvec's plane-1 estimate (§44.3) is it with F a row's sign
bits, one a dimension, and the planes the query's four bits a dimension; a bit-sliced index's
`sum(x)` under a filter, the section after this one, is it with F the filter's container and the
planes the column's slices, a roaring container each. The identity is one; the operands are
transposed. lionvec's many-bit operand is the query: made once a scan, in memory, short (dimsp / 64
words, 24 at 1536 dimensions), met by thousands of rows' sign bits, and kept **interleaved**, a
word's four planes side by side, `planes[w * 4 + j]`, so that one vector holds them against the row's
word broadcast. A bit-sliced index's many-bit operand is the stored column: a slice is a posting set
of its own, a container per container key in whatever representation suits it - the high slices of
small values sparse ARRAYs or nothing, the low ones BITSETs or NARROWs (§38) - inserted into and
vacuumed one slice at a time as any posting set is, so its planes are **strided**: each its own
512-word payload (a BITSET's; 64 k words a NARROW's), wherever its page holds it. Interleaving
slices on disk would make one item of 4 KB a slice that no container operation reads, that every
insert rewrites whole, and whose empty high slices still cost their words; de-interleaving lionvec's
query would cost its kernel the one-vector-a-word load. So the layouts stay as their owners need
them, and this module takes both: one kernel for the identity, below the container library and
lionvec, frontend-safe as lion_container.c is (c.h, pg_bitutils and libpgcommon).

### The interface (`lion_planes.h`)

    /* per-plane counts: counts[j] = sum over w < nwords of popcount(bits[w] AND plane j's word w) */
    void   lion_planes_count_interleaved(const uint64 *bits, const uint64 *planes,  /* [w * k + j] */
                                         uint32 nwords, uint32 k, uint32 *counts);
    void   lion_planes_count_strided(const uint64 *bits, const uint64 *const *planes, /* [j][w] */
                                     uint32 nwords, uint32 k, uint32 *counts);
    /* sum over j < k of 2^j counts[j], modulo 2^64; k <= 64 */
    uint64 lion_planes_dot_interleaved(const uint64 *bits, const uint64 *planes, uint32 nwords, uint32 k);
    uint64 lion_planes_dot_strided(const uint64 *bits, const uint64 *const *planes, uint32 nwords, uint32 k);
    /* 64 x 64 bit matrix, in place: bit c of word r to bit r of word c */
    void   lion_planes_transpose64(uint64 *m);
    /* n values of nbits (1 .. 64) to nbits planes of ceil(n / 64) words, and back */
    void   lion_planes_scatter_interleaved(const uint64 *values, uint32 n, uint32 nbits, uint64 *planes);
    void   lion_planes_scatter_strided(const uint64 *values, uint32 n, uint32 nbits, uint64 *const *planes);
    void   lion_planes_gather_interleaved(const uint64 *planes, uint32 n, uint32 nbits, uint64 *values);
    void   lion_planes_gather_strided(const uint64 *const *planes, uint32 n, uint32 nbits, uint64 *values);

STRIDED takes an array of k pointers, so that k payloads that lie on k pages, or anywhere, need no
copy; a caller whose planes are one array at a stride builds the k pointers. nwords and k are any,
0 included: a BITSET's 512, a NARROW's 64 k, lionvec's dimsp / 64. A scatter pads the last word with
zeros past value n - 1 and leaves out a value's bits from nbits up; a gather writes exactly n values
and does not read the padding as one. Nothing allocates; every array is the caller's.

**Counts, not sums.** A count is at most 64 nwords, a uint32 below 2^26 words. A weighted sum is
not bounded so: 64 slices over a container's 32,768 rows weigh to (2^64 - 1) 32,768, past any
uint64, and a column's sum over many containers further. So the count functions return per-plane
counts and the caller weighs them as its sum needs - a bit-sliced index into int128, a signed
column's top slice negatively - and the `dot` functions are the convenience for a caller that
knows `(2^k - 1) 64 nwords` is below 2^64, lionvec's being at most 121,920 (k = 4, 127 words);
past that they wrap, deterministically, and every implementation wraps alike.

### Kernels

Each count function runs one of four implementations (below), every one returning the same counts
to the bit. Every kernel takes the planes four at a time, a group, whose four sums stay in
registers through one pass over the words; the last k % 4 planes are a shorter group. bits is read
once a pass, from L1 after the first.

- **portable** and **POPCNT**: a word at a time, four sums, one a plane, so that neither their adds
  nor POPCNT's false dependency on its destination chain the words; the word's popcount
  `lion_popcount64()` (the builtin where the target has the instruction, `pg_popcount64()` where not,
  as §3's portable kernel counts) or the POPCNT instruction.
- **AVX2**: each byte counted a nibble at a time with VPSHUFB (Muła, as §3 and lionvec count), the
  byte counts added over 31 vectors, 248 a byte at most, before VPSADBW sums them into 64-bit lanes.
  INTERLEAVED, lionvec's: a word's four planes are one vector, ANDed with the bits' word broadcast,
  lane j counting plane j; up to four groups a pass, a word's 16 planes, so that a pass over 64
  interleaved planes reads each cache line once - a group a pass read each line twice and took a
  fifth longer. STRIDED: four words of the bits against four of each of the group's planes, one
  vector a plane, as §3 counts an AND.
- **AVX-512**: AVX2's, each lane's word counted whole by VPOPCNTDQ into its 64-bit sum, on 256-bit
  vectors (`avx512f,avx512vl,avx512vpopcntdq`, as lionvec's, §44.3): no 512-bit instruction runs.

Where a vector would reach past the caller's array - the last nwords % 4 words of a STRIDED pass,
the last k % 4 planes of an INTERLEAVED one at its last words - AVX2 reads a zero-padded copy and
AVX-512 a masked load (`_mm256_maskz_loadu_epi64`), which reads nothing past the lanes it keeps;
elsewhere the last planes' vector reads the next word's planes into its spare lanes, whose sums are
dropped. The unit test holds every array in an exact-size heap allocation, so a sanitized build sees
a read one byte past.

Two things the first version did and this one does not, both found by the timings. Each group's sums
were arrays of vectors indexed in a loop over the group's planes; GCC kept them in memory, and four
STRIDED planes took longer than four calls of one (AVX2 671 ns against 450, AVX-512 397 against
250, 512 words); they are named registers now (446 and 195). And at lionvec's shape - four planes,
24 words - the weighted sum went through the counts of any k: a call more, 64 counts on the stack
with its canary, a loop of variable shifts, 22 - 28 ns against `lionvec_plane_dot()`'s 11 - 15 with
AVX-512. Every INTERLEAVED kernel now has a pass of constant stride for k = 4, and the weighted sum a
function for each implementation that weighs its lanes in registers (`planes_dot4_*()`): 16 ns
against 15. *(2026-10-26, when lionvec took its plane 1 from here, §44.3: a third. The portable
`planes_dot4_portable()`, the one of the four without a target of its own, was inlined into
`lion_planes_dot_interleaved()`, and its loop's registers made the dispatch save six and grow a
frame on every call, whichever kernel it then jumped to - AVX2's estimate 39.2 ns against lionvec's
36.5. It is `pg_noinline` now, and the dispatch a test of k, a load of the choice and a jump.)*

### One choice of implementation (`lion_simd_*`)

The extension chose its SIMD kernels twice, by the same tests written twice: lion_container.c's
`bits_kernel_best()` (AVX2, else POPCNT, else portable, §3) and lionvec's `lionvec_kernels_init()`
(AVX-512 with VPOPCNTDQ, AVX2, POPCNT, §44.3). The choice is now one, here:

- `LionSimdImpl` - `LION_SIMD_PORTABLE`, `_POPCNT`, `_AVX2`, `_AVX512` (AVX2 and AVX-512F, VL and
  VPOPCNTDQ), and `LION_SIMD_AUTO`, the best - moves from lion_container.h, where it was the unit
  tests' alone; `lion_simd_has()` is whether the build has one and the CPU runs it
  (`__builtin_cpu_supports()`, which also checks that the OS saves the registers);
  `lion_simd_best()` the best of those; `lion_simd_current()` what every kernel runs, resolved at its
  first call to the best - as PostgreSQL's `pg_popcount64` resolves at its first - and read through an
  inline function, a load and a compare; `lion_simd_force()`, in a `-DFRONTEND` build, makes every
  kernel run another, or the best again, and refuses (false, nothing changed) one the build or the
  CPU lacks; `lion_simd_f16c()` is whether the build knows F16C (GCC 11, clang 18) and the CPU has it,
  for lionvec's halves, not an implementation of its own nor forced.
- The compile-time side moves with it: `LION_HAVE_X86_SIMD` (GCC 5 or clang 6 on x86-64, and not
  `LION_NO_SIMD`), `LION_HAVE_X86_AVX512` (GCC 8, clang 8), `LION_HAVE_X86_F16C`, `LION_TARGET()`,
  and the portable kernels' `lion_popcount64()`.
- lion_container.c keeps its seven whole-bitset passes - COUNT, RUNS, AND_COUNT, AND, OR, ANDNOT,
  OR_NEW - as they were, and picks among their three kernels by `lion_simd_current()`
  (`bits_kernel_of()`) where a function pointer started at a resolver did; AVX-512 runs its AVX2
  kernel, which is what `bits_kernel_best()` picked on such a CPU. Each kernel stays a function the
  dispatch calls (`pg_noinline`), as it was behind the pointer. `lion_container_simd_force()` and
  `lion_container_simd_current()` keep their signatures: force() is `lion_simd_force()`, and so
  forces every kernel that follows the choice, and current() reports the kernel the passes run, AVX2
  under AVX-512. The passes take what they took: through the library, one pair of BITSETs in L1, the
  fastest of six alternated runs before and after, AVX2 `and_cardinality()` 94.1 / 94.2 ns,
  `and_raw()` 109.2 / 109.0, `bitset_recount()` 88.9 / 89.3, `or_inplace()` 113.8 / 113.4 (this
  section's machine, below; on the Cascade Lake Xeon at 2.8 GHz without VPOPCNTDQ where this work
  began, 125.0 / 126.3, 128.2 / 130.2, 104.3 / 105.8, 134.4 / 134.7), and container_test passes
  under every forced implementation with the same 3,139,381 checks as before (2,887,036 without the
  x86-64 kernels), under AddressSanitizer and UBSan too.
- lion_vec_math.c is unchanged: lionvec still chooses its own set, under its own `LIONVEC_HAVE_*`
  tests, until it takes its kernels from here ("Not done"). *(Since 2026-10-26 it does, §44.3,
  "Kernels": every kernel of lionvec's dispatches on `lion_simd_current()`, under `LION_HAVE_X86_*`,
  and its plane 1 is `lion_planes_dot_interleaved(bits, planes, nwords, 4)`.)*

### The transpose

The 64 x 64 bit matrix, word r its row r and bit c its column c, transposed in six rounds as
Hacker's Delight's 7-3 transposes 32 x 32: round j = 32, 16, .., 1 swaps the off-diagonal j x j
blocks of every 2j x 2j block, word k's columns from j up for word k + j's below j (bit j of k
clear) - a mask, two shifts and three XORs a pair, 192 pairs. Round j exchanges bit j of a bit's
row index with bit j of its column index, so the rounds commute, and all six exchange every bit of
the two: the transpose. The planes of 64 values are the first nbits rows of the transpose of the
values (scatter), and 64 values the transpose of their planes padded with zero rows (gather); for
nbits up to p, a power of two below 64, each needs only part of the work. The scatter needs only
rows below p: round j < p mixes rows below p among themselves, and round j >= p, which runs
first, need make only its pairs' first rows, j half-swaps. The gather runs the rounds the other
way, j = 1 .. 32, on rows of which those from p up are zero: rounds j < p mix rows below p, and
round j >= p splits each row k below j into itself and row k + j. A word of 4-bit values - lionvec's
query, a column of 16 values - takes 60 half-swaps and four swaps rather than 192.

### Measured

Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz (family 6, model 207: Emerald Rapids; AVX-512 with VPOPCNTDQ, and F16C), a VM
